The Western Grimoire

The Western Grimoire

Being an account of the magical tradition from the Greek Magical Papyri to the modern revival: Hermetic, alchemical, Solomonic, Kabbalistic, Rosicrucian and folk; with the sources of each dated and attributed, and the practices set out so that they may be performed

Twenty-nine chapters · with seventy-five diagrams and seven plates

The Western Grimoire. This edition is assembled from primary and scholarly sources, each of which is dated and attributed in the Sources & Bibliography. Where a source is out of copyright this is marked; where it is not, it is cited rather than reproduced at length.

The text of the Emerald Tablet in Chapter 6 is Isaac Newton’s, from Keynes MS 28, King’s College Library, Cambridge, in the transcription of The Chymistry of Isaac Newton (Indiana University, 2010). The ritual texts in Chapters 7, 8, 15 and 20 are drawn from Mathers’s translation of the Key of Solomon (1889) and from Crowley’s Liber O (1909), both in the public domain. The planetary herbs in Chapter 20 are Culpeper’s, from The Complete Herbal (1653). All diagrams were drawn for this book.

This text has been through repeated rounds of source verification, the later ones adversarial, and they are not finished. What they find, including the errors they find in the corrections themselves, is recorded in the note at the head of the bibliography rather than quietly removed. A count is deliberately not given here: it would be one more number in the book with nothing to check it.

Presented for historical, educational and research purposes as part of humanity’s spiritual heritage.

When a source tells you a text is ancient, check the date yourself. It is often findable in a few minutes, and it is frequently not what you were told.

The closing advice of this book

Important Safety Warning

This grimoire describes practices drawn from living and historical traditions. Approach it with care:

  • Proper preparation and protection are essential
  • Use only for ethical intentions
  • Respect the forces involved
  • Follow all safety protocols
  • Begin with beginner-level content only

How to read this book

Every source in this grimoire is dated and attributed. Where a teaching commonly presented as ancient turns out to be medieval, early-modern or modern, the chapter says so and gives the date. This is not scepticism for its own sake; it is the only way a book claiming to rest on primary sources can be checked. Knowing that a practice was written in 1888 rather than in remote antiquity takes nothing away from it; it tells you what you are actually holding.

Difficulty: Beginner foundational, safe to begin alone   Adept assumes the foundations   Advanced historical or demanding material   Reference background, not practice

Chapter IIntroduction to the Tradition Beginner

Six bodies of practice stand behind this book, and a reader will almost always meet them mixed: the Hermetic philosophy of Roman Egypt, alchemy, the Solomonic conjuring books, Kabbalah as Christian Europe took it up, the Rosicrucian episode, and the folk charms that were never anybody’s system at all. They are not one tradition. They were made in different centuries by people with different aims, in Greek and Arabic and Latin and Pennsylvania German, and several of the men who made them would have been appalled to be shelved together. What joins them is late. From the fifteenth century each was read in the light of the others, and by 1900 the whole accumulation had been fitted into a single curriculum that a single order could teach in a single set of rooms.

The oldest of the six goes first, and not only because it is oldest. It supplied the vocabulary the other five were later described in, so a reader who does not have it will keep meeting its words without knowing whose they are. The Hermetic tradition grew out of the meeting of Greek philosophy and Egyptian religion in Roman Alexandria and reached us through Arabic, Byzantine and Renaissance hands. Its central conviction is that the cosmos is intelligible, that it is ordered by correspondence rather than by accident, and that a person willing to work at it can come to know that order directly rather than on authority. Every claim in the last two sentences is genuinely ancient. A great deal of what is now taught under the same name is not, and this book’s whole method is to say, at every step, which is which.

The name on the door

The tradition is named for Hermes Trismegistus, Hermes the Thrice-Greatest, and the name is itself a summary of the meeting that produced it. In Ptolemaic Egypt the Greek settlers identified their Hermes, god of speech and writing, with Thoth, the ibis-headed Egyptian god of the moon, of reckoning and of the scribal art, lord of the sacred word. The epithet grew out of Egyptian usage rather than Greek: Egyptian piety intensified a god’s greatness by repeating it, and the decree carved on the Rosetta Stone still calls him, in its Greek, “Hermes the great and great”: Mead’s study of the epithet traces the path from that doubled “great” to the superlative “thrice-greatest,” and finds Hermes already trismegas in a Greek magical prayer and thrice-blessed in inscriptions. To late antiquity he was not a god so much as the most ancient of sages: the books that circulated under his name were held to preserve the primordial wisdom of Egypt, older than Plato, older than Moses. The Renaissance believed exactly that, and built on it; the belief was wrong, and Chapter 2 tells the story of how it was formed and how it fell. What matters here is the shape of the claim: a body of writing whose authority rested on its supposed antiquity, and whose actual content (late-antique, Greek-Egyptian, philosophically serious) turned out to matter more than the false date ever did.

The primary text speaks

Before any modern summary, hear the corpus itself. The first treatise of the Corpus Hermeticum (the Poimandres, in Mead’s English the “Man-Shepherd”) opens the whole literature with a scene of instruction:

It chanced once on a time my mind was meditating on the things that are, my thought was raised to a great height, the senses of my body being held back — just as men are who are weighed down with sleep after a fill of food, or from fatigue of body. Methought a Being more than vast, in size beyond all bounds, called out my name and saith: What wouldst thou hear and see, and what hast thou in mind to learn and know? And I do say: Who art thou? He saith: I am Man-Shepherd, Mind of all-masterhood; I know what thou desirest and I’m with thee everywhere. [And] I reply: I long to learn the things that are, and comprehend their nature, and know God. This is, I said, what I desire to hear. He answered back to me: Hold in thy mind all thou wouldst know, and I will teach thee.

That is the tradition’s mission statement (to learn the things that are, and comprehend their nature, and know God) and it is put as a request any reader can make. The eleventh treatise states the method, in the most audacious passage the corpus contains. Mind is speaking to Hermes:

If, then, thou dost not make thyself like unto God, thou canst not know Him. For like is knowable to like [alone]. Make, [then,] thyself to grow to the same stature as the Greatness which transcends all measure; leap forth from every body; transcend all Time; become Eternity; and [thus] shalt thou know God. Conceiving nothing is impossible unto thyself, think thyself deathless and able to know all, — all arts, all sciences, the way of every life. … Think that thou art at the same time in every place, — in earth, in sea, in sky; not yet begotten, in the womb, young, old, [and] dead, in after-death conditions. And if thou knowest all these things at once, — times, places, doings, qualities, and quantities; thou canst know God. But if thou lockest up thy soul within thy body, and dost debase it, saying: I nothing know; I nothing can; I fear the sea; I cannot scale the sky; I know not who I was, who I shall be; — what is there [then] between [thy] God and thee?

Everything else in this book (the meditations, the rituals, the tables of hours and herbs, the laboratory) descends from some historical attempt to take those two passages seriously: to treat the knowledge of the order of things as a practice rather than an opinion. The square brackets in both quotations are Mead’s own editorial marks, and the ellipsis omits one sentence on collecting the senses of all creatures into oneself.

The shape of the literature

“Hermetic” covers more ground than any one shelf. Scholarship divides the ancient material into the philosophical Hermetica (the treatises on God, cosmos and mind quoted above) and the technical Hermetica: astrology, alchemy, the properties of stones and plants, and the making of talismans, all likewise under Hermes’ name and often older than the philosophical treatises. The later tradition kept both streams, and then the other five strands attached themselves to them one after another. That accumulation is what a book on this subject has to cover, and one table maps it:

How to use this book

Every chapter heading carries one of three tags. Beginner chapters assume nothing and are safe to work from directly. Advanced chapters assume the beginner material and, where they are operative, assume the protections that go with it. Reference chapters are history and apparatus; they are for reading and checking rather than working. Two honest paths run through the book. The reader’s path takes the chapters in order, and the book is arranged so that every claim is dated before it is used. The practitioner’s path is shorter and starts with four weeks of foundations: first the regimen of Chapter 16 and a working journal, with the breathing and the vibration of a divine name from Chapter 7; second, the opening and closing of Chapter 8, performed plainly until they are familiar; third, the Lesser Banishing Ritual of the Pentagram from Chapter 15, daily; fourth, the Middle Pillar of Chapter 13 added to the banishing, and the first review of the journal against the month’s record. Everything further (talismans, scrying, the hours, geomancy, evocation) builds on that footing, and each chapter states its own prerequisites. Neither path requires belief; both require the journal, because the tradition’s own test is whether the record bears the claim out.

The seven principles that almost every modern introduction puts first are the right place to see this book’s method in action, because they are the tradition’s most famous summary and its most instructively misdated one.

The Seven Hermetic Principles

1. The Principle of Mentalism: “The All is Mind; the Universe is Mental.” The fundamental nature of reality is mental, and all phenomena are manifestations of a Universal Mind.

2. The Principle of Correspondence: “As above, so below; as below, so above.” There is harmony and correspondence between the different planes of existence, such that what is learned of one informs understanding of another. (This is the principle with the deepest pedigree of the seven, and the familiar wording is itself a modern compression of it, as Chapter 6 sets out; three others are also attested in the ancient material, as the note below explains.)

3. The Principle of Vibration: “Nothing rests; everything moves; everything vibrates.” All matter and energy exist in constant motion, differing in frequency rather than in kind.

4. The Principle of Polarity: “Everything is dual; everything has poles; everything has its pair of opposites.” Opposites are identical in nature and different only in degree, so that heat and cold, or love and hate, are positions on a single scale.

5. The Principle of Rhythm: “Everything flows, out and in; everything has its tides; all things rise and fall.” Phenomena manifest in cycles, and the pendulum swing in one direction implies its return.

6. The Principle of Cause and Effect: “Every cause has its effect; every effect has its cause.” Nothing happens by chance; what looks like chance is a cause not yet perceived.

7. The Principle of Gender: “Gender is in everything; everything has its masculine and feminine principles.” All creation proceeds from the interaction of an active and a receptive principle, on every plane and not merely the physical.

Where these principles actually come from

These seven principles derive from The Kybalion, published in 1908 under the pseudonym “Three Initiates” and generally attributed to William Walker Atkinson (1862–1932), a pioneer of the American New Thought movement. They are not found as a set in the ancient Hermetic writings.

Some of the material has genuine ancestry. Nicholas E. Chapel, in the most detailed study of the question, finds at least four of the seven principles clearly attested within Hermetic sources: mentalism, correspondence, polarity and gender have real footing in ancient and medieval Hermetic texts. Others do not. Chapel’s specific claim about vibration is an argument about origin: the principle “originated in the middle of the 18th century with the British philosopher and medical doctor David Hartley (1705–1757),” and is by now so common in modern spiritual writing “that it bears no comment.” That derivation is Chapel’s own reconstruction across some hundred and sixty years; his supporting citation is to a study of Hartley’s associationism rather than to anything linking Hartley to Atkinson, so it is given here as his argument rather than as a documented line of descent. His overall conclusion is that “the longstanding supposition that The Kybalion is consonant with Hermetic philosophy as an historical current is one that is erroneous and in need of revision.”

The title is itself a puzzle. Chapel notes that the word “takes the form of a Greek noun, but has no meaning in that language or any other,” and judges it “the more likely explanation that the title was chosen as an allusion” to Kabbalah or to Cybele, “to insinuate a link to antiquity.”

None of which means the seven principles are worthless. They are a lucid, teachable summary that has introduced more people to Hermetic thinking than any ancient text ever did, and they are set out above in full for that reason. But they are a 1908 formulation, and a book that claims to rest on primary sources has to say so. Chapter 2 deals with the attested ancient material.

What the tradition is for

Beneath the various formulations, ancient and modern, the Hermetic project is consistent in its aims. It holds that the universe is not inert: that it has structure, intelligence and direction, and that these can be investigated. It holds that the human being stands in a peculiar position, participating in both the material and the intelligible orders, and is therefore capable of understanding a cosmos that most of what exists cannot. And it holds that this understanding is transformative: to know the order of things truly is to be altered by knowing it.

This is why the tradition has always been simultaneously philosophical and practical. The meditations in Chapter 7 and the ritual structures in Chapter 8 are not decorations on the philosophy; they are how the philosophy is meant to be tested. The Hermetic claim is not that you should believe the cosmos is ordered, but that you can find out.

On ethics

The ethical position of this literature deserves stating directly, because it is easy to lose among the warnings and the symbolism. Every serious current in this tradition treats knowledge as inseparable from the character of the person holding it. The Hermetic texts frame ascent as purification: what has to be put down is not ignorance in the abstract but greed, deceit, cruelty, self-importance. The Rosicrucian manifestos made the healing of the sick without payment their first practical commitment. Agrippa insisted the magus must also be a devout philosopher, and drew a hard line against sorcery. The Ars Notoria asks for memory and understanding, not for power over anyone.

The practical form this takes is simple enough to state and difficult to keep. Do not work to coerce, injure, deceive, or override another person’s will; this rules out a considerable amount of what the historical grimoires happily supply, which is one reason this book presents that material descriptively. Do not treat other people’s crises as an opportunity. Do not charge the desperate. Do not confuse the sensation of insight with the fact of it, and keep the habit of checking your conclusions against something outside your own enthusiasm. Where a practice touches on health, treat it as a complement to medicine and never a substitute; Chapter 16 returns to this.

These are not rules imposed on the tradition from outside. They are what the sources themselves say, when read carefully; and they are considerably more demanding than any warning box.

Chapter IIThe Hermetica and Their Transmission Reference

The genuine foundation of Hermetic philosophy is a body of Greek writing attributed to Hermes Trismegistus: “Hermes the Thrice-Greatest,” a figure identified with the Egyptian Thoth and understood by his readers as an ancient Egyptian sage. These are the Hermetica. They are real, they are substantial, and their history of transmission is one of the more remarkable episodes in European intellectual life, largely because for two centuries everybody was wrong about how old they were.

What the Corpus Hermeticum is

The Corpus Hermeticum is a selection of seventeen Greek treatises: numbered I to XVIII, with no treatise XV transmitted. It survives as a collection whose date and compiler are unknown; it is first attested in Byzantium, in the writings of Michael Psellos (c. 1017–1078), who is a reader of the collection rather than its compiler, and the surviving manuscripts are late medieval and later. The religio-philosophical Hermetica themselves were, for the most part, produced in a relatively short span: between the late first and the third century CE on the common dating, though Christian Bull argues that some of the underlying material is older, stemming from at least as early as the first century BCE. They are the product of Roman-era Alexandria: Greek in language and philosophical vocabulary, Egyptian in much of their religious frame, and shaped by the Platonism of their period.

Alongside the Corpus proper stand several related texts. The Asclepius survives mainly in a Latin translation, with some Greek and Coptic fragments. The Nag Hammadi discovery yielded three Hermetic tractates in Codex VI: The Discourse on the Eighth and Ninth (VI,6); the Prayer of Thanksgiving (VI,7) with its Scribal Note (VI,7a); and that prayer also appears among the Greek Magical Papyri, a connection worth noting; and a single continuous excerpt of the Asclepius, chapters 21–29 (VI,8). Further material survives as excerpts in Stobaeus (among them the long Kore Kosmou, the “Virgin of the World”) and as papyrus fragments.

The seventeen treatises

Because the collection is small enough to know whole, here it is whole. Mead numbers the treatises by his own count and sets the older editions’ numbering in parentheses beside it, and the two diverge because the second treatise of those editions, the General Sermon, is lost. That is why his table carries a (XV.), which the modern numbering does not: current editions run the collection from I to XVIII and leave XV empty. The three ways of counting disagree about the labels and agree about the contents, which are seventeen surviving treatises. The one-line summaries are this book’s.

The Prayer of Thanksgiving

This book has referred three times to the one piece of Hermetic liturgy that survives complete (at Nag Hammadi, among the papyri of Chapter 9, and in the Latin Asclepius) without ever printing it. Here it is, from the close of the Asclepius, in G. R. S. Mead’s translation of 1906.

The frame deserves to be kept with it. As the prayer is about to begin, Asclepius whispers a suggestion: that they add incense and unguents. Trismegistus is appalled: “this is like to profanation of our sacred rites... For naught is there of which He stands in need, in that He is all things, or all are in Him. But let us worship, pouring forth our thanks. For this is the best incense in God’s sight, — when thanks are given to Him by men.” A tradition that filled Chapter 20 with suffumigations begins from a text that refuses them.

[We give] Thee grace, Thou highest [and] most excellent! For by Thy Grace we have received the so great Light of Thy own Gnosis.

O holy Name, fit [Name] to be adored, O Name unique, by which the Only God is to be blest through worship of [our] Sire, — [of Thee] who deignest to afford to all a Father’s piety, and care, and love, and whatsoever virtue is more sweet [than these], endowing [us] with sense, [and] reason, [and] intelligence; — with sense that we may feel Thee; with reason that we may track Thee out from the appearances of things; with means of recognition that we may joy in knowing Thee.

Saved by Thy Power divine, let us rejoice that Thou hast shown Thyself to us in all Thy Fullness. Let us rejoice that Thou hast deigned to consecrate us, [still] entombed in bodies, to Eternity. For this is the sole festival of praise worthy of man, — to know Thy Majesty.

We have known Thee, yea, by the Single Sense of our intelligence, Thy Light supreme, — O Thou true Life of life, O Fecund Womb that giveth birth to every nature! We have known Thee, O Thou completely filled with the Conception from Thyself of Universal Nature! We have known Thee, O Thou Eternal Constancy!

For in the whole of this our prayer in worship of Thy Good, this favour only of Thy Goodness do we crave; — that Thou wilt keep us constant in our Love of knowing Thee, and let us ne’er be cut off from this kind of Life.

Text: Asclepius 41, in G. R. S. Mead, Thrice-Greatest Hermes, vol. II (1906), pp. 389–90; Mead translated Hildebrand’s Latin text of 1842. The square brackets are Mead’s, marking words supplied by the translator. After the prayer the text ends: “With this desire we [now] betake us to [our] pure and fleshless meal”: the shared vegetarian supper that closed the observance. The same prayer survives in Coptic at Nag Hammadi (VI,7) and in Greek in the Mimaut papyrus (PGM III); those versions have no public-domain translation, and Mead’s Latin-based rendering is used here for exactly that reason. Augustine, De civitate Dei XVIII.39, in the translation of Marcus Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, ser. 1, vol. 2, ed. Philip Schaff (1887): the words quoted above, and even after Moses himself, were collated against that text for this edition.

The Divine Pymander

The first treatise of the Corpus, the Poimandres or Divine Pymander, the “Divine Shepherd”, describes the creation of the cosmos and the nature of the divine, and it remains the best entry point to the collection. Its teaching, in summary:

  • The Divine Mind, Nous, is the source of all creation
  • Human beings contain a divine element capable of being awakened
  • Knowledge of the divine comes through direct experience rather than through belief
  • The path to that knowledge runs through purification and contemplation

What makes the Poimandres compelling is that it is written as a report rather than a doctrine. The narrator describes an experience (a vision, a voice, a sequence of understandings) and the reader is invited to a method, not asked for assent. That posture runs through the whole collection and explains a great deal about the tradition it founded.

The ascent through the zones

The Poimandres ends with the two passages that organised everything after them. The first is the ascent: after death, the narrator is taught, the man of Gnosis rises through the seven planetary zones, and at each he hands back the vice that zone had lent him:

To the first zone he gives the Energy of Growth and Waning; unto the second [zone], Device of Evils [now] de-energized; unto the third, the Guile of the Desires de-energized; unto the fourth, his Domineering Arrogance, [also] de-energized; unto the fifth, unholy Daring and the Rashness of Audacity, de-energized; unto the sixth, Striving for Wealth by evil means, deprived of its aggrandisement; and to the seventh zone, Ensnaring Falsehood, de-energized. And then, with all the energizings of the Harmony stript from him, clothed in his proper Power, he cometh to that Nature which belongs unto the Eighth, and there with those-that-are hymneth the Father.

Every planetary ladder in this book (the hours of Chapter 20, the sphere-by-sphere ascent of the Middle Pillar in Chapter 13, the very idea that the planets index stages of a work) has this passage for an ancestor, with one difference worth noticing: here the planets are not powers to be courted but customs posts, and what is paid at each is a vice. The second passage is the commission. Told that the end of those who have Gnosis is to be made one with God, the narrator hears:

Why shouldst thou then delay? Must it not be, since thou hast all received, that thou shouldst to the worthy point the way, in order that through thee the race of mortal kind may by [thy] God be saved?

And the treatise closes with the narrator in the street: “O ye people, earth-born folk, ye who have given yourselves to drunkenness and sleep and ignorance of God, be sober now, cease from your surfeit, cease to be glamoured by irrational sleep!” The philosophical corpus, in other words, understands itself as a teaching with an obligation attached, the knower points the way, and that is the frame in which every practice in this book was originally imagined.

The transmission, and the great misdating

Here is where the story becomes genuinely interesting. Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) had been set to translate the complete works of Plato into Latin for his patron Cosimo de’ Medici, a commission of enormous significance for the Renaissance, when a manuscript of the Corpus Hermeticum reached Florence and Cosimo ordered him to translate Hermes first. The exemplar survives: Laurentianus LXXI, 33. He completed that translation (treatises I–XIV only, titled Liber de potestate et sapientia Dei and known ever after as the Pimander) in 1463, dedicating it to Cosimo, who died the following year. It was first printed at Treviso by Gerardus de Lisa on 18 December 1471, in an edition Ficino neither prepared nor authorised; that printing date is the one usually quoted, and it is not the date of the translation. Lodovico Lazzarelli (1447–1500) worked on the material as well.

Ficino interrupted Plato because he believed these texts were far older than Plato: the work of an Egyptian sage of remote antiquity, first of the prisci theologi, the ancient theologians, and the ultimate source from which Plato’s own theology descended. Recovering them was therefore more urgent than translating a comparatively recent philosopher.

A correction to a story often told about Ficino

It is frequently said that Ficino believed the Hermetica older than Moses. He did not. Following Augustine’s genealogy, which he reproduces at the head of his own preface, Ficino placed Hermes Trismegistus several generations after the time of Moses’s birth. Augustine, De civitate Dei XVIII.39, has Hermetic philosophy flourishing long before the sages and philosophers of Greece but after Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, “and even after Moses himself.” The exact number of steps is not recoverable: the genealogy is corrupt in the received text of Augustine, and Yates calls Ficino’s version of it garbled. The pre-Mosaic dating was one position available in Renaissance Hermeticism, and various later Hermetists and magi held it, but it should not be attributed to Ficino himself. What Ficino claimed was priority over the Greeks, not over scripture, which was quite enough to place these texts at the centre of European thought.

He was mistaken, and the correction came from Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), the classical scholar. In his De rebus sacris et ecclesiasticis exercitationes XVI (London, 1614), written against Baronius’s Annales, Casaubon argued that the Greek Hermetica were written not in ancient Egypt but partly out of Plato and the Platonists and partly out of Christian scripture, and that their vocabulary was later than the Greek current even around the birth of Christ. The English here is a summary of his argument rather than a translation of any single sentence; his own dating formula is primis illis seculis nascentis Christianismi, “in those first centuries of nascent Christianity.” He gives no numeric range, and the ones often quoted in his name are modern glosses. The philology was decisive. The Hermetica were not primordial Egyptian revelation but Graeco-Egyptian writing of the Roman period.

The misdating is the reason the tradition exists

It would be easy to file Casaubon’s finding as a debunking and move on. That would miss the most important thing about it. The error is what made Hermeticism matter.

Had Ficino known these were second-century texts (roughly contemporary with the Church Fathers, plainly indebted to Platonism) he would very likely have finished the Plato first, and the Corpus Hermeticum might have remained a minor curiosity of late antique philosophy. Because he believed he was recovering the oldest wisdom in the world, the Hermetica were placed at the centre of Renaissance thought, and from there they shaped Ficino, Pico, Agrippa, Bruno, Dee, the alchemists, the Rosicrucian authors, and eventually every tradition covered in this book.

The dating was wrong. The influence was entirely real. And a tradition secure enough to record how it was founded on a philological mistake is in a stronger position than one that cannot mention it.

The Emerald Tablet

One short text deserves separate treatment, and gets it: the Emerald Tablet, the Tabula Smaragdina, is the single most quoted item in the entire Hermetic literature, and Chapter 6 gives its full text, its transmission and its commentary tradition. The essential point belongs here, though, because it bears directly on the question of what “ancient Hermetic” means. The Tablet is not ancient Egyptian. It is first attested in Arabic, in the Kitāb Sirr al-khalīqa wa-ṣanʿat al-ṭabīʿa (the Book of the Secret of Creation), of the late eighth or early ninth century.

This places the Tablet firmly in the Arabic-Islamic tradition that preserved, developed and transmitted so much of this material to medieval Europe: a debt Western esoteric writing has often obscured. The Latin versions on which every later European reading depends are translations from Arabic, beginning in the twelfth century. When the Tablet is described as a text of remote Egyptian antiquity, an entire and decisive stage of the tradition is being erased.

Reading the Hermetica today

For a reader who wants the primary texts rather than summaries, the standard modern scholarly translation is Brian Copenhaver’s Hermetica (1992), which gives the Greek Corpus and the Latin Asclepius with a substantial introduction and notes; M. David Litwa’s Hermetica II (2018) covers the Stobaean excerpts, papyrus fragments and ancient testimonies. Walter Scott’s four-volume Hermetica (1924–36) (completed after his death by A. S. Ferguson, who wholly authored the fourth volume) is older and its editorial choices are now contested, but it remains foundational. G. R. S. Mead’s Thrice-Greatest Hermes (1906) is out of copyright and widely available online, which is why it is the version most readers encounter; but it is a Theosophically-inflected translation from before Scott’s work, and it should be read alongside Copenhaver rather than instead of him.

Chapter IIISacred Geometry & Symbols Beginner

Nothing in this chapter has a power of its own. A circle drawn on a floor does not hold anything in or out, and a triangle does not attract. What the tradition found in a handful of figures was something weaker and more useful: that a few of them recur so persistently, in crystal and shell and orbit and the branching of plants, that they can be used as a vocabulary. A symbol of this kind is a compressed argument, a way of holding several relations in mind at once, which is a thing prose does badly and a drawing does well. That is the defensible version of the claim, and it is the one this chapter works from. The indefensible version, that the recurrence proves a designer, is not needed by any practice in this book and is not made here. The figures below were taught as objects of contemplation rather than as decoration, and that is how they are set out.

The fundamental forms

The Circle represents unity, wholeness and the infinite. Having neither beginning nor end, it stands for the eternal, and for that which contains without being contained. In practice it is also the boundary: the ritual circle of Chapter 8 and the Solomonic tradition is this figure put to work, defining an inside and an outside.

The Triangle represents the threefold structure that recurs across the tradition: heaven, earth and the human realm; or in alchemical terms the three principles of Chapter 5. Its orientation carries meaning: point upward for the ascent of the volatile and the aspiration of spirit, point downward for descent, manifestation and the fixed.

The Square represents stability, foundation, and the four elements. It is the figure of the material world and of earthly manifestation: four walls, four directions, four winds. Where the circle bounds, the square builds.

The Pentagram represents the five elements (the four with a fifth, quintessence or spirit, added) and the human microcosm. Drawn with a single unbroken line, it stands for the human being as a reflection of the cosmos, arms and legs and head at the five points. It is the central figure of the banishing practice in Chapter 15, where its specific documented history is given.

The Hexagram, two interpenetrating triangles, represents the union of the ascending and descending currents: the visual statement of “as above, so below.” In alchemical contexts it also encodes the elements by their combination of upward and downward triangles with and without a bar.

The Tree of Life

The diagram that organises most Western ceremonial practice is the Qabalistic Tree of Life: ten sephiroth, or emanations, connected by twenty-two paths. It came into this tradition from Jewish mysticism, was extensively reworked by Christian Cabalists of the Renaissance, Agrippa among them, and reached modern practice through two translations and an order: Knorr von Rosenroth’s Latin of the 1670s and 80s, Mathers’s English of 1887, and then the Golden Dawn, which mapped tarot, astrology, colour and Hebrew letter onto every path. Chapter 4 follows that route with the dates, and says what the diagram is a picture of.

Two points of honesty are owed here. First, the Christian and occult Cabala of the Renaissance is a genuine tradition with real intellectual achievements, but it is not identical to Jewish Kabbalah and should not be presented as though it speaks for it; the correspondences layered on by nineteenth-century orders are their own contribution. Second, the elaborate tables of correspondence familiar from modern handbooks (this path to that tarot trump, that sephirah to this planet and colour) are largely Golden Dawn constructions of the late nineteenth century. They are coherent, they are useful, and they are not ancient.

Constructions, not decorations

The forms above are usually met as pictures. They were originally met as constructions: things you make with a compass and a straightedge, in a fixed order, where each step is forced by the last. That difference matters, because a figure you have built has taught you something a figure you have looked at has not.

The foundational one is the vesica piscis, and it is the first proposition of Euclid. Draw a circle. Put the compass point anywhere on its circumference and draw a second circle of the same radius. The two overlap in a pointed oval, the vesica; and if you join the two centres to either point of the oval, you have an equilateral triangle, exactly, without having measured an angle. Euclid opens the Elements with this construction because it is the cheapest way to get a known shape out of nothing but a repeated radius.

Everything else follows cheaply. Keep stepping the same radius around the first circle and it divides the circumference into exactly six: the hexagon, and the six-petalled rosette that fills the pattern the popular literature calls the Flower of Life. The tradition read enormous significance into the fact that the radius measures its own circle six times. It is a fact about circles. Whether it is more than that is a question this chapter cannot settle, but the fact itself is free, checkable in two minutes, and genuinely surprising the first time.

The construction, as a contemplation

  1. Compass, straightedge, paper. No ruler markings, no protractor. The constraint is the practice.
  2. Draw the first circle. Note where you chose to put the centre, and that nothing determined it.
  3. Second circle, centre on the first circle’s edge, same radius. The vesica appears.
  4. Join the two centres to one point of the vesica. You now have an equilateral triangle, and you did not construct it; it was already implied by the two circles.
  5. Step the radius round the first circle: six marks, meeting exactly. Join them for the hexagon.
  6. The pentagon, which does not come free. The radius steps round its circle six times exactly: never five. To divide a circle in five, the line must first be cut in the golden section, which is why Euclid must build the whole of Book II before the pentagon of Book IV. The working construction: draw a diameter, and a second diameter at right angles to it (bisect the straight angle at the centre). Mark the midpoint of one radius. Set the compass on that midpoint, open it to the top of the vertical diameter, and swing an arc down to cut the horizontal diameter. The distance from the top of the vertical to that cut is the side of the inscribed pentagon; step it round the circle five times, and it closes exactly. Join every second point for the pentagram.
  7. Stop and look before interpreting. The tradition holds that the order of the figures is not arbitrary, and asks the reader to sit with that. Test that against what you have drawn rather than against the claim. Note what the two constructions have taught between them: six is native to the circle, and five must be earned, which is a fact of geometry, whatever else the tradition made of it.

The five solids

The three-dimensional counterpart is the set of Platonic solids: the five convex figures whose faces are all the same regular polygon. There are five and there cannot be a sixth: a proof, not a doctrine, and it closes Euclid’s Elements. Plato assigns four to the elements in the Timaeus and the fifth to the whole:

SolidFacesAssigned to
Tetrahedron4 trianglesfire: the sharpest, the most cutting
Cube6 squaresearth: the most stable, the one that stacks
Octahedron8 trianglesair
Icosahedron20 triangleswater: the roundest, the most mobile
Dodecahedron12 pentagonsthe whole: the heavens, the fifth thing

The assignments are Plato’s reasoning about shape and behaviour, not measurements: fire is the tetrahedron because it is the most acute, earth the cube because it alone tiles space. This is not physics and was never quite meant as physics. It is the correspondence principle of Chapter 1 applied to solid geometry, and it is the direct ancestor of the elemental attributions used in the ritual chapters of this book.

Where the ten and the twenty-two come from

This book uses the Tree of Life in nine chapters, and this is the one that says where its numbers come from. What the diagram is a picture of, the doctrine of emanation it descends from, is Chapter 4. The numbers come from one short, strange, very early text: the Sepher Yetzirah, the Book of Formation. It is not a Hermetic work and it is not a grimoire; it is a Jewish cosmological treatise, its date disputed across several centuries, and it is the reason every diagram in this tradition has ten circles and twenty-two lines.

It opens by announcing both numbers at once:

In thirty-two wonderful Paths of Wisdom did Jah, Jehovah Tzabaoth, the God of Israel, the Elohim of the living, the King of ages, the merciful and gracious God, the exalted One, the Dweller in eternity, most high and holy — engrave his name by the three Sepharim: Numbers, Letters, and Sounds.

Ten are the ineffable Sephiroth. Twenty-two are the Letters, the Foundation of all things; there are Three Mothers, Seven Double and Twelve Simple letters.

Thirty-two paths, made of ten and twenty-two. That is the entire architecture of the diagram in Fig. 2, stated in two sentences perhaps sixteen centuries before the Golden Dawn drew it. The ten are the sephiroth, and the twenty-two are the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, which is why the paths of the Tree are lettered rather than merely numbered, and why the correspondences of Chapter 22 attach to letters at all.

The subdivision matters as much as the total. Three Mothers, seven Double, twelve Simple: three letters for the elements, seven for the planets, twelve for the signs of the zodiac. Every correspondence table in this book (the planetary hours of Chapter 20, the elemental attributions of Chapter 15, the sigil work of Chapter 22) is a descendant of that three-way division. It is the oldest layer of the system, and it is doing the structural work everywhere.

“Ten and not nine, ten and not eleven”

The text is emphatic on the number in a way that reads oddly until you notice what it is guarding against. Section 4: “Ten is the number of the ineffable Sephiroth, ten and not nine, ten and not eleven. Understand this wisdom, and be wise in the perception.”

That insistence bears directly on a problem the later tradition never resolved. The Middle Pillar exercise of Chapter 13 uses a centre at the throat called Daath, which is not one of the ten. Later Qabalah calls it the non-sephirah, the empty place on the Tree, and the manoeuvre is transparently a way of having eleven while insisting on ten. The Sepher Yetzirah saw the temptation coming and forbade it by name. Whether the later tradition was right to do it anyway is a real question; that it was doing something the founding text prohibits is not.

Two images from the text are worth carrying, because they say more about how this diagram was originally meant than any modern commentary. The sephiroth, it says, “have the appearance of the Lightning flash, their origin is unseen and no end is perceived”: a sequence of descent, not a static chart. And: their “ending is even as their origin, as a flame arising from a burning coal.” The Tree in Fig. 2 is drawn as furniture. Its source describes it as something happening.

The glyphs of the seven and the four

One family of symbols is used on almost every page of this book’s tables and has not yet been read as symbols: the sigils of the seven planets, and the four element-triangles. The element signs are pure geometry: the two triangles of the hexagram, barred and unbarred: fire points up, water points down, air is fire barred, earth is water barred; superimpose all four and the hexagram returns. The planetary glyphs are compounds of three strokes: the circle, the crescent and the cross. The Sun is a circle about a point; the Moon a crescent; Venus a circle over a cross; Mars a circle driven into an arrow; Mercury all three strokes at once: crescent, circle and cross in a column; Jupiter a crescent rising over a cross; Saturn a cross over a crescent, the Sun’s opposite number in the old scheme of dignities. The popular reading of the three strokes (circle for spirit, crescent for soul, cross for matter, so that each glyph diagrams a different balance of the three) is a tidy mnemonic and is used as such in the modern literature; it is a later systematisation, not an ancient doctrine, and the glyphs themselves grew by scribal abbreviation long before anyone read them this way. Both facts can be true at once: the mnemonic works, and it was applied after the fact.

Proportion

The proportional side of sacred geometry concerns ratios that recur in growth and in classical design: the relation of a diagonal to a side, the interval ratios that produce consonance in music, and above all the division of a line “in extreme and mean ratio,” as Euclid calls it: cut so that the whole is to the greater part as the greater part is to the lesser. That cut is the golden section, about 1.618 to 1, and it is not mystical in origin: it is what the pentagon is made of. Every diagonal of a regular pentagon cuts every other in exactly this ratio, and the pentagram contains a smaller pentagon, which contains a smaller pentagram, without end: the figure is self-similar, and that, not any modern diagram, is why this ratio belongs to the five-pointed star and why Euclid needed it before he could construct the pentagon at all. The Pythagorean discovery that harmony can be expressed as simple whole-number ratios is the root of the whole enterprise, and it is the reason this tradition has always taken mathematics to be a spiritual discipline rather than a merely useful one. That a plucked string divided in half sounds the same note an octave higher is a fact about the world, and it was received as a revelation about the world.

A caution belongs here, in keeping with the rest of this book. A great deal of popular writing on sacred geometry claims to find the golden ratio in the Parthenon, the Great Pyramid, and the proportions of the human body, with a precision the measurements do not support. The genuine cases (in phyllotaxis, in certain spirals, in deliberate Renaissance design) are interesting enough without the invented ones. Contemplating a form for what it actually is remains the practice; contemplating a form for what a diagram claims about it does not.

Sources: Pythagorean ratio theory as transmitted through Platonic and Neoplatonic writing. Agrippa, De occulta philosophia (1533), Books I–II, for elemental and celestial correspondence. Tree of Life correspondences in their modern form: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn (1888 onward), published in Regardie, The Golden Dawn (1937–40). Constructions: Euclid, Elements I.1 for the vesica and the equilateral triangle, and the concluding proposition of Book XIII, that no sixth regular solid exists. The elemental assignment of the five solids: Plato, Timaeus 55d–56c. The compass-and-straightedge contemplation above is this book’s own arrangement of a standard construction. Sepher Yetzirah, quoted from the translation of William Wynn Westcott, Sepher Yetzirah: The Book of Formation and the Thirty Two Paths of Wisdom, 2nd ed. (1893), ch. I, sections 1, 2, 4, 6 and 7. Note that Westcott, who translated it, is one of the three founders of the Golden Dawn in Chapter 13: the line from this text to the modern diagram runs through him personally. The dating of the original is disputed across several centuries and no attempt is made to settle it here. A widely circulating scan of a later Westcott edition is a 1996 reset carrying its own copyright; the 1893 printing used here does not.

Chapter IVKabbalah and Its Transmission Adept

The Tree of Life is a diagram of a doctrine, and the doctrine is emanation: that the divine, considered as infinite and without attribute, becomes knowable only by descending through ten stages, each issuing from the one before. The diagram is drawn in Chapter 3 and is not redrawn here. What follows is the doctrine it depicts, the literature that doctrine comes from, and the route by which a body of Jewish mystical writing became the skeleton on which English ceremonial magic was built. That route has names and dates in it, and runs through three books.

The Ein Sof, and what emanation means

Behind the ten sephiroth stands the doctrine the diagram exists to depict: the Ein Sof, the Boundless: the divine considered as infinite, without attribute, and therefore without anything a diagram could show. The sephiroth are not parts of it. They are how it becomes knowable at all. Ginsburg, whose 1865 essay is the spine of this chapter, puts the mechanism plainly:

the medium by which the En Soph made his existence known in the creation of the world are ten Sephiroth or intelligences, which emanated from the Boundless One… At first the En Soph, or the Aged of the Aged, or the Holy Aged, as he is alternately called, sent forth from his infinite light one spiritual substance or intelligence.

Three consequences follow, and all three change how the diagram in Chapter 3 should be read.

The first is that the Tree is a record of a descent, not a filing system. Chapter 3 notices this already, in the Sepher Yetzirah’s image of the sephiroth as a lightning flash whose origin is unseen; the doctrine of the Ein Sof is why that image is the right one. Each sephirah issues from the one before. A table of correspondences can be read in any order. This cannot.

The second is that the top of the diagram is not the top of the system. Kether is the first emanation, not the source; the source is not on the page and cannot be. Modern handbooks that treat Kether as the divine simply lose the distinction the whole structure exists to make.

The third is that the sephiroth are, in Ginsburg’s account, both infinite and finite: “infinite and perfect when the En Soph imparts his fulness to them, and finite and imperfect when the fulness is withdrawn.” They are not ten things. They are one thing at ten degrees of withdrawal.

The ten by name

The ten deserve their names in the reader’s hand before any correspondence is hung on them. The table gives the modern spellings beside Ginsburg’s English, and the station each holds on the figure his essay prints: the Heavenly Man, the Archetypal Man, the ten drawn on a human body standing inside the oval of the Boundless, which his plate labels “The Endless.” That plate is the ancestor of every body-centred use of the Tree, including the Middle Pillar of Chapter 13, and Ginsburg’s exposition of it ends in a sentence worth the whole table: “It is this form which the prophet Ezekiel saw in the mysterious chariot, and of which the earthly man is a faint copy.”

#NameGinsburg’s EnglishOn the Heavenly Man
1Ketherthe Crownthe crown upon the head
2ChokmahWisdomthe head, right side
3BinahIntelligencethe head, left side: with the first triad, “the heart or the understanding”
4Chesed (Gedulah)Mercy, or Love; also Greatnessthe right arm, “distributing life”
5Geburah (Pachad)Justice; Judicial Strengththe left arm, distributing “death”
6TipherethBeauty, or Mildnessthe chest, uniting the two
7NetzachFirmnessthe right leg
8HodSplendourthe left leg
9YesodFoundation, or the Basis“the basis and source of all things”
10MalkuthKingdom; also Shechinah“the harmony of the whole Archetypal Man”

Ginsburg’s arrangement of the ten is the one every later diagram keeps. The three on the right are the Pillar of Mercy; the three on the left, “representing the principle of rigour,” the Pillar of Judgment; the four in the centre, “representing mildness,” the Middle Pillar. And the ten resolve into a “trinity of triads”: the first triad “represents the intellect; hence this triad is called the Intellectual World”; the second “represents moral qualities; hence it is designated the moral or Sensuous World”; the third “represents power and stability,” the material world. Above the whole structure, later Qabalah interposed three veils between the Ein Sof and Kether, and Mathers’s introduction gives their names as the tradition received them: “the primal AIN, Ain, the negatively existent One, and the AIN SVP, Ain Soph, the limitless Expansion; while of even the AIN SVP AVR, Ain Soph Aur, the illimitable Light, only a dim conception can be formed.”

Why one Tree is not enough: the four worlds

The ten do not happen once. In the developed system they repeat at four levels, each produced by the one above it, and each containing a complete set of ten. Ginsburg names them in the older English spellings, which are worth seeing because they are the ones the Victorian occultists read:

I. The World of Creation, or the Briatic World, also called The Throne, which is the abode of pure spirits, and which, like its parents, consists of ten Sephiroth, or Emanations. The Briatic World, again, gave rise to II. The World of Formation, or the Jetziratic World, which is the habitation of the angels, and also consists of ten Sephiroth; whilst the Jetziratic World, again, sent forth III. The World of Action, or the Assiatic World… which contains the Spheres and matter.

Above those three stands the World of Emanation, the Atziluthic. Modern writing spells them Atziluth, Briah, Yetzirah and Assiah, and the arithmetic is the point: forty sephiroth, not ten, and any statement of the form this sephirah means that thing is incomplete until it says which world it is in. This is the part of the system that modern correspondence tables most often flatten, and flattening it is what turns a cosmology into a lookup table.

The Zohar, and who wrote it

The central text is the Zohar, the Book of Splendour: a vast Aramaic commentary on the Torah, and the source of nearly everything in the two sections above. The tradition assigns it to Rabbi Simeon ben Jochai, a second-century sage. Ginsburg tells the received story without disguising that it is a story:

No one, however, dared to write it down, till Simon ben Jochai, who lived at the time of the destruction of the second Temple. Having been condemned to death by Titus, Rabbi Simon managed to escape with his son and concealed himself in a cavern where he remained for twelve years… Scarcely had his spirit departed, when a dazzling light filled the cavern, so that no one could look at the Rabbi.

It is a good story and it is the wrong century. The Zohar appears in Castile at the end of the thirteenth century, in the hands of one man, Moses de León, who published it, sold it, and said he was copying an ancient manuscript. Nobody else ever saw the manuscript. The case that de León wrote it was made in print by Adolph Jellinek at Leipzig in 1851 and by Heinrich Graetz at Leipzig in 1863, and Ginsburg, reviewing the evidence in 1865, reports it as proven: he cites Graetz for the page “where other facts are given, proving that Moses de Leon is the author of the Sohar.”

The evidence is of a familiar kind. Ginsburg’s most telling item is not a document but a mistake: de León, quoting scripture in a work published under his own name, misquotes it and then explains the misquotation; and the same error, with the same explanation built on it, appears in the Zohar. A second-century Galilean does not inherit a thirteenth-century Spaniard’s slip of memory. Ginsburg notes drily that commentators who did not know where the blunder came from “express their great surprise that the Sohar should explain a mis-quotation.”

How far this book follows that

The dating case set out here is the one made between 1851 and 1865, because those are the sources this edition can print. A great deal of twentieth-century scholarship has gone over the same ground and is in copyright; none of it has been consulted for this chapter, and the reader should not take the absence of a modern citation as evidence that the question stopped there. What can be shown from public-domain material is narrower and still striking: the thirteenth-century attribution was argued, in print, in the standard literature, more than thirty years before the text reached English occultism; and it reached English occultism with that argument printed inside it.

How it reached the English magicians

The Zohar is in Aramaic, which almost no Victorian occultist read. It arrived through two translations, and knowing which two explains a great deal about what the Golden Dawn thought it was working with.

The first is Christian Knorr von Rosenroth’s Kabbala Denudata, a Latin anthology of kabbalistic material published in the 1670s and 1680s. Ginsburg records that the Latin of the Idra Rabba and the Idra Suta, the Greater and Lesser Assemblies, is in its second volume, Frankfurt-on-the-Maine, 1684. Rosenroth is the reason the material was available to Christian Europe at all, and the reason it arrived with a Christian frame already fitted to it.

The second is S. L. MacGregor Mathers’s The Kabbalah Unveiled of 1887: the same man, and the same London publisher, as the Key of Solomon of 1889 in Chapter 10. Its title page is exact about what it is: three books of the Zohar, not the Zohar, “translated into English from the Latin version of Knorr von Rosenroth, and collated with the original Chaldee and Hebrew text.” The three are the Book of Concealed Mystery and the Greater and Lesser Holy Assemblies: precisely the sections Ginsburg says Rosenroth had put into Latin. Mathers describes his own method in the preface, and it is more careful than his reputation suggests:

My translation is principally taken from the Latin version of Knorr von Rosenroth, but I have throughout collated it with the original Chaldee and Hebrew text, and in many instances have translated directly therefrom, especially whenever the Latin rendering seemed unreliable.

So: English out of Latin out of Aramaic, checked against the Aramaic where the Latin looked wrong. Not a translation at one remove exactly, and not a direct one either. A reader building an argument on a particular English word in Mathers is standing on Rosenroth unless Mathers says otherwise, and Mathers does not usually say.

The voice of the English Zohar

What the Victorian reader actually met in Mathers deserves a hearing, because it is better than its reputation. His introduction lays out the written Kabbalah in four heads: “the Sepher Yetzirah and its dependencies; the Zohar with its developments and commentaries; the Sepher Sephiroth and its expansions; the Asch Metzareph and its symbolism”; and defines its central working term in a sentence this book’s sigil chapters could take as a motto: “The term ‘path’ is used throughout the Qabalah to signify a hieroglyphical idea, or rather the sphere of ideas, which may be attached to any glyph or symbol.” Then the translation proper opens, with the first sentence of the Book of Concealed Mystery and Mathers’s own gloss upon it:

“The Book of Concealed Mystery is the book of the equilibrium of balance.” What is here meant by the terms “equilibrium of balance”? Equilibrium is that harmony which results from the analogy of contraries, it is the dead centre where, the opposition of opposing forces being equal in strength, rest succeeds motion. It is the central point. It is the “point within the circle” of ancient symbolism. It is the living synthesis of counterbalanced power. Thus form may be described as the equilibrium of light and shade; take away either factor, and form is viewless.

“The term balance,” he continues, “is applied to the two opposite natures in each triad of the Sephiroth, their equilibrium forming the third Sephira in each ternary”, which is Ginsburg’s trinity of triads, restated as a principle of design. The text then hangs the whole structure in the negative: “Equilibrium hangeth in that region which is negatively existent”; and Mathers’s gloss on negative existence is the source of the three veils quoted above. His introduction also lists the problems the doctrine addresses (the Supreme Being, the cosmogony, the creation and destiny of angels and man, the soul, the revealed law, “the transcendental symbolism of numerals,” the mysteries of the Hebrew letters, “the equilibrium of contraries”), a syllabus that maps, item for item, onto the chapters of this book’s own practicum.

The thing Mathers is not given credit for

Here is what makes the transmission worth a chapter rather than a footnote. Mathers did not conceal the dating problem. He printed it. Section 5 of his own introduction says that on the author and origin of the Qabalah he “cannot do better than give the following extract from Dr. Ginsburg’s Essay on the Kabbalah”; and then reproduces Ginsburg at length, the same Ginsburg who had just concluded that a thirteenth-century Spaniard wrote the book.

The caveat was in the English Zohar from its first page, put there by the man who translated it. What happened afterwards is that the tradition kept the text and dropped the introduction. That is a different failure from the one this book usually documents, and a more interesting one: not a source that hid its dating, but a readership that skipped it.

Kabbalah, Cabala, Qabalah

The three spellings are commonly said to mark three traditions: Kabbalah for the Jewish original, Cabala for the Christian adaptation of the Renaissance, and Qabalah for the Hermetic and occult version that runs from the Golden Dawn to the present. The convention is useful and this book follows it. Know that it is a convention and not a rule, and that it postdates the material it sorts.

Where the Q comes from is documented, at least. Mathers, in 1887, noted that the word “has been spelt in a great variety of ways: Cabala, Kabalah, Kabbala, &c.” and stated his own choice and his reason: “I have adopted the form Qabalah, as being more consonant with the Hebrew writing of the word.” He was making a transliteration decision, not founding a school. The school came afterwards and took the spelling with it.

What the Christian Cabala actually took

Ginsburg opens his essay by listing who in Christendom had been captured by this material, and the list is a roll-call of names already in this book: Raymond Lully, John Reuchlin, Pico della Mirandola, Cornelius Agrippa, van Helmont, Robert Fludd, Henry More. Agrippa is the author of the book that Chapter 22 catches Barrett copying; Fludd stands beside Maier in the Rosicrucian material of Chapter 12. The Christian Cabala is not a side channel to the tradition this book describes. It is one of its main arteries, and the sephiroth reached Agrippa before they ever reached an English magician.

What that adaptation did with the material is a separate question, and Chapter 3 states the caution that governs it: the Christian and occult Cabala is a genuine tradition with real achievements, and it is not identical to Jewish Kabbalah and should not be made to speak for it. This chapter adds only the mechanism. The Christian readers met the sephiroth in Latin, in an anthology assembled by a Christian Hebraist who was looking for confirmations of his own theology, and they met the Zohar in the same way. What reached them was already selected.

The seventy-two-fold Name, and what the Goetia did with it

One product of this reading technique became more famous than the technique itself, and Agrippa prints it entire. His chapter heading is its own summary: How the Hebrew Mecubals draw forth the sacred names of Angels out of the sacred writ, and of the seventie two Angels, which bear the name of God. The general rule comes first, and it is a rule about where to look rather than what to find: “wheresoever any thing of divine essence is expressed in the Scripture, from that place the name of God may rightly be gathered; but in what place soever in the Scripture the name of God is found expressed, there mark what office lies under that name.” A caution follows it that is easy to pass over and worth keeping: “that of good spirits we receive the names of good spirits, of evill the names of evill,” and “let us not confound black with white, nor day with night, nor light with darkness.”

Then the operation. Three consecutive verses of Exodus each run to exactly seventy-two letters, and Agrippa sets them out as a single figure:

There is a certain text in Exodus conteined in three verses, whereof every one is writ with seventy two letters, beginning thus: The first, Vajisa; the second, Vajabo; the third, Vajot: which are extended into one line, viz. the first, and third from the left hand to the right, but the middle in a contrary order, beginning from the right to the left, is terminated on the left hand: then each of the three letters being subordinate the one to the other, make one name, which are seventy two names, which the Hebrews call Schemhamphoræ: to which if the divine name El or Jah be added, they produce seventy two trissyllable names of angels.

Three lines of seventy-two letters, the middle one written backwards, read as columns rather than as rows: each column of three letters is a name, and a divine ending makes each name an angel. The arithmetic is the whole of the method, and it is the same habit of counting that produced the twenty-two paths and the ten sephiroth of this chapter. What the names are then said to govern is stated in one sentence, and the reach of it is the point:

whereof every one carries the great name of God, as it is written: My Angel shall go before thee; observe him, for my name is in him. And these are those that are set over the seventy two Celestial quinaries, and so many Nations, and tongues, and joynts of mans body, and cooperate with the seventy two seniors of the Synagogue, and so many disciples of Christ.

A quinary is five degrees of the zodiac, and seventy-two of them is the circle entire. The same number is then made to carry the nations of the earth, the languages, the joints of the body, the elders of the Sanhedrin and the disciples: a single count reconciling astronomy, anthropology and two scriptures at once. Agrippa’s table of the names follows on the next leaf, set sideways across the page, each name in Hebrew with its Latin form beside it. Those Latin forms are given below exactly as that printing has them.

The list is printed here as it stands on the leaf, which means it is printed with its faults. The same name, Ieiazel, is set twice, at thirteen and at forty. Mchekiel at sixty-four and Roehel at sixty-nine are evidently misprints, and the letters on the page are unambiguously those; a reader who has met these names elsewhere will know them as Mehekiel and Rochel. Mihæl at forty-eight carries the ligature the printing gives it. None of this is corrected above, because a list of angelic names is exactly the kind of material where silent tidying accumulates into a tradition, and the point of printing from the leaf is to be able to say what the leaf says.

A name of God at the head of a list of demons

The seventy-two here are angels, and each is said to carry the name of God. The seventy-two of Chapter 11 are the spirits of the Goetia, and they are not these. The two sets share nothing but a number, and the number is not a coincidence in either case: the zodiac has seventy-two quinaries whichever kind of spirit is being distributed around it.

What is worth noticing is what the printed Goetia does with the word. In the edition this book reads, the catalogue of the seventy-two spirits opens under a single line of capitals, standing alone above the first of them: SHEMHAMPHORASH. Then, directly beneath it, “(1.) Bael. The First Principal Spirit is a King ruling in the East.” The word occurs nowhere else in that printing. No angel is named, no derivation is given, and no explanation is offered for setting a name of God over a list of demons. Whatever was once meant by it, what survives in the text as printed is the title and nothing behind it.
