Ginsburg, The Kabbalah (1865), read in the 1920 verbatim reprint of the first edition, Cornell copy cu31924075115380: the En Soph and the emanation of the sephiroth, the four worlds in his Briatic / Jetziratic / Assiatic spellings, the legend of Simon ben Jochai in the cavern, the misquotation argument, and the citations of Jellinek (1851) and Graetz (1863) for the authorship of the Zohar, are all his. The ten-by-name table follows his plate of the Heavenly Man and his exposition at pp. 92–93 of that reprint, both read on the page images; the plate labels the oval “The Endless” and gives Love and Justice for the fourth and fifth, and the pillars and the trinity of triads come from the same pages. Mathers, The Kabbalah Unveiled (1887), Wellcome copy b24884443: the title page for what the book contains and what it was translated from, the preface for his account of his own method, Introduction §5 for the spelling and for his reproduction of Ginsburg, and §§23–30 at pp. 14–16 for the four heads, the definition of “path,” the equilibrium passage with its gloss, the three veils and the list of problems.

Three readings are repaired in the quotations above and are declared here. The Mathers scan renders Rosenroth as B-osenroth and Bosenroth, its fount confusing R with B; the same confusion gives Babbi for Rabbi in the Ginsburg scan, and creaiion for creation. Nothing else in the quoted passages is altered, and the ellipses are marked. Where the two scans carry the same sentence, Ginsburg’s opening as Mathers reprints it, the 1887 setting is the cleaner and is the one quoted. The Hebrew and Aramaic is unreadable in both text layers and none of it is reproduced here. Rosenroth’s Kabbala Denudata is named on Ginsburg’s and Mathers’s authority and was not consulted. Twentieth-century scholarship on the Zohar is in copyright and none of it has been used. The reading of the Tree as a descent rather than a table, and the observation about the four worlds and modern correspondence tables, are this book’s own.

Chapter VAlchemical Foundations Adept

Alchemy is the art of transformation, and its literature is the most systematically misread body of writing in this tradition. The popular account, that alchemists were failed chemists trying to make gold, is too crude, but the correction usually offered for it is a matter of live scholarly dispute, and this book will not pretend otherwise. Lawrence Principe and William Newman have argued, in “Some Problems with the Historiography of Alchemy” (2001) and in Principe’s The Secrets of Alchemy (2013), that reading alchemy as essentially an inner discipline is a nineteenth-century invention, traceable to Mary Anne Atwood in 1850 and to Ethan Allen Hitchcock, and that, in their words, they “find no indication that the vast majority of alchemists were working on anything other than material substances toward material goals.” Against them, Hereward Tilton, Wouter Hanegraaff and others hold that this corrects too far and, as Mike Zuber summarises the critics, “downplays important topics in favour of chemical content and experimental technique.” What almost nobody now defends is the sharp either/or; Stanton Linden, whom this chapter cites below, holds that all three goals (metallic, medical and spiritual) are at times simultaneously present in the same treatise. Metals are the language in which the work is described (metallurgy supplied a vocabulary of purification, dissolution and change of state that nothing else in the ancient world could match) and what else the metals were is exactly what is argued about.

One sentence often offered as evidence for the symbolic reading deserves to be traced, because it does not survive the tracing. The claim that neither Michael Maier nor Heinrich Khunrath ever claimed to have produced gold, and that their alchemy was therefore symbolic rather than operative, circulates as an unsourced sentence in the Wikipedia article on Rosicrucianism, where no scholar is named for it. The specialists say something else. Hereward Tilton, Maier’s biographer, writes that Maier “dedicated his life to the quest for the highest goal of alchemy: the philosophers’ stone”: a substance held in Maier’s day to “transmute lead into gold, heal the sick, and even reverse the aging process.” Tilton records Maier’s first laboratory experiments during his internship of 1592–95, his journey in 1603 to the gold and silver mines of Hungarian Carpathia and his first alchemical experiment at Easter 1604, his co-authorship in 1616 of Francis Anthony’s printed defence of aurum potabile, and, in the last year of his life, his having produced an aurum potabile “far excelling” Anthony’s. Peter Forshaw, reporting Tilton, notes that gold-making “may not have been the main goal of Maier’s practice, which was more concerned with the use of gold as aurum potabile (drinkable gold) in chemical medicine, but it was nevertheless part of his training and repertoire,” that “many of the quotes in Atalanta fugiens have their sources in medieval chrysopoetic literature,” and that the tendency to relegate visual forms of alchemy to a “spiritual quest” “should also be reconsidered.” Nor were these two men associates: Tilton records that Maier met Khunrath in Danzig and came to regard him as a fraud, a Betrüger. The narrow claim, that no surviving text has either man announcing a successful transmutation, may well be true. The conclusion the popular account draws from it is not one any specialist draws.

What the alchemists asked of the operator

The grimoires of Chapter 8 open with washing. The alchemical corpus opens with something harder to fake. The Sophic Hydrolith, one of the treatises in The Hermetic Museum, begins its instruction not with apparatus but with the operator’s condition; and the passage is the alchemical answer to the ablutions:

In the first place, let every devout and God-fearing chemist and student of this Art consider that this arcanum should be regarded, not only as a truly great, but as a most holy Art (seeing that it typifies and shadows out the highest heavenly good). Therefore, if any man desire to reach this great and unspeakable Mystery, he must remember that it is obtained not by the might of man, but by the grace of God, and that not our will or desire, but only the mercy of the Most High, can bestow it upon us.

For this reason you must first of all cleanse your heart, lift it to Him alone, and ask of Him this gift in true, earnest, and undoubting prayer. He alone can give and bestow it.

Whatever one makes of the metaphysics, notice the structure of the claim: the work cannot be commanded, only received, and the first vessel to be cleansed is the operator. That is the same instruction the Key of Solomon gives as a bath and the Heptameron gives as six days of washing: stated here as an inward condition instead of a procedure. It is also the reason the literature is so hard to use as a manual: it keeps insisting that the decisive variable is not in the apparatus.

The three principles

Sulfur: Soul. The active principle: consciousness, will, the animating and combustible element that drives change. In the operator, that which initiates.

Mercury: Spirit. The mediating principle: intuition, imagination, the volatile element that passes between states and carries influence from one to another. In the operator, that which perceives and connects.

Salt: Body. The fixed principle: form, stability, the residue that remains after burning. In the operator, that which persists and can be built upon.

To these the tradition adds the four elements as states rather than substances (earth for the solid and fixed, water for the fluid and receptive, air for the mobile and mediating, fire for the transformative) and, in most systems, a fifth, quintessence, standing outside the four as their principle of coherence.

Where the matter is to be found

The Glory of the World, in the same collection, answers the tradition’s central riddle, what the prima materia actually is, by refusing to name it and telling you where to look instead:

“I will tell you where you may find it. The first spot is on the summit of two mountains; the second, in all mountains; the third, among the refuse in the street; the fourth, in the trees and metals the liquid of which is the Sun and Moon, Mercury, Saturn, and Jupiter. There is but one vessel, one method, and one consummation.”

The third of those is the famous one, and it recurs throughout the corpus: the matter of the Great Work is something universally available and universally despised: refuse in the street. Whether that points at a substance, at a psychological condition, or at nothing at all is precisely the dispute this chapter opened with, and the text is constructed so as not to settle it.

The seven metals

The alchemist’s palette is seven metals, and the tradition never lists them without their planets: the metal in the crucible and the planet in the sky are the same nature at two removes, which is why the timing chapters of this book and the metal-graded seals of the Goetia use one vocabulary. Agrippa’s survey of what stands under each planet (Book I of the Occult Philosophy, in the English of 1651) assigns the metals with reasons attached, and the reasons are the instructive part. Under Saturn: “Amongst Metals, Lead, and Gold, by reason of its weight, and the golden Marcasite.” Under the Sun: “Amongst Metals, Gold by reason of its splendor, and its receiving that from the Sun which makes it cordiall.” The rest of the series stands in the adjacent chapters: tin (with silver and gold again, “by reason of their temperateness”) under Jupiter; iron and “red Brass,” with “all fiery, red, and sulphureous things,” under Mars; copper under Venus; quicksilver under Mercury, “which moves all things indistinctly”; silver under the Moon.

MetalPlanetThe character it carries
leadSaturnweight, slowness, the dark beginning: the work starts here
tinJupitertemperateness; the benign, easy-working metal
ironMarsthe fiery and sharp; the metal of edges
goldthe Sunsplendour; incorruptible, “cordiall”: the work ends here
copperVenusthe joining metal, of mirrors and vessels
quicksilverMercurythe runner between states, liquid metal, neither and both
silverthe Moonthe reflective, the white stage embodied

Two things in Agrippa’s assignment repay attention. First, gold appears three times (under Saturn for its weight, under Jupiter for its temperateness, under the Sun for its splendour), which is the clearest small proof this book can offer that a correspondence is an argument about qualities and not an entry in a lookup table: the same metal answers three planets for three different reasons. Second, the series is a ladder with a direction. The work begins in lead and ends in gold; begins, that is, in Saturn and ends in the Sun: the same road the ascent of Chapter 2 climbs sphere by sphere, run through matter instead of through the soul. The doctrine beneath it, common to the whole literature, is that the metals are one substance at different degrees of maturity, ripening in the earth toward gold; the operations of this chapter are, on the tradition’s own understanding, a hastening of that ripening; and the assay of Chapter 29 shows what that belief looked like when it met the cupel.

The stages of the work

The magnum opus is described in stages, most often by colour. The Latin names familiar from modern writing are conventionally set beside a Greek sequence that is among the oldest technical vocabulary in the tradition: exactly, for the first three; less so for the fourth:

  • Nigredo: the blackening, Greek melanosis. Putrefaction and dissolution; the breaking down of what was.
  • Albedo: the whitening, leukosis. Washing and purification; what remains once the dross is gone.
  • Citrinitas: the yellowing, xanthosis. The transitional stage.
  • Rubedo: the reddening, iosis. The completed work; the union of what had been separated.

Colour change of this kind is already the substance of the earliest surviving Greek alchemy. The Physika kai mystika attributed to pseudo-Democritus is concerned with whitening base metals to silver and yellowing them to gold; ancient testimony describes four books under the name: on gold, on silver, on stones and on purple. Whether all four of the Greek stage-names in the modern lists occur in that text is a question for its critical edition (Matteo Martelli, The Four Books of Pseudo-Democritus, 2013), which could not be obtained for this edition. Zosimos of Panopolis, who quotes Mary the Jewess constantly, is reported to have credited her with knowledge of the colour changes; the claim is widely repeated, and reaches this book through Raphael Patai’s 1982 Ambix article, which could not be obtained and against which it was therefore not checked. How many stages there are was never settled. The four-colour form is the older, and from about the fifteenth or sixteenth century many writers reduced the colours to three, citrinitas being absorbed into rubedo or simply dropped, which is why modern accounts differ on whether there are three or four. That dating reaches modern readers chiefly through Jung, Psychology and Alchemy §333, who hedges it as “about the fifteenth or sixteenth century” and attributes the change to “inner psychological reasons” rather than to anything in the texts.

Read as an account of interior change the sequence is uncomfortably recognisable. Something held together comes apart; there is a period in which nothing is left but the fact of having come apart; what survives is smaller and cleaner than what went in; and only afterwards is there any integration worth the name. The alchemists insisted the stages cannot be skipped and cannot be hurried, and that nigredo is not a failure of the work but its beginning. Whatever one makes of their metallurgy, that is a serious psychological observation, and it is why this literature found readers in the twentieth century among people with no interest in furnaces at all.

The operations

Alongside the colour stages the tradition describes sequences of operations: the named procedures by which the work advances. The most influential English list is George Ripley’s Twelve Gates, from the Compound of Alchymy: a poem completed in 1471 and dedicated to Edward IV, but not printed for another hundred and twenty years, when Raph Rabbards set it forth in London from Thomas Orwin’s press in 1591: calcination, solution, separation, conjunction, putrefaction, congelation, cibation, sublimation, fermentation, exaltation, multiplication, and projection. (The second gate is Solution in Ashmole’s Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum of 1652, followed here, and Dissolution in the 1591 print.)

A rival scheme of fourteen stages goes under the name of Samuel Norton, great-grandson of Thomas Norton: it begins with purgation, sublimation and calcination and ends with multiplication in virtue and multiplication in quantity. Where it comes from matters, because it is almost always mis-cited. It is not in Norton’s English Key of Alchemy of 1578, which he says he “divided into eight several parts or treatises” and which contains no such list. The fourteen are the operations numbered through Mercurius redivivus, a Latin tract published at Frankfurt in 1630 by the York physician Edmund Deane, whose title page describes it as begun by Norton (inchoatus) and issued auctior & perfectior, enlarged and improved. How much of the numbering is Norton’s and how much Deane’s cannot be settled from the printed book; the names are Latin, and the English forms in circulation are translations.

A caution is owed here, and it comes from the scholarship rather than from scepticism. Stanton J. Linden, introducing The Alchemy Reader (Cambridge, 2003), p. 17, writes that “there is nothing approaching uniformity and consistency in the names assigned to these stages, or to the nature of the processes described, their order, or even their number.” Anyone presenting a single definitive sequence of alchemical operations is presenting one author’s scheme as though it were the tradition’s. Ripley’s twelve are worth knowing because they were widely copied, not because they are canonical.

What the operations do share is a shape. Something is broken down, separated into components, purified, recombined with what it was separated from, and then stabilised: with fermentation and multiplication at the end suggesting that a completed work becomes capable of propagating itself. Whether read as metallurgy or as biography, that arc is the same one the colour stages describe.

How the heat was actually controlled

Read enough alchemical recipes and a gap opens between what they say and what you could do. They call constantly for a gentle heat, a moderate heat, a heat like that of a hen sitting; and a modern reader has no idea what that means with a stove in front of them. It is the single most practical thing missing from the tradition as it is usually presented, and it is not missing from the tradition itself. It is stated plainly, in English, in 1653.

John French (very probably the “J.F.” who two years earlier had put Agrippa into the English this book quotes in Chapter 22, though as Chapter 10 notes the initials have also been read as James Freake) published The Art of Distillation in London in 1653, subtitled a treatise of the choicest spagyricall preparations. He opens by saying that the degrees of heat are principally four, and the list is the whole control system of the art:

DegreeFrench’s source of heatWhat it is forIn a kitchen
FirstOnly a warmth: horse dung, the Sun, warm water and its vapourPutrefaction and digestion: the long standing that changes a substance without driving anything offAn airing cupboard, a warm windowsill, a yoghurt maker
SecondSeething water and its vapour; also of ashesDistilling what is subtle and moist, and rectifying any spirit or oilA pan of simmering water: a double boiler
ThirdSand, and filings of ironDistilling what is subtle and dry, or gross and moistA sand bath: a tray of sand on the heat
FourthA naked fire: close, open, or with a blastMetals and minerals, and hard gums such as amberNo kitchen equivalent. Chapter 29.

Three things follow from that table, and they are worth more than any recipe.

First, the heat is chosen by what the material is, not by how fast you want to go. A warmth for putrefaction; boiling water for the subtle and moist; sand for the dry. French is explicit that many of the lower distillations can be done over a naked fire and are, in a copper still; but that minerals cannot be done any other way. Heat is a tool with four settings, and the recipes assume you know which one they mean.

Second, the second degree is Maria the Jewess’s bath, whose descent to us is set out later in this chapter: the apparatus from Berthelot’s reproduction of the Greek manuscript figures, the name from the medieval Latin balneum Mariae. Fourteen hundred years separate the Alexandrian apparatus from the Southwark physician, and it is still the water bath, still doing the same job, and still carrying her name into every French kitchen as the bain-marie. Only the heart scarab of Chapter 22, in use across some two thousand years, outlasts it.

Third, and this is the useful one, the safety line this book draws falls exactly on French’s fourth degree. That is not a coincidence and it is not modern squeamishness. His own scheme separates the operations that need only warm water from the operations that need an open forge, and the second set is the set that works on metals and minerals. Everything this book gives you is in his first three degrees. Everything it refuses is in his fourth.

The vessels, and what the operations mean in the hand

The named operations of the tradition sound abstract until you know which vessel each one happens in. French supplies the correspondence, and once you have it the recipes stop being mysterious:

  • Digestion and putrefaction: material left standing at the first degree for a long period, commonly forty days. Nothing is driven off; the substance is allowed to change. This is the step the spagyric tincture below performs when the jar stands for a month.
  • Distillation: in an alembic over the bath, or a retort in sand. The volatile part rises, condenses and is caught.
  • Rectification: distilling the product again to purify it, and again. French describes taking a spirit through several rectifications.
  • Cohobation: the distillate poured back onto what it came from, and distilled again. Repeated, this is how the tradition strengthens a spirit without adding anything to it.
  • Circulation: the operation with the best vessel. A pelican is a closed glass body with one or two arms curving from the neck back into its own belly, so that what rises condenses and returns continuously without ever leaving. Sealed, at moderate heat, for a month. French says of the matter simply that it must be put in at the top, which afterwards must be closed up.

What circulation is, and why the vessel is shaped like that

A pelican does not remove anything and does not add anything. It takes a sealed quantity of matter and puts it through the same ascent and descent, over and over, for weeks. Nothing enters, nothing leaves, and the operator does nothing but maintain the heat.

It is difficult to look at that vessel and not see what the literature saw in it. The bird was supposed to wound its own breast to feed its young from itself; the vessel returns its own substance to itself indefinitely; and the solve et coagula of the whole tradition is exactly a dissolution followed by a reconstitution, repeated until something is fixed. Whatever a month in a pelican does chemically, the alchemists had an apparatus that performed their central metaphor continuously, in the corner of the room, while they waited. Keep that in mind before deciding the imagery came first.

The fourth degree, and why this chapter stops there

French’s fourth degree (the naked fire, and the metals and minerals it is for) is where the historical literature becomes genuinely dangerous, and where this chapter prints history and no procedure. Distilling minerals produces corrosive and volatile products; the seventeenth-century laboratory did it in rooms that killed people slowly, and its practitioners knew and said so. The first three degrees, applied to plants, are kitchen operations and are given in full below.

The fourth degree has its own chapter. Chapter 29 gives six metal and mineral operations (calcination, the regulus of antimony, cupellation, the strong waters, amalgamation and the corrosive sublimate) written for a reader with a real laboratory, hazard first, with the modern controls that make them survivable and the historical toll of doing them without.

The Greco-Egyptian foundation

The earliest substantial alchemical material is Greek, from Roman Egypt, and two figures dominate it.

Zosimos of Panopolis (fl. c. 300 CE) is the earliest alchemical writer whose substantial corpus survives under his own name; the Physika kai mystika attributed to pseudo-Democritus is older but survives incompletely and under a pseudonym. He is the channel through which nearly everything earlier survives, and his writing is a strange and compelling mixture of technical procedure and recorded vision: the dream-sequences in which he is instructed by priests at an altar are among the oldest first-person accounts of anything resembling initiatory experience in this tradition.

Mary the Jewess (Maria Hebraea), whom Zosimos quotes as an authority already of the past, worked in Greco-Roman Egypt, most likely between the first and third centuries CE: the specialist literature declines to place her in a particular city, and the usual attachment to Alexandria comes from general reference works rather than from anything Zosimos says. F. Sherwood Taylor and Edmund von Lippmann place her among the first alchemical writers, no later than the first century; others read Zosimos’s manner of quoting her as evidence for a later date. Nothing narrows it further. She is credited with describing three pieces of apparatus, and the credit is technical rather than legendary. The tribikos is a three-armed alembic for distillation, whose technical details Zosimos says were transmitted by Mary; hers is the earliest description that survives, though Zosimos does not call it the first, and whether she devised the still or only described it is not known. The kerotakis is a reflux vessel in which metals laid on a heated palette were exposed to rising vapours, a luted condensing cover returning the condensate to the base. It is often called airtight, and often called the ancestor of Soxhlet’s extractor of 1879; neither claim belongs to the specialist literature on her apparatus, the cover being vented by a small hole and Soxhlet going unmentioned in the standard survey. And the bain-marie, the double boiler, carries her name: the medieval Latin balneum Mariae is thought to have been introduced by Arnald of Villanova in the fourteenth century, and the lexicographers derive it from Marie-la-Juive, who is said to have invented or improved the technique. Said, not shown: von Lippmann pointed out that water-baths are described by Hippocrates, Theophrastus, Dioscorides and Pliny long before her. She is named among the alchemists listed in Ibn al-Nadīm’s tenth-century Kitāb al-Fihrist. (The oddly specific figure of fifty-two, repeated in many popular accounts, could not be checked against Dodge’s translation of the Fihrist for this edition, and is therefore not given here.)

The tribikos survives as a drawing, not only as a description

What is easy to miss in the secondary literature is that these instruments are not merely written about. They are drawn, in the Byzantine manuscripts that carry the Greek alchemical corpus, and Berthelot reproduced the drawings in 1887 from the manuscript of St Mark and its relatives. His commentary on figure 15 identifies the parts, and the names are the interesting thing:

  • the vessel is an alambic à trois récipients: a still with three receivers, the three βικία that give the instrument its name;
  • the furnace carries two words written one above the other, the place of the burning and the place of the flame;
  • the flask below is a λωπὰς of unburnt sulphur;
  • and the two tubes are named for fingers: the rising one is the λιχανὸς σωλήν, the index tube, and the descending one the ἀντίχειρος σωλήν, the thumb tube.

A manifold of tubes named after the fingers of a hand is not the sort of thing a later writer invents while paraphrasing. It is workshop vocabulary, and it is the detail that lets the same instrument be recognised across manuscripts that otherwise disagree about its shape: Berthelot notes that by the time the figure is redrawn in one later copy it has drifted towards the glass alembics of his own grandfather’s century.

Two sayings are attributed to her. One is a formula for union: join the male and the female, and you will find what is sought. The other is the celebrated Axiom of Maria: one becomes two, two becomes three, and out of the third comes the one as the fourth. Neither is given in quotation marks here, and for a plain reason: they reach English through a chain of translations, and for the Axiom the wording everyone reproduces descends through Jung’s Psychology and Alchemy rather than from any named translator of Zosimos. The union formula’s English has not been traced to a named translator at all. Jung took the second seriously enough to build on it at length. Not everything attached to her name is sound (the Byzantine chronicler George Syncellus, writing about 810, reports the alleged initiation of Democritus in Egypt by Ostanes, Mary the Jewess and Pammenes, which is chronologically impossible: Democritus belongs to the fifth century BCE) but the apparatus comes through Zosimos and stands. The Axiom does not: Jung traced it to the treatise ascribed to Christianos, whom Berthelot placed at about the beginning of the seventh century, and cited it from Berthelot’s edition of the Greek alchemists rather than from Zosimos.

And the construction itself survives, in Zosimos’s words, quoting hers. It is not an allusion. It is a specification, and a builder could work from it:

Je vais te décrire le tribicos. On appelle ainsi la construction en cuivre transmise traditionnellement par Marie. Voici en quels termes : Fabrique, dit-elle, trois tubes de cuivre laminé et aminci, d’une épaisseur dont voici la mesure : ce sera à peu près celle d’une poêle en airain, à faire cuire les gâteaux ; la longueur sera d’une coudée et demie… Après avoir luté les jointures avec de la pâte de farine, adapte aux extrémités des tubes des récipients en verre, grands et forts, afin qu’ils ne cassent pas en raison de la chaleur de l’eau qui entraîne la matière distillée.

I am going to describe the tribikos to you. So is called the copper construction handed down by tradition from Maria. Here are the terms: Make, she says, three tubes of copper, rolled and thinned, of a thickness of which here is the measure — it will be about that of a brazen pan for baking cakes; the length will be a cubit and a half… After luting the joints with flour paste, fit to the ends of the tubes glass receivers, large and strong, so that they do not break from the heat of the water that carries over the distilled matter. (English by this book, from Berthelot’s French.)

Read that as an engineer would. The wall thickness is gauged against a cake pan, because the reader has one and does not have a micrometer. The length is a cubit and a half. The joints are sealed with flour paste. And the glass receivers are specified large and strong so that they do not crack, which is a failure this writer has plainly had, and is warning the next person about.

The passage the ellipsis covers is the assembly: three orifices at the end of the copper vessel, fitted to the tubes and soldered eccentrically to the upper receiver that takes the volatile part, with the three tubes meeting the neck of the small receiver by a pin through the thumb-tube so that the two index-tubes sit laterally. The copper vessel then stands over an earthenware matrass. This book prints the apparatus and not an operation: what the matrass holds, and what is done with what comes over, is the chemistry, and it is outside what this chapter gives.

Why this is the oldest thing of its kind

A still with one outlet gives you a distillate. A still with three, taken off at different heights and led to separate receivers, gives you fractions: different products collected separately from a single charge. That is the principle of fractional distillation, and it is being described here in the third or fourth century, transmitted from a writer earlier still, in a vocabulary borrowed from the human hand.

It is also worth noticing what the description does not contain: no invocation, no timing, no purity requirement, nothing of the operator’s condition. Set beside the rest of this book it reads like a different literature entirely, and in an important sense it is. Somebody was building equipment.

The axioms of the serpent

The oldest surviving explanation of what the ouroboros means is not a modern gloss. It is a short article in the Greek corpus, and Berthelot prints it under the heading Le serpent Ouroboros. It opens by telling you outright that it is a cipher:

Voici le mystère : Le serpent Ouroboros (mordant sa queue), c’est la composition qui dans son ensemble est dévorée et fondue, dissoute et transformée par la fermentation. Elle devient d’un vert foncé, et la couleur d’or en dérive. C’est d’elle que dérive le rouge appelé couleur de cinabre : c’est le cinabre des philosophes.

Here is the mystery: the serpent Ouroboros (biting its tail) is the composition which as a whole is devoured and melted, dissolved and transformed by fermentation. It becomes a dark green, and the colour of gold derives from it. From it derives the red called the colour of cinnabar: it is the cinnabar of the philosophers. (English by this book, from Berthelot’s French.)

The serpent is not a symbol of eternity here. It is a diagram of a process: one substance consuming itself and coming out changed, with the colour sequence of Fig. 2 above read off its body: the article goes on to give the beast a saffron belly, a dark green head, four feet for the four imperfect metals and three ears for the three sublimed vapours. Then, in four lines, the sentences that the whole later tradition quotes without knowing where they came from:

L’Un fournit à l’Autre son sang ; et l’Un engendre l’Autre. La nature réjouit la nature ; la nature charme la nature ; la nature triomphe de la nature ; et la nature maîtrise la nature ; et cela non pas pour telle (nature) opposée à telle autre, mais pour une seule et même nature, (procédant) d’elle-même par le procédé (chimique), avec peine et grand effort.

Or toi, mon ami très cher, applique ton intelligence sur ces matières et tu ne tomberas pas dans l’erreur ; mais travaille sérieusement et sans négligence, jusqu’à ce que tu aies vu le terme (de ta recherche).

The One furnishes the Other its blood; and the One begets the Other. Nature gladdens nature; nature charms nature; nature triumphs over nature; and nature masters nature — and that not as one nature opposed to another, but as one and the same nature, proceeding from itself by the process, with pain and great effort. Now you, my dearest friend, apply your intelligence to these matters and you will not fall into error; but work seriously and without negligence, until you have seen the end of your search. (English by this book.)

One word, and why it is not the famous one

The sentence everyone knows is nature rejoices in nature. That is not what Berthelot’s French says. His verb is réjouit, transitive and active: nature gladdens nature, one thing acting on another. Rejoices in renders the Greek middle voice, and it reaches English through a different route than the one this book took.

The literal rendering is given above because that is what the edition in front of this book actually prints. The familiar wording is not wrong, and it may be closer to the Greek, but it is not a translation of Berthelot, and quietly using it here while labelling it as this book’s own English would be precisely the fault this chapter objects to a few pages earlier, where it declines to put the Axiom of Maria in quotation marks because the version everyone reproduces descends through a chain of translations rather than from any text.

The difference is not merely grammatical. Nature gladdens nature describes an action with an agent and an object, which is what the surrounding four clauses all describe: charming, triumphing over, mastering. Nature rejoices in nature describes a state. The first belongs to a set of operative axioms; the second reads like contemplation.

Berthelot’s own footnote identifies these as les axiomes du Pseudo-Démocrite, which places them earlier than Zosimos and makes them among the oldest operative sayings in this book. Two things are worth drawing out. The insistence that it is one and the same nature, not two opposed ones, is the point on which this tradition differs from every dualism it is usually confused with. And the closing address is not doctrine at all: it is a working instruction, from one operator to another, and what it asks for is not purity or grace but attention, seriousness, and the willingness to keep going. That sentence would not be out of place in a laboratory notebook.

What comes next in the article, and why it is not printed

The passage above is sections 1 to 4. Section 5 follows immediately and is omitted here: it directs the operator to sacrifice a serpent, flay it, and make a footstool of the flesh. It is said outright so that the quotation is not read as complete when it is not, and it is left out under the same rule that governs the rest of this book: nothing requiring harm to an animal is printed as an operation, however old, and however plainly the whole thing is meant as an allegory of the metals.

The operative tradition and its transmission

Physical laboratory alchemy was, of course, also real, and it deserves its historical due. Its practitioners developed distillation, sublimation and crystallisation, identified acids and salts, built the apparatus (alembic, retort, athanor, the vessels above) and produced the observational groundwork on which chemistry was later built. Robert Boyle and Isaac Newton both worked in this tradition, and what kind of work it was is still argued. Lawrence Principe’s The Aspiring Adept (1998) argues that Boyle’s alchemical interests were “serious and persistent, constituting a significant and influential dimension of his life, thought, and works,” that his alchemy was of a distinctly traditional type grounded in chrysopoeia, and that Boyle took a keen interest in connections between alchemy and the supernatural. Newton wrote and transcribed about a million words on alchemy: laboratory notebooks, indices of alchemical substances, and transcriptions from other sources. The papers surfaced at a Sotheby’s sale in 1936, and it took the twentieth century some time to absorb what they were: William Newman reads them as experimental chymistry rather than religious search, a reading not every scholar shares.

The textual lineage runs deep. Two of the key early documents, Leyden papyrus X and the Stockholm papyrus, came out of the same reconstructed Theban group as the Greek Magical Papyri of Chapter 9: the clearest single piece of evidence that late antique alchemy and late antique magic were one enterprise. From there the tradition passes into Arabic hands, where it was transformed and considerably advanced: Jābir ibn Ḥayyān, Ibn Umayl, Abū Bakr al-Rāzī, and the Sirr al-khalīqa that carries the earliest text of the Emerald Tablet: the subject of Chapter 6. Latin Europe received the whole inheritance in translation from the twelfth century onward, beginning with Robert of Chester in 1144. The great early-modern flowering (Paracelsus, Sendivogius, Maier’s Atalanta fugiens, the Rosary of the Philosophers, Splendor Solis, the emblem books with their images of kings drowning and suns turning black) builds on that Arabic foundation, a debt the European sources acknowledge far more readily than their modern popularisers do.

Safety Warning for Alchemical Practices

Spiritual and contemplative alchemical work should be undertaken with proper preparation and, ideally, guidance; the process can be intense and should be approached gradually.

Physical laboratory alchemy is a separate matter, and this chapter does not provide procedures for it. The historical recipes call for mercury, antimony, lead, arsenic compounds and corrosive acids, handled with heat in unventilated rooms. These substances cause irreversible neurological and organ damage, and the harm is frequently cumulative and unnoticed until advanced. Chronic mercury poisoning is well documented among historical practitioners. There is no traditional protection, purification or intention that alters the toxicology. Those operations are given, hazard first, in Chapter 29, which is written for a reader who already has a fume hood, a chemistry qualification and a waste-disposal route. If you do not have those three things, read the history and leave the materials alone.

The spagyric separation

There is one laboratory operation this chapter can give in full, because every step of it is kitchen-safe: the spagyric preparation of a plant: the three principles of this chapter applied to the one kingdom where separating them harms nobody. The word is Paracelsus’s coinage, from the Greek spao and ageiro: to separate and to recombine. That pair of verbs is the whole of alchemy in miniature, and this is the honest way to experience the structure of the work with your own hands.

The separation of the three principles in a plant

  1. Choose the plant from the table in Chapter 20, and gather or begin the work in its planet’s day and hour. Use a culinary herb (rosemary, sage, melissa) nothing from the poison rows.
  2. Extract the Sulfur and Mercury. Chop the dried herb and cover it with strong drinkable spirit in a sealed jar. In the tradition’s vocabulary the alcohol is the Mercury, the mediating spirit, and what it draws from the plant (the aromatic, virtuous part) is the plant’s Sulfur, its soul. Keep the jar warm and dark, shaking daily, for a philosophical month of twenty-eight days.
  3. Separate. Strain the tincture off and set it aside, sealed. Keep the exhausted plant body: the caput mortuum, the dead head.
  4. Calcine the Salt. Burn the dried plant body outdoors in a steel or earthen vessel until it is black, then keep it in the fire until the ash goes from black through grey toward white: nigredo to albedo, literally and visibly. Grind the ash fine.
  5. Recombine. Add the ash to the tincture, seal, and let it circulate in gentle warmth for some days; then filter. The three principles, separated, purified and reunited, which is the definition the chapter opened with.

What you have made is a spagyric tincture of the sort sold in any herbalist’s shop, and the point was never the product. The point is that you have now performed, in miniature and in safety, the sequence the whole literature describes: dissolution, separation, purification by fire, recombination; and watched the colour stages happen in a dish rather than in a diagram.

Modern Practice

Contemporary practitioners work the alchemical sequence almost entirely as an interior discipline, often keeping a written record structured by the stages: noting what is dissolving, what is being washed, what has survived. Some work with plant alchemy or spagyrics, which uses herbal tinctures and distillation and stays within the safety envelope of ordinary kitchen chemistry. C. G. Jung’s reading of the alchemical corpus as a symbolic account of individuation has been enormously influential and is how most readers now encounter this material; it is a twentieth-century interpretation of the texts rather than what their authors said they were doing, and the two readings belong together.

Chapter VIThe Emerald Tablet Adept

The Emerald Tablet is the shortest text in this book and the most consequential. In a few hundred words it supplied Western alchemy with its founding statement, its governing image, and its most quoted line. Nearly every alchemical work from the twelfth century to the eighteenth cites it, glosses it, or assumes it. Newton translated it. Jung read it. It has been printed thousands of times.

It is also not what most readers are told it is. It is not ancient Egyptian, it was not carved on emerald, and the sentence everybody knows from it is not in it. All three of those facts are well established, and none of them diminishes the text: they make its actual history considerably more interesting than the legend.

The text

Below is Isaac Newton’s English rendering of the Tablet, from Keynes MS 28 in King’s College Library, Cambridge (ff. 2r–v). The same manuscript carries the Latin text of the vulgate and Newton’s own Latin commentary; B. J. T. Dobbs argued, mainly from the handwriting, that the English was made some years after the Latin and from a French version rather than directly from the Latin: the Newton Project’s catalogue points to the Bibliothèque des philosophes (1672–8), which Newton owned and names on the same leaf. Newton’s version is given here in preference to a modern one for three reasons: it is out of copyright, it is the rendering most often reproduced in popular anthologies and online, and Newton’s choices as a translator are themselves part of the commentary tradition.

Tis true without lying, certain & most true. That which is below is like that which is above & that which is above is like that which is below to do the miracles of one only thing

And as all things have been & arose from one by the mediation of one: so all things have their birth from this one thing by adaptation.

The Sun is its father, the moon its mother, the wind hath carried it in its belly, the earth is its nourse. The father of all perfection in the whole world is here. Its force or power is entire if it be converted into earth.

Separate thou the earth from the fire, the subtile from the gross sweetly with great indoustry. It ascends from the earth to the heaven & again it descends to the earth & receives the force of things superior & inferior.

By this means you shall have the glory of the whole world & thereby all obscurity shall fly from you. Its force is above all force. For it vanquishes every subtile thing & penetrates every solid thing.

So was the world created. From this are & do come admirable adaptations whereof the means (or process) is here in this.

Hence I am called Hermes Trismegist, having the three parts of the philosophy of the whole world. That which I have said of the operation of the Sun is accomplished & ended.

Text: Isaac Newton, Keynes MS. 28, King’s College Library, Cambridge, ff. 2r–2v, from The Chymistry of Isaac Newton, ed. William R. Newman (Indiana University, 2010), normalised transcription by John A. Johnson. Newton’s spelling and ampersands are retained. The manuscript sets the text as eleven verses; they are grouped here into seven, and the full stop after “the whole world” is editorial: the manuscript has none there, nor after “one only thing.” Newton wrote “(or process)” above the line as a gloss on “the means.” The folio heading, three cancelled letters before “fly from you,” and Newton’s closing cross-references on f. 2v are not reproduced. The third English rendering of the Tablet, given later in this chapter, is quoted inside The Glory of the World in The Hermetic Museum, Restored and Enlarged, trans. A. E. Waite, 2 vols (1893); the wording is therefore Waite’s, at one remove from the Latin.

Where it actually comes from

The Tablet is an Arabic text. Its oldest known recension appears in the Kitāb Sirr al-Khalīqa wa-Ṣanʿat al-Ṭabīʿa, the Book of the Secret of Creation and the Art of Nature, compiled in Arabic in the late eighth or early ninth century. The precise dating is contested in the scholarship: Julius Ruska placed it in the sixth to eighth centuries, Paul Kraus around 813–833, Ursula Weisser around 750–800. The work presents itself as a translation of a treatise by Apollonius of Tyana, Balīnūs in the Arabic, which is itself a pseudepigraphic frame rather than a real attribution.

The Tablet also appears, in a somewhat shorter version with lines missing, in the Second Book of the Element of the Foundation (Kitāb Usṭuqus al-Uss al-Thānī) attributed to Jābir ibn Ḥayyān. And it turns up in two further Arabic settings: Ibn Umayl’s tenth-century Book of the Silvery Water and the Starry Earth, later translated into Latin as the Tabula Chemica, which quotes the Tablet and glosses it clause by clause; and towards the end of the long version of the pseudo-Aristotelian Sirr al-Asrār, the Secret of Secrets, also tenth century.

That discovery narrative belongs to the Sirr al-Khalīqa itself, not to any later source, and it is the origin of the story every popular account repeats. Balīnūs is directed by an apparition (in Ruska’s description, the heavenly archetype of Apollonius in the form of an old man) into a dark subterranean chamber beneath a statue of Hermes, where a figure seated on a throne holds an emerald tablet and a book. It is a literary device of the eighth- or ninth-century Arabic tradition, not a record of an excavation, and it is a vault rather than a pyramid: the pyramid of the popular retellings is a later accretion.

How it reached Europe

The Latin transmission runs through several independent channels, and knowing which one a given version descends from explains most of the variation between printed texts:

  • Robert of Chester, 1144: the Book on the Composition of Alchemy, the Latin Morienus. Some manuscripts carry an explicit dating the translation to 11 February 1144, and that date is independent of the prologue. It is generally considered the first Latin translation of an Arabic alchemical treatise, and marks the point at which this whole literature enters Europe; but the attribution to Robert is less settled than the date: his name comes only from a prologue which Dapsens concludes is genuinely Robert’s work yet was probably not written for this text.
  • The vulgate version, probably twelfth century, tentatively attributed to Plato of Tivoli (active c. 1134–1145). It survives embedded in an anonymous Latin compilation of commentaries on the Tablet (known variously as the Book of Hermes on Alchemy, the Book of Dabessus or the Book of the Rebis) itself translated from a now-lost Arabic original. This is the most widely circulated version and the basis of every later edition: including the version behind Newton’s English.
  • Hugo of Santalla, c. 1145–1151: translated the Book of the Secret of Creation itself, and so gives the Tablet closest to its oldest known Arabic form. It does not appear to have circulated widely: the translation survives in a single manuscript contemporary with the translator (Paris, BnF lat. 13951) and one copy, and the Tablet spread in Europe not from this version but from the Secret of Secrets.
  • Philip of Tripoli, thirteenth century: translated the Secret of Secrets, which became, by some measures, the most popular book of the Latin Middle Ages, carrying the Tablet along with it.

What appeared in 1541 (in De Alchemia, from Johann Petreius at Nuremberg, edited by “Chrysogonus Polydorus”, most likely a pseudonym for Andreas Osiander) is what the bibliographic literature calls the editio princeps of the Tablet, and it was the first to set the text beside the commentary of Hortulanus; that pairing shaped how the text was read for centuries. It was not, however, the Tablet’s first appearance in print. A different Latin version, the one carried inside the Secret of Secrets, was already in print by 1501 at the latest, Alessandro Achillini’s Bologna edition prints it complete, and possibly in the incunable editions of the 1480s, though the collations are ambiguous on the alchemy section. The two are not the same translation: the Secret of Secrets version opens Veritas ita se habet et non est dubium, the vulgate Verum sine mendacio certum et verissimum.

The commentary tradition

The Tablet’s history is largely a history of people disagreeing about what it means, and the disagreement divides along a fault line that runs through this entire book: laboratory or interior.

Hortulanus (Ortolanus), about whom almost nothing is known beyond what he says of himself, was probably active in the first half of the fourteenth century. His is the commentary that circulated most widely in print (published with the Tablet in 1541, reprinted in 1545, reissued in 1560 as the Compendium alchimiae under Johannes de Garlandia’s name, and again in 1571) and he read the text as an operative one: a cryptic recipe describing laboratory processes under cover names, in which the Sun and Moon stand for alchemical gold and silver. He could not translate the obscure word telesmus either. He left it standing and glossed it; in the Elizabethan English of The Mirror of Alchimy (London, 1597) the gloss reads that the Philosopher “calleth the worke, the Father of all the Telesme: that is, of all secret, or of all treasure of the whole worlde.”

The word was obscure because it was not Latin. The vulgate’s translator met the Arabic ṭilasm, could not place it, and transliterated it as telesmus: the texts spell it variously (telesmus, telesmum, telesmi, thelesmi; the 1597 English telesme). Behind the Arabic is a Greek word built on the verb teleō, to complete or to perform a rite, though the witnesses differ over its form; the same Arabic word reaches English as “talisman.” The oldest Arabic recension calls the one thing abū al-ṭilasmāt, father of talismans.

Albertus Magnus commented on the vulgate in On Minerals, around 1250. Roger Bacon edited and annotated the Latin Secret of Secrets (Philip of Tripoli’s version, not a translation of his own) believing it a genuine work of Aristotle. Robert Steele, its 1920 editor, held that Bacon cited it throughout his career; Steven Williams has since argued that the edition belongs to the end of Bacon’s life, around 1280, and Bacon’s heavy use of the text is documented from the 1260s rather than from his earliest writings. Either way it illustrates how much intellectual weight a misattribution can carry.

Johannes Trithemius, in the early sixteenth century, moved the reading decisively away from the laboratory and toward metaphysics, identifying the Tablet’s “one thing” with the Pythagorean monad and the anima mundi, the soul of the world. That is an early and influential instance of the metaphysical reading; Debus records it being taken up by Dee, Agrippa and Gerhard Dorn. The move is visible on the page in a letter of his to Germain de Ganay, printed in 1613 among the epistles appended to the Polygraphia. Trithemius recites the Tablet with the arithmetic of unity written into it: Quod est superius, est sicut quod est inferius … quia solis unitatibus constat omnis numerus ad perpetranda miracula unius rei multa: the miracles of the one thing are worked because every number is built of unities alone. The alchemists who take the text as furnace instruction are dismissed in the same letter as simiarum discipuli, hostes naturae (apes’ pupils, enemies of nature) and the new reading is stated outright: Nostra philosophia coelestis est non terrena: our philosophy is celestial, not earthly. Whether the twentieth-century psychological readings descend from it or merely resemble it is not something the scholarship establishes.

Newton made his own interpretive choice at that same word. Where the Latin vulgate reads pater omnis telesmi, Newton’s own Latin copy of the Tablet, on a later leaf of the same manuscript, reads pater omnis perfectionis, and his English follows it: “The father of all perfection in the whole world is here.” The substitution therefore stands in the Latin rather than in an act of Englishing, and whether the reading was his own or one he inherited is not settled. Add to this that Newton’s commentary in the same manuscript reads the text as chemistry, in terms of mercury and sulphur. The word did not make a cosmologist of him.

“As above, so below” is not in the Emerald Tablet

The most quoted sentence in Western esotericism is a paraphrase, and a recent one. The vulgate’s second verse, in Robert Steele and Dorothea Waley Singer’s translation, reads: “That which is above is like to that which is below, and that which is below is like to that which is above.” (Witnesses of the vulgate differ over which half comes first; the Latin behind Newton’s version above begins with the lower. The sense is unaffected: the verse is symmetrical.) The oldest Arabic recension runs differently again: its second line, inna al-aʿlā min al-asfal wa-l-asfal min al-aʿlā, says that the uppermost is from the lowermost and the lowermost from the uppermost. (Arabic as edited by Ursula Weisser; the English here is a literal gloss rather than a published translation, and is given without quotation marks for that reason.)

Note that the Arabic says the levels derive from each other, where the vulgate says they resemble each other. The Latin translators did not agree among themselves: Hugo of Santalla, working directly from the Book of the Secret of Creation, has Superiora de inferioribus, inferiora de superioribus (“from”, not “like”) and the Secret of Secrets version has the levels respondent, correspond. The vulgate was made from a different and now-lost Arabic compilation, so where the shift entered cannot be established.

The compressed form (“as above, so below”) was popularised by Helena Blavatsky in the late nineteenth century, and it was through her that it became the motto of modern occultism and later of the New Age. She does not present it as her own coinage: in Isis Unveiled (1877) she introduces it as something the reader already knows: “Remember the Hermetic axiom: ‘As above, so below; as in heaven, so on earth’” (vol. 1, p. 294); and where she translates the verse itself (vol. 1, p. 507) she renders it “What is below is like that which is above,” not by the maxim. The wording is not the Tablet’s; whether it is hers is not established. This is the same pattern as the Kybalion of Chapter 1: a modern formulation, elegant and genuinely useful, circulating as an ancient one. The maxim is a fair summary of what the verse says. It is simply not a quotation from it.

A third English rendering

This chapter has now printed Newton’s version, and the note above gives Steele and Singer’s. A third exists in this book’s own period range and belongs beside them, because it shows how much the Tablet moves between translators. It appears inside The Glory of the World, one of the twenty-two alchemical treatises of The Hermetic Museum, Englished in 1893; where the Tablet is quoted not as a curiosity but as an authority in an argument, numbered among forty other citations:

THE EMERALD TABLE: It is true, without any error, and it is the sum of truth; that which is above is also that which is below, for the performance of the wonders of a certain one thing, and as all things arise from one Stone, so also they were generated from one common Substance, which includes the four elements created by God. And among other miracles the said Stone is born of the First Matter. The Sun is its Father, the Moon its Mother, the wind bears it in its womb, and it is nursed by the earth. Itself is the Father of the whole earth, and the whole potency thereof. If it be transmuted into earth, then the earth separates from the fire that which is most subtle from that which is hard, operating gently and with great artifice. Then the Stone ascends from earth to heaven, and again descends from heaven to earth, and receives the choicest influences of both heaven and earth. If you can perform this you have the glory of the world.

Set that against Newton. Where Newton has that which is below is like that which is above, this has that which is above is also that which is below: likeness has become identity. Where Newton has the bare one only thing, this interpolates one Stone and one common Substance, which includes the four elements, importing a doctrine the Tablet does not state. And the alchemical treatise it sits in takes its own title from the Tablet’s closing promise: you have the glory of the world.

Three English versions, then, of a text that was already a translation of a translation. None is wrong; each is a reading. This is the ordinary condition of the material, and the reason this book gives the date and the translator every time it prints a sentence.

Reading it

Taken on its own terms, the Tablet describes a single process in a single substance. One thing is the origin of all things. It has a father and a mother, so its production requires a union. It must be separated (earth from fire, subtle from gross) and the separation must be done sweetly, with great industry, which is to say gradually and with attention rather than by force. It then ascends and descends, gathering the powers of what is above and what is below, and returns changed. The result penetrates everything.

Whether that is an account of a metallurgical operation, of the cosmos, or of a person is precisely the question the commentators have argued for eight hundred years, and the text is constructed so as not to settle it. That ambiguity is not a defect of the writing; on any reading of its purpose, it is the writing. The instruction that survives translation into every register is the one in the middle: separate patiently what has been confused, and expect to have to do it more than once.

Sources: Kitāb Sirr al-Khalīqa wa-Ṣanʿat al-Ṭabīʿa, late 8th / early 9th c.; the three datings that disagree are Ruska (1926), p. 166, 6th–8th c.; Kraus (1942), vol. II, pp. 274–75, c. 813–833; and Weisser (1980), p. 54, c. 750–800. The vault frame story is at Ruska, pp. 166–67. Pseudo-Jābir, Kitāb Usṭuqus al-Uss al-Thānī. Ibn Umayl, Book of the Silvery Water and the Starry Earth, 10th c., Latin Tabula Chemica; the Tablet quoted and glossed there at Stapleton, Lewis and Sherwood Taylor, Ambix 3 (1949), sect. XXI, p. 81. Pseudo-Aristotle, Sirr al-Asrār, 10th c., long version; the Latin of the Tablet in Steele (ed.), Secretum secretorum (1920), pp. 115–17. Robert of Chester (1144); vulgate version, 12th c., tentatively Plato of Tivoli (active c. 1134–45); Hugo of Santalla (c. 1145–51), ed. Hudry (1997–99); Philip of Tripoli (13th c.). First printing as a free-standing alchemical text: De Alchemia (Nuremberg, 1541), with Hortulanus’s commentary; but a different Latin version was already in print inside the Secretum secretorum by 1501 at the latest. Hortulanus, probably first half 14th c.; the English of his commentary in The Mirror of Alchimy (1597). Albertus Magnus, On Minerals, c. 1250; Roger Bacon, c. 1275–80, with Williams, Speculum 69 (1994), 57–73, against Steele’s dating; Trithemius, early 16th c., with Debus (2004), p. 415, for the reading’s later adoption.

The letter to Germain de Ganay is quoted from Libri Polygraphiae (Strasbourg: Zetzner, 1613), pp. 31–32, read on the page images of the Internet Archive scan bub_gb_E5TjGI-NlOsC, leaves 716–717; that scan’s text layer is unusable for Latin and supplied no wording. In those quotations the long s is set as s and æ and œ are expanded to ae and oe; the ellipsis omits the clause’s mirrored second half, et quod est inferius, est sicut quod est superius, where the page has an ampersand; and the recipient is named in the French form, the letter’s own address being ô Germane.

English of the vulgate’s second verse: Steele and Singer, “The Emerald Table” (1928).
