Chapter VIIMeditation Practices Beginner

Skipping this chapter to reach the interesting ones is the most common mistake made with material like this, and it reliably produces practitioners who can recite correspondences and cannot sit still for ten minutes. Everything operative in this book assumes an attention that can be directed and held, and that capacity is not native; it is trained, on a schedule, like a physical one. The ancient texts are explicit that the ascent they describe begins with stillness, and the practical writers of every later period agree with them. It is the one prerequisite the whole tradition states out loud and the one a reader in a hurry is most likely to skip.

Basic technique

  1. Find a quiet place to sit, upright but not rigid, where you will not be interrupted.
  2. Close your eyes and bring your attention to the breath: not controlling it, simply following it.
  3. When thoughts arise, notice them and return attention to the breath. This is the practice; the returning is not an interruption of it.
  4. Begin with ten to fifteen minutes daily and increase gradually.
  5. Be consistent rather than ambitious. Ten minutes every day will take you further in a year than an hour once a week.

Two things worth knowing at the outset. The first is that a session in which you notice fifty distractions is not a failed session: noticing is the skill being built, and fifty noticings is fifty repetitions. The second is that progress in this practice is almost invisible from inside it. What changes is not the quality of the sitting but the quality of the rest of the day.

Contemplation of a form

Once bare attention is reasonably stable, the tradition turns it toward an object. Take one of the forms from Chapter 3 (the circle, the triangle, a single sephirah) and hold it in mind, returning to it as you returned to the breath. The aim is not to think discursively about the symbol but to let it remain in attention until it begins to disclose relations you had not put there.

This is the technique the Hermetic texts assume when they describe knowledge arriving as vision rather than as argument. That assumption is visible in the first sentence of the corpus, printed in Chapter 1: the Poimandres opens with the senses of the body held back, and only then does anything appear. The stillness is not preliminary to the vision in that account. It is the condition of it. It is also where honest self-assessment becomes important: the felt sense of profound insight is not evidence of insight, and the practice includes writing down what you thought you saw and reading it again a week later when the atmosphere has worn off.

The discipline of the four elements

A widely used progression takes the elements of Chapter 5 as meditative subjects in turn: sitting with earth as solidity and weight, water as flow and receptivity, air as movement and mediation, fire as transformation. Each is held for a period of days or weeks before moving on. The value of the exercise is diagnostic as much as devotional: most people find one of the four significantly harder than the others, and that difficulty is generally informative.

Vibration

One technique deserves its own heading because everything ceremonial in this book depends on it, and because it is almost always taught badly. To vibrate a divine name is not to say it loudly. It is to sound it so that the body itself carries the sound (chest, throat, the bones of the face) and to hold the meaning of the name in attention while doing so.

The clearest published instruction is also one of the oldest available in English, from Crowley’s Liber O of 1909, which prints it as a preliminary to assuming a godform:

Vibrating a divine name, Liber O (1909)

  1. Stand with arms outstretched.
  2. Breathe in deeply through the nostrils, imagining the name of the God desired entering with the breath.
  3. Let that name descend slowly from the lungs to the heart, the solar plexus, the navel, and so to the feet.
  4. The moment it appears to touch the feet, advance the left foot, throw the body forward, and let the hands shoot out from beside the eyes, breathing the name out through the nostrils with all the force of which you are capable.
  5. Withdraw the left foot and place the right forefinger upon the lips.

The text adds two tests, and they are worth quoting because they set an unusually concrete standard for a spiritual exercise. The first: it is a sign the student is doing it correctly “when a single ‘Vibration’ entirely exhausts his physical strength.” The second, a sign of success perceptible only to the practitioner, is when the name is heard “vehemently roared forth, as if by the concourse of ten thousand thunders,” and appears to proceed “from the Universe, and not from himself.”

That is the ceremonial maximum. For ordinary daily practice, a great deal less will do: sound the name on a single sustained out-breath, low in the chest, until the breath runs out, and feel where in the body it resonates. The rest of this book assumes you can do that much. The full form repays an occasional attempt, if only because it makes the difference between vibrating a name and merely pronouncing one impossible to miss.

A daily sequence

The techniques above are given separately because the sources give them separately; a practice needs them in an order. The following twenty-minute sequence is this book’s own arrangement of the chapter’s contents and claims no other authority. Sit as directed and settle the breath into a slow, even count: the modern convention of equal fourths (in for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four) is as good a regulator as any and is offered as convention, not doctrine. When the breath is steady, take up one contemplation only: a form from Chapter 3, one element of the four, or a single sentence of the Corpus held and turned without commentary. Close with a single vibrated name, as taught above, and write the record before standing up. One object per sitting, the same hour each day, and the journal kept honestly: the discipline is the practice; the contents of any one sitting matter far less than the unbroken series.

Recording the work

Keep a record. Date each session, note its length, and write a sentence or two on what happened without embellishing it. The reason is practical rather than ceremonial: memory is unreliable about interior states, and it edits in the direction of a good story. A written record is the only means you have of distinguishing genuine development from the impression of it, and it is the closest thing this tradition has to an experimental notebook.

Modern Practice

The technique above is essentially what the sources describe, and it needs little updating; but the surrounding context has changed in ways worth naming. Contemporary practitioners have access to a large body of clinical research on meditation that no historical author had, and it broadly supports the basic claims about attention, stress response and emotional regulation while saying nothing either way about the metaphysics. Many now use timers or apps for the practical business of sitting, which is a straightforward improvement over guessing. The one genuinely modern caution: intensive practice can destabilise people with certain psychiatric histories, a risk the historical literature does not discuss because it had no framework for it. If you have a history of dissociation, psychosis or severe trauma, extend the timelines and work with a professional rather than alone.

What a long discipline looked like when somebody wrote one down

Everything above is a modern arrangement of practices that are older than the arrangement. It is worth setting one historical regimen beside it, both because the chapter has been asserting that the practical writers agree and because the specimen is instructive in ways a summary is not. The fullest one in this tradition is the operation of the Book of the Sacred Magic of Abra-Melin the Mage, the manuscript Mathers translated in 1898: six months of daily prayer, morning and evening, lengthening as the months pass until it is three times a day, conducted in a room set aside for it and kept clean. It is the ancestor of the Golden Dawn’s longer workings and of a good deal that came after them, and what it says about the daily conduct of a practice is not what a reader expects from a grimoire.

As for eating, drinking and sleeping, such should be in moderation and never superfluous. It is especially necessary to shun drunkenness, and flee public dinners. Content yourself with eating at your own house, with your family, in the peace and quiet which God hath granted unto you. You should never sleep during the day, but you may in the morning, for after that you have performed your devotions you may if you wish again go to bed to rest yourself. And if it happeneth by chance that you do not rise sufficiently early, that is to say before sunrise, it doth not greatly matter (provided that it be not done of evil intent), and you shall perform your ordinary morning prayer; but you should not accustom yourself to be slothful, it being always better to pray unto God at an early hour.

Note what that passage does. It sets a standard, admits in the same breath that the standard will be missed, declines to treat the miss as a failure, and then declines equally to let the concession become the rule. It doth not greatly matter, followed immediately by you should not accustom yourself to be slothful. That is the tone of somebody who has actually kept a daily practice and watched other people try to. The advice in this chapter to begin with ten or fifteen minutes and let the returning be the practice rather than an interruption of it is the same instinct, four hundred years later.

One further point from the same book bears directly on the vibration exercise above, and it comes with a disagreement attached. The instruction is to use your own language. Mathers summarises it in his introduction as the author’s insistence on “the preferability of employing one’s mother tongue both in prayer and evocation,” for a stated reason: “the absolute necessity of comprehending utterly and thoroughly with the whole soul and heart, that which the lips are formulating.” Then the translator, in the next sentence, takes the other side. “While fully admitting the necessity of this, I yet wish to state some reasons in favour of the employment of a language other than one’s own. Chief, and first, that it aids the mind to conceive the higher aspect of the Operation.” The two positions are worth having in front of you because the choice is a real one and this chapter cannot settle it. Comprehension argues for your own tongue and estrangement argues against it; the text says one thing, the man who put the text into English says the other on the same page, and a reader who has vibrated a Hebrew name without knowing what it means has already been standing on one side of the argument without being told there was one.

Sources: The vibration exercise is Aleister Crowley, Liber O vel Manus et Sagittae sub figura VI, section III, first printed in The Equinox I, no. 2 (1909); the quoted phrases are his. The remaining practices in this chapter are described rather than quoted, and are common to the contemplative literature of several traditions; no single historical source is claimed for them. The regimen and the two sentences on language are from S. L. MacGregor Mathers (trans.), The Book of the Sacred Magic of Abra-Melin the Mage (1898): read on the page images of the Internet Archive scan dli.ministry.10516, the regimen at p. 68 and the exchange about the mother tongue at p. xxxvi of Mathers’s introduction, where the summary of the author’s position and the translator’s objection to it stand in consecutive sentences.

Chapter VIIIRitual Foundations Beginner

A ritual makes an intention expensive. It demands preparation, a particular hour, specific words in a specific order, and the deliberate exclusion of everything else, and anything held to that standard is held with a seriousness that a passing wish cannot reach. That is the mechanism, and the tradition is not at its better moments mystifying about it. It also accounts for the one fact about ritual most in need of accounting for: the structure is remarkably consistent across traditions that share no content whatever, which is easier to explain by the reliability of that effect than by any shared descent.

The basic structure

  1. Preparation: cleanse yourself and the space. Bathe; clear the room of clutter and interruption; put away anything not needed. Historically this stage was elaborate: the Key of Solomon devotes considerable attention to ablution, abstinence and prayer before any operation begins.
  2. Opening: define the space and invoke protection. This is the circle of Chapter 3 made operational, and it is where a banishing such as the one in Chapter 15 is normally performed.
  3. Main work: the central action: a meditation, a contemplation, a stated intention, a consecration.
  4. Closing: give thanks, and close the circle deliberately. Closing matters as much as opening. A ritual left open is a working left unfinished, and in practical terms it means the frame that was meant to contain the work now has nothing to contain it.

Why the frame works

What a rite does, then, is establish a boundary in time and in space: within these words and this hour, attention is on one thing only. Everything below is a way of drawing that boundary and of taking it down again afterwards, which matters as much as putting it up.

This is also why the historical sources are so insistent on precision. Instructions about the hour, the direction faced, the material of an instrument, the exact form of words; these are not arbitrary hurdles. They are the means by which an action is made deliberate. Whether one takes the planetary hours of the Solomonic literature literally or as a discipline of timing, the effect on the operator is much the same.

The circle itself, as the Key builds it

This chapter has consecrated the water, the salt, the sword and the vestments, and has walked a circle in the opening rite: without ever giving the figure its own construction. The Key of Solomon devotes a chapter to it, and the thing it describes is not a chalk ring but a piece of surveying: three concentric circumferences, two squares set corner-on to the quarters, four small circles at the outer square’s angles, and a divine name written in every space the construction opens. It is given below as the Key gives it, and the preparations that precede it (nine days’ continence, the bath on the seventh, the white linen, the last three days fasting “without wind, and without clouds rushing hither and thither over the face of the sky”) belong to it as much as the geometry does.

The Construction of the Circle, from the Key of Solomon

Who carries what. The Master distributes the instruments before anyone walks to the place: “The First Disciple will bear the Censer, the Perfumes and the Spices; the Second Disciple will bear the Book, Papers, Pens, Ink, and any stinking or impure materials; the Third will carry the Knife and the Sickle of Magical Art, the Lantern, and the Candles; the Fourth, the Psalms, and the rest of the Instruments; the Fifth, the Crucible or Chafing-dish, and the Charcoal or Fuel; but it is necessary for the Master himself to carry in his hand the Staff, and the Wand or Rod.”

The three circumferences. “Take thou the Knife, the Sickle, or the Sword of Magical Art consecrated after the manner and order which we shall deliver unto thee in the Second Book. With this Knife or with the Sickle of Art thou shalt describe, beyond the inner Circle which thou shalt have already formed, a Second Circle, encompassing the other at the distance of one foot therefrom and having the same centre.” Mathers’s note explains the count: two circles enclosed between three circumferential lines. In the foot of space between them, toward the four quarters, are traced “the Sacred and Venerable Symbols of the holy Letter Tau”: the cross, as the manuscripts draw it.

The four Names in the band. Between the first and second circles are made four hexagonal pentacles, and between those, four “terrible and tremendous Names of God”: the Supreme Name IHVH between East and South; the Essential Tetragrammatic Name AHIH, Eheieh, between South and West; the Name of Power ALIVN, Elion, between West and North; and the Great Name ALH, Eloah, between North and East.

The squares and the corner circles. “Furthermore, thou shalt circumscribe about these Circles two Squares, the Angles of which shall be turned towards the Four Quarters of the Earth; and the space between the Lines of the Outer and Inner Square shall be half-a-foot. The extreme Angles of the Outer Square shall be made the Centres of four Circles, the measure or diameter of which shall be one foot.” In those four circles are written, at the East AL (El), at the West IH (Yah), at the South AGLA, and at the North ADNI (Adonai); between the two squares, Tetragrammaton.

What is said while drawing. “While constructing the Circle, the Master should recite the following Psalms: — Psalm II; Psalm LIV; Psalm CXIII; Psalm LXVII; Psalm XLVII; Psalm LXVIII. Or he may as well recite them before tracing the Circle.” The fumigations follow; then the Master “should reassemble his Disciples, encourage them, reassure them, fortify them,” place them at the four quarters, “and exhort them to fear nothing, and to keep in the places assigned to them.”

The simpler form. The Second Book gives a plainer way to strike the same figure, and it is the one a reader working alone will actually use: “take thou the Sickle or Scimitar of Art and stick it into the centre of the place where the Circle is to be made; then take a cord of nine feet in length, fasten one end thereof unto the Sickle and with the other end trace out the circumference of the Circle.” A nine-foot radius, struck with a cord from a blade set in the ground, which is why the circles of this tradition are eighteen feet across and why they were drawn out of doors.

Notice what the construction is doing. Every element is a boundary with a name on it: three lines, two squares, four corner circles, and in every interval a name of God, so that the operator stands at the centre of a nested set of enclosures each of which is signed. The instruction to the disciples (keep the places assigned to you, fear nothing) is the same doctrine in the register of stage-management, and it belongs beside the modern banishing of Chapter 15, which achieves the identical enclosure with no chalk at all, in a bedroom, in four minutes. The difference is not belief but real estate.

Tools

The traditional instruments (knife, wand, cup, disc, censer, lamp) correspond to the elements and to the functions of a working: to divide, to direct, to receive, to establish. The grimoire tradition specifies their making and consecration in great detail, often requiring specific materials, timings and inscriptions.

Two practical notes. First, tools are not required to begin; a clear space, an hour and a stated intention are sufficient, and every historical tradition contains practitioners who worked with almost nothing. Second, where the historical instructions call for animal sacrifice, blood, or materials obtained by harming anything, they should be read as history and not followed: the ethical position set out in Chapter 1 takes precedence over textual fidelity, and no serious modern practice depends on those elements.

Washing, and what it is for

How old the preparations are

Fasting, washing and continence before a working read, in the grimoires, like medieval Christian discipline borrowed for magical ends. They are very much older than that. The rubric to the sixty-fourth chapter of the Egyptian Book of the Dead attaches this condition to the recitation, in Budge’s translation:

This chapter shall be recited by a man who is ceremonially clean and pure, who hath not eaten the flesh of animals or fish, and who hath not had intercourse with women.

Cleanness, abstention from flesh and fish, continence: the same three requirements, in the same order, that open the Heptameron and govern the whole first half of the Key of Solomon’s second book. There is no line of transmission to point at here and this book does not assert one. What can be said is narrower and more interesting: the shape of ritual preparation in the Western grimoires is not a Christian innovation, and it was already conventional in Egypt long enough before them that a funerary text could state it in a single sentence and expect to be understood.

Nearly every operative text in this tradition begins with a bath. The Key of Solomon devotes a chapter to it: go to running water, or have warm water ready in a private room, and recite psalms while undressing: Psalm 27, The Lord is my light and my salvation, among them. The garments are then linen, or silk if you can afford it, and white; the book specifies that linen thread should have been spun by a young woman, which is the sort of detail that tells you the text is early modern rather than ancient.

What the washing is for can be said without mystification, because the tradition is not consistent about it and the modern practitioner has to decide. Read one way it is purification in a literal sense. Read another it is a boundary marker: the point at which ordinary time stops. The second reading is the one that survives translation into a life with plumbing, and it is the reason to keep the instruction even if you do not believe the first. Wash, deliberately, before you begin. Put on something you wear for nothing else.

The exorcism of the water, for the bath

From the Key of Solomon, Book II, chapter 5. Undressing, the operator recites, in Mathers’s printing, Psalms 14 or 53, 27, 54, 81 and 105. (Lists differ between manuscripts, and editions that record the variants give a different set again; the sequence above is the one Mathers actually prints.) Entering the water, they say:

I exorcise Thee, O Creature of Water, by Him Who hath created thee and gathered thee together into one place so that the dry land appeared, that thou uncover all the deceits of the Enemy, and that thou cast out from thee all the impurities and uncleannesses of the Spirits of the World of Phantasm, so they may harm me not, through the virtue of God Almighty who liveth and reigneth unto the Ages of the Ages. Amen.

That is the 1889 printing’s wording. The Latin manuscripts run shorter — “cast out from me all impurity and uncleanness, so that no phantasm may enter therein” — and which reading a modern edition gives depends on which witnesses it follows.

Then dress in the consecrated garment and cense yourself before beginning.

Consecrating water and salt

This is the most useful single operation in the grimoire literature, because the result, a bowl of salted water, is what every subsequent purification uses. The Key of Solomon gives it in Book II, and what follows is that procedure, with the text as Mathers printed it in 1889.

The consecration of water and salt

  1. Prepare the censer in the day and hour of Mercury, with the incense of the art (see Chapter 20 for reckoning the hour).
  2. Take a vessel of tin or earthenware and fill it with clear spring water. Have salt ready.
  3. Say over the salt: TZABAOTH, MESSIACH, EMANUEL, ELOHIM GIBOR, YOD HE VAU HE; O God, who art the Truth and the Life, deign to bless and sanctify this creature of salt, to serve unto us for help, protection and assistance in this art, experiment and operation, and may it be a succour unto us.
  4. Cast the salt into the water, and say Psalms 102, 54, 6 and 51.
  5. Make a sprinkler of vervain, fennel, periwinkle, sage, valerian, mint, marjoram, basil and rosemary, gathered in the day and hour of Mercury with the Moon increasing, and bind it with thread spun for the purpose.

Two notes on the text. The divine names in step three vary considerably between manuscripts: Mathers’s reading is given above; other witnesses have Zeuaod, Messiah, Jehova, Nghimanuel, Nghelion, Gibor and several further variants, which is characteristic of this literature and a reminder that no single wording is the wording. And the psalm numbers are given here in the English numbering; the manuscripts use the Vulgate numbering, which runs one lower through most of the Psalter.

If you keep nothing else from the operative tradition, keep this: consecrated water, made deliberately, sprinkled at the start of a working and used to close it. It costs a bowl and five minutes and it does the work that elaborate ceremony is usually reaching for.

The conjuration of the sword

The instruments are consecrated as well as made. Having engraved the divine names on the blade — YOD HE VAU HE, ADONAI, EHEIEH, YAYAI on one side, ELOHIM GIBOR on the other — sprinkle it, cense it, and say:

I conjure thee, O sword, by these names, ABRAHACH, ABRACH, ABRACADABRA, YOD HE VAU HE, that thou serve me for a strength and defence in all magical operations, against all mine enemies, visible and invisible. I conjure thee anew by the holy and indivisible name of EL strong and wonderful, by the name SHADDAI almighty; and by these names QADOSCH, QADOSCH, QADOSCH, ADONAI ELOHIM TZABAOTH, EMANUEL, the First and the Last, Wisdom, Way, Life, Truth, Chief, Speech, Word, Splendour, Light, Sun, Fountain, Glory, the Stone of the Wise, Virtue, Shepherd, Priest, Messiach Immortal; by these names then, and by the other names, I conjure thee, O sword, that thou servest me for a protection in all adversities. Amen.

The same form serves for the knife and the other instruments, with the name of the instrument changed. Note the shape of the thing: it is a list of names, and the list is the operation.

The vestments, and the aspergillum

Two further pieces of the ceremonial apparatus can be given, and they come through a route worth naming. Several grimoires (the Grimorium Verum, the Book of True Black Magic) have no public-domain English text of their own. What exists is A. E. Waite’s Book of Ceremonial Magic, which quotes and summarises them. So what follows is at one remove: Waite’s rendering, not those grimoires speaking directly, and the book says so rather than pretending otherwise.

The sprinkler and the water

Sprinkling is performed with the aspergillum, which, according to the Grimorium Verum, should be composed of mint, marjory and rosemary, bound about with a thread woven by a virgin girl. It should be made on the day and in the hour of Mercury, the moon waxing.

The ewer should be a pot of glazed earth, filled with fresh spring water, in which some salt has been cast. Over it are recited the Psalms Domine, ne in furore tuo arguas me and Domine, exaudi orationem meam — Psalms 6 and 102 — with this prayer:

“O Thou most powerful Lord, my God, my rest, and my life! Do Thou help me, Most Holy Father! In Thee I place my hope, Who art the God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, God of the Angels and Archangels…”

Set that beside the consecration of water and salt given earlier in this chapter from the Key of Solomon. Same operation, same materials nearly, different psalms and a different prayer; and the herbs differ too, mint and marjoram and rosemary here against the nine-herb sprinkler Mathers prints. Two branches of one practice, neither derived from the other.

The assumption of the vestments

All garments, even to the shirt, must be of linen cloth, and when assuming them these words should be recited:

ANTON, AMATOR, EMITES, THEODONIEL, PONCOR, PAGOR, ANITOR — by the virtue of these most holy Angelic Names do I clothe myself, O Lord, in my Sabbath garments, that so I may fulfil, even unto their term, all things which I desire to effect.

Seven angels, two lists

The Key of Solomon prescribes the same rite with a different set of names: Amor, Amator, Amides, Ideodaniach, Pamor, Plaior, Anitor, and calls the robes Vestments of Power rather than Sabbath garments.

Seven angels invoked at the same moment of the same operation, and the two lists agree on exactly two names: Amator and Anitor. Neither can be derived from the other by any plausible scribal slip; they are two traditions remembering the same seven differently. This book prints both because the disagreement is the finding: a reader who meets one list has met a branch, not the tradition.

The circle

The Key of Solomon’s circle is a construction of some complexity, and should be seen in full before deciding what to do with it. Book II, chapter 9: drive the knife into the centre of the working place; take a cord of nine feet; describe the circumference. Mark four regions within it, east, west, south and north. Beyond that circle describe another, leaving an opening toward the north to enter and leave by; beyond that a third at a foot’s distance, with the same opening; and beyond these, pentagrams with the names of the Creator, surrounding the whole. Then a square outside the circles, and a second square set at forty-five degrees to the first so that its angles point to the four quarters, with a censer of lighted charcoal at each of the eight corners.

That is a nine-foot radius, an eighteen-foot circle, and eight burning censers. Almost nobody has ever done it. What the description does establish is the logic of a circle in this tradition: a marked centre, a definite boundary, a controlled point of entry, the quarters distinguished, and the names of God at the perimeter. Every practical modern circle is an abbreviation of that logic, and the abbreviation is legitimate as long as you know which parts you are abbreviating.

A working rite you can actually perform

What follows is this book’s own synthesis, not a historical text: assembled from the elements above and from the banishing of Chapter 15, and offered because a grimoire that describes procedures without ever putting one together is not much use. Every component is dated in the sources line; the arrangement is modern and is mine.

Opening

  1. Prepare. Wash. Put on the garment. Clear the space and set out what the working needs: no more than that.
  2. Set the centre. Stand where the work will be done. Three slow breaths. Say, aloud, in your own words, what this hour is for. Aloud matters; the difference between a stated intention and a held one is most of what ritual is doing.
  3. Purify. Sprinkle the consecrated water at the four quarters and over yourself, beginning in the east and moving sunwise.
  4. Mark the boundary. Walk the circle sunwise, tracing it with the hand or the knife, returning to where you began. See it as a boundary of light, closed and complete.
  5. Banish. Perform the Lesser Banishing Ritual of the Pentagram (Chapter 15), or, if you do not use it, name the four quarters in turn and ask that the space be clear.
  6. Light and incense. Kindle the lamp, then the censer. The Key of Solomon exorcises the fire before the incense goes on it; the practical residue is that you light the fire attentively rather than absently.

Closing

  1. Finish the work. Stop before you are tired, not after.
  2. Give thanks, in whatever terms you honestly hold: to the source of the work, and to anything you called on.
  3. Banish again. The same rite as at the opening. The closing banishing is the one practitioners skip and the one that matters: it is what returns the space to ordinary use.
  4. Open the circle. Walk it widdershins, or simply declare it open, and mean it.
  5. Extinguish the lamp and the coals. Check them.
  6. Ground. Eat something. Write down what happened before you interpret it. See Chapter 15.

Twenty minutes, and it is a complete ceremonial frame. Elaboration is available in every direction (a longer purification, a full Solomonic circle, planetary timing, consecrated instruments) and none of it is a substitute for having done the short form regularly.

Ritual Safety

Begin with simple rituals and work up gradually. Do not attempt advanced or evocatory rituals without proper preparation and grounding. Practical matters deserve equal attention: open flames and candles want a stable surface and a clear space above them, incense wants ventilation, and long periods kneeling or standing in one position want a realistic assessment of your own body. The commonest injuries in ceremonial practice are burns and falls, not spiritual ones.

Modern Practice

Where the historical sources assume a private room, a full night, and access to consecrated ground, most contemporary practitioners have a bedroom and forty minutes. The adaptations are sensible and near-universal: shortened forms of the longer rituals, electric light where open flame is unsafe or prohibited, substituted materials where the traditional ones are unobtainable, protected or endangered. Many practitioners now work seasonally rather than by planetary hour, simply because a calendar is easier to keep than an ephemeris. What has not changed, and what the modern shortcuts most often lose, is the deliberate closing. Practitioners who abbreviate a ritual almost always abbreviate the end of it, and that is the one part the sources treat as non-negotiable.

Sources: Clavicula Salomonis, trans. Mathers’s footnotes supply the gloss on the three circumferential lines and on the Tau, and the transliterations IHVH, AHIH, ALIVN, ALH, AL, IH, AGLA and ADNI are his. Book II, ch. 5 for the bath, its psalms and the exorcism of the water; ch. 6 for the garments; ch. 8 for the instruments and the conjuration of the sword; ch. 10 for the incense and the exorcism of fire; ch. 11 for the consecration of water and salt and for the sprinkler. Manuscript variants of the divine names in the salt formula are recorded in Peterson’s edition of Mathers’s text. Agrippa, De occulta philosophia (1533), Book III, for ceremonial framing. The opening and closing rite given above is this book’s own arrangement of those elements and is not a historical text.

The aspergillum, the ewer and the vesting names: Waite, The Book of Ceremonial Magic (1913 printing), quoting the Grimorium Verum and the Book of True Black Magic, neither of which has a public-domain English text of its own, so the wording is Waite’s rendering at one remove. The variant list of seven vesting angels is from his own footnote comparing the Key of Solomon. The purity condition quoted in the note on the age of the preparations is from the rubric to ch. LXIV of the Egyptian Book of the Dead in Budge’s translation; the edition and page are given in full in Chapter 22, where the same rubric is printed and the caution about Budge as superseded scholarship is set out.

Chapter IXThe Greek Magical Papyri Advanced

Everything else in this book is a reconstruction, an interpretation, or a tradition about a tradition. This chapter is different. The Greek Magical Papyri are the working papers of practising magicians of the Graeco-Roman world, written on papyrus in their own hands, surviving in museum cases in London, Paris, Berlin and Leiden. They are not a later account of what ancient magic might have been. They are ancient magic, in its own words, with the abbreviations and marginal notes still in place.

Scholars call the collection the Papyri Graecae Magicae, abbreviated PGM. The extant texts run from the late fourth century BCE (PGM XL, the curse of Artemisia, an isolated early outlier) and the first century BCE, down to the fifth century CE, with Christian magical texts extending into the sixth on a dating that should be treated as provisional. The bulk of the corpus, however, is third to fifth century CE, and that concentration matters: this is predominantly the magic of late Roman Egypt, not of the Ptolemies. The texts are written mostly in ancient Greek, but also in Demotic Egyptian, in Old Coptic, and in passages of hieratic script and cipher. Individual texts are cited by volume and item number, so that PGM IV. 1266 refers to a specific line of a specific papyrus, the way one would cite any other classical text.

How they came to light

There was never an ancient library called “the Greek Magical Papyri.” The corpus is a modern scholarly assembly, and knowing how it was put together matters for reading it. The papyri surfaced through the antiquities trade from the eighteenth century onward. The largest single group, the so-called Anastasi collection, was assembled by Jean d’Anastasi, who was vice-consul and from 1828 Consul-General of Sweden and Norway at Alexandria, as well as a grain merchant and antiquities dealer at the court of the Ottoman viceroy Muhammad Ali Pasha. He acquired the papyri through local agents at an unknown date before 1828; the first documented transfer is the purchase of the collection, consigned to Livorno in 1826, by the Dutch government in 1828 for the Rijksmuseum van Oudheden at Leiden. He said he had obtained them at Thebes, modern Luxor, and further material went to the British Museum, the Louvre, the Bibliothèque Nationale and the Staatliche Museen in Berlin.

Hans Dieter Betz, who edited the standard English translation, suggests (hedged, and as one of two possibilities alongside a temple library) that about half a dozen of the Anastasi papyri may have come from the collection of a single Theban scholar-bibliophile. The ownership of what is now called the Theban Magical Library remains disputed, and other scholars argue for multiple collectors rather than one. What is not disputed is that the same Theban material included Leyden papyrus X and the Stockholm papyrus, both of them alchemical: fourth-century codices written in the same hand, or very nearly, as PGM XIII. (Two Leiden papyri are easily confused and should not be: Leiden X, P. Leid. I 397, is the alchemical one; Leiden W, P. Leid. I 395, is PGM XIII. The Stockholm papyrus, P. Holm., is now in the Kungliga Biblioteket.) Pause on that detail: the alchemy of Chapter 5 and the magic of this chapter came out of the same context. In late antique Egypt these were not separate disciplines.

Publication was slow, piecemeal and, in one instance, tragic. The first pieces of the corpus into print were PGM XL in 1826 (Petrettini) and PGM XIV in 1843 (Leemans). PGM XII and XIII, often wrongly said to have come first, were described in selections by C. J. C. Reuvens in his Lettres à M. Letronne (1830) and published in full, Greek text with Latin translation and commentary, by Conrad Leemans in 1885. The first scholarly publication in English is credited to Charles Wycliffe Goodwin, who translated PGM V with commentary for the Cambridge Antiquarian Society in 1852. The critical edition is Karl Preisendanz’s, published in two volumes in 1928 and 1931. A projected third volume, containing new texts and the indices, reached galley proofs with a preface dated “Pentecost 1941”; Teubner’s Leipzig house was bombed on 4 December 1943. The proofs themselves survived and circulated as photocopies, most papyrological institutes hold the volume, and the 1941 preface was reprinted in the second edition. A revised edition, with Albert Henrichs, appeared in 1973–74, incorporating the lost third volume’s papyri but omitting the indices. Betz’s English translation, including the Demotic texts, was published by the University of Chicago Press in 1986. Preisendanz’s numbering runs to PGM LXXXI; later finds have been given further numbers by convention.

What is in them

Most of these fragments are pages from spell books. Broadly they fall into two kinds. Some are compilations assembled by collectors: scholarly gatherings of magical writing, made out of interest or for study. Others read like the working manuals of travelling practitioners: a repertoire, formulae for all occasions, the common phrases abbreviated because the owner already knew them by heart.

The range is much wider than the popular image of ancient magic allows. There are summonings of gods and daemons of real gravity, and there are parlour tricks. There are fatal curses and there are love charms. There are cures for impotence and remedies for minor medical complaints. There are folk recipes sitting on the same page as elaborate theurgy. The best known single text in the whole corpus is the invocation now generally called the Mithras Liturgy: a sustained ritual of ascent, and the piece most often anthologised.

Certain features recur throughout and are worth recognising on sight:

  • Voces magicae: strings of words with no meaning in Greek, Egyptian or Hebrew, to be spoken exactly as written. Their power was understood to lie in the sound and the precision, not in any sense they carried.
  • Charaktêres: written signs resembling letters with small circles at their terminals, used as a script of their own.
  • Assumption of a divine identity: rituals in which the practitioner takes on the identity of a deity, through invocation and visualisation, as part of an ascent or an operation.
  • Figurines: repeatedly referenced, in judicial, erotic and curse workings alike, made of materials chosen to suit the spell. Surviving examples turn up across the Mediterranean, generally in places the Greeks associated with the underworld: graves, sanctuaries, bodies of water. Some were found inside lead coffins with the spell inscribed on the outside.
  • Prayers alongside all of it, including the Prayer of Thanksgiving: a text that also turns up among the Nag Hammadi Hermetica.

The formulae are often strikingly close to those found on defixiones (curse tablets or binding spells, katadesmoi in Greek) inscribed on ostraka, amulets and sheets of lead. Some of those tablets date from as early as the late sixth and early fifth centuries BCE (the oldest are Sicilian, from Selinous and probably Himera) and they have been recovered from Sicily, Athens, Asia Minor, Rome and Egypt, in over a thousand texts. Some collections frame the corpus more conservatively as fifth century BCE to fifth century CE. That continuity matters: it means the papyri are not an Egyptian curiosity but a window onto practice across the Graeco-Roman world.

The Headless Rite

Several texts from this corpus are printed here in full, and the rule that selects them needs stating before the first of them. It is not a judgement about which spells are safe. It is this: an operation that acts on nobody but the operator is given entire; an operation aimed at another person is described and not printed. The reasoning is set out at the end of the chapter, and the rule is applied there without exception. This is the first of the texts it admits, and the most consequential in the corpus for everything later in this book: the ancestor of the ceremonial tradition of Chapter 13 and Chapter 15, and a rite that asks nothing of anybody but the operator.

It is PGM V. 96–172, an exorcism. The translation is Charles Wycliffe Goodwin’s, made for the Cambridge Antiquarian Society in 1852 and long out of copyright: the first scholarly publication of any part of this corpus in English, and the same edition this chapter cites above.

An address to the god drawn upon the letter

I call thee, the headless one, that didst create earth and heaven, that didst create night and day, thee the creator of light and darkness. Thou art Osoronnophris, whom no man hath seen at any time; thou art Iabas, thou art Iapos, thou hast distinguished the just and the unjust, thou didst make female and male, thou didst produce seeds and fruits, thou didst make men to love one another and to hate one another. I am Moses thy prophet, to whom thou didst commit thy mysteries, the ceremonies of Israel; thou didst produce the moist and the dry and all manner of food. Listen to me: I am an angel of Phapro Osoronnophris; this is thy true name, handed down to the prophets of Israel. Listen to me, … hear me and drive away this spirit.

I call thee the terrible and invisible god residing in the empty wind, … thou headless one, deliver such an one from the spirit that possesses him. … strong one, headless one, deliver such an one from the spirit that possesses him.

The gaps are in the printed translation, where the papyrus is damaged or Goodwin left the magical names untransliterated. The Greek continues with the passage the modern tradition took up: egō eimi ho akephalos daimōn en tois posin echōn tēn horasin — “I am the headless daemon, having sight in my feet.”

It is the Headless Rite, not the Bornless Rite

Modern occultism knows this text as the Bornless Ritual, and under that name it has been one of the most widely performed pieces of ceremonial magic of the last century. The Greek word is aképhalos: a-, without, and kephalē, head. Goodwin translated it correctly in 1852 as “the headless one,” and the rite’s own imagery, a daemon with its sight in its feet, only makes sense of a figure that has no head.

“Bornless” is not what the word says. This book does not attempt to establish how the reading arose, because it could not verify the usual account; what can be shown is only that the earliest English translation says headless, that the Greek says headless, and that the popular name says something else. That is the pattern of Fig. 1 in miniature, a modern rendering circulating as the ancient one, and it is a fitting thing to find in the one chapter with the largest body of ancient primary material of this book.

Two more spells from the same papyrus

The Headless Rite is the papyrus’s most famous page, but it is not typical of the book it sits in. To show the texture of the working manual itself, here are two further operations from the same manuscript, in the same 1852 translation: both, like the exorcism, acting on nobody but the operator. The first is a consecration; the second is the classic dream-oracle of the corpus.

The ring of Hermes, the ceremony of the beetle

Take a beetle, sculptured as described beneath, place it on a paper table, and under the table a pure linen cloth, and lay under it some olive sticks, and place on the middle of the table a small censer, and offer myrrh and kyphi, and have in readiness a small chrysolite vessel, into which put ointment of lilies, or myrrh, or cinnamon, and take the ring and put it into the ointment, first purifying it from every defilement, and offer in the censer the kyphi and myrrh. Leave it three days, and take it and put it in a pure place.

At the celebration let there lie near at hand some pure loaves, and such fruits as are in season, and having made another sacrifice upon vine sticks, during the sacrifice take the ring out of the ointment, and anoint yourself with the unction from it. Anoint yourself early in the morning, and turning towards the east pronounce the words underwritten.

The carving of the beetle. Carve a beetle upon a precious emerald, bore it and pass a gold wire through, and beneath the beetle carve the holy Isis, and having consecrated it as above written, use it.

Notice what the operation consists of: purification, a fixed waiting period, perfumes, a dawn orientation, and an anointing: the same grammar as the Key of Solomon’s pentacle consecration in Chapter 20, fourteen centuries earlier. The grammar is the continuity; the gods change.

The dream oracle of Hermes

Take of the inner leaves of laurel twenty-eight, and virgin earth, and wormwood seeds, flour, and the herb cynocephalium — ground up together — and make an image of the cloaked Hermes, the moon’s rising being in the Ram, the Lion, the Virgin, or the Archer. And let Hermes hold the herald’s wand. And write the spell upon a sheet of hieratic paper, and having cut off a hair from your head, wrap it up in the paper, and tie it with a Phoenician knot, and place outside an olive branch.

And let the figure lie in a shrine of limewood; and when you wish for an oracular response, place the shrine with the god at your head and invoke, offering frankincense upon an altar. The address begins: Hermes, ruler of the cosmos… — and the answer is expected in the night’s dream.

An incubation rite: the question is prepared by day and the god is expected to answer in sleep. The scrying protocol of Chapter 13 and the record-keeping of Chapter 7 are this operation’s descendants, with the statue exchanged for a notebook. Both texts are given as Goodwin printed them, lightly normalised where the scan mangled a letter; his ellipses mark gaps in the papyrus itself.

An inquiry of the god, without a medium

One further operation from the wider corpus shows what a working manual looks like when it is describing a private rite rather than a public one. It is from the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden: the PGM’s bilingual sister, the same Theban material of this chapter, published by Griffith and Thompson in 1904. Most of the papyrus’s divinations require a boy as medium; this one the operator performs alone, and sleeps.

Inquiry of the god by a table and a dream

Take a table of wood having four feet, upon which no man on earth has ever sat, and put it, it being clean, beside you. Put the table in a clean room in the midst of the place, it being near your head; cover it with a tunic from its head to its feet, and put four bricks under the table before it, one above another, there being a censer of clay before it. Put charcoal of olive-wood on the censer, and put wild-goose fat pounded with myrrh, and make them into balls, and put one on the brazier, and lay the remainder at your side, and pronounce the spell to it.

Then spend the night without speaking to any one on earth, and lie down. And you see the god in the likeness of a priest wearing fine linen.

The invocation begins: I invoke thee who art seated in the invisible darkness and who art in the midst of the great gods…

Griffith and Thompson’s edition marks its uncertainties with question marks in the translation. They are the editors’ honesty about a damaged text rather than hesitation about the sense, and they are not reproduced in the rite above: as this chapter’s sources line records, they were dropped for readability and the uncertainty is described here instead. Note what the rite actually requires: a table nobody has sat on, a clean room, a specific smoke, and silence: the operator’s own preparation doing most of the work, exactly as in the incubation rite of the Headless Rite’s papyrus above.

The so-called Mithras Liturgy

This chapter called it, near the top, the best known single text in the corpus and the piece most often anthologised, and then printed not a line of it. That is the largest thing missing here, and it is fixed below: the text is given entire. It is PGM IV. 475–829, dug out of the great Paris magical papyrus, and it belongs in this chapter on the same rule as the rest: from its first word to its last it acts on nobody but the person performing it. There is no second party in it at all. What it asks for is the sight of the gods and a share in immortality, and the only equipment it names is two amulets and the light of the sun.

Before the text, its name, which is wrong twice over; and the demonstration comes from the translator himself, in the same volume that carries the English. It is not a liturgy. “A Liturgy is a service in which several take part, whereas it is plain that our Ritual was a secret and solemn inner rite for one person only.” And whether it is Mithraic was contested before this translation was printed: “though Cumont in his great work quotes several passages from the unrevised text, he does so only to reject it as a genuine Mithriac document.” Franz Cumont was the founder of the modern study of Mithraism, and he declined to admit this text to it. Read the rite below and the reason is plain enough: the name Mithras occurs in it exactly once, in the opening prayer, and everything after that is Egyptian, Greek and Hermetic. The title is Albrecht Dieterich’s, from Eine Mithrasliturgie (Leipzig, 1903), and it stuck to the text the way “Bornless” stuck to the headless daemon. That is twice in one chapter that the name a text travels under is not the name it gave itself, and in both cases the correction has been available in print for over a century.

Its date and its layers are worth having in the same breath. The Paris papyrus is placed “with every probability as the earliest years of the fourth century A.D.”: late, for a rite so often described as a survival of something much older. And the text is not of one piece: it “has, however, been plainly worked over by a school of Egyptian magicians, who inserted most of the now unintelligible words and names (asēma onomata, nomina barbara, nomina arcana), and vowel-combinations and permutations.” That the older layer was Mithraic and the insertions Egyptian is Dieterich’s argument and Mead’s, not this book’s; what is documented is a fourth-century Egyptian papyrus containing both.

The daggers, and what stands behind them

A dagger, †, stands at sixteen places in the text below. It is not an editorial footnote and it is not damage to the papyrus. It is where the Greek has a magical name and the translator declined to set it: Protect me! †! is an invocation of a name, and For † bids thee [remain] makes no sense as anything else. Mead says as much obliquely at the one place he did print the barbarous syllables in full: “I have retained this specimen of magical chanting to give the reader some idea of one mode of theurgic language.” Retained: that is, out of a set he was otherwise suppressing. The daggers stay in the text below exactly where the 1907 printing puts them. What stands behind each of them is no longer withheld: the Greek Mead was translating is Dieterich’s, Dieterich’s book is in the public domain, and this edition read the names off its pages. They are given here in transliteration, dagger by dagger.

Where the dagger standsWhat the Greek gives

Second Utterance: from out the Depth †oxyoxerthouth
Sixth Utterance: Protect me! †prosymeri

Seventh Utterance: the Seven Fortunes, first to seventhchrepsenthaes, meneschees, mechran, ararmaches, echommie, tichnondaes, erourombries

Read the recovered names against the rite and the pattern is plain: the short ones are addresses (a guardian name for each amulet, a name for the Silence, one name apiece for fourteen door-keepers) and the long strings sit exactly where the rubrics demand a physical act, the hiss and the puff. The names are the operative half the translation withheld, and with them the fifty-two words of Angelical in Chapter 14 have their older counterpart: a working vocabulary nobody has ever read, preserved letter by letter because the letters were the point.

The rite of immortalisation, called the Mithras Liturgy

Prayers and utterances are in italic and rubrics in roman, which is the 1907 printing’s own distinction, stated on its p. 17. The bracketed section headings and the bracketed words inside the text are the translator’s.

I. [The Father’s Prayer.] O Providence, O Fortune, bestow on me Thy Grace — imparting these the Mysteries a Father only may hand on, and that, too, to a Son alone — his Immortality — [a Son] initiate, worthy of this our Craft, with which Sun Mithras, the Great God, commanded me to be endowed by His Archangel; so that I, Eagle [as I am, by mine own self] alone, may soar to Heaven, and contemplate all things.

II. The Invocatory Utterance (Logos). 1. O Primal Origin of my origination; Thou Primal Substance of my substance; First Breath of breath, the breath that is in me; First Fire, God-given for the Blending of the blendings in me, [First Fire] of fire in me; First Water of [my] water, the water in me; Primal Earth-essence of the earthy essence in me; Thou Perfect Body of me — N. N., son of N. N. (fem.) — fashioned by Honoured Arm and Incorruptible Right Hand, in World that’s lightless, yet radiant with Light, [in World] that’s soulless, yet filled full of Soul!

2. If, verily, it may seem good to you, translate me, now held by my lower nature, unto the Generation that is free from Death; in order that, beyond the insistent Need that presses on me, I may have Vision of the Deathless Source, by virtue of the Deathless Spirit, by virtue of the Deathless Water, by virtue of the [Deathless] Solid, and [by virtue of] the [Deathless] Air; in order that I may become re-born in Mind; in order that I may become initiate, and that the Holy Breath may breathe in me; in order that I may admire the Holy Fire; that I may see the Deep of the [New] Dawn, the Water that doth cause [the Soul] to thrill; and that the Life-bestowing Æther which surrounds [all things] may give me Hearing.

3. For I am to behold to-day with Deathless Eyes — I, mortal, born of mortal womb, but [now] made better by the Might of Mighty Power, yea, by the Incorruptible Right Hand — [I am to see to-day] by virtue of the Deathless Spirit the Deathless Æon, the Master of the Diadems of Fire — I with pure purities [now] purified, the human soul-power of me subsisting for a little while in purity; which [power] I shall again receive transmitted unto me beyond the insistent Bitterness that presses on me, Necessity whose debts can never go unpaid — I, N. N., son of N. N. (fem.) — according to the Ordinance of God that naught can ever change.

4. For that it is beyond my reach that, born beneath the sway of Death, I should [unaided] soar into the Height, together with the golden sparklings of the Brilliancy that knows no Death.

5. Stay still, O nature doomed to perish, [nature] of men subject to Death! And straightway let me pass beyond the Need implacable that presses on me; for that I am His Son; I breathe; I am!

III. [The First Instruction.] 1. Take from the [Sun-]rays breath, inhaling thrice [as deeply] as thou canst; and thou shalt see thyself being raised aloft, and soaring towards the Height, so that thou seem’st to be in midst of Air. 2. Thou shalt hear naught, nor man nor beast; nor shalt thou see aught of the sights upon the earth, in that same hour; but all things thou shalt see will be immortal. 3. For thou shalt see, in that same day and hour, the Disposition of the Gods — the Ruling Gods ascending heavenwards, the other ones descending. And through his Disk — the God’s, my Father’s — there shall be seen the Way-of-going of the Gods accessible to sight.

4. And in like fashion also [shall be seen] the Pipe, as it is called, whence comes the Wind in service [for the day]. For thou shalt see as though it were a Pipe depending from His Disk; and toward the regions Westward, as though it were an infinite East Wind. But if the other Wind, toward the regions of the East, should be in service, in the like fashion shalt thou see, toward the regions of that [side,] the converse of the sight. 5. And thou shalt see the Gods gazing intently on thee and bearing down upon thee. Then straightway lay thy dexter finger on thy lips and say:

IV. [The First Utterance.] O Silence! Silence! Silence! The Symbol of the Living God beyond Decay. Protect me, Silence! †!

Next “hiss” forth long: S̄! S̄! Then “puff” saying: †! And thereon shalt thou see the Gods gazing benignly on thee, and no longer bearing down upon thee, but proceeding on the proper order of their doings.

V. [The Second Instruction.] When, then, thou see’st the Upper Cosmos clean and clear, with no one of the Gods (or Angels) bearing down on thee, expect to hear a mighty thunder-clap so as to startle thee. Then say again:

VI. The [Second] Utterance (Logos). 1. O Silence! Silence! I am a Star, whose Course is as your Course, shining anew from out the Depth †.

Upon thy saying this, straightway His Disk will start expanding. 2. And after thou hast said the second utterance — to wit, twice Silence and the rest — “hiss” twice, and “puff” twice; and straightway shalt thou see a mighty host of stars, five-pointed, emerging from His Disk, and filling all the Air. 3. Then say again: O Silence! Silence! And when His Disk is opened [fully] out, thou shalt behold an infinite Encircling and Doors of Fire fast closed. Straightway set going then the utterance that follows, closing thy eyes:

VII. The Third Utterance (Logos). 1. Hear me, give ear to me — N. N., son of N. N. (fem.) — O Lord, who with Thy Breath hast closed the Fiery Bars of Heaven; Twin-bodied; Ruler of the Fire; Creator of the Light; O Holder of the Keys; Inbreather of the Fire; Fire-hearted One, whose Breath gives Light; Thou who dost joy in Fire; Beauteous of Light; O Lord of Light, whose Body is of Fire; Light-giver [and] Fire-sower; Fire-loosener, whose Life is in the Light; Fire-whirler, who sett’st the Light in motion; Thou Thunder-rouser; O Thou Light-glory, Light-increaser; Controller of the Light Empyrean; O Thou Star-tamer!

2. Oh! Open unto me! For on account of this, the bitter and implacable Necessity that presses on me, I do invoke Thy Deathless Names, innate with Life, most worshipful, that have not yet descended unto mortal nature, nor have been made articulate by human tongue, or cry or tone of man:

iōō · oēēe · ōēe · ōoē · iē · ēō · oō · oē · ieō ·
oē · ōoē · ieōoē · ieeō · eē · iō · oē · ioē ·
ōēō · eoē · oeō · ōiē · ōiēeō · oi · iii · ēoē ·
ōuē · ēō · oēe · eōēia · aēaeēa · ēeeē · eeē ·
eeē · ieō · ēeō · oēeeoē · ēeō · euō · oē · eiō ·

3. Utter all these with Fire and Spirit once unto the end; and then begin again a second time, until thou hast completed [all] the Seven Immortal Gods of Cosmos. When thou hast uttered them, thunders and crashings shalt thou hear in the Surround, and feel thyself a-shake with every crash. Then once more utter Silence! [and] the utterance [following it]. 4. Thereon open thy eyes; and thou shalt see the Doors thrown open, and the Cosmos of the Gods that is within the Doors; so that for joy and rapture of the sight thy Spirit runs to meet it, and soars up. Therefore, hold thyself steady, and, gazing steadily into thyself, draw breath from the Divine. When, then, thy Soul shall be restored, say:

VIII. [The Fourth Utterance.] 1. Draw nigh, O Lord!

Upon this utterance His Rays shall be turned on thee, and thou shalt be in midst of them. 2. When, then, thou hast done this, thou shalt behold a God, in flower of age, of fairest beauty, [and] with Locks of Flame, in a white Tunic and a scarlet Mantle, wearing a Crown of Fire. Straightway salute Him with the Salutation of the Fire:

IX. [The Fifth Utterance.] 1. Hail Lord! O Thou of mighty Power; O King of mighty Sway; Greatest of Gods; O Sun; Thou Lord of Heaven and Earth; O God of Gods! Strong is Thy Breath; strong is Thy Might! O Lord, if it seem good to Thee, make Thou announcement of me unto God Most-high, who hath begotten and created Thee!

2. For that a man — I, N.N., son of N.N. (fem.), born of the mortal womb of N.N. (fem.), and of spermatic ichōr, yea, of this [ichōr], which at Thy Hands to-day hath undergone the transmutation of re-birth —, one, from so many tens of thousands, transformed to immortality in this same hour, by God’s good-pleasure, of God transcendent Good —, [a man, I say,] presumes to worship Thee, and supplicates with whatsoever power a mortal hath.

3. Upon this utterance He shall come to the Pole, and thou shalt see Him moving round as on a path. Then gaze intently, and send forth a prolonged “bellowing,” like to a horn-note, expelling the whole breath, with pressure on the ribs, and kiss the amulets, and say first to that upon the right:

X. [The Sixth Utterance.] Protect me! †!

When thou hast uttered this, thou shalt behold the Doors thrown open, and, issuing from the Depth, Seven Virgins, in byssus-robes, with serpent-faces, and golden sceptres in their hands. These are they who are the so-called Heaven’s Fortunes (Tychai). When thou dost see these things, make salutation thus:

XI. [The Seventh Utterance.] 1. Hail Heaven’s Seven Fortunes, Virgins august and good, ye sacred ones who live and eat with †! Ye holiest Protectors of the Four Supports! Hail thou, the First, †! Hail thou, the Second, †! Hail thou, the Third, †! Hail thou, the Fourth, †! Hail thou, the Fifth, †! Hail thou, the Sixth, †! Hail thou, the Seventh, †!

2. There come forth others, too — Seven Gods, with faces of black bulls, in linen loin-cloths, with seven golden fillets on their heads. These are the so-called Heaven’s Pole-lords. And in like fashion unto each of them thou must make salutation with his special name.

XII. [The Eighth Utterance.] 1. Hail Guardians of the Pivot, ye sacred sturdy Youths, who all, at once, revolve the spinning Axis of Heaven’s Circle, ye who let loose the thunder and the lightning, and earthquake-shocks and thunder-bolts upon the hosts of impious folk, but [who bestow] on me, who pious am and worshipper of God, good-health, and soundness of my frame in every part, and proper stretch of hearing and of sight, and calm, in the now present good-hours of this day, O mighty Ruling Lords and Gods of me! Hail thou, the First, †! … Hail thou, the Seventh, †!

2. Now when they [all] are present in their order, here and there, gaze in the Air intently, and thou shalt see lightnings down-flashing, and lights a-quiver, and the earth a-shake; and [then] a God descending, [a God] transcending vast, of radiant Presence, with golden Locks, in flower of age, [clad] in a Robe of brightness, with Crown of gold [upon His Head], and Garments [on His Legs], holding in His Right Hand the golden Shoulder of the Calf. This latter is the Bear that moves the Heaven[-dome], and changes its direction, now up now down, according to the hour. Then shalt thou see lightnings leap from His Eyes and from His Body stars. 3. Straightway send forth a “bellowing” prolonged, with belly-pressure, to start thy senses going all together — prolonged unto the very end, kissing again the amulets and saying:

XIII. [The Ninth Utterance.] †, [O Lord] of me — N. N. — abide with me, within my Soul! Oh! leave me not! For † bids thee [remain].

And gaze intently on the God, with “bellowing” prolonged, and thus salute Him:

XIV. [The Tenth Utterance.] Hail Lord, Thou Master of the Water! Hail, Founder of the Earth! Hail, Prince of Breath! O Lord, being born again, I pass away in being made Great, and, having been made Great, I die. Being born from out the state of birth-and-death that giveth birth to [mortal] lives, I now, set free, pass to the state transcending birth, as Thou hast stablished it, according as Thou hast ordained and made the Mystery.

The seven repetitions of the vowel-string are not decoration, and they answer a question this chapter raised in a bullet point and left hanging. Voces magicae were listed above as one of the features to recognise on sight; that block is what one actually looks like, and the rubric beside it says what it is for: utter the whole string through, then begin again, “until thou hast completed [all] the Seven Immortal Gods of Cosmos.” Seven passes, one for each. The practice was neither secret nor peculiar to magicians. Demetrius, On Interpretation, reports that “in Egypt the priests hymn the Gods by means of the seven vowels, chanting them in order; instead of the pipe and lute the musical chanting of these letters is heard. So that if you were to take away this accompaniment you would simply remove the whole melody and music of the utterance (logos).” The seven Greek vowels, Α Ε Η Ι Ο Υ Ω, answer to the seven spheres, and the string above is those seven sounds permuted, which is why it contains no consonant anywhere in it. Check the block: there is not one.

The hiss and the puff have the same standing. Nicomachus of Gerasa, in the second century, is quoted to the effect that the vowels are root-sounds combined with material elements as speech combines them with consonants, and that “whenever theurgists are awe-struck in any such operation, they make invocation symbolically by means of ‘hissings’ and ‘poppings’ and unarticulated and discordant sounds.” The Greek is syrigmos, a shrill piping or hissing, and poppysmos, a clicking or clucking of lips and tongue: used of birds, of the smack of a kiss, and of the cry “hush.” Rendering them “hiss” and “puff” was the translator’s decision and he said plainly that he was unsure of the second: the precise meaning “escapes me.” So the reader has the rubric exactly, and an honest translator’s doubt about half of it.

What the rite is doing is not in doubt. It is a solitary ascent, worked in stages, each stage gated by a spoken formula and a breath: draw breath from the sun’s rays, rise, meet resistance, command silence, hear thunder, see the disk open, name the god, be received, salute what comes through the doors, and at the end die into the state that transcends birth. Strip the names and the sequence is the ascent of the Poimandres in Chapter 2, the graded vision of Chapter 19, and (in its insistence that the operator hold steady and keep looking while the body shakes) the scrying discipline of Chapter 13. It is also, on the evidence of the text itself, breathwork: three deep inhalations to begin, breath expelled long against the ribs, the whole thing timed to the lungs. That is the operative core, and it is the part no summary of this text ever reproduces.

Reading the Greek settled one more thing: Mead suppressed more than his daggers admit. At “I breathe; I am!” the Greek carries a mystic formula his English passes over without a mark. The Third Utterance’s litany of fire-titles has barbarous names interleaved between the epithets (penpterouni, semesilam, psyrinpheu, iao) all silently dropped. The whole of his Fourth Utterance, “Draw nigh, O Lord!”, is in Greek proselthe, kyrie followed by an unmarked string: archandara photaza pyriphotaza bythix etimenmerophorathenerieprothriphorathi. And at the Fifth, the Greek continues past Mead’s ending with a petition naming the ruler of the day’s hour, thrapsiari morirok: a passage Dieterich sets in italic as the magician-redactor’s own insertion, which is the Egyptian working-over of the text made visible on the page, exactly the layering this chapter described. The daggers were the honest part of the suppression; the rest carried no flag at all.

One thing is honestly missing. The papyrus prescribes a preparation before any of this (a regimen, and the juice of a plant it calls kentritis) and it says how the two amulets are to be made; none of that is in the English translation used here, which begins at the Father’s Prayer and ends at the tenth utterance. Dieterich’s edition prints that closing apparatus entire, in Greek with his German facing, and the sources note says where it stands. A reader who wants to know what the corpus’s most famous text actually says now has everything the century-old public translation contains, with the names it withheld restored from the Greek it translated.

A syncretism, not a survival

The religion of the papyri is a genuine blend rather than a pure inheritance. Greek, Egyptian, Jewish and later Christian elements sit together, sometimes in a single formula. Olympian gods take on the attributes of Egyptian counterparts, or Egyptian deities are addressed by Greek names: Aphrodite, associated with Hathor, is given the epithet Neferihri, from the Egyptian nfr-iry.t, “nice eyes” (PGM IV. 1266). Betz observes that the Greek gods here are frequently not the Hellenised aristocrats of contemporary literature but something closer to the figures of folklore: chthonic, demonic, dangerous.

Betz’s own summary is careful about what this mixture represents: in it, he writes, the indigenous Egyptian religion “has in part survived, in part been profoundly hellenized,” reduced and simplified to ease its assimilation; while Greek traditions were in turn Egyptianised. He is candid that the Jewish material resists explanation, calling its origin and nature “far from clear.” He concludes that what we have is specifically a Greco-Egyptian syncretism rather than a general Greco-Roman one. Janet H. Johnson made the complementary point in 1996: the texts cannot be fully understood from the Greek alone, because the Demotic passages carry part of the argument.

The papyri also sit at the centre of a live scholarly disagreement that any honest reader should know about. Betz treats them as a fraction of a much larger lost literature, a kind of “underground literature” subject to book-burning: citing Acts 19:19, Augustus’s order to burn magical books reported by Suetonius, and later Christian burnings. David Frankfurter reads them very differently: as the productions of innovative members of the Egyptian priesthood during the third- and fourth-century collapse of the temple infrastructure, and therefore far less “underground” than Betz allows. Alan F. Segal goes further still, using the hymns embedded in these supposedly magical texts to question whether the distinction between magic and religion holds up at all in the Hellenistic world. The people who copied these pages, on Segal’s reading, saw no such line.

Why this chapter is not a set of instructions

The operations printed above are given entire; the rest of the PGM are presented here descriptively. That division is deliberate, and it is not a squeamish one. These are historical documents whose interest lies in what they tell us about the people who wrote them: their cosmology, their anxieties, their remarkable willingness to file a summoning of a god next to a cure for a headache. The line this book draws is not between safe and unsafe texts but between operations that act on the operator and operations aimed at somebody else. Reproducing a binding spell against a named person would not make this book more authentic; it would only make it worse. Every rite printed in this chapter falls on the operator’s side of that line (an exorcism the operator speaks over himself, a ring he consecrates, two dreams he goes to sleep to receive, and an ascent he undertakes alone) and every operation this chapter withholds falls on the other. Read them as what they are: the most direct access we have to the ancient practice that everything later in this tradition claims to descend from.

Sources: Preisendanz, Papyri Graecae Magicae (1928, 1931), vol. 1 on the Internet Archive; Betz (1986), in copyright; Faraone and Torallas Tovar (2022), open access, which renumbers the formularies and supersedes Preisendanz. Goodwin, Fragment of a Graeco-Egyptian Work upon Magic (1852), the first scholarly publication of any part of the corpus in English, is the source of the Headless Rite, the ring of Hermes and the dream oracle as printed above, all from PGM V.
