Chapter XThe Solomonic Tradition Advanced

If the Greek Magical Papyri are ancient magic without a famous name attached, the Solomonic literature is the reverse: a large, influential and genuinely important body of texts attached to a name that did not write any of them. Every book in this tradition is pseudepigraphic: attributed to King Solomon, composed many centuries after him, by authors who are almost entirely anonymous. That is not a scandal to be exposed. It was a convention of the genre, and a claim about authority rather than a claim about history. But it does mean that the phrase “the magic of Solomon” describes a literary lineage, not a Judaean one.

The oldest Solomonic book

This chapter has so far begun in the wrong millennium. Behind the medieval and early-modern books stands a much older text, and it is the one in which the whole idea of Solomon commanding demons is first worked out at length: the Testament of Solomon.

Its frame needs telling because everything later descends from it. Solomon is building the Temple. A demon named Ornias is troubling one of the workmen, a boy, draining his strength. Solomon prays; the archangel Michael brings him a ring with a seal; the ring gives him authority over demons; and he uses it to conscript them into building the Temple. He then interrogates them one after another (Ornias, Beelzeboul, Onoskelis, Asmodeus and the rest) each stating its name, its activity, the harm it does, and the angel or name by which it is thwarted.

That interrogation format is the ancestor of the demon catalogues of the Ars Goetia: name, office, appearance, and the means of control. What the later grimoires present as a list, the Testament presents as a series of encounters.

One section deserves particular notice because it shows what the text is actually made of. In chapter XVIII, Solomon summons the thirty-six decans (the decans being the divisions of the zodiac at ten degrees each, an Egyptian astronomical scheme) and each states which part of the body it afflicts and which name cures it. As McCown observes, the surviving decan lists do not agree with each other, but all agree on the underlying proposition, which Celsus had described as an Egyptian belief: that the decans rule diseases, each of a certain part of the body. This is astrological medicine, of the kind Chapter 16 describes, embedded in a demonological text.

How old, and from where

Chester Charlton McCown’s critical edition of 1922 (assembled from manuscripts at Mount Athos, Bologna, Holkham Hall, Jerusalem, London, Milan, Paris and Vienna) remains the standard text, and his conclusions are carefully hedged in a way this book can only approve of.

On date: the Testament as we have it was written “early in the third century.” But its Jewish groundwork may be much older: Josephus shows that ideas of Solomon’s dealings with demons “were common among the Jews already in the first century A.D.”, so the underlying material “may be as early as the first century of the Christian era.” McCown then stops: “At present our data allow no more precise date.”

On provenance he is blunter still. “So far as I am aware, no one has attempted to decide from what part of the ancient world the Test. came — perhaps wisely, for no certain conclusion can be reached.” He names three candidates (Palestine, Egypt, and the province of Asia) and leans, without insisting, toward Galilee, “where Judaism and Hellenism were in the closest contact.”

So: a text of the early third century, resting on first-century material, of uncertain origin, mixing Jewish, Egyptian, Greek and Christian elements. That is roughly a thousand years before the Clavicula, and it means the Solomonic tradition of this chapter has a genuinely ancient root: unlike the Rosicrucian brotherhood of Chapter 12, and like the papyri of Chapter 9.

The Key of Solomon

The Clavicula Salomonis, the Key of Solomon, is the central text. It probably dates to the sixteenth century, possibly the fifteenth (the older attribution to the fourteenth or fifteenth is Waite’s rather than modern scholarship’s) and it belongs to the Italian Renaissance. It is a model example of Renaissance magic: heavily ceremonial, concerned with purification and consecrated instruments, framed throughout in devotional Christian language. Its introduction supplies the traditional legend: that Solomon wrote the book for his son Rehoboam. That is the document’s backstory, not its provenance.

The manuscript tradition is rich and worth knowing, because “the Key of Solomon” is not one fixed book but a family of related texts that differ from copy to copy. The surviving manuscripts date mostly from the late sixteenth to the eighteenth century. Among the notable witnesses are a fifteenth-century Greek manuscript in the British Library (Harley MS 5596), an important Italian manuscript in the Bodleian (Michael MS 276) of around 1600, and an English translation, “The Clavicle of Solomon, revealed by Ptolomy the Grecian,” dated 1572. The Greek text is generally known separately as the Magical Treatise of Solomon; Armand Delatte transcribed one Athens manuscript of it in his Anecdota Atheniensia (1927): not, it should be said, the Harley manuscript. Its contents closely resemble the Clavicula. Priority is not finally settled, but the specialist literature leans to the Greek as the ancestral form, and it is almost certain that the earliest Western version was translated from it.

The version most modern readers have met is S. L. MacGregor Mathers’s English edition of 1889, based on manuscripts in the British Museum: the British Library did not exist until 1973, and the anachronism is a common one. Mathers’s edition is important for a reason beyond its scholarship: he was one of the three founders of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, and it was largely through him that this medieval and early-modern material entered modern ceremonial practice. Nearly every twentieth-century magical order that uses circles, pentacles and consecrated tools is drawing, at some remove, on Mathers’s reading of these manuscripts.

The practical content of the Key is broadly consistent across versions. It concerns the preparation of the operator through ablution, abstinence and prayer; the drawing of the circle as the defined space of the working; the making and consecration of instruments (knife, wand, censer, parchment) each with its own procedure and timing; the planetary hours governing when a given operation may be attempted; and the pentacles, the engraved figures that give the tradition its visual signature.

The forty-four pentacles

The Key’s most-copied contents are its pentacles, and this chapter has described the procedure for making one, in Chapter 20, without ever saying how many there are or what they are for. There are forty-four, grouped by planet, and Mathers’s edition prints them as plates numbered straight through, Figures 11 to 54.

PlanetPentaclesFiguresWhat the set is for
Saturn711–17terror and submission of spirits, adversity, ruin and destruction, defence at night, treasure-guarding spirits driven off
Jupiter718–24protection of the operator, riches and honour, treasure, visions
Mars725–31invoking martial spirits, disease and its cure, victory in war, resisting enemies
the Sun732–38the countenance of Shaddai, transport from place to place, invisibility, deliverance from prison
Venus539–43controlling the spirits of Venus, attracting love, gaining grace and honour
Mercury544–48spirits under the Firmament, opening what is shut, knowledge of hidden things
the Moon649–54opening doors, defence against sorcery and injury, answers in sleep, rain and safety on water

Two of the Saturn set are worth quoting, because between them they show what a pentacle in this literature actually is. The third is a piece of scheduling: “This should be made within the Magical Circle, and it is good for use at night when thou invokest the Spirits of the nature of Saturn,” and Mathers notes that the characters at the ends of its rays are the magical characters of Saturn, with the angels Omeliel, Anachiel, Arauchiah and Anazachia named around it. The second is a small revelation:

Figure 12. — The Second Pentacle of Saturn. — This Pentacle is of great value against adversities; and of especial use in repressing the pride of the Spirits.

Editor’s Note. — This is the celebrated SATOR AREPO TENET OPERA ROTAS, the most perfect existing form of double acrostic, as far as the arrangement of the letters is concerned; it is repeatedly mentioned in the records of mediæval Magic; and, save to very few, its derivation from the present Pentacle has been unknown.

The famous word-square of Roman graffiti (found scratched at Pompeii, and argued over ever since) sits in the Key as a planetary talisman, and Mathers’s claim about its derivation is exactly the sort this book does not repeat unchecked: the square is centuries older than any manuscript of the Key, so the pentacle cannot be its origin, whatever a Victorian editor supposed. What is true and more interesting is the arithmetic he gives with it: twenty-five letters, plus the unity, making twenty-six, the numerical value of IHVH; and the Hebrew versicle around the rim, from Psalm lxxii, also of exactly twenty-five letters. The pentacle is a numerological argument in a circle, which is what the whole class of objects is.

Then the whole set, each with what Mathers gives as its use, in his order. The list is worth having entire because the summary above smooths it, and the unsmoothed version is stranger. Four things show only when the forty-four are read one after another. The first is how much of the collection is not spiritual at all but weather, sleep, locks and travel: three of the six lunar pentacles concern water, rain and journeys, and one of the Mercury set is a lockpick. The second is that the operator is frequently the one in danger, and the pentacle is armour rather than a weapon. The third is that several of them do not stand alone: the second of the Sun is grouped with the one before and the one after it, the third of the Sun adds to the effects of the two preceding, the third of Mercury runs with the fourth, the first of the Moon with the second. The plates are in part a sequence and not a catalogue. The fourth is the plainest, and it is that a handful of them are for hurting people.

The set closes with a note in square brackets, in which the translator stops translating and speaks for himself. He has, he says, restored the Hebrew letters and mystical characters as correctly as he could, and given nearly every versicle in pointed Hebrew rather than in the Latin, so that the occult student need not go looking for it in a Hebrew Bible. Then the admission: the restoration of the Hebrew inside the pentacles “has been a work of immense difficulty, and has extended over several years.” It is the most useful sentence on the page. The plates are not a copy of anything. They are a Victorian reconstruction of manuscripts in which, as his introduction has already said, the letters were “so vilely scribbled as to be actually undecipherable in some instances,” and the man who redrew them says so twice.

The Lesser Key, or Lemegeton

The Lesser Key of Solomon is a separate and later compilation, assembled in the mid-seventeenth century from materials several centuries older. Despite the name it is not an abridgement of the Key; it is its own anthology, in five books:

  1. Ars Goetia: the evocation of seventy-two spirits, each with a name, a rank and a sigil. This is the part of the Lemegeton that everyone has heard of, and the part that has done most to shape the popular idea of grimoire magic.
  2. Ars Theurgia Goetia: spirit princes organised by the points of the compass.
  3. Ars Paulina: angels assigned to the hours of the day and to the degrees of the zodiac.
  4. Ars Almadel: angelic contact by means of a wax tablet and scrying.
  5. Ars Notoria: prayers to strengthen memory, eloquence and understanding.

The layering here is instructive. The Ars Notoria is substantially older than the compilation that contains it: Véronèse’s critical edition traces it from a thirteenth-century version A through a glossed version that appeared at the end of the thirteenth century and survives in three fourteenth-century manuscripts, with the core Flores aurei possibly redacted as early as the later twelfth. What survives as book five is a seventeenth-century composite of that older material. And the Ars Goetia, the most notorious section, has a traceable and rather deflating pedigree. Its ultimate ancestor is the list in Johann Weyer’s Pseudomonarchia Daemonum; but not directly. The proximate source is the English translation printed in Reginald Scot’s Discoverie of Witchcraft, which Peterson attributes to Abraham Fleming rather than to Scot, and whose exemplar he identifies as the expanded edition of 1665, established by the unique errors and spellings that edition introduced. As Peterson puts it, the Goetia “does, in fact, seem dependant on Scot, faithfully copying his frequent mistranslations, elaborations, and omissions.” The list is reordered, four spirits added and one dropped.

Two dates in that paragraph will not sit together, and the difficulty should be stated rather than smoothed. A compilation assembled in the middle of the seventeenth century cannot copy errors that first entered print in 1665. Either the Ars Goetia reached the form we have later than the rest of the Lemegeton, or its compiler worked from one of the earlier printings of the Discoverie, which appeared in 1584 and again in 1651. The descent drawn in Chapter 11 runs the catalogue from the edition of 1584, because that is the printing whose contents that chapter quotes and counts. Which printing the compiler actually had on the table is a separate question, and it is left open here.

Weyer’s own purpose is the sharpest irony in this chapter. Johann Weyer (1515–1588) was a Dutch physician (city physician of Arnhem, later court doctor to the Duke of Cleves) and he catalogued demons in the course of arguing against the witch trials. His De praestigiis daemonum (1563) criticised the Malleus Maleficarum and the witch-hunting of the civil and ecclesiastical authorities, and he was among the first to publish systematic arguments against the persecutions. His position was narrower than it is usually reported to be, and the precision matters. Weyer affirmed the reality and power of demons (fallen angels who used supernatural powers against the kingdom of Heaven and who needed no human help) and concluded on that ground that the pact was pointless and legally void. What he voided was the pact and the maleficia, not the devil. He allowed that alleged acts might be fraud or poisoning, did not object to judicial enquiry of accused witches, and attributed apparently supernatural illness variously to melancholy, poisoning, malingering or unmediated demonic action. He also held learned magicians genuinely culpable, accusing popes, bishops, priests and monks of being magicians in league with the devil; he has been judged more concerned to inculpate magicians than to exculpate women. That judgement is not put in quotation marks here because the wording in circulation could not be traced to a named scholar for this edition, and an unattributed quotation is the one thing this book will not print.

He was also, from about the age of fifteen, a live-in student of Agrippa’s in Antwerp, which is why his denunciation of the spurious Fourth Book carried weight. So the most notorious demon-catalogue in Western magic was compiled by a sceptical physician trying to stop people being burned, by a man who had studied under Agrippa and defended his teacher’s actual work against forgery. It was then lifted, more or less wholesale, into the working grimoire that has carried it ever since.

The Arbatel and the seven governors

The last text in Turner’s 1655 volume is the Arbatel of Magick, first printed in Latin at Basel in 1575, and it is unlike everything else in this chapter. It contains no conjurations, no circles and no seals to draw. It is a book of aphorisms; and its system rests on seven governors called the Olympic spirits, each ruling the affairs of one planet.

GovernorGovernsAs the text states it
AratronSaturn“those things which in Astronomy are ascribed to the power of Saturn”; teaches alchemy, magic and physic; makes the barren fruitful
BethorJupiter“governeth those things which are ascribed to Jupiter”; raises to dignities, reconciles the spirits of the air
PhalegMars“ruleth those things which are attributed to Mars, the Prince of peace”
OchSun“governeth solar things”; gives perfect health, great wisdom, excellent spirits and perfect medicines
HagithVenus“governeth Venereous things”; makes fair, and adorns with beauty
OphielMercury“the governour of such things as are attributed to Mercury”; “he teacheth all Arts”
PhulMoon“governeth Lunary things”; healeth the dropsy; gives the spirits of the water

All seven attributions above are the 1655 text’s own words, not inferred from the order; though the order is itself the Chaldean sequence of Chapter 20, running from Saturn down to the Moon. Note the strangest line in the table: Mars, “the Prince of peace.” Whether that is Turner’s slip, the Latin’s irony, or a genuine doctrine that the planet of war governs the ending of wars, the text does not explain.

The Arbatel’s real distinction is its tone. Where the Lemegeton commands and constrains, the Arbatel advises: it warns that “a man that is a true Magician, is brought forth a Magician from his mothers womb,” that the governors “hear not the false Magicians, but expose them to the deceits of the devils,” and, quoting John the Baptist, that no man can do any thing of himself, except it be given him from above. It is the one book in this chapter that spends more effort on the operator’s character than on his equipment.

Agrippa and the Renaissance transmission

The channel through which all of this reached later practitioners is Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim (1486–1535), whose De occulta philosophia libri tres is the single most important synthesis of Renaissance magical thought. Book I appeared in 1531, published at Paris and Antwerp (the Cologne imprint of that year is often listed alongside them but is unattested in the catalogues); the complete three books followed at Cologne in 1533. The English translation by “J.F.” (probably John French, possibly James Freake) appeared in 1651 and is the version through which the work entered the English-speaking tradition.

The three books ascend deliberately through the levels of a magical cosmos. Book I treats natural or elemental magic: the properties of stones, herbs, animals and the human body, and the “occult virtues” Agrippa held to arise from hidden correspondences between the material world and higher principles. Book II treats celestial magic: stellar and planetary influence, and the construction of talismans to capture it. Book III treats intellectual or divine magic: theurgy, Kabbalah, ceremonial practice. Agrippa insists throughout that the true magus must also be a devout priest-philosopher, and he draws a firm line between holy magic and demonic sorcery, goetia.

Hold on to that line, because the Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy crosses it. Its earliest known imprint is Marburg, 1559, twenty-four years after Agrippa’s death, and it was falsely attributed to him, and contains explicit spirit-summoning instructions of a kind entirely absent from the authentic three books. Weyer, Agrippa’s own former student, identified it as a forgery. Much of what circulates as “Agrippa” in later grimoire literature is in fact this spurious fourth book, which means readers have often taken a pseudonymous appendix for the thing it was attached to.

What the datings add up to

Laid end to end, the Solomonic tradition runs: a legend of Solomon; a fourteenth- or fifteenth-century Italian text claiming him as author; a sixteenth-century sceptic’s demon catalogue; a seventeenth-century compilation that absorbed it; a spurious fourth book attached to a genuine 1533 masterwork; and a nineteenth-century translation by a founder of the Golden Dawn, through which the whole assemblage reached the modern world. Not one link in that chain is ancient. Every link is real, documented, and has a date. That is a more interesting story than the legend, and it is a true one.

The Heptameron

One more text belongs in this chapter, because it is the cleanest working system in the whole Solomonic orbit: the Heptameron, or Magical Elements, attributed (falsely, like everything else here) to the medieval physician Peter de Abano (d. c. 1316). Its first attested appearance is in print in the sixteenth century, and it reached English in the same 1655 volume as the geomancy of Chapter 24, Robert Turner’s translation of the Fourth Book.

Its organising idea is in its title: hepta, seven. One ritual frame, parameterised by the day of the week: each day with its own angel, its own perfume, and its own proper petitions, all riding on the planetary rulerships of Chapter 20. It is the day-side complement to the planetary hours: where the hours tell you when, the Heptameron supplies the who.

DayPlanetAngel of the day
SundaySunMichael
MondayMoonGabriel
TuesdayMarsSamael
WednesdayMercuryRaphael
ThursdayJupiterSachiel
FridayVenusAnael
SaturdaySaturnCassiel

Note the crossing with Chapter 15: the Heptameron’s day-angels put Michael with the Sun and Samael with Mars, where the banishing ritual’s quarter-angels put Michael at the fire quarter. The two systems assign the same names by different logics, day-rule against element, and both are “traditional.” This is the normal condition of the literature, and a practitioner who meets a contradiction between two tables has not found an error; they have found two sources.

The preparation of the working place is pure Key of Solomon discipline, and one passage earns its place for its rhythm alone. The operator, says the text, on the Lord’s day in the new of the moon, is to enter the place “clothed with clean white garments,” exorcise and bless it, and make a circle “with a sanctified coal,” writing the names of the angels in the outer ring and the names of God within; then to enter “fasting, and washed,” praying toward the east: “and that let him do six days, continuing washed.”

The other family: the printed grimoires

Everything above belongs to one tradition, copied by hand and attributed to Solomon. Beside it runs a second, printed rather than copied, French rather than Latin or Italian, and cheaper in every sense: small duodecimo volumes sold through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, promising treasure, invisibility and command of spirits. They are the books most people picture when they hear the word grimoire, and their dates are worth setting out because almost every one of them lies about its own.

A. E. Waite catalogued the family in 1913 and had no patience with it, which makes him a useful guide to the dating even where he is contemptuous of the contents.

BookWhat it claimsWhat it is
Sworn Book of Honorius
Liber Juratus		 the work of a Honorius, master of magic genuinely medieval: fourteenth century, in manuscript, not printed
Grimoire of Honorius the same authority as the above a different book: 1629, and routinely confused with the Sworn Book
Grimorium Verum “Published by Alibeck the Egyptian” at Memphis, 1517 mid-eighteenth century, and Roman
Grand Grimoire
later the Red Dragon		 antiquity by association eighteenth century, no older than the last
True Black Magic a manuscript found at Jerusalem in the Sepulchre of Solomon its own imprint says Rome, 1750
The Black Pullet
and its offspring		 very little, in the end late eighteenth century, and barely pretending

Two men called Honorius

The confusion in the first two rows is old and still current. The Sworn Book is the serious one: a fourteenth-century manuscript work which Waite calls “one of the most historical and notable Rituals” of its kind, and which “has no title or other determinate name, but it appears from the text that it was understood to be the Sworn Book of Honorius.” Its prologue is a remarkable piece of framing: the bishops, deceived by demons, have condemned magic, and in answer the masters of magic are convoked to defend it: eight hundred and eleven of them.

The Grimoire of Honorius is a printed book of 1629 trading on the same name, and Waite notes that it “has been sometimes referred erroneously to the same period of the previous century.” Three hundred years separate the two, one is a manuscript and one is a commercial print, and a modern edition of either is liable to carry a title implying it is the other.

Memphis is Rome

The Grimorium Verum is the clearest case in the genre of an imprint doing the work a text cannot. Its title page offers a translation from the Hebrew by a Dominican Jesuit, two orders which are not the same order, published by Alibeck the Egyptian at Memphis in 1517. Waite’s verdict is one line and it is worth the whole paragraph:

The date specified in the title of the Grimorium Verum is undeniably fraudulent; the work belongs to the middle of the eighteenth century, and Memphis is Rome.

Not a mistaken date but a manufactured one, with a manufactured city and a manufactured translator attached. Separate that from the misdatings elsewhere in this book. Ficino believed the Hermetica ancient and was wrong; Mathers printed the argument against the Zohar’s antiquity in his own introduction. Here nobody is mistaken about anything. The false imprint is the first sentence of the sales pitch, and the buyer in 1750 was expected to enjoy it.

Of the last row Waite is blunter still, and the phrasing is exact enough to be worth quoting: the Black Pullet and its relatives are “quite unserious publications, which can scarcely be called spurious, as they are almost without pretence.” A book has to claim something before it can be accused of claiming falsely.

Why the imprints are evidence

Read the middle column of the table as a set of marketing decisions and a pattern appears. What sells a grimoire is age, foreignness and danger: Egypt, Jerusalem, a Hebrew original, a sepulchre, a date two centuries before the buyer. The same three ingredients recur from 1517-that-is-1750 to the tarot’s Egyptian pedigree in Chapter 25, and they were still working in the nineteenth century.

The practical consequence for a reader is narrow and useful. In this family the title page is not evidence about the book; it is part of the book, and should be read with the same suspicion as anything else inside it.

The Arbatel was first printed in Latin at Basel in 1575. That 1655 wording was read in a modern facsimile whose typographic setting carries its own copyright, which is why the geomancy of Chapter 24 goes to an original printing instead.

The printed grimoires: Waite, The Book of Ceremonial Magic (1911; the 1913 printing is the one cited elsewhere in this book), read from the Internet Archive copy a.-e.-waite-the-book-of-ceremonial-magic. His is the authority for every date in the table above: the fourteenth century for the Sworn Book and his description of it as having no determinate title, 1629 for the Grimoire of Honorius and the error he notes about it, the mid-eighteenth century and Rome for the Grimorium Verum, the Grand Grimoire as no older, and the Black Pullet group as late eighteenth century. The title-page wording of the Grimorium Verum and of True Black Magic, including Alibeck the Egyptian, Memphis, 1517 and the Sepulchre of Solomon, is quoted from his catalogue of the imprints rather than from the books themselves; this edition has seen none of these grimoires and quotes none of their contents. Waite is a hostile witness to this literature and says so freely: remember it when reading his verdicts, though it bears on his opinions rather than on his dates. The observation that a false imprint is a claim rather than a mistake, and the reading of the middle column as marketing, are this book’s own.

Chapter XIDemonology Reference

Every tradition in this book keeps lists: of hours, of herbs, of names of God. Demonology is what happened when the same instinct was turned on the enemy. Its literature is not, for the most part, a literature of horror; it is a literature of filing. Spirits have names, ranks, offices, retinues counted in legions, and fixed hours at which they may be approached. The catalogue is the genre. This chapter reads the catalogue across fifteen hundred years (the oldest surviving interrogation of demons, the Renaissance list printed in order to be disbelieved, the English translation that carried it anyway, and the reply of a king who named both authors in print) and then the working itself, exactly as the sources give it: the conditions, the citation, the binding, and the licence to depart, printed from the same leaves as the catalogue, beside the confutation their own printer set two pages after them.

The ring, and the oldest catalogue

The ancestor of every list in this chapter is a Greek pseudepigraphon in which Solomon himself narrates how the demons were put to work on the Temple. F. C. Conybeare, who put the Testament of Solomon into English in 1898, placed the core of it around the first century of our era (his dating, argued from its debts to the Enoch literature and its nearness to the New Testament’s world) and the text he translated begins not with a rite but with a labour dispute: a demon is taking half of a workman’s pay and food, and the workman is wasting away. Solomon prays, and the help that arrives is an object:

And it came about through my prayer that grace was given to me from the Lord Sabaôth by Michael his archangel. [He brought me] a little ring, having a seal consisting of an engraved stone, and said to me: “Take, O Solomon, king, son of David, the gift which the Lord God has sent thee, the highest Sabaôth. With it thou shalt lock up all the demons of the earth, male and female; and with their help thou shalt build up Jerusalem. [But] thou [must] wear this seal of God. And this engraving of the seal of the ring sent thee is a Pentalpha.”

The pentalpha is the five-pointed star, Conybeare’s note glosses it as five interlaced A’s, and the reader who has met the pentagram in Chapter 8 should notice where this one sits: not drawn in the air but engraved on a stone, worn on the hand, and delegated: Solomon lends the ring to the boy with instructions to throw it at the demon’s chest and say, “In the name of God, King Solomon calls thee hither.” What follows the ring is not an exorcism but an induction. Each spirit brought before Solomon is made to state its name, the star or sign it belongs to, what it does, and, the detail that organises the whole book, the name of the angel by which it is thwarted. Ornias, the pay-stealing demon of the opening, is set to hew stones. Asmodeus gives an account of himself that agrees with the Book of Tobit. Thirty-six spirits of the zodiac’s divisions appear in a block, each with its ailment and its remedy-formula. Name, office, constraint: the entire later literature is already here, and it is a personnel file.

From office-book to print

The medieval heirs of the Testament were manuscript registers, books “of the offices of spirits”, circulating in the same world as the Solomonic handbooks of Chapter 10. What pulled the catalogue into print was, of all things, a book written against the witch trials. In 1577 Johann Weyer (the physician whose De praestigiis daemonum had argued since 1563 that the accused were deluded and ill rather than guilty) appended to his treatise a catalogue he titled Pseudomonarchia daemonum, the false monarchy of demons: sixty-nine spirits with their ranks, shapes, offices and legions, printed as an exhibit of what the conjuring books actually contained. Seven years later Reginald Scot, an English gentleman writing the most radical attack on witch-belief of the century, carried the whole list into English inside The discoverie of witchcraft; and his margin names the source plainly: J. Wierus in Pseudomonarchia dæmonum. Neither man believed a word of it. Both printed it. That is how a working conjuror’s register became the most accessible demon-list in Europe: through two authors who published it to be laughed at, and were read by people who did not laugh.

The inventarie itself

Scot introduces the list with open mockery (conjurors, unlike mere witches, “fetch divels out of hell, and angels out of heaven” and undertake “to doo as much as God himselfe can doo”) and then promises that they “call up by name, and have at their commandement seventie and nine principall and princelie divels, who have under them, as their ministers, a great multitude of legions of pettie divels.” The chapter that follows is headed like a stock-take:

An inventarie of the names, shapes, powers, governement, and effects of divels and spirits, of their severall segniories and degrees: a strange discourse woorth the reading.

Their first and principall king (which is of the power of the east) is called Baëll; who when he is conjured up, appeareth with three heads; the first, like a tode; the second, like a man; the third, like a cat. He speaketh with a hoarse voice, he maketh a man go invisible, he hath under his obedience and rule sixtie and six legions of divels.

Sixty-seven entries follow Baëll, each in the same form. Agares “commeth up mildlie in the likenes of a faire old man, riding upon a crocodile, and carrieng a hawke on his fist,” teaches languages “presentlie,” fetches back runaways, and causes earthquakes. Read as a set, the offices are a mirror held up to the customers: the spirits teach languages, logic, astronomy and “all handicrafts,” find treasure and things hidden, procure “the especiall love of women,” reconcile friends and enemies, confer dignities and overthrow them, and make a man invisible. Nothing in the list wants for the soul; everything in it wants tuition, money, love and standing. Here and there the bureaucratic surface cracks and something older shows through: Phoenix, a great marquess who sings “manie sweet notes” in a child’s voice before the conjuror, “hopeth to returne to the seventh throne after a thousand two hundreth yeares”: a demoted angel counting the years of his sentence.

The arithmetic is kept with the same solemnity. Baëll rules sixty-six legions, Agares thirty-one, Phoenix twenty; and the chapter closes with the driest sentence in the whole literature:

¶ Note that a legion is 6666. and now by multiplication count how manie legions doo arise out of everie particular.

The numbers in this chapter do not add up, and the failure is instructive at every step. Scot’s preface promises “seventie and nine” principal devils. The Latin list he was translating, Weyer’s, contains sixty-nine. And the inventarie Scot actually prints contains sixty-eight: reading the catalogue leaf by leaf and counting the entries shows that Pruflas, Weyer’s fourth spirit, is silently missing from the English, and no edition of Scot notices the loss. Seventy-nine promised, sixty-nine in the source, sixty-eight delivered: three numbers on adjacent pages, no two of them equal. The page teaches the lesson this book keeps meeting: the numbers in this literature are part of the rhetoric, and they should be counted rather than repeated.

The inventarie entire

Because the catalogue is the genre, it is given here whole: every spirit Scot prints, in his order and his spellings, with rank and legions as the inventarie states them. Each entry in the original runs a paragraph (shape, offices, conditions) and a selection is quoted at length below the table; the compressed columns here are an index to the sixty-eight, not a substitute for them. A dash means the entry states no number; Bifrons and Decarabia are given no rank; Haagenti’s thirty-three is stated as “as manie legions as Zagan”; and Paimon’s two hundred are “partlie of the order of angels, and partlie of potestates,” with twenty-five more in the host of the two kings who attend him. Every figure was read on the page it stands on.
