Nine entries at length

The compressed table loses what makes the inventarie worth reading: the operative conditions embedded in the entries, and the personalities. These are the entries a working conjuror needed most, quoted as Scot prints them.

Bileth, whose entry is a protocol in miniature: “When he is called up by an exorcist, he appeareth rough and furious, to deceive him. Then let the exorcist or conjuror take heed to himself, and to allaie his courage, let him hold a hazell bat in his hand, wherewithall he must reach out toward the east and south, and make a triangle without besides the circle; but if he hold not out his hand unto him, and he bid him come in, and he still refuse the bond or chaine of spirits; let the conjuror proceed to reading, and by and by he will submit himselfe, and come in, and doo whatsoever the exorcist commandeth him, and he shalbe safe. … Also, if he be cited by an exorcist, alwaies a silver ring of the middle finger of the left hand must be held against the exorcists face, as they doo for Amaimon.”

Paimon: “Note, that at the calling up of him, the exorcist must looke towards the northwest, bicause there is his house. When he is called up, let the exorcist receive him constantlie without feare, let him aske what questions or demands he list, and no doubt he shall obteine the same of him. … There follow him two hundred legions, partlie of the order of angels, and partlie of potestates. Note that if Paimon be cited alone by an offering or sacrifice, two kings followe him; to wit, Beball & Abalam, & other potentates: in his host are twentie five legions.”

Beliall, in whose entry the brazen vessel appears: “If he will not submit himselfe, let the bond of spirits be read: the spirits chaine is sent for him, wherewith wise Salomon gathered them together with their legions in a brasen vessell, where were inclosed among all the legions seventie two kings, of whome the cheefe was Bileth, the second was Beliall, the third Asmoday, and above a thousand thousand legions. Without doubt (I must confesse) I learned this of my maister Salomon; but he told me not why he gathered them together, and shut them up so: but I beleeve it was for the pride of this Beliall.”

Astaroth: “He talketh willinglie of the creator of spirits, and of their fall, and how they sinned and fell: he saith he fell not of his owne accord. … Let everie exorcist take heed, that he admit him not too neere him, bicause of his stinking breath. And therefore let the conjuror hold neere to his face a magicall ring, and that shall defend him.”

Sidonay, alias Asmoday: “When the conjuror exerciseth this office, let him be abroad, let him be warie and standing on his feete; if his cap be on his head, he will cause all his dooings to be bewraied, which if he doo not, the exorcist shalbe deceived by Amaymon in everie thing. But so soone as he seeth him in the forme aforesaid, he shall call him by his name, saieng; Thou art Asmoday: he will not denie it, and by and by he boweth downe to the ground; he giveth the ring of vertues … he hath under his power seventie two legions.”

Gaap, in whose entry the tradition dates itself: “There were certeine necromancers that offered sacrifices and burnt offerings unto him; and to call him up, they exercised an art, saieng that Salomon the wise made it. Which is false: for it was rather Cham, the sonne of Noah, who after the floud began first to invocate wicked spirits. … It is to be noted, that if anie exorcist have the art of Bileth, and cannot make him stand before him, nor see him, I may not bewraie how and declare the meanes to conteine him, bicause it is abhomination, and for that I have learned nothing from Salomon of his dignitie and office.”

Focalor, the smallest command in the list: “he killeth men, and drowneth them in the waters, and overturneth ships of warre, commanding and ruling both winds and seas. And let the conjuror note, that if he bid him hurt no man, he willinglie consenteth thereto: he hopeth after 1000. yeares to returne to the seventh throne, but he is deceived, he hath three legions.”

Andras, the reason the books keep warning: “he is seene in an angels shape with a head like a blacke night raven, riding upon a blacke and a verie strong woolfe, flourishing with a sharpe sword in his hand, he can kill the maister, the servant, and all assistants, he is author of discords, and ruleth thirtie legions.”

Ose, the strangest office in the catalogue: “he maketh one cunning in the liberall sciences, he answereth truelie of divine and secret things, he transformeth a mans shape, and bringeth a man to that madnes, that he thinketh himselfe to be that which he is not; as that he is a king or a pope, or that he weareth a crowne on his head, Durátque id regnum ad horam” — and the delusion of kingship lasts an hour.

The rest of the catalogue keeps the same texture, and the one-line wonders deserve their line. Orobas “deceiveth none, nor suffereth anie to be tempted”: the one honest spirit in the list. Amduscias, a duke in the shape of a unicorn, gives concerts: “trumpets and all musicall instruments may be heard and not seene,” and trees bend to the conjuror’s will. Decarabia “commeth like a ✱” (the reprint sets a printer’s star where the Latin says he appears as a star in a pentacle) and makes birds fly before the exorcist, tame, drinking and singing. Gomory, the one spirit who appears “like a faire woman, with a duchesse crownet about hir midle, riding on a camell.” Shax steals money out of kings’ houses and “carrieth it backe after 1200. yeares, if he be commanded.” Marchosias “hopeth after 1200. yeares to returne to the seventh throne, but he is deceived in that hope”: the inventarie keeps actuarial tables on redemption, and they all read: denied.

The protocol of audiences

Collect the conditions scattered through the entries and a complete court etiquette emerges. Direction: face the northwest for Paimon, “bicause there is his house.” Posture: for Asmoday, be standing, in the open, and bare-headed: the cap on the head betrays the whole working. Address: call the spirit by name to its face, “Thou art Asmoday,” and it cannot deny itself. Courtesy: Bileth is received “courteouslie,” and glorified “in his pride,” “bicause he saith nothing without other princes.” Defence: the silver ring on the middle finger of the left hand, held against the exorcist’s face for Bileth and Amaymon, and the “magicall ring” held to the face against Astaroth’s breath. Verification: several spirits (Shax, Furfur, Flauros) lie at large and speak truth only inside a triangle. Escalation: the hazel bat and the triangle beyond the circle for a furious Bileth, and the “bond or chaine of spirits” read aloud until submission. And schedule: for the hours are the frame the whole court runs on, the same logic that runs through the planetary hours of Chapter 20: power is real but scheduled, and the operator’s skill is knowing the timetable.

At the end of this material Scot’s margin discloses, with the exactness of a man entering evidence, where it all came from: “This was the work of one T. R. written in faire letters of red & blacke upon parchment, and made by him, Ann. 1570. to the maintenance of his living, the edifieng of the poore, and the glorie of gods holie name: as he himselfe saith.” A jobbing conjuror’s working manuscript, copied out in red and black in 1570 to pay its author’s rent, quoted verbatim by the man who wanted the whole trade abolished; there is no better emblem of how this literature survives. The believers wrote it; the unbelievers published it; the readers decided for themselves.

The forme of adjuring

The fourth and fourteenth chapters of Scot’s fifteenth book print the working itself, from the same manuscript stratum as the hours; and the reprint’s margins collate it with Weyer’s Latin, noting where the parchment and the Pseudomonarchia differ (“fast not in Wier”). It is given here as the sources give it. Read the conditions as a list before the words, because they are the operative doctrine in miniature: the operator must know the name and the office (the inventarie is the prerequisite, not an appendix) must fast and be clean, must never work alone, must offer no sacrifice, and must dismiss what he has called. On the leaf facing the licence, the reprint carries the woodcut of the conjuring knife, its blade graven AGLA: the same consecrated-instrument logic as the sword of Chapter 8.

The forme of adjuring or citing of the spirits aforesaid to arise and appeare

The conditions. “When you will have anie spirit, you must know his name and office; you must also fast, and be cleane from all pollusion, three or foure daies before; so will the spirit be the more obedient unto you. Then make a circle, and call up the spirit with great intention, and holding a ring in your hand, rehearse in your owne name, and your companions (for one must alwaies be with you) this praier following, and so no spirit shall annoie you, and your purpose shall take effect.”

The praier. “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ the ✠ father ✠ and the sonne ✠ and the Holie-ghost ✠ holie trinitie and unseparable unitie, I call upon thee, that thou maiest be my salvation and defense, and the protection of my bodie and soule, and of all my goods through the vertue of thy holie crosse, and through the vertue of thy passion, I beseech thee O Lord Jesus Christ, by the merits of thy blessed mother S. Marie, and of all thy saints, that thou give me grace and divine power over all the wicked spirits, so as which of them soever I doo call by name, they may come by and by from everie coast, and accomplish my will, that they neither be hurtfull nor fearefull unto me, but rather obedient and diligent about me. And through thy vertue streightlie commanding them, let them fulfill my commandements, Amen.” The prayer continues for two further pages in the same register — Holie, holie, holie, Lord God of sabboth, litanies of divine names, the life of Christ recited event by event, the petition for power to draw the spirits, to tie and bind them, and to loose them — and closes Fiat ✠ fiat ✠ fiat, Amen.

The binding. When the spirit is appeared, it is held with a second form. The manuscript gives it for the spirit Bealphares: “I charge thee Bealphares, that thou shalt not depart out of my sight, nor yet to alter thy bodilie shape, that thou art appeared in, nor anie power shalt thou have of our bodies or soules, earthlie or ghostlie, but to be obedient to me, and to the words of my conjuration, that be written in this booke.” And then the terms of the audience: “When he is thus bound, aske him what thing thou wilt, and he will tell thee, and give thee all things that thou wilt request of him, without anie sacrifice dooing to him, and without forsaking thy God, that is, thy maker.”

A licence for the spirit to depart. “Go unto the place predestinated and appointed for thee, where thy Lord GOD hath appointed thee, untill I shall call thee againe. Be thou readie unto me and to my call, as often as I shall call thee, upon paine of everlasting damnation.” If he will not depart, the last conjuration is repeated, and the dismissal made absolute: “that thou depart from this place, without hurt or damage of anie bodie, or of anie deed to be doone; that all creatures may knowe, that our Lord is of all power, most mightiest.” Against outright refusal the manuscript keeps one last escalation, the malediction: “And the malediction of God the father omnipotent, the sonne and the holie ghost, descend upon thee, and dwell alwaies with thee, except thou doo depart without damage of us, or of any creature, or anie other evill deed to be doone: & thou to go to the place predestinated. And by our Lord Jesus Christ I doo else send thee to the great pit of hell.” Yet the forme ends in peace, not in power: “The peace of Jesus Christ bee betweene us and you; in the name of the father, and of the sonne, and of the Holie-ghost: Amen” — and then the opening of John’s Gospel, recited to the words full of grace and truth.

Notice what the sequence refuses as firmly as what it performs. No sacrifice: stated in the plainest terms the manuscript has. No working alone. No dismissal omitted: the licence is not a courtesy but a load-bearing part of the operation, and every later text in this lineage keeps it. The operator who binds and does not loose has, on the tradition’s own account, left the operation unfinished, which is the same doctrine the closing banishing of Chapter 15 carries in the modern curriculum.

The same working, four centuries on: the Goetia’s apparatus

Everything Scot printed in fragments, the Ars Goetia, compiled in the mid-seventeenth century and printed in 1904, systematises. The catalogue grows to seventy-two, the brazen vessel’s own number: the spellings shift (Leraie to Leraje, Sidonay’s alias Asmoday becomes the name), and spirits absent from Weyer and Scot appear: Vassago, Seere, Dantalion, Andromalius among them. Each spirit now has a seal, and the seal is the working instrument: after Samigina’s entry the text says, “And his Seal is this, which is to be worn before the Magician when he is Invocator.” The seals are graded by rank into metals: kings in gold, marquises in silver, dukes in copper, princes in tin, presidents in mercury, earls in copper and silver “alike equal,” and one solitary knight, Furcas, in lead. The binding hours of Scot’s third chapter return converted to clock time: “the Chief Kings may be bound from 9 till 12 o’clock at Noon, and from 3 till Sunset; Marquises may be bound from 3 in the afternoon till 9 at Night, and from 9 at Night till Sunrise … and Counties or Earls any hour of the Day, so it be in Woods, or in any other places whither men resort not, or where no noise is.”

The apparatus is a complete kit, and its continuities with everything above are exact. The Magic Ring or Disc, “to be made in gold or silver … held before the face of the exorcist to preserve him from the stinking sulphurous fumes and flaming breath of the Evil Spirits”: Scot’s silver ring against Bileth and the ring held to the face against Astaroth’s breath, made standard equipment. The Hexagram of Solomon, drawn “on parchment of a calf’s skin, and worn at the skirt of thy white vestment,” shown to the spirits to compel human shape. The Triangle of Art, set outside the circle exactly as Bileth’s entry demanded, now with directions: “this triangle is to be placed toward that quarter whereunto the Spirit belongeth. And the base of the triangle is to be nearest unto the Circle, the apex pointing in the direction of the quarter of the Spirit.” The other requisites: “a sceptre, a sword, a mitre, a cap, a long white robe of linen … also a girdle of lion’s skin three inches broad, with all the names written about it which be round the outmost part of the Magical Circle,” perfumes, a chafing-dish of charcoal, anointing oil, and “fair water to wash thyself in”: with an Adoration at the Bath (“Thou shalt purge me with hyssop, O Lord!”) and another at the Induing of the Vestments, which is the bath-and-garments sequence of Chapter 8 in its goetic dress.

The spoken sequence is likewise the 1570 forme grown formal, and its stations deserve quoting. The First Conjuration opens, in the spelling of the edition’s own archaic appendix, “I invoke and move thee, O thou, Spirit N.: and being exalted above ye in the power of the Most High, I say unto thee, Obey! in the name Beralensis, Baldachiensis, Paumachia, and Apologiae Sedes: and of the mighty ones who govern, spirits, Liachidae and ministers of the House of Death: and by the Chief Prince of the seat of Apologia in the Ninth Legion, I do invoke thee and by invoking conjure thee.” If the spirit refuses, the conjurations escalate to the Curse: the spirit’s name and seal, written and bound into a box, are “choken in sulphurous stinking substances, and burned in this material fire,” while the exorcist declares, “in the name Iehovah and by the power and dignity of these three names, Tetragrammaton, Anaphaxeton, and Primeumaton, I do cast thee, O thou wicked and disobedient Spirit N., into the Lake of Fire”; and the box goes into the flame until the spirit comes, whereupon the fire is quenched and “a sweet perfume” made. Obedience arrived, the register changes completely: “Welcome Spirit N., O most noble king! I say thou art welcome unto me, because I have called thee through Him who has created Heaven, and Earth, and Hell, and all that is in them contained, and because also thou hast obeyed.” The demand is put with the lamen shown: “By the Pentacle of Solomon have I called thee! Give unto me a true answer”; and the working closes with the License to Depart:

O thou Spirit N., because thou hast diligently answered unto my demands, and hast been very ready and willing to come at my call, I do here license thee to depart unto thy proper place; without causing harm or danger unto man or beast. Depart, then, I say, and be thou very ready to come at my call, being duly exorcised and conjured by the sacred rites of magic. I charge thee to withdraw peaceably and quietly, and the peace of God be ever continued between thee and me! Amen!

“After thou hast given the Spirit license to depart, thou art not to go out of the circle until he or they be gone, and until thou shalt have made prayers and rendered thanks unto God.” The same doctrine as the 1570 parchment, the same doctrine as the closing banishing of Chapter 15: the dismissal is part of the operation, and the operator who skips it has not finished working; he has stopped in the middle.

The seventy-two, each with its office

The inventarie above is Weyer’s list in Scot’s English, and it is the older of the two. The Goetia’s own list is the younger, the longer and the one the modern tradition actually uses, and this chapter has so far described its apparatus without printing its contents. Here they are: all seventy-two, in the order the text gives them, each with the rank it holds, the shape it is said to arrive in, what it is called for, and the number of legions under it. Read down the offices rather than the names and the roster stops looking like a bestiary and starts looking like what it is: an index of wants. Somebody wanted languages, somebody wanted a lost thing found, somebody wanted the thief brought back with the goods, somebody wanted to know what another person was thinking, and somebody wanted a tower built and furnished with weapons.

Three cautions before the list. The first is that the ranks are not decoration: a king is approached differently from a knight, and four of these entries carry explicit handling instructions: Beleth and Berith require the silver ring held to the face, Asmoday must be called abroad with the operator’s head uncovered and challenged by name, and Astaroth must not be let near because of his breath. The second is that several are frankly said to lie: Haures, Shax and Furfur will deceive the operator unless commanded into the triangle first, and Belial does not stay truthful for an hour unless constrained. The third is that a good number of these offices are injuries to other people: sowing discord, taking away sight or hearing, afflicting with sores, drowning men, burning up the operator’s enemies. Those are printed here because they are what the source says and because concealing them would misrepresent the document; they are not printed as instructions, and this book gives no operation aimed at harming a named person. The rule stated at the front of this chapter holds for its roster too.

1. Baël: King, ruling in the East; 66 legions. Appears as divers shapes: sometimes a cat, sometimes a toad, sometimes a man, and sometimes all these forms at once; speaks hoarsely. Office: makes the operator go invisible.

2. Agares (Agreas): Duke, under the Power of the East; 31 legions. Appears as an old fair man riding on a crocodile, a goshawk on his fist, mild in appearance. Office: makes those that stand still run, and brings back runaways; teaches all languages; destroys dignities spiritual and temporal; causes earthquakes. Of the Order of Virtues.

3. Vassago: Prince, of the same nature as Agares; 26 legions. Appears as nothing: the entry gives him no shape. Office: declares things past and to come, and discovers all things hid or lost. Of a good nature.

4. Samigina (Gamigin): Marquis; 30 legions. Appears as a little horse or ass, changing to human shape at the Master’s request; speaks with a hoarse voice. Office: teaches all liberal sciences, and gives account of the souls of those that died in sin.

5. Marbas: President; 36 legions. Appears as a great lion, afterwards human at the Master’s request. Office: answers truly of things hidden or secret; causes diseases and cures them; gives wisdom and knowledge in the mechanical arts; changes men into other shapes.

6. Valefor: Duke; 10 legions. Appears as a lion with an ass’s head, bellowing. Office: a good familiar; but tempts those he is familiar to into stealing.

7. Amon: Marquis, great in power, and most stern; 40 legions. Appears as a wolf with a serpent’s tail vomiting flame; at command, a man with dog’s teeth set in a raven’s head, or a man with a raven’s head simply. Office: tells all things past and to come; procures feuds, and reconciles controversies between friends.

8. Barbatos: Duke, appears when the Sun is in Sagittarius, with four noble kings and their troops; 30 legions. Appears as nothing further: the entry describes his retinue and not his shape. Office: gives understanding of the singing of birds and the voices of other creatures, such as the barking of dogs; breaks open hidden treasure laid by the enchantments of magicians; knows all things past and to come; conciliates friends and those in power. Of the Order of Virtues, of which some part he retains still.

9. Paimon: King, very obedient unto Lucifer; observed towards the West; 200 legions. Appears as a man crowned most gloriously, seated on a dromedary, preceded by a host of spirits with trumpets, cymbals and all other music; a great voice, roaring at his first coming, his speech such that the magician cannot understand unless he compels him. Office: teaches all arts and sciences and other secret things; declares what the earth is and what holds it up in the waters, and what mind is and where it is; gives and confirms dignity; binds any man subject to the magician; gives good familiars. Of the Order of Dominations. Called alone he must be made an offering, and two kings attend him, Labal and Abalim, with twenty-five legions of Potentates.

10. Buer: President; 50 legions. Appears as Sagittary itself, which the text says is his shape when the Sun is there. Office: teaches philosophy moral and natural, the logic art, and the virtues of all herbs and plants; heals all distempers in man; gives good familiars.

11. Gusion: Duke, great and strong; 40 legions. Appears as a xenopilus. Office: tells all things past, present and to come, and shows the meaning and resolution of any question asked; conciliates and reconciles friendships; gives honour and dignity.

12. Sitri: Prince; 60 legions. Appears as at first a leopard’s head with the wings of a gryphon; after the command of the Master of the Exorcism, human shape, and that very beautiful. Office: inflames men with women’s love and women with men’s, and causes them to show themselves naked if it be desired.

13. Beleth (Bileth, Bilet): King, mighty and terrible; 85 legions. Appears as rides a pale horse, trumpets and all other music playing before him; very furious at his first appearance. Office: causes all the love that may be, of men and of women, until the Master Exorcist has had his desire fulfilled. Of the Order of Powers. He must be met with a hazel wand struck out toward the south and east and commanded into a triangle outside the circle; if he will not enter it at threats, the bonds and charms are rehearsed before him. He is then to be received courteously, and the operator must wear a silver ring on the middle finger of the left hand, held against the face: the scan’s footnote says it is to protect him from the flaming breath of the enraged spirit.

14. Leraje (Leraikha, Leraie): Marquis, great in power; 30 legions. Appears as an archer clad in green, carrying a bow and quiver. Office: causes great battles and contests, and makes wounds made with arrows by archers putrefy. He belongs to Sagittary.

15. Eligos: Duke; 60 legions. Appears as a goodly knight carrying a lance, an ensign and a serpent. Office: discovers hidden things and knows things to come, and of wars, and how the soldiers will or shall meet; causes the love of lords and great persons.

16. Zepar: Duke; 26 legions. Appears as red apparel and armour, like a soldier. Office: causes women to love men and brings them together in love; also makes them barren.

17. Botis: President and Earl; 60 legions. Appears as at the first show an ugly viper; at the magician’s command a human shape with great teeth and two horns, carrying a bright sharp sword. Office: tells all things past and to come, and reconciles friends and foes.

18. Bathin: Duke, mighty and strong; 30 legions. Appears as a strong man with the tail of a serpent, sitting on a pale-coloured horse. Office: knows the virtues of herbs and precious stones, and can transport men suddenly from one country to another.

19. Sallos (Saleos): Duke, great and mighty; 30 legions. Appears as a gallant soldier riding a crocodile, a ducal crown on his head, but peaceably. Office: causes the love of women to men and of men to women.

20. Purson: King; 22 legions. Appears as comely, like a man with a lion’s face, carrying a cruel viper and riding a bear; many trumpets sounding before him. Office: knows all things hidden, discovers treasure, and tells all things past, present and to come; can take a body either human or aerial; answers truly of all earthly things both secret and divine, and of the creation of the world; brings forth good familiars. His legions are partly of the Order of Virtues and partly of Thrones.

21. Marax: Earl and President, written Morax in some codices, though the 1904 editor prefers Marax; 30 legions. Appears as a great bull with a man’s face. Office: makes men very knowing in astronomy and all other liberal sciences; gives good familiars, wise, knowing the virtues of herbs and of precious stones.

22. Ipos: Earl and Prince, mighty; 36 legions. Appears as an angel with a lion’s head, a goose’s foot and a hare’s tail. Office: knows all things past, present and to come; makes men witty and bold.

23. Aim: Duke, great and strong; 26 legions. Appears as a very handsome man in body, but with three heads: the first like a serpent, the second like a man having two stars on his forehead, the third like a calf; rides a viper and carries a firebrand. Office: with the firebrand he sets cities, castles and great places on fire; makes the operator witty in all manner of ways, and gives true answers unto private matters.

24. Naberius: Marquis, most valiant; 19 legions. Appears as a black crane fluttering about the circle; speaks with a hoarse voice. Office: makes men cunning in all arts and sciences, but especially in rhetoric; restores lost dignities and honours.

25. Glasya-Labolas: President and Earl, mighty; 36 legions. Appears as a dog with wings like a gryphon. Office: teaches all arts and sciences in an instant, and is an author of bloodshed and manslaughter; teaches all things past and to come; if desired, causes the love both of friends and of foes; can make a man go invisible.

26. Buné (Bimé, Bim): Duke, strong, great and mighty; 30 legions. Appears as a dragon with three heads, one like a dog, one like a gryphon, and one like a man; speaks with a high and comely voice. Office: changes the place of the dead and causes the spirits under him to gather together upon sepulchres; gives riches, and makes a man wise and eloquent; gives true answers unto demands. He has two seals, and the printing notes that the last is the best.

27. Ronové: Marquis and Earl; 19 legions. Appears as a monster. Office: teaches the art of rhetoric very well; gives good servants, knowledge of tongues, and favours with friends or foes.

28. Berith (Beale, Beal, Bofry, Bolfry): Duke, mighty, great and terrible; the two other names were given him by men of later times; 26 legions. Appears as a soldier in red clothing, riding a red horse, a crown of gold upon his head; speaks with a very clear and subtle voice. Office: gives true answers past, present and to come; turns all metals into gold; gives dignities and confirms them unto man. The ring must be used in calling him forth, as with Beleth.

29. Astaroth: Duke, mighty and strong; 40 legions. Appears as a hurtful angel riding on an infernal beast like a dragon, carrying a viper in his right hand; his breath is noisome, and he must in no wise be let approach too near: the magician holds the magical ring near his face and that will defend him. Office: gives true answers of things past, present and to come, and discovers all secrets; will declare wittingly how the spirits fell, and the reason of his own fall; makes men wonderfully knowing in all liberal sciences.

30. Forneus: Marquis, mighty and great; 29 legions. Appears as a great sea-monster. Office: teaches and makes men wonderfully knowing in the art of rhetoric; causes men to have a good name and the knowledge and understanding of tongues; makes one beloved of his foes as well as of his friends. His legions are partly of the Order of Thrones and partly of Angels.

31. Foras: President, mighty; 29 legions. Appears as a strong man in human shape. Office: gives men the understanding of the virtues of all herbs and precious stones; teaches the arts of logic and ethics in all their parts; if desired makes men invisible, and to live long, and to be eloquent. The 1904 editor notes that one or two codices read “invincible” for “invisible,” and that the majority read invisible.

32. Asmoday (Asmodai): King, strong and powerful; first and choicest under the power of Amaymon, and goes before all other; 72 legions. Appears as three heads: the first like a bull, the second like a man, the third like a ram; the tail of a serpent, flames of fire issuing from his mouth, and feet webbed like a goose’s; sits upon an infernal dragon and bears a lance with a banner. Office: gives the ring of virtues; teaches arithmetic, astronomy, geometry and all handicrafts absolutely; gives true and full answers; makes one invincible; shows where treasure lies and guards it. He is called abroad, the exorcist standing on his feet the whole time with his cap off; if it be on, Amaymon will deceive him. As soon as he is seen in the shape aforesaid he is to be asked “Art thou Asmoday?”, which he will not deny, and by and by he will bow down to the ground.

33. Gäap: President and Prince, mighty; 66 legions. Appears as a man, when the Sun is in some of the southern signs, going before four great and mighty kings as if he were a guide to conduct them on their way. Office: makes men insensible or ignorant, and in philosophy and all the liberal sciences makes them knowing; causes love or hatred; teaches the operator to consecrate those things that belong to the dominion of Amaymon his king; delivers familiars out of the custody of other magicians; answers truly and perfectly of things past, present and to come; carries and re-carries men very speedily from one kingdom to another. He was of the Order of Potentates.

34. Furfur: Earl, great and mighty; 26 legions. Appears as a hart with a fiery tail; being brought within the triangle he takes upon himself the form of an angel; being bidden, he speaks with a hoarse voice. Office: never speaks truth unless compelled or brought up within the triangle; wittingly urges love between man and woman; raises lightnings, thunders, blasts and great tempestuous storms; gives true answers of things secret and divine, if commanded.

35. Marchosias: Marquis, great and mighty; 30 legions. Appears as at first a wolf with gryphon’s wings and a serpent’s tail, vomiting fire; after a time, at the exorcist’s command, the shape of a man. A footnote records that one badly written seventeenth-century codex might be read “ox” for “wolf,” and the editor adds in brackets that for him the spirit appeared always like an ox, and very dazed. Office: a strong fighter. He was of the Order of Dominations. He told his chief (Solomon) that after 1,200 years he had hopes to return to the Seventh Throne.

36. Stolas (Stolos): Prince, great and powerful; 26 legions. Appears as a mighty raven at first before the exorcist; afterwards he takes the image of a man. Office: teaches the art of astronomy, and the virtues of herbs and precious stones.

37. Phenex (Pheynix): Marquis; 20 legions. Appears as the bird phoenix, having the voice of a child; he sings many sweet notes before the exorcist, which he must not regard, but by and by must bid him put on human shape. Office: speaks marvellously of all wonderful sciences if required; is a poet, good and excellent, and willing to perform requests. He too has hopes to return to the Seventh Throne, after 1,200 years more, as he said unto Solomon.

38. Halphas (Malthus, Malthous, Malthas): Earl; 26 legions. Appears as a stock-dove; speaks with a hoarse voice. Office: builds up towers and furnishes them with ammunition and weapons, and sends men-of-war (warriors, or men-at-arms) to places appointed.

39. Malphas: President, mighty and powerful; 40 legions. Appears as at first a crow; afterwards human shape at the exorcist’s request; speaks with a hoarse voice. Office: builds houses and high towers; brings to knowledge enemies’ desires and thoughts, and what they have done; gives good familiars. If a sacrifice is made to him he receives it kindly and willingly; but he will deceive the one who does it.

40. Räum: Earl, great; 30 legions. Appears as at first a crow; afterwards human shape at the exorcist’s command. Office: steals treasure out of kings’ houses and carries it whither he is commanded; destroys cities and the dignities of men; tells all things past, what is, and what will be; causes love between friends and foes. He was of the Order of Thrones.

41. Focalor (Forcalor, Furcalor): Duke, mighty and strong; 30 legions. Appears as a man with gryphon’s wings. Office: slays men and drowns them in the waters, and overthrows ships of war, for he has power over both winds and seas; but he will not hurt any man or thing if commanded to the contrary by the exorcist. He hopes to return to the Seventh Throne after 1,000 years.

42. Vepar (Vephar): Duke, great and strong; 29 legions. Appears as a mermaid. Office: governs the waters and guides ships laden with arms, armour and ammunition; at the exorcist’s request causes the seas to be right stormy and to appear full of ships; makes men die in three days by putrefying wounds or sores, causing worms to breed in them.

43. Sabnock (Savnok): Marquis, mighty, great and strong; 50 legions. Appears as an armed soldier with a lion’s head, riding a pale-coloured horse. Office: builds high towers, castles and cities and furnishes them with armour; afflicts men for many days with wounds and with sores rotten and full of worms; gives good familiars at the exorcist’s request.

44. Shax (Shaz, Shass): Marquis, great; 30 legions. Appears as a stock-dove, speaking with a voice hoarse but yet subtle. Office: takes away the sight, hearing or understanding of any man or woman at the exorcist’s command; steals money out of the houses of kings and carries it again in 1,200 years; fetches horses or any other thing if commanded; discovers all things hidden and not kept by wicked spirits; gives good familiars, sometimes. He must first be commanded into the triangle, or he will deceive the operator and tell him many lies.

45. Viné (Vinea): King and Earl; 36 legions. Appears as a lion (or, in some codices, with the head of a lion) riding upon a black horse and bearing a viper in his hand. Office: discovers things hidden, witches, wizards, and things present, past and to come; at the exorcist’s command builds towers, overthrows great stone walls, and makes the waters rough with storms.

46. Bifrons (Bifröus, Bifrovs): Earl; 6 legions. Appears as a monster; after a while, at the exorcist’s command, the shape of a man. Office: makes one knowing in astrology, geometry and other arts and sciences; teaches the virtues of precious stones and woods; changes dead bodies and puts them in another place; lights seeming candles upon the graves of the dead.

47. Uvall (Vual, Voval): Duke, great, mighty and strong; 37 legions. Appears as a mighty dromedary at the first; after a while, at the exorcist’s command, human shape; and he speaks the Egyptian tongue, but not perfectly. The 1904 editor adds a footnote: he can nowadays converse in sound though colloquial Coptic. Office: procures the love of woman; tells things past, present and to come; procures friendship between friends and foes. He was of the Order of Potestates or Powers.

48. Haagenti: President; 33 legions. Appears as a mighty bull with gryphon’s wings at first; afterwards human shape at the exorcist’s command. Office: makes men wise and instructs them in divers things; transmutes all metals into gold; changes wine into water, and water into wine.

49. Crocell (Crokel): Duke, great and strong; 48 legions. Appears as an angel, speaking something mystically of hidden things. Office: teaches the art of geometry and the liberal sciences; at the exorcist’s command produces great noises like the rushings of many waters, although there be none; warms waters, and discovers baths. He was of the Order of Potestates, or Powers, before his fall, as he declared unto King Solomon.

50. Furcas: Knight; 20 legions. Appears as a cruel old man with a long beard and a hoary head, riding upon a pale-coloured horse, a sharp weapon in his hand. Office: teaches the arts of philosophy, astrology, rhetoric, logic, cheiromancy and pyromancy, in all their parts, and perfectly.

51. Balam (Balaam): King, terrible, great and powerful; 40 legions. Appears as three heads: the first like a bull, the second like a man, the third like a ram; the tail of a serpent, and flaming eyes; rides upon a furious bear and carries a goshawk upon his fist; speaks with a hoarse voice. Office: gives true answers of things past, present and to come; makes men go invisible, and also witty.

52. Alloces (Alocas): Duke, great, mighty and strong; 36 legions. Appears as a soldier, or warrior, riding upon a great horse; his face like a lion’s, very red, with flaming eyes; his speech hoarse and very big. Office: teaches the art of astronomy and all the liberal sciences; brings good familiars.

53. Camio (Caim): President, great; 30 legions. Appears as the bird called a thrush at first; afterwards the shape of a man carrying a sharp sword. He seems to answer in burning ashes, or in coals of fire, and is a good disputer. Office: gives men the understanding of all birds, the lowing of bullocks, the barking of dogs and other creatures, and also of the voice of the waters; gives true answers of things to come. He was of the Order of Angels, but now rules over legions of spirits infernal.

54. Murmur (Murmus, Murmux): Duke and Earl, great; 30 legions. Appears as a warrior riding upon a gryphon, with a ducal crown upon his head; his ministers go before him with great trumpets sounding. Office: teaches philosophy perfectly; constrains souls deceased to come before the exorcist to answer such questions as he may wish to put to them. He was partly of the Order of Thrones and partly of that of Angels.

55. Orobas: Prince, great and mighty; 20 legions. Appears as a horse at first; after the exorcist’s command, the image of a man. Office: discovers all things past, present and to come; gives dignities and prelacies, and the favour of friends and foes; gives true answers of divinity and of the creation of the world. He is very faithful unto the exorcist, and will not suffer him to be tempted of any spirit.

56. Gremory (Gamori): Duke, strong and powerful; 26 legions. Appears as a beautiful woman with a duchess’s crown tied about her waist, riding on a great camel. Office: tells of all things past, present and to come, and of treasures hid and what they lie in; procures the love of women both young and old.

57. Osé (Oso, Voso): President, great; 30 legions. Appears as a leopard at the first; after a little time the shape of a man. Office: makes one cunning in the liberal sciences and gives true answers of divine and secret things; changes a man into any shape the exorcist pleases, so that he who is so changed will not think any other thing than that he is in verity that creature or thing he is changed into. The printing gives his legions as 30 and then hangs on that figure a footnote reading Should be 30, adding that these seventy-two great spirits are all princes and leaders of numbers. A note correcting a number to itself corrects nothing, and the only figure it can have been written against is a smaller one that this setting has quietly reset to agree with its own footnote. The absurdity belongs to the printing, and it stands here because it is the sharpest single mark of which edition this roster was read from.

58. Amy (Avnas): President, great; 36 legions. Appears as a flaming fire at first; after a while the shape of a man. Office: makes one wonderful knowing in astrology and all the liberal sciences; gives good familiars, and can bewray treasure that is kept by spirits.

59. Oriax (Orias): Marquis, great; 30 legions. Appears as a lion (or, in some codices, with the face of a lion) riding upon a horse mighty and strong with a serpent’s tail, holding in his right hand two great serpents hissing. A footnote asks whether the serpent’s tail belongs to the horse or to the marquis. Office: teaches the virtues of the stars, and to know the mansions of the planets and how to understand their virtues; transforms men; gives dignities, prelacies and confirmation thereof, and favour with friends and with foes.

60. Vapula (Naphula): Duke, great, mighty and strong; 36 legions. Appears as a lion with gryphon’s wings. Office: makes men knowing in all handcrafts and professions, also in philosophy and other sciences.

61. Zagan: King and President, great; 33 legions. Appears as a bull with gryphon’s wings at first; after a while human shape. Office: makes men witty; turns wine into water, and blood into wine, also water into wine; turns all metals into coin of the dominion that metal is of; can even make fools wise.

62. Volac (Valak, Valu, Ualac): President, mighty and great; 38 legions. Appears as a child with angel’s wings, riding on a two-headed dragon. Office: gives true answers of hidden treasures, and tells where serpents may be seen, which he will bring unto the exorciser without any force or strength being employed by him.

63. Andras: Marquis, great; 30 legions. Appears as an angel with a head like a black night raven, riding upon a strong black wolf, a sharp and bright sword flourished aloft in his hand. Office: sows discords. If the exorcist have not a care, he will slay both him and his fellows.

64. Haures (Hauras, Havres, Flauros): Duke, great; 36 legions. Appears as a leopard at first, mighty, terrible and strong; after a while, at the exorcist’s command, human shape with eyes flaming and fiery, and a most terrible countenance. Office: gives true answers of all things present, past and to come; but if he be not commanded into the triangle he will lie in all these things, and deceive and beguile the exorcist. He will talk of the creation of the world and of divinity, and of how he and other spirits fell; destroys and burns up those who are the exorcist’s enemies should he so desire it; and will not suffer him to be tempted by any other spirit.

65. Andrealphus: Marquis, mighty; 30 legions. Appears as a peacock at first, with great noises; after a time human shape. Office: teaches geometry perfectly, and makes men very subtle therein, and in all things pertaining unto mensuration or astronomy; can transform a man into the likeness of a bird.

66. Cimejes (Cimeies, Kimaris): Marquis, mighty, great, strong and powerful; he rules over all spirits in the parts of Africa; 20 legions. Appears as a valiant warrior riding upon a goodly black horse. Office: teaches perfectly grammar, logic and rhetoric, and discovers things lost or hidden, and treasures.

67. Amdusias (Amdukias): Duke, great and strong; 29 legions. Appears as a unicorn at first; at the exorcist’s request he stands before him in human shape, causing trumpets and all manner of musical instruments to be heard, but not soon or immediately. Office: causes trees to bend and incline according to the exorcist’s will; gives excellent familiars.

68. Belial: King, mighty and powerful, and was created next after Lucifer; 50 legions. Appears as two beautiful angels sitting in a chariot of fire; speaks with a comely voice, and declares that he fell first from among the worthier sort, that were before Michael and other heavenly angels. Office: distributes presentations and senatorships, and causes the favour of friends and of foes; gives excellent familiars. He must have offerings, sacrifices and gifts presented unto him by the exorcist or he will not give true answers; and even then he does not tarry one hour in the truth unless he be constrained by divine power.

69. Decarabia: Marquis, great; 30 legions. Appears as a star in a pentacle at first; after, at the exorcist’s command, the image of a man. Office: discovers the virtues of birds and precious stones, and makes the similitude of all kinds of birds fly before the exorcist, singing and drinking as natural birds do.

70. Seere (Sear, Seir): Prince, mighty and powerful, under Amaymon King of the East; 26 legions. Appears as a beautiful man riding upon a winged horse. Office: goes and comes, and brings abundance of things to pass on a sudden; carries or re-carries anything whither the operator would have it go, or whence he would have it from; can pass over the whole earth in the twinkling of an eye; gives a true relation of all sorts of theft, and of treasure hid. He is of an indifferent good nature, and willing to do anything the exorcist desires.

71. Dantalion: Duke, great and mighty; 36 legions. Appears as a man with many countenances, all men’s and women’s faces, holding a book in his right hand. Office: teaches all arts and sciences unto any; declares the secret counsel of any one, for he knows the thoughts of all men and women and can change them at his will; causes love, and shows the similitude of any person, and shows the same by a vision, let them be in what part of the world they will.

72. Andromalius: Earl, great and mighty; 36 legions. Appears as a man holding a great serpent in his hand. Office: brings back both a thief and the goods which be stolen; discovers all wickedness and underhand dealing; punishes all thieves and other wicked people; discovers treasures that be hid.

Two features of the list only appear once it is read whole. One is the hope of return: Marchosias told Solomon that after twelve hundred years he had hopes of returning to the Seventh Throne, Phenex says the same, and Focalor puts it at a thousand years. Three of the seventy-two are on a sentence rather than in a state, and expect to go back. The other is the register of the fall: nine of them are given a former rank in the celestial orders: Agares and Barbatos of the Virtues, Paimon of the Dominations, Marchosias also of the Dominations, Gäap and Uvall of the Potestates, Crocell of the Potestates before his fall as he declared unto Solomon, Räum of the Thrones, Camio of the Angels, with Purson and Forneus divided between two orders apiece. Belial says he fell first, from among the worthier sort that were before Michael. This is not a bestiary of monsters. It is a demoted civil service, and it remembers its former grades.

Where the seals are

Every entry above ends, in the source, with a sentence this book has not reproduced: and his Seal is this, which thou shalt wear as a Lamen before thee. Each of the seventy-two has an individual character: a line figure to be drawn, worn on the breast during the working, and shown to the spirit as the token it owes obedience to. They are the most reproduced images in the whole of this literature.

The printing this chapter works from does not contain them. The 1916 edition sets the text and refers to the figures, its footnotes to Buné point at “Figure 30” and “Figure 31”, but prints no plates; both scans of it examined for this edition run from the first spirit to the last without a single seal. Two scans catalogued elsewhere as the edition of 1904 do carry seals, and neither is a printing: both are modern digital settings, laid on blank white with no paper under the type, and what they took the figures from is stated nowhere in them. A redrawing is somebody else’s reading of a plate, and an unsourced reproduction dropped into a reset is worse than a redrawing, because it cannot be traced even to a reading. Seventy-two sigils supplied from such a source would be indistinguishable on the page from seventy-two real ones.

What could be reached is Waite. Plate IV is one page of his roster as the seals stand in it, engraved and captioned beside the entries they belong to. The copy is not the London first edition of 1898: it is the Chicago reproduction of 1910, whose title page says in one line that it is faithfully reproduced from the London edition and in the next that all rights are reserved. That is the third de Laurence piracy this edition has had occasion to read, after the Goetia the roster above comes from and the tarot of Chapter 25. One thing follows from the dates and should be said plainly: Waite printed in 1898 and Mathers and Crowley in 1904, so whatever these figures are, they are not the 1904 plates and cannot be. They are Waite’s, out of the manuscripts he worked from, and that is how they are offered here.

The instruments, and the hours

The roster above ends every entry at the seal, and the seals reached this chapter through Waite rather than through the printing it works from. What that printing does give whole is everything the seal is worn with and everything it is worn for, and it specifies that to the inch and to the colour. This is the part of the apparatus a reader can actually make, and none of it has been in this chapter.

Two objects are carried on the body and one is held in the hand, and they are not interchangeable. The pentagram of Solomon, gold or silver, hangs on the breast and carries the required spirit’s seal on its back; it is the badge of authority, and the text says plainly what it is for: to preserve thee from danger, and also to command the Spirits by. The hexagram of Solomon, on calf’s parchment, hangs at the skirt of the vestment under a linen cover and is produced only when the spirit has appeared, to force it into human shape. And the magic ring, or rather disc, gold or silver, bright yellow with black letters, is held up in front of the operator’s face: for a stated and startlingly physical reason: to preserve him from the stinking sulphurous fumes and flaming breath of the Evil Spirits. That is the same object Beleth, Berith and Astaroth each require by name in the roster above. The fourth thing is the vessel of brass, the container Solomon is said to have shut the spirits into, with its own privy seal to cover it.

The last piece of the apparatus is a timetable, and it is the most practical page in the book. Rank does not only decide how a spirit is addressed; it decides what metal its seal is cut in and what hours it can be bound at all. A reader who wants to know why the roster bothers to give every spirit a rank has the answer here.

RankOf the 72Seal cut inHours at which it may be bound
Kings9gold9 till 12 at noon, and from 3 till sunset
Dukes23coppersunrise till noonday, in clear weather
Princes and Prelates7tinany hour of the day
Marquises15silver3 in the afternoon till 9 at night, and from 9 at night till sunrise
Presidents14mercuryany time excepting twilight at night, unless the king they are under be invoked
Earls, or Counts10copper and silver, alike equalany hour of the day, so it be in woods, or other places whither men resort not, or where no noise is
Knights1leadfrom the dawning of day till sunrise, or from 4 o’clock till sunset

Those counts do not add to seventy-two, and the reason is in the source rather than in the arithmetic: several spirits hold two ranks at once and appear in two of the lists. Viné is both king and earl, Glasya-Labolas both president and earl, Botis both president and earl, Marax and Ronové likewise. The editor of 1904 says so in a note, adds that prince and prelate seem to be used interchangeably, and then does something worth watching: he observes that the metals as given exclude iron, and therefore Mars, from a system that otherwise assigns one metal to each of the seven planets (lead to Saturn, tin to Jupiter, iron to Mars, gold to the Sun, copper to Venus, mercury and mixtures to Mercury, silver to the Moon) and proposes that earls’ seals should probably be iron. That is a conjecture repairing a symmetry, not a reading of any manuscript, and it is marked as one here because the table above prints what the text says rather than what the pattern wants. It is the same move this book has watched other editors make, and the same correction.

The quarrel over the whole subject

The catalogue travelled inside an argument, and the argument was about killing people. Weyer’s De praestigiis daemonum held that the women being burned as witches were melancholic, deceived or ill: a physician’s verdict entered against a legal machine. Scot went further than Weyer, further than almost anyone in his century, and denied the crime outright: the confessions were extracted, the wonders were tricks and delusions, and the conjurors’ books were the vanity of “couseners.” The reply came from a head of state. James VI of Scotland, not yet James I of England, published his Daemonologie at Edinburgh in 1597, and its preface declares its targets by name:

…against the damnable opinions of two principally in our age, wherof the one called SCOT an Englishman, is not ashamed in publike print to deny, that ther can be such a thing as Witch-craft: and so mainteines the old error of the Sadducees, in denying of spirits. The other called WIERUS, a German Phisition, sets out a publick apologie for al these craftes-folkes, whereby, procuring for their impunitie, he plainely bewrayes himselfe to haue bene one of that profession.

The king’s logic deserves attention: Scot is wrong because denying witches denies spirits; Weyer, by defending the accused, proves he must be one of them. In 1603 James took the English throne, and a new and harsher Witchcraft Act followed in 1604. Behind all three books stands the manual this chapter describes and does not quote: the Malleus Maleficarum, first printed about 1486, the inquisitors’ handbook whose questions the confessions answered: Chapter 27 shows what happened when a twentieth-century reader mistook those confessions for ethnography. Weyer and Scot lost their argument for a century, and then won it completely; it is their books, not the king’s, that read as the modern position. A reader who wants the catalogue’s later career (the Goetia’s seventy-two spirits, seals and operative apparatus, compiled in the mid-seventeenth century and printed in 1904) will find every stage of it dated in Chapter 10 and the bibliography.

What this chapter is and is not

The operation above is printed as its sources print it: a working text of 1570, carried into type by the century’s great sceptic, with his confutation standing two pages after it on the same leaves; and this book prints both, because the reader is owed the pair. Its conditions are the sources’ own and are not decoration: never alone, fasting before, no sacrifice ever, and the licence to depart always given. The Goetia’s later and more elaborate apparatus (seals, brass vessel, seventy-two spirits) is dated in Chapter 10 and left in its own editions, which are cited there. The tradition treats the approach to these powers as governed, conditional and dangerous from the Testament’s ring onward, and its protective frame, the banishing that opens and closes every working, is given in full in Chapter 15.

Modern Practice

What survives of demonology, for a modern reader, is mostly the debate. Weyer’s move (to look for illness before crime, and to insist that a confession extracted is not a fact established) is one of the tradition’s genuine gifts to the modern world, and it was made by a man who fully believed in the devil. The catalogue survives differently: as a mirror. Its offices (languages, knowledge, love, standing, hidden money) are a complete inventory of what its buyers lacked, and reading it that way tells more truth about the sixteenth century than any list of legions. The modern occult revival re-adopted the Goetia as a working text; this book’s treatment of that adoption is in Chapter 10 and Chapter 27.

Chapter XIIRosicrucian Mysteries Reference

The Rosicrucian tradition is the most influential body of Western esoteric thought whose founding organisation probably never existed. That sentence needs stating plainly at the outset, because almost everything written about the Rosicrucians for four hundred years has depended on which half of it the writer chose to emphasise. The manifestos are real, dated and enormously consequential. The Brotherhood they describe cannot be shown to have existed at all.

The three manifestos

Three anonymous texts appeared in Germany and then across Europe in quick succession:

  • Fama Fraternitatis Rosae Crucis (The Fame of the Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross): circulating in manuscript among German occultists from around 1610, and published at Cassel in 1614. It announces the existence of a secret brotherhood and narrates the travels, education and death of a figure called “Father Brother C.R.C.”
  • Confessio Fraternitatis (The Confession of the Brotherhood of R.C.): printed at Cassel by Wilhelm Wessel in 1615, in Latin, appended to Philippus a Gabella’s Secretioris Philosophiae Consideratio brevis, responding to the confusion and criticism the Fama had provoked and elaborating the programme further.
  • The Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz: published in 1616: an allegorical romance in seven days, structurally quite unlike the two documents preceding it.

What they promised was a universal reformation of humanity, by means of a science built on esoteric truths of the ancient past: knowledge concealed from ordinary understanding that offered insight into nature, the physical universe and the spiritual realm, and which had supposedly been kept secret until the intellectual climate was ready for it. The programme was set out extensively but cryptically, in the languages of Qabalah, Hermeticism, alchemy and Christian mysticism: precisely the subjects the learned readership of the period was studying most avidly. The stated aims are worth setting down plainly: universal reformation, the advance of spiritual and scientific knowledge, the healing of the sick, and the teaching of divine wisdom.

The legend of C.R.C.

As the manifestos tell it, Christian Rosenkreuz was born in 1378 and lived 106 years. He studied in the Middle East under a succession of masters: a detail that has invited speculation about Sufi influence, which shaped a number of Western esoteric currents. During his lifetime the order was said to comprise no more than eight members, each of them a physician and all “bachelors of vowed virginity.” Each swore to heal the sick without accepting payment, to keep the fellowship secret, and to find a replacement for himself before he died. Three such generations were said to have passed between about 1500 and about 1600: by which time, the Fama claims, scientific, philosophical and religious liberty had grown enough that the public might finally benefit, and the brotherhood was now seeking good men.

Read as literature this is superb: a lineage, a rediscovered tomb, a sealed vault of knowledge, and an open invitation the reader has no way to accept. Read as history it has no corroboration of any kind.

The vault, in the manifesto’s own words

The tomb of Christian Rosenkreuz is the image the whole Rosicrucian episode turns on, and this book gives it exactly as the Fama tells it rather than as later writers summarise it. The discovery is an accident of building work. A brother, altering the house, lights on the memorial table of brass that carries the names of the Brethren, and means to move it to a better vault:

In this table stuck a great naile somewhat strong, so that when it was with force drawn out it took with it an indifferent big stone out of the thin wall or plaistering of the hidden door, and so unlooked for uncovered the door, whereat we did with joy and longing throw down the rest of the wall and cleared the door, upon which was written in great letters — Post CXX Annos Patebo, with the year of the Lord under it.

After a hundred and twenty years I shall open. They wait until morning (the text says they let it rest that night because they would first consult their Rota) and then:

In the morning following we opened the door, and there appeared to our sight a vault of seven sides and seven corners, every side five foot broad, and the height of eight foot. Although the sun never shined in this vault, nevertheless, it was enlightened with another sun, which had learned this from the sun, and was situated in the upper part in the center of the sieling. In the midst, instead of a tomb-stone, was a round altar, covered with a plate of brass, and thereon this engraven: — A. C. R. C. Hoc universi compendium unius mihi sepulchrum feci. Round about the first circle or brim stood, Jesus mihi omnia. In the middle were four figures, inclosed in circles, whose circumscription was, 1. Nequaquam Vacuum. 2. Legis Jugum. 3. Libertas Evangelii. 4. Dei Gloria Intacta.

This vault we parted in three parts, the upper part or sieling, the wall or side, the ground or floor. … Every side or wall is parted into ten squares, every one with their several figures and sentences. … The bottom again is parted in the triangle, but because therein is described the power and rule of the Inferior Governors, we leave to manifest the same, for fear of the abuse by the evil and ungodly world.

The Latin should be translated rather than admired: A. C. R. C.: this compendium of the universe I made in my lifetime to be my tomb; Jesus is all things to me; and the four circumscriptions, By no means a vacuum, The yoke of the law, The liberty of the gospel, The untouched glory of God. Every detail is a doctrine in miniature. The vault is seven-sided, on the planetary number this book meets in every chapter. It is lit by an artificial sun “which had learned this from the sun”: a made thing that has taken instruction from a natural one, which is the whole Hermetic programme in a lamp. Its walls are divided into ten squares apiece, the sephirotic number of Chapter 4. And it withholds: the floor is left undescribed on the stated ground that the ungodly would abuse it: the withholding of Chapter 19, performed rather than discussed.

Whether any such vault existed is a question the rest of this chapter answers. What is certain is that the description worked: the seven-sided chamber was built, physically, more than two centuries later, by the Golden Dawn, as the Vault of the Adepti in which its Adeptus Minor grade was conferred. A room described in a pamphlet of 1614 by an author who called the whole thing a ludibrium became a room people stood in.

The furore

The reception is the part of this story that actually happened, and it was extraordinary. Europe in 1614 was sliding toward the Thirty Years’ War; the promise of a spiritual and intellectual transformation landed in a continent primed for it. Between 1614 and 1620 roughly four hundred books, pamphlets and manuscripts were published discussing the Rosicrucian documents, favourably and otherwise. Serious philosophers took up the worldview: Michael Maier, Robert Fludd, Thomas Vaughan, later Elias Ashmole. The manifestos drew on Heinrich Khunrath’s Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae (first printed Hamburg, 1595), itself indebted to John Dee’s Monas Hieroglyphica (1564); the invitation that opens the Chymical Wedding is marked with Dee’s Monas symbol.

The peak came in 1622, when two mysterious posters appeared on walls in Paris within days of each other. The first began: “We, the Deputies of the Higher College of the Rose-Croix, do make our stay, visibly and invisibly, in this city.” The second closed: “The thoughts attached to the real desire of the seeker will lead us to him and him to us.” Nobody has ever established who put them up.

One consequence outlived all the others. The idea of an invisible college of natural philosophers, corresponding across borders and pooling discoveries, was taken up by the network around Kepler, Dee, Rheticus and Tycho Brahe, and passed into the group that met weekly in London from about 1645 to conduct experiments. Robert Boyle wrote of “the cornerstones of the Invisible (or as they term themselves the Philosophical) College.” That body became the Royal Society in 1660. The Rosicrucian manifestos are, by a genuinely traceable route, among the ancestors of the modern scientific academy.

Who wrote them

The attribution is not what the manifestos claim, though it is less settled than it is often made to sound. Roland Edighoffer, writing in the Brill Dictionary of Gnosis & Western Esotericism (2005), traces the manifestos to the “Learned and Christian Society” that Johann Valentin Andreae established at Tübingen in 1610: a small circle of close friends, notably Christoph Besold and Tobias Hess, who together conceived of and constructed the Rosicrucian myth. Recent scholarship refines this rather than overturning it: Andreae is widely accepted as the principal author, probably working with Tobias Hess, while Besold’s participation has been specifically doubted, and a minority of scholars exclude Andreae altogether. What is not seriously contested is that the manifestos came out of this Tübingen milieu rather than from an existing brotherhood.

Andreae (1586–1654) went further than being suspected. In his autobiography (the Vita ab ipso conscripta, unpublished in his lifetime and printed only much later) he acknowledged the Nuptiae Chymicae as his own work, listing it among juvenilia he assigns to 1602–1603. He gives no age; born 17 August 1586, he was then about sixteen or seventeen. And he was dismissive about it. Of that group of youthful writings he says the others perished, but this one survived:

… Superfuerunt e contra Nuptiae Chymicae, cum monstrorum foecundo foetu, ludibrium, quod mireris a nonnullis aestimatum et subtili indagine explicatum, plane futile et quod inanitatem curiosorum prodat.

Rendered as literally as the difficult clauses allow: the Chymical Wedding survived by contrast, with its foetus fruitful of monsters, a ludibrium, which you may wonder was esteemed by some and expounded with subtle investigation, plainly futile, and disclosing the emptiness of the curious. (Waite, reading the phrase about monsters, took it to refer not to the book’s contents but to its progeny: the ridiculous commentaries it spawned.) Elsewhere Andreae is blunter still: in the Vita’s second book he speaks of his Invitations to the Fraternity of Christ as set in opposition to “that Rosicrucian ludibrium,” and in the Menippus of 1617 the Fraternity is “only a ludibrium for the curious,” in which those who followed an artificial path instead of the simple way of Christ were deceived.

What ludibrium means, and what it does not

Everything in this chapter’s reading of Andreae turns on one Latin word, and care with it pays. Lewis & Short give ludibrium (from ludus, play) as mockery, derision, wantonness; a laughing-stock, butt, jest or sport; and abuse done to a woman. Neither “hoax”, a fraud passed off as true, nor “lampoon”, a satire against a named target, is what the Latin says, and no authority cited here translates it either way: Waite renders it “jest” or “fantasy,” Yates “a play, a comic fiction.” Those two popular glosses are also incompatible with each other. A classical lexicon cannot by itself bound a word written in the seventeenth century, so the strongest form of the point is about the record rather than the dictionary: the harder English is read back into Andreae. (Waite 1924, p. 188, does at one point list the possibilities as “jest, hoax or fantasy,” and the one study devoted to the word (Willard, 2010) argues a Menippean-satire reading.)

The scholarship divides. Paul Arnold (1935) translated it “une farce” and concluded Andreae had told us the whole affair was a joke; Charles Webster (1970) calls the ludibrium phrases “derisive terms.” Frances Yates argued at length for a different reading: ludibrium “could be a play, a comic fiction,” and given Andreae’s high regard for theatre as a moral and educative instrument, she read the Rosicrucian material as “not a hoax, but a dramatic presentation of a profoundly interesting religious and intellectual movement.”

The defensible statement is therefore narrower than “Andreae called it a hoax.” Andreae’s later references to the Rosicrucian material are genuinely dismissive and at times derisive: plane futile is his own phrase. But he called it a jest or a fiction, not a fraud, and the stronger English glosses have been read back into him.

Two further cautions belong here, and both cut against the simple story. First, the text published at Strasbourg in 1616 cannot be the unrevised juvenile draft: it contains references to the manifestos of 1614 and 1615, so whatever Andreae wrote as a teenager was substantially reworked, and Yates doubted the two were the same work at all. Second, A. E. Waite is routinely miscited on this. His 1887 sentence that Andreae “considered the Rosicrucian manifestoes a reprehensible hoax” (The Real History of the Rosicrucians, p. 240) is a report of Andreae’s contempt, deployed as an argument against his authorship; and in the same book Waite rejects both the “frolicsome imposture” reading of the manifestos (p. 225) and the ludibrium reading of the Chymical Marriage (p. 234). In The Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross (1924) he argued at greater length that the hoax hypothesis should be dropped (pp. 122 n., 207), while continuing to insist on Andreae’s disdain (p. 206). He was never the authority for the hoax reading he is quoted as supplying.

Some scholars have suggested Andreae distanced himself from the movement to protect a clerical career from the religious and political authorities of the day, and that reading cannot be ruled out. That reading is at least as old as Waite, who proposed a secret-society oath as the reason (1887, pp. 240–41); it remains a conjecture, and the evidence for it is thin.

When did real Rosicrucians appear?

Edighoffer is blunt on the central question: “there is no proof that the Brotherhood of the Rose Cross described in the Fama Fraternitatis ever existed, and it is only in the 18th century that actual organizations calling themselves ‘rosicrucian’ first come into existence.” He dates the first creation of a Rosicrucian order in Germany to 1763; though that date deserves a footnote of its own. Edighoffer infers it from a later controversy between “Phoebron” (Bernhard Joseph Schleiss von Loewenfeld) and Baron von Ecker und Eckhofen, whose pamphlet Der Rosenkreuzer in seiner Blösse Edighoffer dates 1782 and the British Library 1781. It is an inference from a polemic, not a documented act of foundation, and Edighoffer does not name the body in the sentence itself; the surrounding discussion indicates the Gold- und Rosenkreuzer, the Order of the Golden and Rosy Cross. He offers three other candidate moments in the same entry; 1710, 1761 and 1777, of which he says only 1777 “signal[s] the ‘official’ foundation.” Renko Geffarth’s archive-based study of the order is summarised by its reviewer as covering circles that existed “from around 1760 until sometime after 1790” (Michael Driedger, H-German, Feb. 2010): a statement about their duration, not a rival founding date. Every Rosicrucian order that has ever operated (the Order of the Golden and Rosy Cross, formally constituted in the 1760s–1770s out of a Rosicrucian literary milieu traceable to about 1750, the Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia from the 1860s, the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn (1888), the Rosicrucian Fellowship (1909), AMORC (incorporated 1915)) postdates the manifestos by at least 140 years. They are its descendants, not its survivors.

What survives the correction

Almost everything of value, as it happens. A literary invention that produced four hundred books in six years, drew in Fludd, Maier and Ashmole, seeded the Invisible College, and still animates active orders four centuries later is not diminished by being an invention; it is one of the most productive fictions in European intellectual history. Andreae’s contempt for what he had started is a fact about Andreae, not a verdict on what his readers built.

A point often made about the alchemical writing of the Rosicrucian circle should be handled with care. It is true, so far as the surviving texts go, that neither Maier nor Khunrath announces a successful transmutation, and Maier does present the Brothers of the Rose Cross as existing to advance the inspired arts and sciences. The inference usually drawn from this, that their alchemy was therefore symbolic rather than operative, is not one the specialists draw; it circulates as an unsourced sentence in the Wikipedia article on Rosicrucianism, and the tracing that undoes it is set out in Chapter 5. Nor were Maier and Khunrath associates: Tilton records that Maier met Khunrath in Danzig and came to regard him as a fraud.
