Three quotations in this chapter are printed without an established source, and are flagged rather than dressed up. The English of the two Paris placards of 1622 is in wide circulation and no edition or translator for it could be traced; the French originals do not survive in a form this book was able to consult, and even the placards’ existence rests on contemporary report rather than on a surviving copy. Robert Boyle’s phrase about the cornerstones of the Invisible College comes from his correspondence of the later 1640s; the letter was not consulted directly and the wording is given as it circulates. A reader building an argument on any of the three should go behind this book.

Chapter XIIIThe Golden Dawn Curriculum Advanced

Almost nothing a modern reader will meet as advanced practice is older than the 1880s. The scrying, the godforms, the pathworking and the ladder of grades were assembled by one London order between 1888 and 1903, out of older parts, into a syllabus that had not existed before and has been the standard ever since. That is not a complaint. It is a considerable piece of work and this chapter sets it out. But a reader who takes it for the inheritance of Alexandria will misread every one of its sources, so the provenance comes first and the practices after it. What follows is descriptive throughout: these are the techniques the sources contain, with their actual dates, so that a reader can tell what they are looking at and decide what is worth pursuing under proper guidance.

The order was the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, founded in 1887–88 by three Freemasons (William Robert Woodman, William Wynn Westcott and Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers), with the Isis-Urania Temple formally established in London in 1888. The order’s foundational documents, the Cipher Manuscripts, were written in English in Trithemius cipher; Westcott decoded them in 1887 after receiving them from A. F. A. Woodford the previous year. Those manuscripts outline the grade rituals and set out a graduated curriculum covering Hermetic Qabalah, astrology, divinatory tarot, geomancy and alchemy: outlines rather than full texts, from which the rituals as performed were elaborated. That curriculum is, in substance, the modern Western magical syllabus.

The grade structure

The Golden Dawn organised its teaching into ten numbered grades across three tiers, each mapped to a sephirah of the Tree of Life and running downward from 10 to 1, preceded by a preliminary Neophyte grade (0=0) that stands outside the series:

  • First Order: Neophyte (0=0), Zelator (1=10), Theoricus (2=9), Practicus (3=8), Philosophus (4=7)
  • Second Order: Adeptus Minor (5=6), Adeptus Major (6=5), Adeptus Exemptus (7=4)
  • Third Order: Magister Templi (8=3), Magus (9=2), Ipsissimus (10=1)

The First Order taught theory (correspondence, symbolism, divinatory systems) and the Second Order taught magic proper, including scrying, astral travel and alchemy. The Third Order was, in practice, understood as belonging to those beyond ordinary membership. The graduated structure is itself the point: material was withheld until earlier material had been demonstrated. It is a sound pedagogical judgement, and it is one no longer available to a book. Regardie put the order’s teaching into print between 1937 and 1940, and everything described below has been public ever since, so withholding it here would conceal nothing from anyone. The practices are therefore given whole, and given in the order the curriculum used, because the sequence is the part of the grade system that a book can still supply. Chapter 19 takes up the part it cannot.

The practices

Scrying. Sustained soft-focus attention on a reflective or featureless surface (black mirror, bowl of water, crystal) until imagery arises. The Ars Almadel of the Lemegeton uses a wax tablet for a related purpose, and scrying is among the techniques the Golden Dawn’s Second Order explicitly taught. What the technique actually reliably produces is the mind’s own imagery under conditions of reduced sensory input; whether it produces more than that is the question the tradition exists to ask, and it is not answerable by assertion in either direction. The discipline is to record what arises before interpreting it.

Assumption of godforms. Building the image of a deity around oneself in visualisation and speaking or acting from within it. This has a genuine ancient parallel (the Greek Magical Papyri contain rituals in which the practitioner assumes the identity of a deity through invocation and visualisation, as part of an ascent or operation (see Chapter 9)), which makes it one of the few advanced techniques here with attested antiquity behind it, even if its modern form is a Golden Dawn reconstruction rather than a continuous inheritance.

The Middle Pillar and pathworking. The Middle Pillar exercise circulates energy through the central sephiroth of the Tree; pathworking traverses the twenty-two paths in structured visualisation, using the correspondences described in Chapter 3. Both belong to the modern Qabalistic system rather than to any ancient source. Their fullest published form comes through Israel Regardie, whose The Golden Dawn: The Original Account of the Teachings, Rites and Ceremonies of the Hermetic Order appeared in four volumes between 1937 and 1940: the publication that broke the order’s secrecy and made this entire body of technique publicly available. It remains in print.

The Enochian material. The system of angelic communication and language recorded by John Dee and Edward Kelley in the 1580s, subsequently reworked by the Golden Dawn into something considerably more systematic than Dee left it. Anyone working with Enochian material should know which layer they are handling: Dee’s diaries and the Golden Dawn’s redaction are different objects.

Working the practices

Descriptions are of limited use without procedure, so the four practices named above are given here as procedures. All four are modern: that is the finding of this chapter, not a caveat bolted onto it.

The Middle Pillar

  1. Stand or sit upright. Perform the banishing of Chapter 15. Breathe evenly until the breath is regular.
  2. Above the head, formulate a sphere of brilliant white light, and vibrate Eheieh (eh-heh-YEH): the name of Kether. Hold it until it is steady.
  3. At the throat, a sphere of soft grey. Vibrate YHVH Elohim (ye-ho-WAU e-loh-HEEM): the name of Daath.
  4. At the heart, a sphere of gold. Vibrate YHVH Eloah ve-Daath (ye-ho-WAU e-LOH-ah ve-DAH-ath): Tiphareth.
  5. At the groin, a sphere of violet. Vibrate Shaddai El Chai (shah-DYE el KHYE): Yesod.
  6. At the feet, a sphere of olive, russet, citrine and black. Vibrate Adonai ha-Aretz (ah-doh-NYE ha-AH-retz): Malkuth.
  7. When all five stand, circulate: bring the light down the left side of the body on the out-breath, up the right on the in-breath, several times; then up the front and down the back; then draw it from the feet up the central column and let it fountain from the crown to fall around you.
  8. Let the images go. Ground as in Chapter 15.

A word on provenance, since this book insists on it. The Middle Pillar in this form was published by Israel Regardie in The Middle Pillar (1938) and his text is in copyright; what is given above is a description of the procedure rather than his wording. The divine names are the standard Qabalistic names of the sephiroth concerned and are much older than the exercise that arranges them.

Scrying

  1. Work at night or in low, even light, with the speculum (black mirror, dark bowl of water, crystal) at a comfortable distance, angled so that it reflects nothing in particular. A reflection of your own face defeats the exercise.
  2. Banish. State what you are seeking, once, aloud, and then set the question down.
  3. Rest the eyes on the surface with the focus slightly soft. Blink normally. Do not stare: staring produces eye strain and afterimages, which are the commonest thing mistaken for a vision.
  4. Wait. Twenty minutes is a session. Cloudiness, dimming or a sense of depth usually precede imagery, and often nothing else follows, which is normal.
  5. When imagery arises, do not interpret it in the moment. Note it. If it is a figure, it is legitimate to ask it to name itself and to test whether it remains consistent; inconsistency under questioning is information.
  6. Close deliberately: cover the speculum, banish, write the record, then eat something.

The reason for the discipline in step five is not superstition about spirits. It is that the material is generated at least partly by you, and interpretation offered while the imagery is still arriving contaminates what arrives next. Record first, interpret later: days later, for preference.

Assumption of a godform

  1. Choose the form before you begin, and know its attributes, its posture and its name. Do not improvise this.
  2. Banish. Stand in the posture of the form.
  3. Build the image around you, not in front of you: the size, the headdress, the colours, the weight of it. Take the time this needs; it is the whole exercise.
  4. Vibrate the name as set out in Chapter 7, feeling it fill the form rather than the body.
  5. Speak or act from within it, briefly. Brevity is a safety measure, not modesty.
  6. Take it off. Let the image dissolve deliberately; state your own name aloud; banish; ground. This step is not optional and is the one that gets skipped.

The ancient parallel noted above is real, the papyri contain rituals of exactly this shape, but the modern form is a Golden Dawn reconstruction, and the Egyptian godforms it uses are the Egypt of the nineteenth-century imagination as much as of the monuments.

Pathworking a single path

  1. Choose the path and know it before you begin. A path on the Tree runs between two named sephiroth; it carries a Hebrew letter and, in the modern system, a trump of the tarot. Take the Tree from Chapter 3, Fig. 2, and the letter-and-trump attribution from Chapter 25; and note there that the two tables printed in that chapter disagree on twenty-one cards out of twenty-two. Pick one table and stay inside it for the whole of a working. Mixing them is the commonest way to make a nonsense of this exercise, and it produces a nonsense that feels like a result.
  2. Work upward, and only one path at a time. You enter from the lower sephirah and travel to the higher, never the reverse; and the first paths worked are those rising out of Malkuth. A path whose lower end you have not visited is not available to you, which is the whole of the pacing this system supplies.
  3. Banish, as in Chapter 15. Write down, before you start, the path’s two ends, its letter, its trump and its colour, and then put the note aside. The point of writing it first is that afterwards you will not be able to tell what you knew going in.
  4. Establish the lower sephirah. Build its scene: its name vibrated as in Chapter 7, its colour, its number. Hold it until it is steady and is somewhere you are standing rather than something you are picturing. This usually takes longer than the journey does.
  5. Make the trump a door. Build the card at the size of a doorway, in front of you, with the Hebrew letter on it. Do not enter until it is stable enough to look away from and find again. Then pass through.
  6. Travel. Let the path present what it presents and do not steer. Where a figure appears, it is legitimate to require it to give the letter of the path or the name of the sephirah you are going to, and to note whether it can; and whether it gives the same answer twice. Inconsistency is information, exactly as in scrying above. A figure that turns hostile when tested is a reason to close, not a reason to argue.
  7. Arrive, and stay briefly. Reach the upper sephirah, vibrate its name, and remain a short time. Brevity here is deliberate: the failure mode of this exercise is not fright but absorption.
  8. Return by the same path. Back down through the same door, through the lower sephirah, and out. Do not exit sideways, do not step off onto a second path, and do not simply open your eyes and stop.
  9. Let the images go. Banish, ground, eat something, and write the record before you interpret a line of it.

Two properties of that procedure are worth naming, because they are what make it a system rather than a reverie. The first is that the map constrains the territory: the path has two fixed ends and a fixed symbol, so a vision that has nothing to do with either is recognisably off the path, and the operator can tell. Free visualisation has no such property and cannot be wrong. The second is that the order of working is forced (upward, from Malkuth, one path at a time), which reproduces in solitary practice the one thing the grade structure supplied and publication removed. A reader who works the paths in the order they find interesting has kept the imagery and thrown away the method.

A note on what is and is not attributed

The Golden Dawn’s founding, dates, grade structure, Cipher Manuscripts and curriculum are well documented, as is Regardie’s publication. What is not settled, and this book will not pretend otherwise, is exactly which of these techniques the order invented outright and which it inherited or adapted from earlier sources. The scholarly record establishes that the Second Order taught scrying, astral travel and alchemy; it does not cleanly establish the origin of each individual exercise. Where this chapter says “Golden Dawn,” read it as “systematised and transmitted by the Golden Dawn,” which is defensible, rather than “invented there,” which in several cases is not yet demonstrated.

What this chapter cannot give, and the reason

Two operations named above are described here and not printed, and the reason in both cases is access to a text rather than any judgement about the practice.

Rising on the planes (the extended astral working the Second Order taught alongside scrying) is set out in the order’s own papers, whose fullest publication is Regardie’s and is in copyright. The earliest printing is Crowley’s, in The Equinox vol. I (1909–13), which is long out of copyright; but no scan of an original printing of that volume could be reached for this edition. What circulates instead is modern re-keyed text (the Celephais Press and Ordo Templi Orientis electronic editions, set from transcriptions and carrying their own notices) and in the case of the 1919 Blue Equinox the electronic edition’s own preface states that its editor never had a hard copy to work from. A transcription of a public-domain text is not the text; it is somebody else’s reading of it, and it can carry a later editor’s emendations silently. The Liber O passages in Chapter 7 and Chapter 15 stand on exactly that footing, and the unresolved question recorded there about one line of the pentagram ritual is unresolved for this reason and no other.

The Ars Almadel, named above for its wax tablet, is a scrying rite the operator performs alone and would belong here on this book’s own rule. Waite prints the operation in full: the four coloured tablets, the candles of the same wax, the gold or silver seal, the twenty spirits of the four altitudes. But the printings that carry it, The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts (1898) and The Book of Ceremonial Magic (1911), could not be reached in a scan: the one photographic copy located is a 1973 reprint behind a lending restriction, and the two freely available texts are a 2018 commercial e-book and a transcription made for a website in 2001–02. Neither is a page image of a printing, and this book does not quote what it has not seen set in type. The rite is named here so that a reader knows it exists and knows what would have to be found.

Advanced Practice Warning

These practices assume extensive preparation and, in their original setting, years of graded work under supervision. The graded structure existed for a reason and its removal by publication was not an unmixed improvement. Two specific cautions. Sustained visualisation and evocatory work can be genuinely destabilising, and the tradition’s own literature contains ample evidence of practitioners who came apart; if you have a history of psychosis, dissociation or mania, this material is not for solitary work. And the commonest failure here is not dramatic; it is the slow inflation of the practitioner’s sense of their own significance, which the grade systems were partly designed to check.

Modern Practice

Regardie’s publication changed this material permanently: what was once transmitted in a temple over years is now available in a single volume, and every modern practitioner is in some sense working from a leaked syllabus. Contemporary orders descended from the Golden Dawn still use graded curricula, while a large majority of practitioners now work solo from published sources. The honest assessment is that solitary work loses the two things the original structure supplied (pacing, and someone else’s eyes on your conclusions) and that practitioners who compensate deliberately, through written records and a peer or teacher who will disagree with them, do markedly better than those who do not.

Sources: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, founded 1887–88 by Woodman, Westcott and Mathers; Isis-Urania Temple, London, 1888; the original order fractured in 1903. Cipher Manuscripts, in the Trithemius cipher, decoded by Westcott in 1887. Howe, The Magicians of the Golden Dawn (1972), for the grade numbering: the descending 10–1 series maps the ten sephiroth, with a preliminary 0=0 outside it. Regardie, The Golden Dawn (1937–40), is in copyright; note that he was not first into print, Crowley having published order material in The Equinox from 1909. PGM for the ancient parallel to godform assumption, in Betz (1986). The Middle Pillar exercise follows the procedure published by Regardie, The Middle Pillar (1938), in copyright: described, not quoted; the sephirotic divine names are older than the exercise. The scrying, godform and pathworking procedures are this book’s own arrangement of practices the order’s published papers describe; the pathworking adds nothing beyond an order of operations, its Tree being the one drawn in Chapter 3 and its letter-and-trump attributions the two tables set side by side in Chapter 25.

On the texts this chapter could not reach, The Equinox vol. I and the 1919 Blue Equinox in any original printing, and Waite’s printings of the Ars Almadel of 1898 and 1911, the identifiers examined were equinox-v1n1, oto-equinox-vol-3-no-01-the-blue-equinox, bookofblackmagic00wait, book-of-ceremonial-magic-by-a.-e.-waite and a.-e.-waite-the-book-of-ceremonial-magic; the first two and the last two are modern re-keyings or transcriptions rather than page images, and the third is access-restricted. A page-image copy of the 1898 book was found afterwards, BookOfBlackMagicWaite, and it does not close this gap: it names the Almadel in its survey of the Lemegeton without printing the operation. The wax talisman, the seal of gold or silver and the four colours of the choirs belong to the revision of 1911, and that is the printing whose pages were not reached. The 1898 copy is used in Chapter 11 for the seals, which it does print.

Chapter XIVEnochian Advanced

Enochian is not one thing. It is three, laid down two and a half centuries apart: the diaries John Dee kept in the 1580s, the folio in which those diaries were first printed in 1659, and the working system the Golden Dawn built out of them after 1888. Only the first is a primary source, and almost everything a modern practitioner would recognise belongs to the third. Knowing which layer a given piece of Enochian comes from is the whole of the difficulty, and the rest of this chapter is the evidence for telling them apart.

What Dee and Kelley actually did

Between 1581 and 1587 John Dee (mathematician, astrologer to Elizabeth I, owner of the largest private library in England) held several hundred sessions in which a scryer looked into a crystal and reported what appeared there, and Dee wrote it down. Out of those sessions came a corpus: an angelic alphabet, a set of long texts in a language its recipients called Angelical, a great many tables of letters, and instructions for their use.

The critical fact about the arrangement is one Dee states himself, and it governs everything downstream. He did not see anything. Casaubon, editing the diaries in 1659, puts it plainly: Dee “himself saw nothing (for so himself acknowledgeth in some places) but by Kelley’s eyes, and heard nothing but with his ears.” The scryer for most of the corpus was Edward Kelley, and everything in it reached the page through him.

Even the beginning of the record is not Kelley’s. The manuscript of the earliest sessions,

British Library Sloane MS 3188, runs from 22 December 1581 to 23 May 1583 and opens with a different scryer altogether, Barnabas Saul. Kelley arrives after him and stays.

How it got into print, and who wanted it there

The diaries sat in manuscript for seventy years. They were printed in 1659 by Meric Casaubon: a Doctor of Divinity, and the son of the Isaac Casaubon who in 1614 demolished the ancient dating of the Hermetica in Chapter 2. The family has a claim to have twice redirected the history of Western esotericism, both times by publishing something.

The title page states the contents and the intent together, and it reads best as the editorial document it is:

A True & Faithful Relation of What passed for many Yeers Between Dr. John Dee (A Mathematician of Great Fame in Q. Eliz. and King James their Reignes) and Some Spirits: Tending (had it Succeeded) To a General Alteration of most States and Kingdomes in the World… Out of The Original Copy, written with Dr. Dees own Hand: Kept in the Library of Sir Tho. Cotton, Kt. Baronet. With a Preface Confirming the Reality (as to the Point of Spirits) of This Relation: and shewing the several good Uses that a Sober Christian may make of All.

Read the last sentence again. Casaubon is not publishing a magical handbook. He is publishing an exhibit. The preface exists to confirm that the spirits were real and to show what a sober Christian should conclude from that, which, in his view, is that Dee was destroyed by them.

The fraud hypothesis is older than you think

The modern explanation of Enochian is that Kelley invented it and imposed on a credulous old man. That explanation is not modern. Casaubon states it in 1659, in the preface, as an objection he has to deal with: is it not possible, he asks, “that Kelley being a cunning man, and well practised in these things might impose upon the credulity of Dr. Dee (a good innocent man) and the rather, because by this office under the Doctor he got 50l. by the year”: fifty pounds a year being Kelley’s salary as scryer.

Casaubon calls the suggestion “plausible as it is proposed” and then rejects it, on the ground that a careful reader of the whole record will “find it far otherwise.” He rejects it because he has a third explanation available that the modern reader does not: that the spirits were there, and were evil. The point worth keeping is not who was right. It is that the argument was joined at the first printing, by the editor, in public, and that the corpus has never at any time been free of it.

What Casaubon concluded about the spirits he states without hedging. Of the suggestion that good angels were involved:

such as appear in form of Angels of Light, such as deluded Dr. Dee, and daily doth those that hunt after Revelations, and Prophecies, and unlawful Curiosities, I grant it. But that any good Angels did ever meddle in a practice commonly attended with so much imposture, impiety, cousenage as this commonly is, I shall not easily grant.

And of Dee himself he is generous, which is what makes the verdict land. Dee was, he writes, “so good, so innocent, yea, so pious a man, and so sincere a Christian”; and the question that troubles Casaubon is why God would permit such a man “to be so deluded and abused… by evil Spirits, even to his dying day, for ought we know.” The first printed Enochian is a book published by a churchman who thought its author sincere, its contents genuine, and its source damnable.

The third layer, and why this chapter stops

What most modern practitioners mean by Enochian is not the diaries. It is the system the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn assembled from them in the late nineteenth century: the four Watchtowers worked as a coherent scheme, the elemental and Tarot attributions laid across the tables, the pronunciation conventions, the grade structure the material was fitted into. That work is a genuine construction and a considerable one. It is also a construction, and it is not in Dee.

This book gives no Enochian operation, and the reason is specific rather than squeamish. The workable system is in copyright and the public-domain source is not a workable system. The Golden Dawn material reached print chiefly through Regardie between 1937 and 1940 and remains in copyright; this book’s practice, set out in the bibliography, is to describe such material and not reproduce it. What is free of copyright is Casaubon’s 1659 folio, and that is a transcript of conversations, not a set of instructions: the tables are there, and so are the angelic names, but the method for using them as the orders use them is the orders’ own.

An honest chapter can therefore give you the history, the provenance, the layers and the caution, and it cannot hand you a rite without either infringing a copyright or inventing one and calling it Dee’s. It does the first and declines the second.

What the free source does contain: a Call, entire

The section above is right that the folio is a transcript rather than a manual, and it has been understating what the transcript holds. The tables are in it, and the angelic names; and so are the Calls: the long invocations in the Angelical tongue, set down word by word as Kelley reported them from the stone, with Dee’s English against each word and a syllabified pronunciation in the margin. A chapter that says the language exists and never lets the reader see a line of it is hiding the most concrete thing the public-domain source has. Here, therefore, is one entire, exactly as the 1659 folio prints it across pp. 207–208: the Call of the Thirty Aethyrs, the one Call that is used with each of the thirty in turn, its name inserted; and the one the later tradition worked hardest.

Read the middle column downward and Dee’s own English runs: one while let her be known, and another while a stranger, because she is the bed of an harlot and the dwelling place of him that is fallen. O you heavens arise, the lower heavens underneath you let them serve you. Govern those that govern, cast down such as fall, bring forth with those that encrease, and destroy the rotten. No place let it remain in one number. Adde and diminish until the stars be numbred. Arise, move, and appear before the covenant of his mouth, which he hath sworn unto us in his justice. Open the mysteries of your creation, and make us partakers of undefiled knowledge.

Three things in that table are worth more than any modern commentary on it. The first is that the language behaves like a language: od is “and” and recurs as “and”; torzu is “arise” both times it appears; madriiax and oadriax are “heavens” and “lower heavens.” Whatever produced it was consistent with itself across a long text dictated letter by letter. The second is the interruptions, which the folio prints and this book keeps in its note below: the curtain drawn and undrawn mid-Call, and Gabriel breaking in with “Move not, for the place is holy.” The record is of a séance, and it never stops looking like one. The third is what the Call is for: it asks for the mysteries of creation to be opened and for the speaker to be made a partaker of undefiled knowledge. It is a request for knowledge, in the same register as the Poimandres of Chapter 2, four hundred years and one invented language later.

What is still not here is the operation, and the distinction is exact. The folio gives the words and their meaning; it does not give which Aethyr to call for what, what a scryer should expect, how the Call is to be voiced, or what follows from it: the apparatus that turns a text into a practice. That apparatus is the third layer, it is the orders’ own, and the fullest modern account of it is in copyright. A reader who wants to know what the Angelical language is now has fifty-two words of it with the recipient’s own translation. A reader who wants to know what to do with them is looking at the gap this chapter exists to describe.

Which layer are you holding?

Three questions settle it, and they are worth asking of any Enochian source you meet. Is it in Casaubon 1659 or in the manuscripts? Then it is Dee and Kelley, and it is a record of what one man said he saw. Is it a Watchtower worked as an elemental temple, with Tarot and colour attributions? Then it is Golden Dawn, and it is Victorian. Is it a pronunciation guide? Then it is later still, and largely conjectural: the diaries record spellings, not sounds.

None of that makes the later layers worthless. It makes them later, and a practitioner who cannot say which century a technique comes from cannot say what it is evidence of.

Chapter XVProtection & Banishing Adept

None of this is for repelling an attack. The literature is full of hostile spirits and the rites below are worded as though a siege were expected, but what a banishing does in ordinary use is mark a beginning and an end. A practitioner who banishes reliably is one who does not carry the residue of a working into the next working, or into the rest of the day, and that is a real result with a plain explanation. The point is worth making at the start because it decides how the chapter should be read: these are not weapons, and treating them as weapons produces a practitioner who is frightened of their own hobby.

Basic techniques

  1. Visualisation: establish an image of light surrounding you, bounded and complete. Simple, portable, and requires nothing.
  2. Prayer: call upon whatever you understand the divine to be, in your own words or a traditional form. The overwhelming majority of historical protective practice is prayer.
  3. Salt: used across many traditions for purification and boundary-marking, whether scattered, dissolved in water, or laid at a threshold.
  4. Herbs: sage and rosemary are the most commonly used in this tradition, burned or hung. Ventilate if burning, and note that white sage in particular is both ecologically pressured and culturally specific to practices this book does not claim; garden sage and rosemary do the same work in a Hermetic frame.

These four are genuinely sufficient for ordinary purposes, and a practitioner who does them consistently is better protected than one who performs an elaborate ceremony occasionally.

The Lesser Banishing Ritual of the Pentagram

The most widely used banishing in Western ceremonial practice is the LBRP, and it comes from the original Golden Dawn, which places it in the late nineteenth century, not antiquity. It belonged to the First, or Outer, Order: apart from the grade ceremonies it was the only ritual revealed at that level, disclosed to neophytes immediately after initiation, and on R. A. Gilbert’s assessment the nearest thing to a purely magical ritual in the outer curriculum. Its skeleton is genuinely in the Cipher Manuscripts (the banishing-pentagram concept appears on page 14, in what looks like a different hand, and the archangel, element and cardinal-point correspondences are already there) though the Cipher MS nowhere sets the ritual out in full. Its structure has four movements:

  1. The Qabalistic Cross. The practitioner traces a cross on the body, touching forehead, breast and each shoulder while vibrating Hebrew words drawn from the doxology of the Lord’s Prayer, each position corresponding to a location on the Tree of Life.
  2. Formulation of the pentagrams. Beginning in the east and proceeding around the quarters, a pentagram is drawn at each cardinal point while a divine name is vibrated: YHVH in the east, Adonai in the south, Eheieh in the west, AGLA in the north.
  3. Evocation of the archangels. Standing with arms outstretched in the form of a cross (the posture the Golden Dawn called the Calvary Cross, and the position of the godform “Osiris Slain”) four archangels are named at the quarters: Raphael before (east), Gabriel behind (west), Michael at the right hand (south), Auriel at the left (north). The declaration continues in the same breath: “Before me flames the pentagram, behind me shines the six-rayed star,” locating the magician between the pentagram of the microcosm and the hexagram of the macrocosm.
  4. The Qabalistic Cross repeated, closing the ritual as it opened.

Set out in full, and in a form you can work from, it runs as follows. The Hebrew is given unpointed, the pronunciation as the earliest printed version gives it.

The Lesser Banishing Ritual of the Pentagram

  1. The Qabalistic Cross. Face east. Touch the forehead, then the breast, then the right shoulder, then the left, then clasp the hands at the breast, vibrating at each: אתה Ateh ah-TAH — “unto Thee” מלכות Malkuth mal-KOOTH — “the Kingdom” וגבורה ve-Geburah ve-ge-boo-RAH — “and the Power” וגדולה ve-Gedulah ve-ge-doo-LAH — “and the Glory” לעולם אמן le-Olahm, Amen le-oh-LAHM, ah-MEN — “to the ages, amen”
  2. The pentagram in the east. Trace a banishing earth pentagram in the air — beginning at the lower left point, up to the top, and round — with the extended fingers or the wand. Bring the point of the wand to the centre and vibrate: יהוה YHVH ye-ho-WAU
  3. South. Turn sunwise, carrying a line of light at shoulder height from the centre of the eastern pentagram. Trace the same figure and vibrate: אדני Adonai ah-doh-NYE
  4. West. The same, and vibrate: אהיה Eheieh eh-heh-YEH
  5. North. The same, and vibrate: אגלא AGLA ah-goo-LAH
  6. Close the circle. Complete the line back to the east, so that the four pentagrams stand joined in a ring of light at shoulder height.
  7. The archangels. Return to face east. Extend the arms sideways in the form of a cross — the posture the order called the Calvary Cross, and the godform of Osiris Slain — and say: Before me Raphael. Behind me Gabriel. On my right hand Michael. On my left hand Auriel. For before me flames the pentagram, and behind me shines the six-rayed star.
  8. The Qabalistic Cross repeated, exactly as at the opening.

Two textual points, since this book is about texts

The wording of the archangel declaration is not stable. The Golden Dawn form is the one given above, and Graham Wheeler notes that “behind me shines the six-rayed star” is regularly altered in modern versions to “in the column shines the six-rayed star”: the column being the middle pillar of the Tree, with which the magician is identifying. Wheeler dates that variant to Crowley’s “Star Ruby” of 1913. The text of Liber O as it now circulates online in fact reads “For about me flames the Pentagram, and in the Column stands the six-rayed Star,” which would push the variant back to 1909; but this book has not checked that text against the 1909 printing of The Equinox, and an online transcription may carry a later editor’s emendation. The point is recorded here unresolved rather than smoothed over.

The pronunciations are those printed in Liber O: “Ye-ho-wau, Adonai, Eheieh, Agla.” They represent one nineteenth-century English convention, not Hebrew as spoken anywhere. YHVH is not pronounced at all in Jewish practice, and a reader who finds the convention uncomfortable is in good company; substituting Adonai or a silent intention is a recognised solution and the ritual does not stop working.

The ritual’s stated purpose is to banish chaotic or impure forms of the elements from the working space. Its components are plainly Christian and Qabalistic: the Lord’s Prayer doxology, Hebrew divine names, the four archangels, and an association of the quarters with the classical elements by way of the biblical four living creatures.

What is documented and what is not

The LBRP is attributed to the original order of the Golden Dawn, and its structure and content are well attested. Two questions remain genuinely open: who first assembled the formula, and exactly when. Mathers is credited as the principal hand by convention rather than by demonstration, R. A. Gilbert has argued for a larger role for Westcott, and the composition process, in Graham John Wheeler’s words, “remains obscure: the evidence simply does not survive” (Correspondences 8, no. 1, 2020, p. 8). Nothing resembling the ritual existed before the 1880s, and the earliest located manuscript text is datable to the 1890s.

The third question, which earlier materials shaped it, is no longer open. Wheeler’s 2020 source-analysis, by his own account the first anyone has attempted, identifies the ingredients in detail. Éliphas Lévi above all: he first noticed the resemblance between the doxology of the Lord’s Prayer and the sephiroth, and he gives the Qabalistic Cross gesture in recognisable form: the order’s replication of his Hebrew solecisms makes the dependence close to certain. Behind Lévi stand Matthew 6:13 and 1 Chronicles 29:11, by way of a Zohar passage Mathers himself translated in 1887. Agrippa, reaching the order through Barrett’s Magus, supplies the archangel–element correspondences; Ptolemy’s Tetrabiblos supplies the element–direction correspondences onto which Agrippa’s were mapped. Solomonic grimoire practice supplies the divine names at the quarters and the ritual dagger; Freemasonry the circumambulation; medieval rabbinic material the four archangels surrounding the divine throne. The rule about closing the angles of the pentagram appears to come from Goethe’s Faust: the one element borrowed from a work of fiction.

One derivation often repeated should be resisted: the archangel invocation does not descend from the bedtime Shema. What the two share is an earlier ancestor (the Jewish motif of four archangels surrounding God’s throne, the throne being the detail that discriminates) and the before/behind/right/left formula itself runs back through the Seder Rav Amram Gaon to a second-millennium-BCE Mesopotamian exorcism. Claims that the ritual descends from ancient Egyptian or Solomonic practice remain unsupported; the ritual is modern. But its ingredients are now traceable, and the tracing is more interesting than the agnosticism it replaces.

The Lesser Ritual of the Hexagram

The banishing of the pentagram has a companion, and this book has referred to it twice without printing it: the six-rayed star named in the fourth movement above. Liber O gives it immediately after the pentagram ritual, with the instruction that it “is to be performed after the Lesser Ritual of the Pentagram.” It opens with the passage known as the Analysis of the Keyword, which is the most theatrical thing in Western ceremonial practice and also the most compressed: a Latin inscription, read as Hebrew letters, read as a sequence of Egyptian gods, resolving into a single word of light.

The Lesser Ritual of the Hexagram

  1. Stand upright, feet together, left arm at the side, right across the body, holding the wand upright in the median line. Face east.
  2. The Analysis of the Keyword. Say: I.N.R.I. Yod. Nun. Resh. Yod. Virgo, Isis, Mighty Mother. Scorpio, Apophis, Destroyer. Sol, Osiris, Slain and Risen. Isis, Apophis, Osiris, IAO.
  3. The signs. Extend the arms in the form of a cross: the Sign of Osiris Slain. Raise the right arm to point upwards and lower the left to point downwards, elbows square, head turned over the left shoulder so the eyes follow the left forearm: the Sign of the Mourning of Isis. Raise the arms at sixty degrees to each other above the head, head thrown back: the Sign of Apophis and Typhon. Cross the arms on the breast and bow the head: the Sign of Osiris Risen.
  4. Extend the arms again as in the first sign, then cross them again as in the last, saying: L.V.X., Lux, the Light of the Cross.
  5. The four hexagrams. Trace the hexagram of Fire in the east, of Earth in the south, of Air in the west, of Water in the north, as drawn above, vibrating at each: אראריתא ARARITA ah-rah-REE-tah The name is an acrostic: “One is His Beginning: One is His Individuality: His Permutation is One.”
  6. Repeat the Analysis of the Keyword and the signs, exactly as at the opening.

To banish rather than invoke, the ritual is identical except that the direction in which each hexagram is traced is reversed.

One crossing should be marked, because a reader working both rituals in one sitting will walk straight into it. The pentagram ritual above puts air in the east, fire in the south, water in the west and earth in the north. This one, from the same source and four paragraphs later, puts fire in the east, earth in the south, air in the west and water in the north. Liber O sets down both orders and says nothing about the difference, and both stand here as it gives them. Why one book assigns the quarters twice, and differently, it does not explain.

The Greater Ritual of the Hexagram

  1. Used to invoke or banish a planet or a sign of the zodiac rather than an element. Only the hexagram of Earth is used.
  2. Begin tracing from the point of the figure attributed to the planet in question, sunwise, and complete that triangle; then trace the other triangle from its own attributed point and complete it. Liber O gives the rule in the form of a single worked example (to invoke Jupiter, begin from the right-hand point of the lower triangle), which is why some later printings state it as though the lower triangle always came first. It does not; the starting point moves with the planet.
  3. Trace the astrological sigil of the planet in the centre of the hexagram.
  4. For a sign of the zodiac, use the hexagram of the planet that rules the sign, but draw the sigil of the sign in the centre rather than the planet’s.

The point attributions are those of Crowley’s table 777. For which planet governs what, and for choosing the hour, see Chapter 20.

A pentacle of defence

The Solomonic answer to the same problem is an object rather than a rite. Of the forty-four pentacles Mathers prints, one is the exemplary defensive figure, and his description of it is given here exactly as the 1889 first edition has it:

The Fourth Pentacle of the Moon

Figure 52. This defendeth thee from all evil sorceries, and from all injury unto soul or body. Its Angel, Sophiel, giveth the knowledge of the virtue of all herbs and stones; and unto whomsoever shall name him, he will procure the knowledge of all.

Editor’s Note. The Divine Name Eheieh Asher Eheieh, and the Names of the Angels Yahel and Sophiel. The versicle is: “Let them be confounded who persecute me, and let me not be confounded; let them fear, and not I.”

Notice what the versicle does not ask for. It names persecutors, but every clause of it asks for the bearer’s own preservation: the operation is defensive throughout, which is why it is printed here and most of its neighbours are not. And the angel’s side-gift is characteristic of the whole literature: a figure worn against harm also confers the knowledge of the virtues of herbs and stones, which is to say it opens onto Chapter 20. Nothing in this tradition does only one thing.

For how such a figure is made (the metal, the hour, the colours, the silk) see Chapter 20; for the logic of its rings and names, Chapter 22.

Grounding

The most useful protective skill is also the least ceremonial: the ability to return deliberately to ordinary awareness. Eat something. Wash your hands and face. Put your attention on physical sensation: feet on the floor, weight in the chair. Write down what happened and then stop. Speak to someone about something unrelated.

Practitioners who neglect this are the ones who get into difficulty, and the difficulty is nearly always the same: not an external attack but a failure to fully come back, accumulating over weeks into distraction, poor sleep, and a steadily thinner grip on ordinary priorities. If that is happening, the correct response is to stop practising for a while. That option is always available and using it is not a failure.

Modern Practice

Most contemporary practitioners use the LBRP or an abbreviated version of it as a daily practice rather than reserving it for ceremonial occasions, which is a departure from its original place in a graded curriculum and generally a productive one: done daily it becomes a reliable frame rather than a special event. Practitioners uncomfortable with the ritual’s explicitly Judaeo-Christian content have developed numerous adaptations substituting other divine names or dispensing with them; these work, and a reader should know they exist, though the version above is the documented one. The broader modern shift is a demystified reading of what banishing accomplishes: many practitioners now describe it frankly as a psychological boundary-setting technique, and find that describing it that way does not reduce its usefulness in the least.

Sources: Lesser Banishing Ritual of the Pentagram: attributed to the original Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn (founded 1887–88); a First Order ritual; first printed in Crowley, Liber O (1909), then Regardie, The Tree of Life (1932) and The Golden Dawn (1937–40). The Lesser and Greater Rituals of the Hexagram, the Analysis of the Keyword and the four hexagram forms: Crowley, Liber O (1909), section V; the wording of the Analysis and of the hexagram instructions is his. For the sources of the pentagram ritual’s components: Graham John Wheeler, “A Microcosm of the Esoteric Revival: The Histories of the Lesser Banishing Ritual of the Pentagram,” Correspondences: Journal for the Study of Esotericism 8, no. 1 (2020), 5–44: open access under CC BY-NC 4.0, which is not the same as public domain. R. A. Gilbert for the argument that Westcott’s hand was larger than convention allows. Who assembled the formula, and when, remains unresolved; see the note above.

Chapter XVIHealing & Wellness Adept

The Fama of 1614 describes a brotherhood that does not exist, in a manifesto that is probably a fiction, and the first thing it requires of its imaginary members is that they heal the sick without accepting payment. Of everything the Rosicrucian documents promised, that is the part that has aged best, and it is the only part a reader can act on this afternoon. It also sets the standard this chapter is held to: what follows is either something a source actually prescribed, or something modern medicine agrees with, and the two are kept apart on the page.

Principles of Hermetic healing

  • All healing is understood to come from the divine source; the practitioner does not generate it
  • The healer functions as a channel rather than an originator, which is also a safeguard against self-importance
  • Healing addresses the whole person: body, mind and spirit, none of them treated in isolation
  • Prevention is better than cure, and regimen matters more than intervention

The fourth of these deserves the longest look, because it is where the historical tradition and modern medicine agree most completely. The Hermetic and Paracelsian writers took sleep, diet, air, exercise, work and companionship to be the substance of health rather than its background. That is an unglamorous position and it was correct.

The historical practice

Historically, healing in this tradition drew on several strands. Herbalism, systematised through the doctrine of correspondences that assigned plants to planets and planets to organs: the material of Agrippa’s first book. Astrological medicine, timing treatment by the heavens and reading the chart for constitutional tendency. Amulets and charms, ubiquitous in the ancient evidence: a substantial portion of the Greek Magical Papyri consists of remedies and phylacteries for entirely ordinary complaints, alongside the grander material. Prayer and laying on of hands, the oldest and most widespread element. And Paracelsian iatrochemistry, which took the alchemical tradition into medicine and, for all its errors, moved European practice toward specific remedies for specific conditions.

The physicians of the Rosicrucian legend were, in the setting of the manifestos, ordinary doctors: the healing described was practical care given freely, not miracle-working. That framing is a useful corrective to how the subject is often presented now.

Paracelsus and the signature of things

The figure who did most to shape this material is Paracelsus (1493 or 1494–1541), and his contribution was to insist that disease comes from outside and is specific: against the humoral orthodoxy, which held it came from inside and was a matter of balance. From that follows the search for specific remedies, which is the ancestor of pharmacology, and much of the strangeness of the tradition besides.

The strangeness is the doctrine of signatures: the belief that a plant’s form advertises its use, so that the walnut resembling a brain is good for the head and the lungwort with its spotted leaf is good for the lung. It is an inference from the correspondence principle of Chapter 1; if the above and the below answer to each other, a thing’s appearance should disclose its virtue. As a research method it is unreliable; as a mnemonic in a world without pharmacopoeias it did real work; and as an illustration of how a metaphysical principle turns into a practice it is the clearest example in this book.

Culpeper, whose planetary herbs are tabulated in Chapter 20, is working inside this system. When he assigns a herb to Mars and an inflammation to Mars, the assignment is the diagnosis and the prescription at once. The system is coherent. It is also, in a great many particular cases, wrong, and the chapter’s warning below is not a modern imposition on it: several of its own practitioners said as much.

The vow, and what it was for

Return to the detail this chapter opened with, because it repays attention. The Fama requires each brother “to profess nothing but to cure the sick, and that gratis”; and look at what that commits them to. A physician who may not charge cannot select patients by their means. The vow is not primarily about generosity; it is a constraint on whom the healer may serve, and it removes the mechanism by which medicine sorts itself by wealth.

Of everything the manifestos promised (the invisible college, the universal reformation, the secret tomb) this is the commitment that has aged best, and it is the one that would still be difficult to keep.

Energetic work

Contemporary practice in this area centres on directing attention and intention toward another person, whether by laying on of hands, at a distance, or through visualisation of light. If you do this work, a few things follow from the tradition’s own commitments. Ask permission: working on someone without their knowledge violates the ethical position of Chapter 1 whatever the intention behind it. Ground afterwards, as in Chapter 15. Make no diagnostic or prognostic claims. And attend to your own state: practitioners who do this work while depleted tend to make it about themselves.

The still-room: how the medicines were actually made

“Potions” is the storybook word; the historical word is preparations, and the tradition wrote them down in exact and practical detail. Culpeper, whose planetary herbs are tabulated in Chapter 20, closes his herbal with a section headed “Directions for making Syrups, Conserves, &c.”: the working end of astrological medicine, addressed “for your instruction-sake, kind countrymen and women.” His three ways of making a syrup are a fair sample of the whole craft:

Syrups made by infusion are usually made of flowers, and of such flowers as soon lose their colour and strength by boiling, as roses, violets, peach flowers, &c. They are thus made: Having picked your flowers clean, to every pound of them add three pounds or three pints, which you will (for it is all one) of spring water, made boiling hot; first put your flowers into a pewter pot, with a cover, and pour the water on them; then shutting the pot, let it stand by the fire, to keep hot twelve hours, and strain it out.

Then syrups by decoction, for roots and barks that can stand the boiling; and syrups by juice, for herbs pressed fresh. Behind those stand the rest of the still-room’s repertoire (conserves, distilled waters, oils, ointments and poultices) each with its own directions in the same plain voice. Two things are worth seeing in this. First, the method is the timing: the herb is gathered in its planet’s day and hour, exactly as Chapter 20 prescribes, and the preparation is where that timing was supposed to be captured and kept. Second, there is nothing arcane in the procedure itself; it is kitchen technique, and deliberately so; Culpeper’s whole polemical project was to put medicine into the hands of people who could not pay a physician.

The warning below applies with full force: these are seventeenth-century medical directions reproduced as history. The form (infusion, decoction, expression) is simply good extraction technique and is used in every kitchen; the uses Culpeper assigns to the results are pre-modern medicine and are not to be followed against illness.

The thirty-six decans of sickness

This chapter said above that a substantial portion of the ancient evidence is remedies and phylacteries for ordinary complaints, and then printed none of it. The oldest systematic example is also the most startling, because it joins three things this book has kept in separate chapters (the astrology of the decans, the demonology of Solomon, and medicine) into a single working table. In the Testament of Solomon, the text this book quotes in Chapter 11, there come before the king “thirty-six spirits, their heads shapeless like dogs, but in themselves they were human in form; with faces of asses, faces of oxen, and faces of birds.” They announce themselves as “the thirty-six elements, the world-rulers of this darkness”: the decans of the zodiac, three to each sign, the same thirty-six that Chapter 21 gives as divisions of the circle. Each then states, in turn, which part of the body it attacks and exactly what defeats it. It is a complete medical demonology with the cures attached, and it reads like a hospital intake ledger written by an exorcist.

The table below gives all of them, in the text’s own order and numbering. Two entries, the fourth and the twenty-second, are missing from the surviving Greek, and the gaps are kept rather than papered over: the manuscript loses two decans, so this table has thirty-four rows.

Read as a set, the remedies sort themselves into a small grammar. The commonest is the name-formula: an angel’s name plus the demon’s own, spoken (Michael, imprison Ruax) on the principle this book met in the papyri and meets again in every conjuration: to know the name is to hold the thing. Then the worn writing: names on paper at the neck or ear, on tin at the loins for a urinary complaint, on copper for the ribs; and the copper must come from a ship that missed its anchorage, a failed thing turned against a failing body. Then the kitchen pharmacy: coriander on the lips for fever, laurel seeds in oil, salt rubbed into oil for lingering disease; and Conybeare’s own footnote points out that Pliny prescribes coriander for exactly the same complaint, which is his evidence for dating the text to Pliny’s age. And once, wonderfully, no magic at all: the thirtieth decan is a swallowed fish-bone, and the remedy is a bone from the same fish and a cough.

What this table is doing in a healing chapter is the point. It is the ancestor, in working form, of everything this chapter has described: the assignment of body parts to celestial powers: compare the planetary body of Fig. 1, which does with seven planets what this does with thirty-six decans; the amulet with the written name, which Chapter 22 traces through the whole tradition; and the conviction that disease is a personal agent that can be addressed, which Paracelsus’s specific-cause doctrine is a rationalised descendant of. None of it is medicine, and the warning below covers all of it. But a reader who wants to know what ancient healing magic actually looked like, complaint by complaint, now has the fullest surviving specimen entire.

The regimen

The oldest and least glamorous practice in the chapter, and the one its sources agree on. It is given as a discipline rather than as medicine.

  1. Sleep, first. The tradition ranks it before all interventions, and so does the modern evidence.
  2. Air and movement daily, outdoors where possible. Both are in the classical list of the non-naturals: the things not intrinsic to the body that nonetheless determine its state.
  3. Food as regimen, not event. The Hermetic and Paracelsian writers treat diet as the substance of health rather than its background.
  4. Work that is yours, and rest that is genuinely rest.
  5. Company. Isolation is treated in this literature as a condition to be corrected, not a neutral circumstance.
  6. Review the six weekly, in writing, and change one thing at a time. The tradition’s claim is that the six together are the treatment.

Nothing here is occult, and that is the finding rather than a disappointment. When the sources of this book are read for what they actually recommend most often, this is what comes back.

On Health and Medicine

Nothing in this chapter is a substitute for medical care. Do not delay diagnosis or treatment, and do not discontinue prescribed medication, in favour of any practice in this book. Do not offer prognoses, discourage anyone from seeing a doctor, or represent spiritual practice as treatment for a serious condition: the historical record of harm here is extensive and it falls hardest on the frightened and the desperate.

Herbal preparations are not exempt from this: plants contain active pharmacology, several traditional remedies are outright toxic, and interactions with prescribed drugs are common and sometimes severe. Consult a physician or pharmacist before combining them with medication, and treat historical herbals as history rather than as dosing guidance.

Used as a complement to proper care (for calm, for meaning, for the considerable value of attentive presence) this material has a real contribution to make. Used as a replacement, it kills people.

Modern Practice

Responsible contemporary practitioners position this work explicitly as complementary, and many now work alongside conventional care rather than in competition with it: in hospice and chaplaincy settings, in pain management, in support of patients under active treatment. That represents a genuine and fairly recent maturation of the field. Practitioners also now have research literature on placebo effects, therapeutic presence and the measurable value of unhurried attention, which offers a plausible and unembarrassing account of why sitting with a frightened person helps. Where the historical tradition claimed to cure, the honest modern claim is narrower and more defensible: this work can reliably reduce suffering, and it does not treat disease.

Sources: Fama Fraternitatis (1614) on healing the sick without payment. Agrippa, De occulta philosophia (1533), Book I, on herbal and planetary correspondence. PGM for ancient remedies, amulets and phylacteries (Betz, 1986). Paracelsus (1493 or 1494–1541) for iatrochemistry. Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (1653), “Directions for making Syrups, Conserves, &c.”, quoted verbatim. The thirty-six decans of sickness: F. C. Reading the leaves was required: the scan’s text layer garbles the names (Sphattdfo for Sphandôr, BobtI for Bobêl, Htphisikireth for Hêphêsikireth), and the names are the content. The quotations in the table are Conybeare’s English as printed, with his accents; the descriptions of the afflictions are compressed. The fourth and twenty-second entries are wanting in the Greek and are recorded as gaps, as are the two places (§§75, 92) where his footnotes mark a lacuna. The observation that Agchoniôn’s diminishing name is the ABRACADABRA device is this book’s; the Pliny parallel for coriander (§87) is Conybeare’s own footnote, citing Nat. Hist. xx. 20.

Chapter XVIIProsperity & Abundance Beginner

The law of attraction is not ancient, and this is the chapter where the dating work of this book earns its keep. The doctrine that thought directly produces material circumstance comes from the American New Thought movement of the late nineteenth century, the same movement that produced The Kybalion in 1908, and it runs from there through the positive-thinking literature to the prosperity industry of the present day. What the older sources hold is close enough to be mistaken for it and different in a way that matters: prosperity there is the sufficiency of all good things, health and wisdom and competence and love among them, and money is one good that behaves badly when treated as the only one. The distinction is not a euphemism for having less money. It is the difference between a claim that can fail and a claim that cannot.

Principles of prosperity

  • Prosperity follows from alignment with the order of things rather than from force applied against it
  • Service to others creates abundance: a claim about how goods actually circulate, not only a moral instruction
  • Gratitude reorients attention toward what is present rather than what is absent
  • Generosity multiplies prosperity, and hoarding reliably impoverishes the hoarder in the ways that matter

Where this chapter has to be careful

No other subject treated here has been commercialised so thoroughly, and knowing the lineage is what explains the odd sensation the doctrine produces: it feels Hermetic and sits awkwardly with every actual text. That is because it descends from the tradition’s vocabulary and not from its argument.

The ancient Hermetica are not about acquisition. Their concern is the ascent of the soul and the shedding of what binds it; and among the things to be shed, in the Poimandres’s account, is greed. A tradition whose foundational vision treats acquisitiveness as an impediment cannot straightforwardly be made into a wealth technique, and the attempt requires quietly dropping most of what the source says.

The practical harm is specific and worth naming. Doctrines that make prosperity a direct product of correct thinking imply, unavoidably, that poverty is a product of incorrect thinking, which blames the poor for structural conditions and lands hardest on people already in difficulty. It is also the mechanism by which a great deal of money is extracted from desperate people by teachers selling the technique. Where a practice in this area asks for significant payment on the promise of return, that is the point to stop.

Where the modern doctrine comes from

The lineage can be dated precisely, which is the most useful thing this chapter can offer. It does not begin in Egypt.

DateStep
1840s–60sPhineas Quimby’s mental healing in New England: the root of New Thought, and a healing doctrine before it is a wealth doctrine.
1908The Kybalion, Chicago. Mentalism as the first principle: “The All is Mind; the Universe is Mental.” See Chapter 1.
1910Wallace D. Wattles, The Science of Getting Rich: the doctrine in its bare form, and the direct ancestor of everything after it.
1937Napoleon Hill, Think and Grow Rich: the same claim, mass-market.
2006The Secret, which cites Wattles as its origin and sells the doctrine to a global audience as ancient wisdom.

Wattles should be read in his own words rather than paraphrased, because he is admirably unhedged. His first chapter opens: “There is a Science of getting rich, and it is an exact science, like algebra or arithmetic. There are certain laws which govern the process of acquiring riches; once these laws are learned and obeyed by any man, he will get rich with mathematical certainty.”

That is not a claim about attitude or diligence. It is a claim about physical law. And Wattles saw clearly what follows from it, and accepted it. His third chapter is titled “Is Opportunity Monopolized?” and answers itself in its first sentence: “No man is kept poor because opportunity has been taken away from him; because other people have monopolized the wealth, and have put a fence around it.”

Whatever else that is, it is a falsifiable claim about the world, made in 1910, and the twentieth century has not been kind to it. It is also the exact point at which the doctrine becomes cruel: if no one is kept poor by circumstance, then everyone poor is poor by their own thinking. The prosperity industry has never resolved this, because it cannot: the promise and the blame are the same sentence read from two ends.

What the older sources actually say

Set that beside the Hermetica. The Poimandres describes the soul’s ascent through the seven planetary zones, handing back at each the thing that zone had lent it, and the list is printed in full in Chapter 2 rather than repeated here. Two details of it bear on this chapter and are worth stating exactly, because the loose version of them is easy to reach for. The wealth item is the sixth zone and not the first: the first is the Energy of Growth and Waning, which is a lunar idea rather than an appetite for money. And what the sixth zone takes back is not the wish to be well off but, in the text’s own words, “Striving for Wealth by evil means.” The qualifier is there and should not be dropped: what is surrendered is a particular vice, getting money wrongly, and not prosperity as such. What can be said, and it is enough for the argument, is that no item in that list is a technique for obtaining anything. Every one of them is something the soul puts down in order to rise, and the sixth stands in company with arrogance, audacity and falsehood, which tells you how it was classed.

Mead, editing the list, works out what the sixth item is made of, and the analysis is worth having because it settles the point this chapter turns on. Setting the seven zones beside the twelve torments of the thirteenth treatise, he reads “Getting Wealth by evil means (6)” as “a combination of Guile (9) and Avarice (6).” The vice is a compound, and guile is half of it. He adds one further distinction, and it is fatal to any attempt to read the passage as a rule of life: in the Poimandres, he says, what is described is “the process of transformation in the case of a good man after death,” whereas the thirteenth treatise sets out “the Way of Rebirth in a living man.” The seven-zone list is an account of what a soul lays down on its way out of the world. It was never a programme for conduct inside it, in either direction.

This does not make the tradition hostile to competence or to having enough. What it does mean is that a wealth technique cannot be derived from these texts without inverting them. The modern doctrine did not grow out of ancient Hermeticism; it borrowed its vocabulary. That is a specific, checkable claim, and it is the reason this chapter exists.

What prosperity magic actually looked like

The older tradition did have a prosperity operation, and setting it beside the modern doctrine is the clearest way to see the difference between them. It is Renaissance, it is documented to the page, and it is an object rather than a mental technique: the talisman of Jupiter. Agrippa’s Three Books of Occult Philosophy, in the English of 1651, gives the whole specification. “The second is called the table of Jupiter, which consists of a Quaternian drawn into it self, containing sixteen particular numbers, and in every line, and Diameter four, making thirty four. Now the Sum of all is 136.” And then the claim: “They say that if it be impressed upon a Silver plate with Jupiter being powerfull, and ruling, it conduceth to gain, and riches, favor, and love, peace, and concord, and to appease enemies, to confirm honors, dignities, and counsels, and dissolve enchantments if it be engraven on a corall.”

The contrast is the point of printing it. The Renaissance operation is falsifiable and modest: a made thing, a planetary hour, a specific list of effects, and “they say” in front of all of it. The modern doctrine is unfalsifiable and total: thought produces circumstance, and failure proves only that one thought wrongly. A reader who wants the tradition’s prosperity magic has it above, with its construction in Chapter 22, its astral timing in Chapter 23 and its consecration in Chapter 20. A reader who wants money for thinking has been sold something, and this chapter has already said by whom.

Practice

What the tradition genuinely supports here is modest and useful. A gratitude practice, the deliberate daily enumeration of what is actually present, reliably shifts attention, and attention shapes judgement. Clarity of intention: writing plainly what you are working toward and what you are prepared to do for it, which is more often revealing than motivating. Regular generosity, fixed in advance rather than decided by mood. And the discipline of examining what you actually want, since a good deal of what presents itself as a desire for money is a desire for security, or standing, or the freedom to stop doing something: all of which have more direct routes.

None of this is a technique for obtaining money without working, and the tradition never claimed otherwise. What it offers is a defensible relationship to material things: enough is a real quantity, it is generally nearer than it appears, and the pursuit of more than enough has a documented history of costing people the other goods on the list.

A prosperity discipline, offered as what it is

This is modern, it is this book’s own arrangement, and it makes no claim to alter circumstance by thought. It is a discipline of attention, which is the part of the older material that survives translation.

  1. Keep the ledger honestly. Once a week, write down what came in and what went out. Not a budget: a record. Most of what people believe about their own finances does not survive contact with a written record.
  2. Name sufficiency. Write the figure that would be enough, and the date you last had less than it. The tradition’s claim is that prosperity is sufficiency of several goods rather than maximisation of one; that claim is testable against your own ledger.
  3. Give something away weekly: money, work or time, in an amount fixed in advance rather than by feeling. The tradition holds that goods circulate; whether or not that is metaphysics, it is a check on hoarding.
  4. Note one thing already present. Aloud, at the same point in the week. Gratitude here is not a technique for acquiring more; it is a correction to the habit of registering only what is absent.
  5. Do the work in front of you. Wattles’s one durable observation, stripped of the metaphysics, is that people who act on present opportunity do better than people who wait for a better one.

Sources: Corpus Hermeticum I on the shedding of greed in the soul’s ascent. The seven-zone list is printed in Chapter 2 from Mead, Thrice-Greatest Hermes (1906), vol.
