The weekly discipline above is this book’s own and is not historical.

Chapter XVIIISeasonal Celebrations Beginner

Four of the eight festivals in this chapter are facts about the tilt of the planet. The other four are agricultural quarter days with a long history of their own. The wheel that joins all eight is younger than the paperback book, assembled between the 1940s and the 1950s and given its modern names in the 1970s, and this chapter dates each stage of that assembly rather than presenting the finished article as immemorial. What survives the dating intact is the reason to keep the calendar at all: the solstices and equinoxes arrive on time whether or not the practitioner is enthusiastic this month, which is exactly what a practice anchored to nothing but its own enthusiasm lacks.

The four solar stations

  • Spring Equinox (around 20 March in the northern hemisphere): renewal and new beginnings. Light and dark in balance, with light increasing. Traditionally a point for starting work and for setting intentions that will be tested over the growing season.
  • Summer Solstice (around 21 June): the peak of solar energy, the longest day. A point of fullness, and, in most traditional readings, of recognition that fullness is also a turning: the light begins to withdraw from here.
  • Autumn Equinox (around 22 September): harvest and gratitude. Balance again, with dark increasing. A point for assessment: what actually came of the year’s work, honestly counted.
  • Winter Solstice (around 21 December): inner light and contemplation, the longest night. Traditionally the most inward of the four, and the one most widely marked across cultures, since the return of the light after the longest night is the most reliably consoling fact available to people without calendars.

Practitioners in the southern hemisphere should reverse these: the astronomical events are shared but the seasons are not, and observing a “spring” equinox in March in Australia inverts the meaning of the whole cycle. A surprising amount of published material silently assumes the northern hemisphere.

The cross-quarters

Many practitioners also mark the four traditional British and Irish season-opening quarter days, at the beginning of February, May, August and November: Imbolc (1–2 February), Beltane (1 May), Lughnasadh or Lammas (1 August) and Samhain (1 November). These are conventionally called cross-quarter days, but they are not true midpoints; as Hutton notes, the eight dates form “two equal-armed crosses, imposed on each other in a slightly crooked pattern, some five weeks apart and some seven weeks apart.” Together with the four solar stations they make up the eightfold “Wheel of the Year.”

It should be said plainly that the Wheel as a unified system is a mid-twentieth-century construction, and that it was assembled by stages rather than designed in one act. In Wicca the quarter days came first, standing alone in the earliest surviving liturgy of the 1940s; the solstices were added around 1953; the equinoxes only after Witchcraft Today went to press in 1954; and the eight reached equal status in early 1958, when Gardner’s coven objected collectively and Gardner gave way: a sequence Ronald Hutton reconstructs from the testimony of four surviving members. Ross Nichols’s Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids is a recipient rather than a co-originator: on Hutton’s account Nichols seceded in 1964 and promptly instituted “the new Wiccan pattern of eight festivals” as one of his Druidic innovations. The often-repeated story that Gardner and Nichols harmonised the calendar together during a naturist retreat is unsourced, and the reverse claim, that Nichols conceived it first, comes from a rival Druid order rather than from scholarship. The phrase “Wheel of the Year” was in use for the cycle of eight observances by the mid-1960s.

Three of the eight names are later still, and not British. Yule is a genuinely old midwinter name, but Ostara, Litha and Mabon were applied to the spring equinox, summer solstice and autumn equinox by the Californian Wiccan Aidan Kelly, by his own account for a “Pagan-Craft” calendar of 1974, and spread through the magazine Green Egg, only entering British Pagan usage in the 1980s. The words themselves are older: Litha and Ostara are Bede’s month-names (Ostara reaching modern usage via Jacob Grimm), and Mabon is Mabon ap Modron of Welsh myth, a derivation Hutton notes British scholars might find “preposterously inappropriate.” What Kelly did was apply existing words, not coin them.

The individual festivals have genuine historical antecedents of varying strength (the Gaelic quarter days are attested, the solstices are astronomical) but the eightfold wheel as a single system is recent, and it is not Hermetic in origin at all. This needs saying because the Wheel is frequently presented as an unbroken ancient inheritance. It is a good framework, genuinely useful, well balanced, and now the practice of a great many people. It is also about seventy years old. Both things are true and neither needs hiding.

What the antecedents actually say

Two claims in the paragraphs above are doing a lot of work and have so far been asserted rather than shown: that the Gaelic quarter days are attested, and that Litha and Ostara are Bede’s month-names. Both are checkable in a few lines, and the two cases turn out to be very unlike each other, which is the useful part.

Take the English side first. Bede, writing about 725, breaks off from the Church calendar to explain what the old English months were called, because, as he says, it seems to him unfitting to describe other nations’ reckoning and pass over his own. The whole basis of the modern festival name is this:

Eostur-monath, qui nunc Paschalis mensis interpretatur, quondam a Dea illorum quæ Eostre vocabatur, et cui in illo festa celebrabant, nomen habuit: a cujus nomine nunc Paschale tempus cognominant, consueto antiquæ observationis vocabulo gaudia novæ solennitatis vocantes.

Eostur-month, which is now rendered as the Paschal month, once took its name from a goddess of theirs called Eostre, in whose honour they held feasts in it; and by her name they now call the Paschal season, giving the joys of the new observance the customary name of the old. That is the entire ancient record of Eostre. One sentence, one author, and no other mention of her anywhere in the surviving literature of the Anglo-Saxons or of any related people. Jacob Grimm, in 1835, reasoned from Bede’s Eostre to a Germanic Ostara, and it is Grimm’s reconstruction, not Bede’s sentence, that reached the twentieth century and became the name of a festival. The chain is short and every link in it is visible, which is more than can usually be said.

The other name comes from the same chapter and is weaker still, because in Bede it is not a goddess and not a festival:

Lida dicitur blandus, sive navigabilis, quod in utroque mense et blanda sit serenitas aurarum, et navigari soleant æquora.

Lida means gentle, or navigable, because in both of those months the air is mild and the seas are usually fit for sailing. It is a remark about weather and shipping. Whatever is being marked at midsummer under that name, Bede is not the authority for it.

Those are two sentences out of a short chapter, and the chapter repays being read whole, because whole it says something the two sentences on their own do not. Bede is not writing about festivals. He is explaining a calendar, and he glosses every month in it:

Roman monthEnglish nameWhat Bede says it means
JanuaryGiulinamed from the turning of the sun toward the increase of the day, one month going before it and one following
FebruarySol-monath“the month of cakes,” which they offered in it to their gods
MarchRhed-monathnamed from their goddess Rheda, to whom they sacrificed in it
AprilEostur-monathnamed from their goddess Eostre, in whose honour they held feasts in it
MayThri-milchibecause the cattle were milked three times a day, such once was the plenty of Britain
June and JulyLidagentle, or navigable, the air being mild and the seas fit for sailing in both
AugustVueod-monaththe month of tares, because they are then most abundant
SeptemberHaleg-monaththe month of sacred rites
OctoberVuinter-fyllethwinter and full moon compounded, because winter began at that month’s full moon
NovemberBlod-monaththe month of immolations, because the cattle that were to be killed were then vowed to their gods
DecemberGiulicalled by the same name as January

Three things in that list bear directly on the modern cycle. The first is that Bede names two goddesses and not one. Rheda is in exactly the same position as Eostre, attested in this sentence and nowhere else in the surviving literature, and nobody has built a festival on her. Whatever argument supports Ostara supports Rheda equally, and the fact that the twentieth century took up one and ignored the other is a fact about the twentieth century. The second is that nine of the eleven glosses are agricultural or astronomical rather than divine: cakes, three milkings, tares, the full moon that starts winter, the month the meat is vowed. This is a farming calendar with two goddesses in it, not a liturgy. The third is that the two names the modern wheel borrowed are the two that sit closest to the solar stations, which is why they were available to borrow.

Bede also records what the English did at midwinter, and it is better attested than anything the wheel puts there:

Incipiebant autem annum ab octavo Calendarum Januariarum die, ubi nunc natale Domini celebramus. Et ipsam noctem nunc nobis sacrosanctam, tunc gentili vocabulo Modranicht, id est, matrum noctem appellabant: ob causam ut suspicamur ceremoniarum, quas in ea pervigiles agebant.

They began the year on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, where we now celebrate the Lord’s birth. And that same night, now most holy to us, they then called by the heathen word Modranicht, that is, mothers’ night, on account, as we suppose, of the ceremonies which they performed through it in vigil. A named night, a date, a practice held all night, and a hedge (ut suspicamur, as we suppose) where the author does not know. That is a stronger record than the one sentence about Eostre, and no modern festival is named for it.

And then the sentence that settles what shape the old English year had:

Item principaliter annum totum in duo tempora, hyemis videlicet, et æstatis dispartiebant: sex illos menses quibus longiores noctibus dies sunt æstati tribuendo, sex reliquos hyemi.

They divided the whole year principally into two seasons, winter and summer, giving to summer the six months in which the days are longer than the nights, and the remaining six to winter. Two seasons, six months each, divided at the equinoxes by the length of the day. Not four stations and not eight. The oldest English description of the native year is a two-part year with a midwinter vigil in it, and the eightfold wheel is not a worn-down version of that. It is a different object, assembled from different materials, as the dating above shows.

Now the Gaelic side, and the difference is immediate. Sanas Cormaic, the glossary attributed to Cormac mac Cuilennáin and put together around the turn of the tenth century, has an entry that does not merely name a day but describes what was done on it:

Belltaine ‘May-day’ i.e. bil-tene i.e. lucky fire, i.e. two fires which Druids used to make with great incantations, and they used to bring the cattle [as a safeguard] against the diseases of each year to those fires [in marg.] they used to drive the cattle between them.

An etymology, a practice, a purpose and the people who performed it. That is an antecedent in a sense the Eostre sentence is not, and the contrast is worth holding on to when anyone tells you the eight festivals are equally ancient. They are not equally anything. One of the cross-quarters has a tenth-century description of cattle driven between two fires against murrain; one of the solar stations has a single line of Bede about a goddess nobody else mentions, and another has a line about the sailing season. The bracketed words in the Belltaine entry are the Victorian editors’ own, marking what they supplied and what stood in the margin of the manuscript, and they are left visible here for the same reason they were printed there.

Observance

What to actually do is simple, and the tradition’s own emphasis falls on regularity rather than elaboration. Mark the day. Note where the sun rises and sets, which is the observation the whole system rests on and which almost nobody makes. Review the season that is ending and name what you are carrying into the next. Eat something appropriate to the time of year. If you keep the record recommended in Chapter 7, read back to the previous station: four entries a year, read in sequence, will tell you more about your own development than any amount of daily introspection.

A single structure serves all eight stations, which is the practical advantage of an eightfold wheel over eight unrelated festivals. What changes between them is the question asked, not the form.

An observance for any of the eight

  1. Observe first. Go outside near sunrise or sunset and note where on the horizon the sun stands. Write it down. Over a year these notes become the only part of this that is not interpretation.
  2. Open as in Chapter 8: the short form is sufficient and appropriate here.
  3. Light one candle for the season closing and one for the season opening. At the winter solstice, light the second from the first.
  4. Read back to your record from the previous station. Read it aloud. This is the heart of the practice and it takes five minutes.
  5. Name, aloud, one thing the closing season completed and one thing it did not. Neither needs to be significant.
  6. Ask the question of the station (below), and write the answer without editing it.
  7. Eat something of the season, deliberately, as part of the rite rather than after it.
  8. Close as in Chapter 8. Extinguish the first candle; let the second burn down safely.
The questions are this book’s own, not traditional. The dates are for the northern hemisphere; in the southern, the solar stations shift by six months and the quarter days conventionally follow them.
StationApprox. dateThe question
Winter solstice (Yule)21 DecWhat is worth carrying through the dark?
Imbolc1–2 FebWhat has begun that is not yet visible?
Spring equinox20 MarWhere am I out of balance, and in which direction?
Beltane1 MayWhat am I willing to commit to in public?
Summer solstice21 JunWhat is at its height, and what does that cost?
Lughnasadh (Lammas)1 AugWhat is ready to be harvested, and what am I refusing to cut?
Autumn equinox22 SepWhat is finished? Say it plainly.
Samhain1 NovWho and what am I carrying that is no longer here?

The names Ostara, Litha and Mabon are deliberately absent from that table: as the dating above establishes, they were applied to the solar stations in California in the 1970s. Use them if you like them (many practitioners do, and nothing depends on it) but the solstices and equinoxes had no such names before then, and the table above says only what can be dated.

The deeper purpose of seasonal practice is the correspondence of Chapter 1 put to use: the cycles of the year, of a life, and of the alchemical work of Chapter 5 are held to be the same pattern at different scales. Winter is nigredo. Whether one takes that as metaphysics or as metaphor, it is a genuinely steadying thing to have available in February.

Chapter XIXGreater Mysteries Advanced

Every tradition in this book claims a summit: a body of knowledge reserved for those who have prepared for it, spoken of in the sources with deliberate reticence. This chapter is about what that reticence has actually meant historically, and what it means for a reader holding a book that claims to contain the whole thing.

The Path of Initiation

The path to the Greater Mysteries, as the tradition describes it, involves:

  1. Mastery of the foundational practices
  2. Purification of body, mind and spirit
  3. Development of the spiritual faculties
  4. Service to humanity
  5. Direct experience of the divine

Two features of that list deserve notice. It is sequential, and the sequence is not decorative: nothing in the tradition suggests the later items are available to someone who has skipped the earlier. And service sits fourth: before the culmination, not after it. Whatever else the Greater Mysteries were held to be, they were not understood as a private attainment.

What “mystery” meant

The word carries a specific historical sense that has largely been lost. In the ancient mystery cults (Eleusis, Samothrace, the Mithraic grades) a mystery was not a puzzle or a secret doctrine but something undergone. The initiate at Eleusis was not told a fact; they were put through an experience, and the prohibition on disclosure concerned that experience rather than any proposition about it. This is why ancient sources can be simultaneously insistent about secrecy and unembarrassed about publishing their philosophy: the philosophy was never the secret.

The Hermetic texts inherit this structure. The Poimandres reports a vision rather than arguing a case, and its claim that knowledge of the divine comes through direct experience and not through belief is a statement about method. What cannot be transmitted in writing is not information being withheld; it is an experience that writing cannot contain. Michael Maier, defending the Rosicrucians in 1617, placed their origins in exactly this lineage (“the mysteries of Eleusis and Samothrace, the Magi of Persia, the Pythagoreans”) a genealogy that says more about how the seventeenth century understood itself than about actual descent, but which locates the aspiration accurately.

Lesser and Greater

The distinction in this chapter’s title is not decorative, and it is older than the orders of Chapter 13. In the ancient mystery traditions the Lesser Mysteries and the Greater were separate stages with separate subjects, and G. R. S. Mead, editing the Hermetic sermons in 1906, states the division plainly: the subject of the Lesser Mysteries was genesis, birth; and “Rebirth was that of the Greater.”

That single sentence organises the whole subject. The Lesser Mysteries concern how a thing comes to be: cosmology, the descent of the soul, the structure of the world. Those are the subjects of Chapter 2 and Chapter 3, and they can be taught. The Greater concern palingenesia, being born again; and the tradition’s consistent claim is that this cannot be taught, only undergone.

Whether one accepts the claim or not, it explains the shape of every institution in this book. A curriculum can deliver the Lesser. The Greater is why the curricula all end in a grade that no examination can confer, and why the literature turns, at exactly that point, from instruction to report.

The one initiate who wrote it down

That turn from instruction to report has one ancient witness who was put through the thing himself and then wrote about it in the first person. Lucius Apuleius of Madaura, a Platonist of Roman North Africa born about 125, is the author of a defence speech against a charge of magic that he delivered and won, and of a novel of transformations whose eleventh and last book leaves the comedy behind and describes an initiation into the mysteries of Isis. It is the only first-person account of a mystery initiation to survive from antiquity. What makes it useful here is not that it describes the rite. It is that it refuses to.

Notice first what he prints without hesitation. The goddess appears to Lucius on a beach at night and declares herself, and the declaration is a piece of theology given entire, with the list of names under which the one power is worshipped across the whole Mediterranean:

The whole earth worships my godhead, one and individual, under many a changing shape, with varied rites and by many diverse names. There the Phrygians, first-born of men, call me the mother of the gods that dwells at Pessinus; there the Athenians, sprung from the soil they till, know me as Cecropian Minerva; there the wave-beaten Cyprians style me Venus of Paphos; the archer Cretans, Diana of the hunter’s net; the Sicilians, with their threefold speech, Stygian Proserpine; the Eleusinians, the ancient goddess Ceres. … the Egyptians mighty in ancient lore, honour me with my peculiar rites and call me by my true name, Isis the Queen.

That is the doctrine of this chapter’s opening pages, stated by a second-century novelist: one power, many rites, many names, and no reason at all to keep any of it quiet. He publishes it. He publishes the preparation too, and it is recognisable from every other chapter in this book: ten consecutive days of abstinence from the pleasures of the table, no living thing eaten and no wine drunk, then a bath, then a sprinkling with pure water by the priest, then a linen robe that no man had yet worn. Only at the door does the account stop, and it stops by turning to face the reader:

Perchance, eager reader, thou burnest to know what then was said, what done. I would tell thee, were it lawful for me to tell, and thou shouldst know all, were it lawful for thee to hear. But both tongue and ear would be infected with like guilt did I gratify such rash curiosity. Yet since perchance it is pious craving that vexes thee, I will not torment thee by prolongation of thine anguish. Hear then and believe, for what I tell is true. I drew nigh to the confines of death, I trod the threshold of Proserpine, I was borne through all the elements and returned to earth again. I saw the sun gleaming with bright splendour at dead of night, I approached the gods above, and the gods below, and worshipped them face to face. Behold, I have told thee things of which, though thou hast heard them, thou must yet know naught.

Three things in that paragraph are worth slowing down over. The refusal is in the second person: it is not a report that the mysteries were secret, which is what every other ancient source gives, but the secrecy operating on the page, on the reader, in the present tense. What he offers instead of the rite is a list of four impossible things in the perfect tense, and they are the same four the ascent literature of Chapter 9 works in: a border approached, a threshold crossed, a passage through the elements, a return. And the last sentence takes back what the paragraph appeared to give. To have heard and still to know nothing is exactly the distinction this chapter began with, between a philosophy that can be published and an experience that cannot be transmitted, and here the two sit in one paragraph with the seam showing.

The caution is that the Metamorphoses is a novel. Lucius is a character, the ass is a fiction, and how much of the Isiac ritual in Book XI is reportage rather than invention is disputed and is likely to stay so. What the book is unarguably evidence of is narrower and still worth having: it is what a well-educated man of the second century, writing for readers who could walk to an Iseum and check, thought an initiation was shaped like. And the shape he reached for is the one this chapter has been describing from every other direction. A preparation that is mostly abstinence and washing, an exclusion of everyone not initiated, a night that is not described, and a claim afterwards in the perfect tense that something has already happened to the speaker which the reader has no way to verify.

The rebirth sermon

The Hermetic corpus contains one text devoted to the Greater subject, and it is the nearest thing the philosophical Hermetica has to a rite. The Secret Sermon on the Mountain, the thirteenth treatise, is a dialogue in which Hermes brings his son Tat through rebirth. Tat asks to be taught it, and is told that it cannot be taught in the ordinary way: that it comes when it will, that the one reborn is not the person who asked, and that Hermes himself cannot describe it except by pointing. Then, rather than explain, he performs it. Follow the mechanism exactly, because it is the ancestor of every graded working in this book. Tat is not given a doctrine; he is emptied and refilled. Twelve torments hold the ordinary self (ignorance, sorrow, intemperance, desire, unrighteousness, avarice, error and the rest) and against them Hermes calls in ten Powers, one at a time, each driving out its opposite as it arrives:

Gnosis of God hath come to us, and when this comes, my son, Not-knowing is cast out.

Gnosis of Joy hath come to us, and on its coming, son, Sorrow will flee away to them who give it room. The Power that follows Joy do I invoke, thy Self-control. O Power most sweet! Let us most gladly bid it welcome, son! How with its coming doth it chase Intemperance away!

Now fourth, on Continence I call, the Power against Desire. … This step, my son, is Righteousness’ firm seat. … We are made righteous, son, by the departure of Unrighteousness. Power sixth I call to us, — that against Avarice, Sharing-with-all. And now that Avarice is gone, I call on Truth. And Error flees, and Truth is with us.

When the tenth Power has come the arithmetic completes itself (“when the Ten is come, my son, that driveth out the Twelve, the Birth in understanding is complete”) and what has been born is not an opinion but a new subject: “This is, my son, Rebirth — no more to look on things from body’s view-point.” Tat asks the obvious question, whether this new body can dissolve as the old one will, and the answer is the sermon’s hinge:

Tat. Tell me, O father: This Body which is made up of the Powers, is it at any time dissolved?

Her. Hush, [son]! Speak not of things impossible, else wilt thou sin and thy Mind’s eye be quenched. The natural body which our sense perceives is far removed from this essential birth. The first must be dissolved, the last can never be; the first must die, the last death cannot touch. Dost thou not know thou hast been born a God, Son of the One, even as I myself?

Three habits of this rite run through everything that follows. It is graded: the Powers arrive in order and the order is not negotiable, which is the logic every grade system in Chapter 13 inherits. It is silent: “be still and solemn silence keep,” Hermes says at the turning point, and the treatise closes by binding Tat not to broadcast it, “in order that we may not be calumniators of the All unto the multitude”: the withholding this chapter describes, stated by the text itself rather than reported of it. And it is a death: the language throughout is of striking a tent and leaving it, and the initiate is told he has already been born a god, in the perfect tense, before he feels any different. Every mystery-grade in this tradition is a rehearsal of that grammar.

The pattern recurs everywhere in this book: the graded curriculum that withholds, the alchemical stages that cannot be hurried, the banishing repeated daily until it becomes a frame rather than an event. This is the same claim in different vocabularies: that certain changes are structural, take time, and cannot be arrived at by being told about them.

Grades and the structure of withholding

The organisational expression of all this is the graded system: the ten Golden Dawn grades of Chapter 13, the Rosicrucian degrees, the Masonic rites. Their logic is pedagogical before it is dramatic. Material is withheld until earlier material has been demonstrated, because the earlier work is what makes the later work legible; and because a technique reached too early tends to be absorbed into whatever the practitioner already wanted to believe.

The systems also functioned, less admirably, as instruments of authority. Grades create hierarchy, hierarchy creates deference, and the history of esoteric orders is substantially a history of schism over who held which grade legitimately. The original Golden Dawn fractured in exactly this manner in 1903, fifteen years after its founding, when Waite and Blackden took possession of Isis-Urania at that spring’s annual meeting. Nothing was dissolved: Waite ran his branch until he closed it in 1914, and the Stella Matutina and Alpha et Omega continued for decades, mostly moribund by the Second World War. A reader encountering claims of high initiatory rank is entitled to notice that such claims have a poor historical record and are unfalsifiable by design.

The honest position of this chapter

A book cannot confer initiation, and this one does not claim to. What has actually happened over the last century is that nearly all of the material formerly reserved to the grades has been published: Regardie’s four volumes of Golden Dawn ritual between 1937 and 1940, Mathers’s editions of the Solomonic texts, Betz’s translation of the Papyri, critical editions of the Hermetica. The secrets are in print. Anyone can read them today.

And the result is instructive: the availability of the material turned out not to be the thing that mattered. What the grade systems supplied was not information but sequence, supervision, and other people who would tell you when you were wrong. Those remain scarce, and they were never in the books to begin with. The genuine Greater Mystery, on the evidence of the century since publication, is that reading the syllabus and doing the work are entirely different activities.

Greater Mysteries Warning

This material is not to be taken lightly. It assumes dedication, preparation and, in every historical setting, guidance. Approach it with respect, and with a working suspicion of your own conclusions. The characteristic failure at this level is not danger but self-deception: the practitioner who has read everything, experienced something, and concluded that they have arrived. The tradition’s own remedy is the fourth item on the list above, which is difficult to fake and tends to correct the rest.

Sources: The Secret Sermon on the Mountain (Corpus Hermeticum XIII), quoted from Mead, Thrice-Greatest Hermes, vol. The square brackets are Mead’s. The first ellipsis marks a lacuna he himself flags in a footnote, “something has here evidently fallen out in the text,” and the second omits his fifth Power; both are declared rather than passed over. Chapter XXCorrespondences, Timing & Ingredients Adept

Everything operative in this book eventually needs three things the earlier chapters have only gestured at: when to work, what to work with, and how to make the object. This chapter supplies them. It draws almost entirely on one source (the Key of Solomon in Mathers’s 1889 translation, out of copyright and freely available) because a single coherent system used consistently is worth more than a synthesis assembled from six systems that disagree.

One caution before the tables. Correspondence tables have a way of acquiring an authority they have not earned. As Chapter 3 notes, the elaborate tables in modern handbooks are largely Golden Dawn constructions of the late nineteenth century, and even the older material below varies between manuscripts. These are the attributions of a tradition, recorded and dated. They are not laws of nature, and a practitioner who cannot say where a correspondence comes from is not using a tradition but repeating one.

The planetary hours

This is the oldest and most useful piece of magical timekeeping, and it is genuinely simple once the one counter-intuitive part is understood: a planetary hour is not sixty minutes.

The Key of Solomon sets out the doctrine directly. The hours of day and night together are twenty-four, and each is governed by one of the seven planets “in regular order, commencing at the highest and descending to the lowest.” The order it gives is the Chaldean order, by apparent speed, slowest first; and it gives the Hebrew names with them:

OrderHebrewPlanetMetalDay ruled
1ShabbathaiSaturnLeadSaturday
2TzedeqJupiterTinThursday
3MadimMarsIronTuesday
4ShemeshSunGoldSunday
5NogahVenusCopperFriday
6KokavMercuryMixed metalWednesday
7LevanahMoonSilverMonday

The rule of the planets “begins from the dawn at the rising of the Sun on the day which takes its name from such planet,” and each following hour goes to the next planet in the order, returning to the top of the list after the seventh. So on Saturday, Saturn rules the first hour, Jupiter the second, Mars the third, the Sun the fourth, Venus the fifth, Mercury the sixth, the Moon the seventh; and Saturn the eighth, and so on round.

Reckoning the hour

  1. Find today’s sunrise and sunset for your location, and tomorrow’s sunrise.
  2. Daylight length ÷ 12 = the length of one hour of the day. Night length ÷ 12 = one hour of the night. In London in June the day-hour runs to about eighty-two minutes and the night-hour to about thirty-eight; at the equinoxes both are sixty. This is what “unequal hours” means and it is why the reckoning has to be done afresh each time.
  3. The first hour of the day begins at sunrise and is ruled by the planet of the weekday.
  4. Count forward through the Chaldean order, one planet per hour, wrapping round after the Moon.
  5. The first hour of the night begins at sunset and simply continues the count: hour 13 of the day-and-night sequence.

Worked example. A Wednesday on which the sun rises at 06:00 and sets at 18:00. Daylight is twelve hours, so each day-hour is sixty minutes. Wednesday is Mercury’s, so 06:00–07:00 is Mercury; 07:00–08:00 the Moon; 08:00–09:00 Saturn; 09:00–10:00 Jupiter; 10:00–11:00 Mars; 11:00–12:00 the Sun; 12:00–13:00 Venus; and 13:00–14:00 Mercury again. The eighth hour of any day returns to the day’s own planet, which is a useful check on your arithmetic.

A consequence worth noticing, because it is the elegant part of the system: count twenty-four hours forward from sunrise on any day and you land on the planet that rules the next day of the week, in exactly the order the week actually runs. The seven-day week and the Chaldean order generate each other.

The same rulers, at the scale of ages

The system did not stop at hours and days. In a short tract dedicated to the Emperor Maximilian (De Septem Secundeis, “of the seven secondaries, that is, the intelligences or spirits moving the orbs after God”) Johannes Trithemius runs the same seven rulers across history itself. The proem states the scheme in one sentence: the lower world is governed under God by seven spirits set over the seven planets from the beginning of heaven and earth, quorum unusquisque mundum annis gubernat trecentis quinquaginta quatuor mensibusque ex ordine quaternis: each of whom in his turn governs the world for three hundred and fifty-four years and four months. The tract then walks the reigns from creation, dated to the day: Orifiel, the spirit of Saturn, rules first; Anael of Venus takes over on the 24th of June in the year of the world 354; Zachariel of Jupiter arrives on the 26th of October in 780; and the rotation continues from there. Two clauses are worth carrying away. Orifiel autem nomen est officij, non naturae: Orifiel is the name of an office, not of a nature: even at the scale of world-ages the planetary ruler is a function, exactly as the hour-tables above treat theirs. And the dedication closes with a scruple worth imitating: the doctrine is laid before the Emperor non asserendo, sed referendo: not by asserting, but only by reporting. The boldest extension of planetary rulership in the literature arrives marked as a report, not a claim, and that is the spirit in which this chapter passes it on.

The tract does not stop at three. It walks the whole first circuit of the seven, each reign dated to the day and closed with the year it ran to, and the circuit is worth having entire, because only when the seven are set out together does it become clear that the scheme is an arithmetic before it is a prophecy. Every reign is the same length. The dates are simply 354 years and 4 months laid end to end from the creation.

ReignGovernorPlanetBeginsRuns to
FirstOrifielSaturn15 March, year of the world 1354, month 4
SecondAnaelVenus24 June, 354, month 4708, month 8
ThirdZacharielJupiter26 October, 780 as printed1063
FourthRaphaelMercury24 February, 10631417, month 4
FifthSamaelMars26 June, 14171771, month 8
SixthGabrielthe MoonOctober, 1771, month 82126
SeventhMichaelthe Sun24 February, 21262480, month 4

One entry in that column will not add up, and it is the printing’s fault rather than the scheme’s. Anael is said to run to the year 708 and Raphael to begin in 1063, so the reign between them has to begin in 708 and cannot begin in 780: 780 with 354 years and 4 months upon it reaches 1134, and the tract itself ends that reign at 1063. The 1613 sheet has transposed two figures. The month survives the error and confirms the reading, because Anael ends in the eighth month and Zachariel is given as beginning in the eighth month, on the 26th of October. It is printed here as it stands, with the correction beside it rather than folded into it.

After Michael the wheel turns again to Orifiel and the same seven repeat in the same order, so the whole of history is seven names on a loop of two thousand four hundred and eighty years. That is the entire mechanism. Everything else in the tract is Trithemius fitting events to it, and the fitting is where it becomes visibly fragile. He records, without appearing to notice the damage, that the chronology the scheme runs on is not agreed: the Hebrews date the Flood to the year of the world 1656, which falls sub regimine Martis, under the government of Mars; but the Septuagint, Isidore and Bede put it at 2242, which falls in a different reign altogether. A system that assigns the character of an age to its planetary governor cannot survive a five-hundred-year disagreement about when the ages begin, and he prints the disagreement anyway.

What each planet is held to govern

The Key of Solomon’s own list, condensed. It is given here as the text gives it, including the parts a modern practitioner will decline to use: the book’s position on those is set out below the table.

PlanetProper to
SaturnSummoning the souls of those who died naturally; fortune good or ill to buildings; familiar spirits in sleep; success or failure in business, possessions, goods, seeds and fruits; acquiring learning; and, the text is candid, destruction, death, hatred and discord.
JupiterObtaining honours; acquiring riches; contracting friendships; preserving health; “arriving at all that thou canst desire.”
MarsWar; military honour; courage; overthrowing enemies; and ruin, slaughter, cruelty and discord.
SunTemporal wealth, hope, gain, fortune, divination, the favour of princes; dissolving hostility and making friends.
VenusForming friendships; kindness and love; “joyous and pleasant undertakings”; travelling.
MercuryEloquence and intelligence; promptitude in business; science and divination; apparitions; answers about the future; also thefts, writings, deceit and merchandise.
MoonEmbassies, voyages, envoys, messages, navigation; reconciliation; love; acquiring merchandise by water.

Roughly a fifth of that list is for harming people. The book prints it because a source should be reported as it stands rather than tidied, and because pretending the grimoire tradition was uniformly benign is its own kind of falsification; this is a literature that contains cursing, and Chapter 9 has already shown the same range in the ancient material. The ethical position of Chapter 1 is not suspended for interesting sources. Read those entries; do not work them.

Planetary herbs

The standard English source for this is Nicholas Culpeper’s The Complete Herbal of 1653, which assigns nearly every plant it treats to a planet in the opening line of its “Government and virtues” section: “It is an herb of Mercury,” “under the dominion of the Moon.” Culpeper serves better than a modern table for three reasons: he is out of copyright, he states the attribution for each plant individually so it can be checked, and he is arguing a case rather than reciting one. He was a radical who translated the College of Physicians’ Latin pharmacopoeia into English against their wishes, and the astrology is load-bearing in his medicine, not decorative.

The table below was compiled by reading his attributions directly, plant by plant, and is a selection rather than the whole herbal.

PlanetHerbs, as Culpeper assigns them
SaturnComfrey, crosswort, mullein, black hellebore, amaranthus, wintergreen, polypody of the oak, mosses
JupiterAgrimony, houseleek (sengreen), liverwort, scurvygrass, samphire, dandelion, costmary, clove gilliflowers, roses, chicory, henbane
MarsAnemone, masterwort, mustard, hyssop, barberry, sweet basil, carduus benedictus, gentian, madder, all-heal, crowfoot, horseradish, savine
SunAngelica, marigold, celandine, saffron, garden rue, peony, centaury, lovage, tormentil, mistletoe, butterbur, holly
VenusAlkanet, mugwort, daisy, coltsfoot, ground ivy (alehoof), columbine, foxglove, herb Robert, catmint, pennyroyal, parsnip, wood sage, dwarf elder, filipendula
MercuryFennel, parsley, horehound, liquorice, sweet marjoram, wild marjoram, calamint, elecampane, eyebright, germander, lily of the valley, wall rue, smallage, pellitory of the wall, honeysuckle
MoonChickweed, cleavers, watercress, white lily, water lily, purslane, cucumber, clary, wild clary, coralwort, lady’s smock, water caltrops, rattle grass

Three cautions, and they matter more than the table does.

Culpeper is not always consistent with himself. Plantain, for instance, is assigned to different planets in different places in the herbal, and where his own text disagrees it has been left out above rather than resolved by picking a favourite. Where other writers disagree with Culpeper, and they frequently do, there is no adjudicating authority. That is a fact about the tradition, not a defect in this table.

These attributions are for ritual correspondence, not for medicine. That distinction is not one Culpeper drew, and it matters here. Several plants in the table are seriously poisonous: black hellebore, henbane, foxglove and savine are all capable of killing an adult, and savine was used as an abortifacient at doses close to lethal ones. Others interact dangerously with prescribed drugs. Use them as symbols, as things to have on the altar or in the incense, and treat any suggestion in a seventeenth-century herbal about taking a plant internally as a historical statement rather than a dosage.

A herb chosen for correspondence is a mnemonic and a focus. It ties a working to a planet, a day, an hour and a metal in a coherent set, and coherence is most of what a correspondence system is for. Nothing in this book claims the plant acts on the working by an occult virtue of its own; the tradition does claim that, and the reader is at liberty to. What is not at liberty is the pharmacology.

Making a talisman

A talisman, the grimoires say pentacle or medal, is a physical object carrying names, figures or characters, made under specific conditions. The Key of Solomon is unambiguous about how much weight it puts on these: “the whole science and understanding of our Key dependeth upon the operation, knowledge, and use of pentacles.”

The procedure, from the Key of Solomon

  1. Timing. Make them “in the days and hours of Mercury, when the Moon is in an aerial or terrestrial sign”: Gemini, Libra or Aquarius; Taurus, Virgo or Capricorn: “she should also be in her increase.”
  2. Place. A room set apart and newly cleaned, where you will not be interrupted, incensed beforehand. The text asks for a clear sky.
  3. Material. Either the metal proper to the planet (see the table above), or virgin paper: paper used for nothing else and handled by nobody else.
  4. Colours. “Gold, cinnabar or vermilion red, and celestial or brilliant azure blue.” Where the metal itself is used, the text says the colour rule need not be observed.
  5. Completion. Finish within the hour you began in if you possibly can. If you must break off, wait for the proper day and hour to resume: do not simply carry on.
  6. Consecration. Wrap the finished pentacle in fine silk. Set a censer of charcoal with frankincense, mastic and aloes. Standing in a circle with the names of God written between its two rims, face east and hold the pentacle in the smoke, reciting the psalms the 1889 page lists, in its own roman: viii, xxi, xxvii, xxix, xxxii, li, lxxii and cxxxiv.
  7. Keeping. Keep it in the silk. The tradition treats a consecrated object as spent if it is handled carelessly, which is a practice worth keeping whatever one thinks of the metaphysics.

Two remarks. First, those eight are exactly what Mathers prints, in his numbering and his roman numerals, and his page marks the list with a footnote; other witnesses of the Key carry ten. Whether he was counting by the Vulgate Psalter or the English one his page does not say, and the two differ by one number through most of the book, so the figures are left as he set them rather than converted into a numbering he may not have been using. That a list this short varies at all is a fair illustration of how much a “standard” grimoire text can vary. Second, notice what the procedure actually consists of: a defined material, a defined window, a requirement of unbroken attention, and a rule that a lapse means starting again at the proper time. Whatever else it is doing, it is an unusually well-designed instrument for making a person concentrate.

Incense

The Key of Solomon divides perfumes simply (“those which are of sweet odour are for the good, those which are of evil savour are for the evil”) and for the good gives incense, aloes, nutmeg, gum benjamin and musk, with the manuscripts adding saffron, myrrh, costus and nard. Frankincense, mastic and aloes are named for consecrating pentacles.

The fire is kindled fresh, with flint and steel, in a newly glazed earthen vessel, and both fire and spices are blessed before use. For a modern practitioner the durable elements are: charcoal in a heatproof vessel on a stable surface, resins rather than perfumed sticks if you want the historical thing, and a window open. See the safety note in Chapter 8; incense in an unventilated room is a genuine respiratory hazard and the tradition, which worked in larger and draughtier rooms than yours, is no guide here.

Why incense is supposed to work

Every grimoire in this book gives lists of perfumes. Almost none of them says why a particular fume should do anything, and the modern literature inherits the lists without the reasoning. One text does explain, and the detour to reach it pays.

Sepher Raziel, also called Liber Salomonis, survives in an English manuscript of 1564 that ends with the sort of colophon a historian dreams about; it names the scribe, his lodgings, his birthplace, his patron, his patron’s county, and the day:

The booke, entituled Cephar Raziel, contain’g seuen treatises, was written by William Parry of Clyffords Inne by Temple barre in London borne at Northof in the County of Flynt & at the charges of John Gwyne of Llandlos in the county of Mountgomericke Esquire in the year of our lord god a thousand five hunderd threscore & four… Londinij 2o Nouembris 1564. William Parry.

A London law-clerk copying a book of magic to order for a Welsh gentleman, on the second of November 1564, in the sixth year of Elizabeth. There is no better single illustration in this book of who actually owned these manuscripts. Not hermits: propertied men, who paid someone by the hour.

Two different books with one name

This is not the Hebrew Sefer Raziel ha-Malakh first printed at Amsterdam in 1701. That is a separate work. Sloane 3846 belongs to the Latin Liber Razielis tradition compiled at the court of Alfonso X in the thirteenth century, and reached English by a different route entirely. The two share a title and an angel and very little else, and conflating them is the single commonest error made about this text. When a modern source cites “the Book of Raziel,” establish which one it means before believing anything that follows.

Its third book is a treatise on suffumigation, and rather than opening with a table it opens with a mechanism. Two of them, in fact, and they do not agree with each other:

And euermore consider thou the nature of the spirit & of the fumigacion & the spirits be constrayned by their contrary & be comforted by like things. Wherefore it is to witt that as a wise leche in giueing a medicine to a sick man remoueth the sickenes & in ledeth health. So fumigacion remoueth the contrary from the place if it be good. And with euill fumigacion be remoued good spirits & euill spirits also dreadeth for eich thing more loueth health then sicknes. And therefore it is said that Sulphur remoueth both good spirits & euill. And this is probation & pref [profit] after one way. And there [is] another way for lignum aloes gathereth together the spirits of ligni aloes & none other. And Sulphur chaseth them away & this is very reason.

Unpack that and there are two separate theories sitting side by side. The first is medical, and the text says so outright: a fume works as a physician’s medicine works, by removing the contrary and leading in health. Spirits are constrained by their contrary and comforted by their like. On this account incense is a treatment applied to a place.

The second is selective, and it is a different claim: lignum aloes gathereth together the spirits of ligni aloes and none other. Here a fume does not treat anything. It calls its own and is inert towards everything else, the way a name calls one person out of a crowd. Sulphur is the text’s worked example of the difference; it drives off good and evil alike under the first theory, and under the second it summons its own proper spirits, which the text adds are full stronge & penetrate & thicke and slow to leave a room.

That is a far more interesting statement than any correspondence table, and it explains something the tables never do: why the sources disagree about whether a given incense is protective or attractive. They are not disagreeing about the substance. They are working from two different accounts of what a fume is, and the manuscript that preserves them both has the honesty to set them down consecutively and call the second another way.

What was left out, and by whom

Between the two halves of this treatise stand the weekday incense lists and a passage on Hermes’ seven manners of sacrifice. The latter is not printed here: two of the seven are blood sacrifice, which this book does not reproduce as procedure. The omission is stated rather than concealed, because a quotation that closes over a gap reads as complete when it is not.

The bracketed words [profit] and [is] above are the modern transcriber’s insertions, not the 1564 scribe’s, and are left visible for that reason. The abbreviation wch and spellings like leche, witt and eich are the manuscript’s own.

Modern Practice

Most contemporary practitioners keep the planetary hours and drop nearly everything else in this chapter, and that is a defensible reading of what the system is for. The hours cost nothing but arithmetic (there are calculators everywhere, though doing it by hand once is worth the twenty minutes) and they supply the thing the tradition is really offering: a reason to begin at a particular moment rather than whenever you get round to it. Talismans are made now in paper and ink far more often than in engraved metal, which the text itself permits. And the requirement to finish within the hour, or else wait for the next proper one, turns out to be the single most useful instruction in the chapter for anyone whose difficulty is not belief but consistency.

Chapter XXIAstrology Adept

A horoscope is a map of the sky as it stood over one place at one moment. Planetary hours, planetary metals, planetary herbs and the zodiac are all read off it, and none of them means very much until the map exists: they are the furniture, and the chart is the house they go in. That image belongs to William Lilly, whose Christian Astrology of 1647 is the fullest account of the traditional art in English, and it is the argument of this chapter in one sentence.

Two things called a house

First a confusion to clear, because the word does two jobs. Chapter 22 gives the traditional rulerships and says that the Sun and Moon “take one house each” while the other planets take two. That is house in the older sense of domicile: the sign a planet governs, its home in the zodiac. It is not the sense in which an astrologer says “the seventh house.”

The twelve houses are something else entirely: divisions not of the zodiac but of the sky as seen from one place at one moment, fixed to the horizon rather than to the stars. The signs turn; the houses do not. A planet is in a sign because of where it is in its orbit, and in a house because of where the observer was standing and what time it was. Confusing the two is the commonest error in popular astrology, and the two senses of the word are most of the reason for it.

Lilly, and the book that made English astrology

William Lilly’s Christian Astrology of 1647 is the first substantial treatment of the art in English, and it is still the standard reference for the traditional practice because it is exhaustive and because Lilly was working, not compiling. Its title page divides it into the three things astrology actually does:

The first containing the use of an Ephemeris; the erecting of a Scheam of Heaven; nature of the twelve Signs of the Zodiack, of the Planets; with a most easie Introduction to the whole Art of Astrology. The second, by a most Methodicall way, Instructeth the Student how to Judge or Resolve all manner of Questions contingent unto Man… The third, containes an exact Method, whereby to Judge upon Nativities.

Erect the chart; answer a question; read a life. Those are horary and natal astrology with their common groundwork in front of them, and the division has not changed since.

On the houses Lilly is emphatic, and the sentence belongs here whole:

As before we have said there are twelve Signes, and also twelve Houses of Heaven, so now we are come to relate the nature of these twelve Houses; the exact knowledge whereof is so requisite, that he who shall learne the nature of the Planets and Signes without exact judgment of the Houses, is like an improvident man, that furnisheth himselfe with variety of Household-stuffe, having no place wherein to bestow them.

A man who buys furniture and has no house to put it in. That is precisely the condition of a reader who has this book’s tables of planetary correspondence and no chart, and Lilly diagnosed it in 1647.

Lilly’s claim for the scheme is total, and traditional astrology stands or falls on it: “There is nothing appertaining to the life of man in this world, which in one way or other hath not relation to one of the twelve Houses of Heaven.” Twelve compartments, and everything a life contains goes in one of them.

The twelve houses of heaven

The horary art of Lilly’s era assigns every affair of life to one of twelve houses, and no question can be judged until it has been put in its house. The significations in the first table are the traditional ones of that literature, stated generally; Lilly’s own, from the chapter he gives to each house, follow it.

HouseTraditional signification
1the querent: body, life, appearance
2moveable goods, money, what is owned
3siblings, neighbours, short journeys, letters
4the father, land and houses, endings, things hidden in the earth
5children, pleasure, play, ambassadors
6sickness, servants, small animals, the conditions of labour
7the other party: marriage, partners, open enemies, the thief
8death, the partner’s goods, legacies, fear
9long journeys, religion, learning, dreams
10honour, office, the mother, authority, the outcome of ambition
11friends, hopes, the resources of the powerful
12secret enemies, imprisonment, large animals, self-undoing

That table is the tradition in summary. Lilly himself is worth reading in his own words, because the summary tidies him and what he actually wrote is stranger and more useful. He gives a short chapter to each house in turn, and three things show when they are read one after another. The first is how physical the list is: every house rules a part of the body, and the twelve between them run head to foot in order, so the chart is a man as well as a sky. The second is that the houses are not private. Almost every one of them has a public reading beside the personal one, and the pair sit in the same sentence: the second house is the querent’s purse and also a besieged commonwealth’s magazines, the eleventh is your friends and also a king’s exchequer. The third is that the categories are those of a particular place and year, which is 1647 in England, and they do not pretend otherwise: gallislaves and warriners, the Common-Councell of the City of London, whether a town be besieged.

HouseWhat Lilly gives it
First“the life of man, of the stature, colour, complexion, forme and shape of him that propounds the Question, or is borne”; in eclipses and great conjunctions, “the common people, or generall State of that Kingdome where the Figure is erected.” It represents the head and face; it is called the Ascendant, “because when the Sun commeth to the cusp of this house, he ascends, or then ariseth, and is visible in our Horizon”
Second“the estate or fortune of him that asks the Question, of his Wealth or Poverty, of all moveable Goods, Money lent, of Profit or gaine, losse or damage; in suits of Law, it signifies a mans Friends or Assistants; in private Duels, the Querents second; in an Eclips or great Conjunction, the Poverty or Wealth of the people.” It represents the neck, “and hinder part of it towards the shoulders, of colours the green”
Third“Brethren, Sisters, Cozens or Kindred, Neighbours, small Journeys, or inland-Journeys, oft removing from one place to another, Epistles, Letters, Rumours, Messengers: It doth rule the Shoulders, Armes, Hands and Fingers”
Fourth“Judgment of Fathers in general, and ever of his Father that enquires, or that is borne; of Lands, Houses, Tenements, Inheritances, Tillage of the earth, Treasures hidden, the determination or end of any thing; Townes, Cities or Castles, besieged or not besieged; all ancient Dwellings, Gardens, Fields, Pastures, Orchards; the quality and nature of the grounds one purchaseth, whether Vineyards, Cornfields, &c. whether the ground be Wooddy, Stony or barren.” It rules the breast and lungs, and is “the Angle of the Earth, or Imum Cœli”
Fifth“we judge of Children, of Embassadours, of the state of a Woman with child, of Banquets, of Ale-houses, Tavernes, Playes, Messengers or Agents for Republicks; of the Wealth of the Father, the Ammunition of a Towne besieged; if the Woman with child shall bring forth man or woman; of the health or sicknesse of his Son or Daughter that asks the Question.” It rules “the Stomack, Liver, Heart, Sides and Back”; it is “the house of Pleasure, Delight and Meriment”
Sixth“Men and Maid-servants, Gallislaves, Hogges, Sheep, Goats, Hares, Connies, all manner of lesser Cattle, and profit or losse got thereby; Sicknesse, its quality and cause, principal humor offending, curable or not curable, whether the disease be short or long; Day-Labourers, Tenants, Farmers, Shepherds, Hogheards, Neatherds, Warriners; and it signifieth Unkles, or the Fathers Brothers and Sisters.” It rules the lower part of the belly and the intestines, and it is unfortunate, “as having no aspect to the Ascendant”
Seventh“judgement of Marriage, and describes the person inquired after, whether it be Man or Woman, all manner of Love questions, our publique enemies; the Defendant in a Lawsuit, in Warre the opposing party; all Quarrels, Duels, Lawsuits; in Astrology the Artist himselfe; in Physicke the Physitian; Theeves and Thefts; the person stealing, whether Man or Woman, Wives, Sweethearts; their shape, description, condition, Nobly or ignobly borne: in an Annuall ingresse, whether Warre or Peace may be expected: of Victory, who overcomes, and who worsted; Fugitives or run-awayes; Banished and Out-lawed-men.” It rules the haunches, and the navel to the buttocks, and is the Angle of the West
Eighth“The Estate of Men deceased, Death, its quality and nature; the Wils, Legacies and Testaments of Men deceased; Dowry of the Wife, Portion of the Maid, whether much or little, easie to be obtained or with difficulty. In Duels it represents the Adversaries Second; in Lawsuits the Defendants friends. What kinde of Death a Man shall dye. it signifies feare and anguish of Minde. Who shall enjoy or be heire to the Deceased.” It rules the privy parts
Ninth“we give judgement of Voyages or long journies beyond Seas of Religious men, or Clergy of any kinde, whether Bishops or inferiour Ministers; Dreames, Visions, forraigne Countries, of Books, Learning, Church Livings, or Benefices, Advowsions; of the kindred of ones Wife, & sic è contrario.” It rules the fundament, hips and thighs
Tenth“Commonly it personateth Kings, Princes, Dukes, Earles, Judges, prime Officers, Commanders in chiefe, whether in Armies or Townes; all sorts of Magistracy and Officers in Authority, Mothers, Honour, Preferment, Dignity, Office, Lawyers; the profession or Trade any one useth; it signifies Kingdomes, Empires, Dukedomes, Counties.” It rules the knees and hams, and is called “the Medium Cœli, or Mid-heaven”
Eleventh“Friends and Friendship, Hope, Trust, Confidence, the Praise, or Dispraise of any one; the Fidelity or falsenesse of Friends; as to Kings it personates their Favourites, Councellours, Servants, their Associates or Allyes, their Money, Exchequer or Treasure; in Warre their Amunition and Souldiery.” In London, he adds, the tenth house represents the Lord Mayor, “the eleventh the Common-Councell; the Ascendant the generality of the Commoners of the said City.” It rules the legs to the ankles
Twelfth“private Enemies, of Witches, great Cattle, as Horses, Oxen, Elephants, &c. Sorrow, Tribulation, Imprisonments, all manner of affliction, self-undoing, &c. and of such men as maliciously undermine their neighbours, or informe secretly against them.” Saturn “doth much joy in that House, For naturally Saturne is author of mischiefe”; it rules the feet

Lilly ends the chapter by declining to give more, and the sentence is the reason he is worth quoting rather than summarised:

This is the true Caracter of the severall Houses, according to the Ptolomeian Doctrine, and the experience my selfe have had for some yeers: I must confesse the Arabians have made severall other divisions of the Houses, but I could never in my practise finde any verity in them, wherefore I say nothing of them.

He had the Arabic divisions in front of him, he could have printed them and been the fuller book, and he left them out because they had not worked for him. That is a working astrologer telling you the boundary of what he has tested, in a century when almost nobody writing on this subject did so.

The aspects

The aspect is the other half of the machinery: the angular distance between two planets, which decides whether they are held to co-operate. Lilly gives them as simple arithmetic on the circle: “When Planets are one hundred and twenty degrees distant, we say they are in a Trine Aspect… When two Planets are one hundred and eighty degrees distant, we call that Aspect an Opposition.”

AspectDegreesTraditional reading
Conjunction0°the two act as one, for good or ill according to the planets
Sextile60°opportunity, requiring something of the native
Square90°obstruction; the classic hard aspect
Trine120°ease, and the ease is not always a favour
Opposition180°confrontation, or a matter brought to a head

The divisions are the circle cut by two, three, four and six: the same arithmetic as the polygons of Chapter 3, applied to the sky. That is not a coincidence anybody hid; it is why the aspects are the ones they are.

Horary: the question as the moment

The second of Lilly’s three books is given to horary, and it is the branch least familiar to a modern reader. A horary chart is not cast for a birth. It is cast for the moment the question was asked, and read as an answer to that question. Lilly’s second book is a long catalogue of worked examples (whether the querent will live long, where a lost thing is, whether a marriage will hold) with the chart for each and his judgment of it.

Whatever one makes of the premise, the method has a property worth noticing: it is falsifiable in a way natal astrology is not. A nativity is read against a whole life and can absorb almost any outcome. A horary question has an answer, usually soon, and Lilly published his charts and his judgments together so that a reader could check them. That is a more exposed position than most of the tradition takes.

How old is this, actually

The parts of astrology have very different ages, and the tradition tends to present them as one thing. What can be said briefly: omen astrology, celestial events read as signs for a king or a kingdom, is Mesopotamian and ancient. The horoscope as this chapter describes it, cast for an individual with an ascendant and twelve houses, is Hellenistic and much later; the machinery in Fig. 1 belongs to the Greek-speaking Mediterranean, not to Babylon. Ptolemy, writing in the second century, systematised what he received rather than inventing it. The material then passed through Arabic astronomy and returned to Latin Europe in the twelfth century, and Lilly is the end of that line in English, printing in 1647.

Of those stages this edition has consulted Ptolemy and Lilly directly and takes the rest from general reference. The dates are given because the shape matters, and they are flagged here rather than asserted with a citation this book cannot supply.

Seven planets, and why this book keeps it that way

Chapter 22 notes that modern astrology reassigns three of the traditional rulerships to planets Ptolemy could not see, and that the older scheme is used here because everything else in this book predates the telescope. The same holds for the whole chapter. The system described above is the one Lilly practised: seven planets, the traditional rulerships, whole aspects rather than the finer modern set. It is internally consistent, it is what every source in this book means when it says Mars, and it has the advantage of being a system somebody actually used rather than a compromise between two.

Sources: Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), read from the Wellcome copy b30338724: the title page for the threefold division; Book I, ch. VII, “Of the twelve Houses, their Nature and signification,” for the passage on the houses, the improvident man and his furniture, and the claim that nothing in a life falls outside the twelve; the same chapter at pp. 50–56, leaves 84–90, read by eye on the page images for the signification of each house in turn and for the closing refusal of the Arabic divisions; and Book I for the aspects and their degrees.

Long s is set as round s and the scan’s broken word-spacing is closed up; period spellings (Household-stuffe, Signes, Scheam, Zodiack) stand. Three readings are repaired and declared: the scan gives Houles for Houses where the long s defeats it, exa& for exact, and variety ol HoLifholdftuffe for variety of Household-stuffe; in the aspect passage Afped is read as Aspect and Offofition as Opposition. For the twelve significations the text layer was not used at all: it loses whole words of this printing rather than merely garbling them, and Caracter, Ptolomeian, Gallislaves and Sweethearts are absent from it for the whole volume, so that passage was read by eye and its oddest readings checked again under magnification.

Ptolemy’s domiciles are cited in Chapter 22 and not requoted. The table of aspects, its third column, and the whole of the dating note are this book’s own; the readings given for each aspect are the common traditional ones and are not any single author’s wording. The observation that horary is more exposed to falsification than natal astrology is this book’s, and is offered as an observation about method and not as a defence of the premise.

Chapter XXIISigils, Seals & Symbols Adept

A sigil is a name or an intention compressed into a line. That is the whole of the idea, and everything else in this chapter is a method for doing the compressing. The tradition has several, of different ages and very different standing, and they are worth keeping apart: some are ancient scripts nobody can read, some are Renaissance number-work, and one is a twentieth-century invention that most people now assume is old.

A caution belongs at the head of this chapter rather than buried in it. The meanings given below are the meanings the tradition assigns. They are conventions: widely shared, long-lived, internally coherent conventions, but conventions. A symbol does not carry its sense the way a stone carries its weight.

How the planetary glyphs are built

The seven planetary signs are not arbitrary marks. They are assembled from three elements, and once that is visible they stop needing to be memorised.

The planets and what they signify

GlyphPlanetSignifiesMetalDay
Sunthe centre, vitality, the self that does not changegoldSunday
Moonreflection, cycle, memory, the tidal part of a lifesilverMonday
Mercuryspeech, exchange, crossing between statesmixed metalWednesday
Venusattraction, harmony, what draws things togethercopperFriday
Marsseverance, force, the cut that separatesironTuesday
Jupiterexpansion, mercy, increase and its dangerstinThursday
Saturnlimit, time, structure, the boundary of a thingleadSaturday

The metals and the days are the Key of Solomon’s, set out with the hours in Chapter 20. The significations are the common stock of the astrological and magical literature and cannot be traced to a single author.

The twelve signs

The zodiac glyphs complete the symbolic alphabet this chapter has been assembling, and they matter operatively: the talisman timing of Chapter 20 is stated in signs (“the Moon in an aerial or terrestrial sign”), and the geomantic figures of Chapter 24 each carry one. Each sign is an element in one of three modes (cardinal beginning, fixed sustaining, mutable dissolving) so the twelve are the four elements of this book run through three phases.

GlyphSignElementModeTraditional ruler
AriesfirecardinalMars

SagittariusfiremutableJupiter
CapricornearthcardinalSaturn
