The rulerships are the traditional scheme, from Ptolemy’s Tetrabiblos: the two luminaries take one house each (the Sun Leo, the Moon Cancer) and each planet takes two, arranged symmetrically outward from the luminaries in Chaldean order. Modern astrology reassigns three of them to planets Ptolemy could not see; the older scheme is used here because everything else in this book predates the telescope.

The elements, the principles and the metals

The alchemical symbols of Chapter 5 work on the same logic of assembly. The four elements are one triangle with one modification:

SignElementThe rule
Firetriangle, apex up: ascending, hot and dry
Watertriangle, apex down: descending, cold and moist
Airfire’s triangle with a bar: ascending, but bounded
Earthwater’s triangle with a bar: descending, bounded

Two triangles and two bars encode four things and their relations to each other, which is an efficient piece of design and the reason the scheme lasted. Superimpose the fire and water triangles and you have the hexagram of Chapter 3: everything above and everything below, in one figure.

The oldest inscribed amulet

Every seal in this chapter joins a figure to a written name. That marriage is far older than the kameas, and the oldest documented instance is Egyptian: the heart scarab, a beetle of green stone carved with a formula and laid on the body of the dead. It is attested from the Twelfth Dynasty to the Roman period: some two thousand years of continuous use for a single amulet type, which no object in the rest of this book approaches.

What makes it belong here rather than in a museum catalogue is that the Egyptian texts state the specification: the material, the finish, the placement, the anointing, and the words to be recited over it. Budge summarises the rubrical direction belonging to the sixty-fourth chapter at page 152 of his first volume, where it stands as a note to a different chapter altogether:

Behold, make a scarab of green stone, wash it with gold and place it in the heart of a man (i.e., the deceased), and it will perform for him the “opening of the mouth”; anoint it with āntu unguent, and recite over it as a charm the following words:— “My heart, my mother; my heart, my mother!” etc.

Two rubrics, one scarab, and an error the whole literature repeats

Budge prints a second rubric for what is manifestly the same amulet, and the two do not agree. Attached to Chapter XXXB at page 151, from the Papyrus of Ȧmen-ḥetep:

These words are to be said over a scarab of green stone encircled with a band of refined copper and [having] a ring of silver, which shall be placed on the neck of the khu.

And the rubric to Chapter LXIV, translated in full at page 222: the last page of that volume:

And behold, thou shalt make a scarab of green stone, with a rim plated (?) with gold, which shall be placed in the heart of a man, and it shall perform for him the “opening of the mouth.” And thou shalt anoint it with ānti unguent, and thou shalt recite over it [these] enchantments:—

Same stone, same charm, same opening of the mouth; and then copper and silver, worn at the neck against gold, set in the heart. Two incompatible specifications for one amulet, in one volume, on facing subjects. This book prints both and adjudicates neither: the disagreement is older than any modern editor and is not resolved by preferring the famous one.

And the famous one is habitually miscited. The wording everybody quotes, wash it with gold and place it in the heart, belongs to the rubric of Chapter LXIV, not to Chapter XXXB, which is where secondary writing routinely attaches it. The copper-and-silver rubric is the one that actually stands with the XXXB text.

One smaller thing, recorded because harmonising it would be a small dishonesty: the unguent is āntu at page 152 and ānti at page 222, in the same printing, for the same word in the same rubric. That is the book disagreeing with itself, not a transcription slip, and both spellings are given above where they occur.

The formula it introduces (the thirtieth chapter, the one actually inscribed on the amulets) opens as the dead man’s own speech at the weighing of the heart:

My heart my mother, my heart my mother, my heart my coming into being. May there be nothing to resist me at my judgment; may there be no opposition to me from the Tchatcha; may there be no parting of thee from me in the presence of him that keepeth the scales. Thou art my Ka within my body, which knitteth together and strengtheneth my limbs.

Read as a piece of amulet design it is remarkable. The object is addressed to a court, the heart is being asked not to testify against its owner, and the inscription is written in the first person of the wearer, to be spoken by someone who cannot speak. That is a solution to a problem no other amulet in this book has to solve, and it is why the scarab carries text at all rather than only a figure.

On Budge, honestly

E. A. Wallis Budge’s translations are the reason most English readers have met this material at all, and they are also, by common consent among Egyptologists, superseded: his grammar predates the decisive advances in the field and his renderings are freely archaising. They are used here because they are the only versions out of copyright, and the same rule this book applies to Mead applies to Budge: an old translation honestly labelled is better than a modern one paraphrased. Where a word matters, the reader should check a current edition.

Tchatcha, left untranslated above, is Budge’s transliteration of the divine assessors at the judgment: he glosses it elsewhere as the “Chiefs.”

Two more, and what they have in common

The scarab is not the only amulet in this literature that comes with a specification. Two others do, and printing them together shows something neither shows alone.

The first is the buckle of Isis, the tjet. Its chapter is four lines long, and its rubric is longer than its text:

The Chapter of a buckle of carnelian

Saith Osiris Ani, triumphant: “The blood of Isis, the charms of Isis, the power of Isis, are a protection unto me, the chief, and they crush that which I abhor.”

Rubric. This chapter shall be said over a buckle of red jasper (or carnelian) which hath been dipped in water of ānkham flowers and inlaid in sycamore wood, and hath been placed on the neck of the shining one. If this chapter be inscribed upon it, it shall become the power of Isis, and it shall protect him; and Horus, the son of Isis, shall rejoice when he seeth it. No way shall be impassable to him, and one hand shall extend unto heaven, and the other unto earth.

The second is the ṬeṬ of gold, the pillar. Budge prints its rubric twice, from two different manuscripts, and the versions differ. The one attached to the Nebseni papyrus reads, in his word-for-word rendering:

Shall be said chapter this over a ṬeṬ of gold laid upon a body of sycamore wood, washed in water of ānkham flowers, and placed on the neck of shining one this.

The later recension gives the same object without the flower-water, and adds something no other amulet in the book receives: a date: it shall set him in his place on the day of the new year. Everywhere else in this literature the amulet is timeless; here alone there is a calendar.

The consecration is general, not particular

Set the two rubrics side by side and the same three operations appear in both, for two entirely different objects made of two different materials:

  • washed or dipped in water of ānkham flowers;
  • set in sycamore wood;
  • placed on the neck of the shining one.

A red stone knot and a gold pillar have nothing in common as figures, and yet they are prepared identically. That makes the flower-water lustration a general consecration for amulets rather than a quirk of one chapter: the Egyptian counterpart of the water and salt of Chapter 8, applied to the object rather than to the room. No popular treatment of either amulet mentions it, because the rubrics are almost never printed with the texts they belong to.

It also explains a confusion these rubrics invite, and the confusion is worth naming because the two ingredients are near neighbours in the same literature. The heart scarab above takes āntu or ānti unguent, and not ānkham; but ānkham is a real ingredient of amulet consecration in exactly this literature, two chapters away, in water rather than in oil. A slip of that kind is a transplant rather than an invention, which is the harder sort to catch, and it is available to anyone who reads these two rubrics out of order.

One further condition in the buckle rubric is the hinge of this whole chapter: if this chapter be inscribed upon it. The stone dipped in flower-water and set in sycamore is not yet the power of Isis. It becomes so when the words are cut into it. Object, preparation and text are three separate requirements, and the third is the one that does the work, which is the same claim the seals below make in a different idiom two and a half thousand years later.

Agrippa’s own words

The method of drawing a seal out of a square is usually described from the general literature; it does not need to be. The 1651 English translation is on the Internet Archive in full, as a scan of the Early English Books microfilm; it does not surface on a title search because the identifiers in that collection are machine-generated. What follows is Agrippa’s own account, from that printing.

He begins by saying what the tables are, and the answer is not that they are lucky numbers:

It is affirmed by Magicians, that there are certain tables of numbers distributed to the seven planets, which they call the sacred tables of the planets, endowed with many, and very great vertues of the Heavens, in as much as they represent that divine order of Celestiall numbers, impressed upon Celestials by the Idea’s of the divine mind, by means of the soul of the world, and the sweet harmony of those Celestiall rayes, signifying according to the proportion of effigies, supercelestiall Intelligencies, which can no other way be expressed, then by the marks of numbers, and Characters.

For materiall numbers, and figures can do nothing in the mysteries of hid things, but representatively by formall numbers, and figures, as they are governed, and informed by intelligencies, and divine numerations, which unite the extreams of the matter, and spirit to the will of the elevated soul, receiving through great affection, by the Celestiall power of the operator, a power from God, applyed through the soul of the universe, and observations of Celestiall constellations, to a matter fit for a form, the mediums being disposed by the skill, and industry of Magicians.

Read that second paragraph slowly, because it is the operative theory of this entire chapter in one sentence. Material numbers and figures can do nothing. The engraved square is not the agent. What acts is a chain: God, through the soul of the universe, through the constellations, through the skill of the operator, into a matter made fit to receive a form. The seal is the last link and the least of them. Nothing in the later literature of talismans improves on this as a statement of what a talisman is supposed to be doing, and a great deal of it forgets the sentence entirely.

Then the rule of derivation, given once, for Saturn, and assumed thereafter:

The first of them is assigned to Saturn, and consists of a square of three, containing the particular numbers of nine, and in every line three every way, and through each Diameter making fifteen. Now the whole sum of numbers is fourty five. Over this are of Divine names set such names as fill up the numbers with an Intelligency to what is good, with a spirit to what is bad, and out of the same numbers is drawn the seal, or Character of Saturn, and of the spirits thereof, such as we shall beneath ascribe to its table.

Three things follow from those four lines, and together they are the whole system. The names are not chosen for their meaning: they are chosen because their letters fill up the numbers of the square. Each planet gets exactly two such names, an Intelligence answering to what is good and a spirit answering to what is bad, and the tradition never explains the pairing further. And the seal is drawn out of the same numbers, which is why the tracing method given earlier in this chapter works at all: the figure and the name are two expressions of one arithmetic.

The table Agrippa prints on the facing pages sets the numbers against the names. Here are the first two exactly as page 243 has them, with the numerals in his margin:

Page 243, in Agrippa’s own setting

Divine names answering to the numbers of Saturn.
3. Ab · 9. Hod. · 15. Iah. · 15. Hod. · 45. Jehovah extended.
45. Agiel. The Intelligence of Saturn.
45. Zazel. The spirit of Saturn.

Divine names answering to the numbers of Jupiter.
4. Abab. · 16. · 16. · 34. El Ab.
136. Johphiel. The Intelligence of Jupiter.
136. Hismael. The spirit of Iupiter.

Forty-five is the sum of every number in the three-by-three square. Agiel and Zazel are both marked 45, and so is Jehovah extended: the divine name, the Intelligence and the spirit all answer to the same total. That is the mechanism, visible on one page.

The remaining five planets are set out in the same form, all on page 243, with the squares and seals following from page 244: Graphiel and Barzabel for Mars, Nachiel and Sorath for the Sun, Hagiel and Kedemel for Venus (with Bne Seraphim as “The Intelligencies of Venus,” plural, for Venus alone), Tiriel and Taphthartharath for Mercury, and for the Moon a fuller hierarchy than any other planet receives: Hasmodai “the spirit of the Moon,” Schedbarschemoth Schartathan “the spirit of the spirits of the Moon,” and Malcha betharsisim hed beruah schehalim “The Intelligency of the Intelligence of the Moon”: the 1651 page’s own descriptors, singular and plural exactly as set there.

How much of this was actually read

Pages 239, 243 and 244 of the 1651 printing were opened as page images and read directly: the two blockquotes, the Saturn and Jupiter panel, and every name-form above come from the leaves themselves, down to the page’s “Iupiter” and its singular “Intelligency.” The scan’s text layer is no help here and was not relied on: the long s defeats it constantly, and it renders tables as “caoles,” Idea’s as “1des’s,” divine order as “Tine order,” Agiel as “Agicl” and Graphiel as “Grzphicl.” The 3×3 square of Saturn in Fig. 3 stands in the same orientation the 1651 page prints, rows 4·9·2, 3·5·7, 8·1·6.

Paracelsus disagrees, and first attacks the field

Agrippa indexes everything to the planets. That is so nearly universal in the later literature that it is easy to take for the only system there is. It was not, and the dissent comes from the most famous physician of the century.

Before Paracelsus will give a character at all, he clears the ground, and the passage could serve as an epigraph for this book. He is describing the characters other practitioners draw:

There are many such-kinde of words found amongst them, which have no affinity at all with the Idioms of the Latine, Greek, or Hebrew Tongues, neither with any other; which cannot possibly be interpreted by any man, nor rendred into any other Tongue. Therefore I speak not without cause, and say, That we are not to credit all Letters, Characters or Words, but to keep to those onely which are true, and have been often proved, and taken out of the Foundation of Truth.

A sixteenth-century magical writer applying source-criticism to magical signs, on the ground that a word belonging to no known language and interpretable by nobody is not thereby profound. He is even unimpressed by novelty as a selling point, noting drily that such characters are said to be found out and devised by themselves. Set that beside the voces magicae of Chapter 9, where the untranslatable name is precisely the point, and you have two coherent and irreconcilable views of what an unintelligible word is for.

Having cleared the field he prints two, and only two:

Two Triangular Figures, cutting one another thorow with a cross, are so painted or engraven, that they do include and divide themselves into seven spaces within, and do make six corners outwardly, wherein are written six wonderful Letters of the great Name of God, to wit, Adonaj, according to their true order.

There is another which excelleth the former in power and virtue, and this hath three Hooks cutting one another through by a cross, and are so delineated, that by their mutual intersection they include six spaces, and outwardly five angles, wherein are written five syllables of the supream name of God; to wit, Tetragrammaton, also according to their true order.

I would have put down the Figures themselves; but because you may happily finde them in many other places and Books, I have the rather omitted them.

The first is a hexagram, described by construction rather than named: two triangles crossed, seven interior spaces, six outward points, one letter of ADONAY to each point. The second is a five-angled figure carrying the five syllables of Te-tra-gram-ma-ton. In both, the geometry comes first and the Name is then distributed into the compartments according to their true order: the figure is a container with a fixed number of places, and the name has to fit it.

And then the sentence that has frustrated readers for four centuries: he does not draw them, because you can find them elsewhere. Notice that this is the same instinct that produced the passage above. He will not print a figure to pad a book.

Two authorities, two indexes, one operation

This is where Paracelsus and Agrippa come apart, and the difference is not cosmetic.

Agrippa indexes to the planets. Seven squares, and from each square an Intelligence and a spirit whose letters fill the same numbers: Agiel and Zazel at forty-five, and so on. The arithmetic of the square generates the names and the seal alike.

Paracelsus indexes to the divine name. His two chief characters are not planetary at all; they are geometric vessels sized to hold ADONAY and Tetragrammaton, and the count that matters is the count of syllables and points, not a magic sum. Where he does give a set of seals in series, in his treatise on the signs of the zodiac, they are keyed to the parts of the body each sign rules, and the planets enter only as election and metal.

So the two great sixteenth-century authorities on talismans disagree about what a seal is filed under. This book prints the divergence instead of merging them, because merging them is what produced the modern impression of a single unified “system of planetary seals” that no source actually states.

What the two men do agree on is the thing that matters most, and Paracelsus states it as a rule of concurrence:

Characters, Letters, and Signes, &c. have several virtues and operations; wherewith also the nature of Metals, the condition of Heaven, and the influence of the Planets, with their operations, and the significations and proprieties of Characters, Signes, and Letters, and the observation of the times, do concur and agree together… but every one is to be prepared in his own proper time, and helpeth such and such infirmities, and no other; as drink is to be taken within the body, and not otherwise.

Four things must concur: the metal, the state of the heavens, the planetary influence, and the election of the time. Miss one and you have an ornament. That is Agrippa’s chain of causes restated by a physician, and it is the reason Chapter 20 spends as long as it does on the hour. The analogy at the end is characteristically blunt: a seal made in the wrong hour fails the way medicine fails when it is not swallowed.

What became of that book

Agrippa’s Book II is the source of nearly every planetary square, intelligence and spirit-name in circulation, and it reached most later readers through an intermediary rather than directly. The intermediary deserves a meeting, because the way it handled its source is a lesson in exactly what this book is for.

In 1801 Francis Barrett published The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer in London, for Lackington, Allen and Co. of the Temple of the Muses. Its title page describes the contents and then makes a claim:

Forming a complete system of delightful knowledge and abstruse science; such as is warranted never before to have been published in the English Language.

Here is how Barrett’s Part II opens, in his chapter on the four elements:

Therefore, there are four elements, the original grounds of all corporeal things, viz. fire, earth, water, and air, of which elements all inferior bodies are compounded; not by way of being heaped up together, but by transmutation and union; and when they are destroyed, they are resolved into elements.

And here is Agrippa, in the English of 1651: a hundred and fifty years before Barrett went to press:

There are four Elements, and originall grounds of all corporeall things, Fire, Earth, Water, Aire, of which all elementated inferiour bodies are compounded; not by way of heaping them up together, but by transmutation, and union; and when they are destroyed, they are resolved into Elements.

It is the same sentence. It continues being the same sentence: earth dissolved becomes water, made thick becomes earth again, evaporated passes into air, kindled into fire, cooled after burning becomes earth or stone or sulphur, and this is shown by lightning. Fire hot and dry, earth cold and dry, water cold and moist, air hot and moist. The Stoics called the heavy elements passives and the light ones actives. Plato distinguished them another way and assigned three qualities to each. Barrett follows Agrippa clause for clause, in order, with the spelling modernised and the occasional word turned round, Agrippa’s earth becoming dirty becomes Barrett’s earth being moistened, and no acknowledgement anywhere on the page.

Why this is in the book and not in a footnote

Barrett is not a villain and The Magus is not worthless. It is handsomely engraved, it gathered scattered material into one place, and it is the channel through which the nineteenth-century revival (and therefore the Golden Dawn, and therefore most of Chapter 13) received this tradition at all. A great deal of what a modern practitioner takes for ancient magic arrives by way of a compilation printed in the year Nelson took Copenhagen.

But set the title page against the text. Never before published in the English Language, printed over a chapter that had been available in English since 1651. That is the mechanism this whole book exists to make visible, caught in one volume: material is transmitted, the transmitter’s name replaces the source’s, and within a generation the compilation is the tradition. It is the same movement that turned a New Thought pamphlet of 1908 into the Seven Hermetic Principles (Chapter 1), and a 1610 Tübingen jeu d’esprit into an ancient brotherhood (Chapter 12).

The reader can check this one personally, which is the point of printing both passages. Both editions are free, both are scanned, and the parallel runs for pages.

Seals from the squares

The most systematic sigil method in the Western tradition is Renaissance, and it is arithmetic. Each planet is assigned a kamea (a magic square whose rows, columns and diagonals all sum alike) of a size matching the planet’s order in the Chaldean sequence: Saturn 3×3, Jupiter 4×4, Mars 5×5, Sun 6×6, Venus 7×7, Mercury 8×8, Moon 9×9. The scheme is set out in Agrippa’s De occulta philosophia, Book II, in the chapter titled “Of the tables of the Planets, their vertues, forms, and what Divine names, Intelligencies, and Spirits are set over them.”

The square of SaturnReading it
492Every row, column and diagonal sums to 15; the whole square sums to 45. This is the only 3×3 magic square that exists, up to rotation and reflection: a mathematical fact, not a magical claim, and one reason the figure impressed people who met it.
357
816

Tracing a seal on a kamea

  1. Choose the planet whose nature suits the work, from the table above.
  2. Write the name (of the intelligence, the spirit, or the intention) in Hebrew letters, and take each letter’s numerical value.
  3. Reduce each value to fall within the square: for the 3×3 of Saturn, values run 1 to 9, so 300 becomes 3 and 40 becomes 4. The conventions for reducing differ between authorities, and this is where two practitioners working “the same” method get different figures.
  4. Mark the first number on the square with a small circle, then draw a line to the cell of the next number, and so on to the last, ending with a short bar.
  5. The resulting figure is the seal. It is drawn on the metal or the paper of Chapter 20, in the planet’s hour.

What the method actually does is turn a word into a path. Nothing about the line is arbitrary once the name and the square are fixed; but nothing about it is inevitable either, since the reduction rules are conventions.

Signs nobody can read

Against all that stands the oldest layer, the charaktêres of Chapter 9: letter-like shapes with small rings at their terminals, thick through the magical papyri and the curse tablets, and not decipherable. They are not a cipher for words, they encode no name, and no key has ever been found, which makes them the honest limit of a chapter about meanings. Some signs in this tradition mean something. Some are older than the traditions that explain them, and the explanations came later.

Between the two sits John Dee’s Monas Hieroglyphica (Antwerp, 1564), a single composed glyph (Moon, Sun, cross and the sign of Aries stacked into one figure) about which Dee wrote a whole book of theorems. It is the most ambitious sigil in the tradition: an attempt to compress the entire cosmos into one mark, made by a man who thought the compression would be legible to anyone who understood it. Almost nobody has.

Modern Practice

The method most people now mean by “sigil magic” is none of the above. It was set out by the artist Austin Osman Spare in the early twentieth century: write the intention as a sentence, strike out repeated letters, and combine what remains into a single abstract figure, which is then charged and deliberately forgotten. It is elegant, it works on its own terms, and it is about a hundred years old: not medieval, not Solomonic, and owing nothing to the kameas. It is included here because it is what a reader is most likely to encounter, and because a book that dates the Kybalion ought to date this too. Spare died in 1956, so his own writings remain in copyright; the method is described here rather than quoted.

Chapter XXIIITalismanic & Astral-Image Magic Advanced

A talisman is two things joined: an image, and a moment. The figure comes from the seals and sigils of Chapter 22, the timing from the planetary days and hours of Chapter 20, and the tradition’s claim is that together they do what neither does alone: a figure cut at the right moment takes an impression from the sky, the way wax takes one from a seal. This chapter sets out the machinery that claim needs; and the large hole in the middle of its literature.

Three ways to cut the same circle

Astral-image magic needs the sky divided, and it inherited three divisions that do not agree. The twelve signs of thirty degrees are familiar. The thirty-six faces or decans of ten degrees each divide the signs evenly, three to a sign, and govern the demon-lists of Chapter 10. The twenty-eight mansions of the Moon do not divide the signs at all, and that is the interesting part.

Agrippa gives the reason and the arithmetic together. The Moon “measureth the whole Zodiack in the space of twenty eight dayes,” so the circle is cut into twenty-eight, and each mansion “containeth twelve degrees, and one and fifty minutes, and almost twenty six seconds.”

Check that figure, because it is exact. Twelve degrees fifty-one minutes and about twenty-six seconds is 360 divided by 28, to the second. Agrippa is not approximating a tradition; he is reporting a division of the circle, and the boundaries he then lists confirm it: the second mansion begins at twelve degrees fifty-one minutes twenty-two seconds of Aries, the third at twenty-five degrees forty-two minutes fifty-one seconds, the fourth at eight degrees thirty-four minutes seventeen seconds of Taurus. The mansions walk straight through the signs without stopping at them.

The twenty-eight, entire

A chapter that names the mansions and does not list them is no use to anybody, so here they are: all twenty-eight as the 1651 English gives them, with the alternative names it records, what each name means, and the virtues attributed to each. Agrippa opens the chapter with the arithmetic and its authorities (the Moon measures the whole zodiac in twenty-eight days, so “the wise-men of the Indians and ancientest Astrologians have granted twenty eight Mansions to the Moon, which being fixed in the eight sphere, do enjoy (as Alpharus saith) diverse names and proprieties from the diverse Signs and Stars which are contained in them”) and gives each mansion a span of “twelve degrees, and one and fifty minutes, and almost twenty six seconds” on the authority of Abraham. He states the exact beginning for the first seven and then says the rest follow “in the like order and number of degrees, minutes and seconds”; the Begins column therefore carries a figure only where he prints one, and a dash where the reader is to continue the count.

Read the virtues column as a whole and the character of the system shows: these are not blessings and curses but windows, each opening on a mixed set of affairs: the same mansion that frees captives strengthens prisons, the one that helps harvests hinders seamen. Captives, buildings, journeys, harvests, marriage and merchandise recur through all twenty-eight, which is a fair portrait of what the people consulting this system actually worried about. Agrippa closes the chapter by pointing beyond it: “in these twenty eight Mansions do lye hid many secrets of the wisdom of the Ancients, by the which they wrought wonders on all things which are under the circle of the Moon; and they attributed to every Mansion his resemblances, Images, and seals, and his president intelligences.” The images he means are the ones this chapter gives above.

What the mansions were for

The virtues Agrippa assigns are startlingly concrete, and reading a few in a row tells you more about the practice than any description of it. The first mansion, Alnath, the horns of Aries, “causeth discords, and journies.” The second “conduceth to the finding of treasures, and to the redeeming of captives.” The third, the Pleiades, is “profitable to Saylers, Huntsmen, and Alchymists.” The fourth, Aldebaran, causes “the destruction and hindrances of buildings, fountains, wels, of gold mines, the flight of creeping things,” and begets discord. The fifth “helpeth to the return from a journey, to the instruction of scholars, it confirmeth edifices, it giveth health and good will.”

Sailors, scholars, builders, wells, prisoners. This is not a contemplative system. It is a calendar for deciding when to do a specific job, and the mansion names are the giveaway about where it came from: Alnath, Allothaim, Athoray, Aldebaran, Alchatay, Alhanna. They are Arabic, transliterated through Latin, and Agrippa says as much: he credits “the wise men of the Indians and ancientest Astrologians,” cites one authority as Alphares and another as Abraham, and is transmitting a system he did not invent.

The images, and whose they are

For the faces, Agrippa gives images: a figure to be seen, and cut. He is explicit about his source and it is not the one most readers assume: “there are besides in the Zodiack thirty six images, according to the number of the faces, of the which (as Porphyry saith) Teucer the Babylonian long since wrote, who was a most ancient Mathematician, after whom the Arabians also wrote of these things.” The first face of Aries then ascends as

the image of a black man, standing and clothed in a white garment, girdled about, of a great body, with reddish eyes, and great strength, and like one that is angry; and this image signifieth and causeth boldness, fortitude, loftiness, and shamelessness.

Seven further chapters give the images of the planets, Saturn through the Moon. All of it is in print, in English, from 1651, and out of copyright.

These are Agrippa’s images, and not the ones you were looking for

The decan images most readers come to this subject for are the Picatrix’s, and the bibliography of this book records why they are not here: no public-domain edition of the Picatrix exists in any language, and the images “are not obtainable from any public-domain source.” That note also anticipates exactly the move this chapter might have made, and forbids it (substituting Agrippa’s images for the Picatrix’s “which is what circulates) would be the same error in a different direction.”

So the images above are given as what they are: Agrippa’s, from a line he traces to Porphyry and Teucer. They overlap the Picatrix tradition and they are not identical to it, and a reader who needs the Picatrix decans specifically still has to go to an edition this book cannot reproduce. The gap is stated rather than filled with something that would pass for it.

The planetary images, as Agrippa gives them

The faces above are one of two sets of images in Book II, and the other is the one a reader of this chapter is more likely to want, because it is the set a talisman is actually cut from. Seven short chapters, one to a planet, give the figures themselves. They are printed here entire. Read together they make three things plain that a description of them cannot. Every image is a person, not a sigil or a character: a crowned man, an armed man, a naked maid, a woman cornuted. Every one is tied to a material and a moment, so that the figure alone is never the whole instruction. And the purposes are almost all defensive or civil, prolongation of life, concord, memory, safe travelling, the increase of the fruits of the earth, with the frankly coercive ones confined to Mars.

The speaking image of Saturn and Mercury deserves a second look, because it is the most completely specified election in this book and the least achievable. Nine conditions have to hold at once, and two of them fight: Mars must be combust by the Sun, which puts him within a few degrees of it, while also aspecting neither Saturn nor Mercury, who are themselves required to be in conjunction with each other. Whether such a chart occurs at all in a given century is a question the text does not raise. What it shows is the direction the whole practice was moving in: the figure becomes almost incidental, a beautiful man in cast metal, and the entire weight of the operation shifts onto the moment. That is the argument the end of this chapter makes, and it is Agrippa who makes it first.

The moment, and why the whole thing is an argument about time

An image alone is a picture. What the tradition claims is that an image cut while the relevant part of the sky is doing the relevant thing becomes something else. That is why this material sits in astrological literature rather than in books of drawing: an election is a chart, and a talismanic election is a chart chosen rather than observed: see Chapter 21.

The practical machinery is distributed across three chapters, and this names it in one place. The hour and the day come from Chapter 20. The metal or stone comes from the same place, and the reason a Saturn talisman is lead is that the correspondence is supposed to be a real affinity and not a mnemonic. The figure comes from Chapter 22 if it is a seal or a kamea, and from Agrippa’s image chapters if it is an astral image. The consecration comes from Chapter 8. The fourth coordinate is the one the mansions supply: where the Moon is.

Chapter XXIVGeomancy Adept

Geomancy is the divination system this tradition actually used. It is not the best known, tarot has long since taken that place, but it is older in Europe, it was in the Golden Dawn curriculum listed in Chapter 13, and unlike almost everything else in this book it is completely specified. Sixteen figures, a fixed procedure for generating and combining them, and a single figure at the end that answers the question. Nothing is left to the reader’s intuition until the very last step.

The name means divination by earth, and the Arabic name it translates (ʿilm al-raml, the science of the sand) describes the original method: marks made at random in sand or dust. It entered Latin Europe in the twelfth century with the same wave of translation from Arabic that carried the Emerald Tablet: the movement Chapter 6 traces, and the collection this chapter follows also contains a treatise on astronomical geomancy under the name of Gerard of Cremona.

What Agrippa says the art actually runs on

The treatise this chapter follows opens by asking the awkward question that any system of random marks has to answer, which is what makes the marks mean anything. It gives two answers and prefers the second. The first is the one the reader expects: that the older practitioners directed the lot to spirits, and “therefore they first used certain holy incantations and deprecations, with other rites and observations, provoking and alluring spirits of this nature hereunto.” Then it sets that aside.

Another power there is that doth direct and rule this lot or fortune, which is in the very soul itself of the projector, when he is carried to this work with some great egress of his own desire, for this art hath a natural obedience to the soul itself, and of necessity hath efficacy and is moved to that which the soul itself desires; and this way is by far more true and pure: neither matters it where or how those points are projected: therefore this art hath the same radix with the art of Astrological questions: which also can no otherwise be verified, unless with a constant and excessive affection of the Querent himself.

Three things in that are worth holding on to. The first is the flat statement that the randomising does not matter: neither matters it where or how those points are projected. Whatever the art is doing, it is not doing it through the sand. The second is the condition it puts in the randomiser’s place, which is the querent’s own wanting, and wanting of a particular intensity: a great egress of desire, a constant and excessive affection. A question asked idly is, on this account, not a question. The third is the phrase the same radix with the art of Astrological questions, which makes this chapter and the horary of Chapter 21 two branches of one thing rather than neighbours. Lilly’s art needs a real question asked at a real moment; so does this one, and for the same stated reason. Having settled that, the treatise turns to the mechanics: “first it is to be known, that all figures upon which this whole art is founded are only sixteen, as in this following table you shall see noted, with their names.”

The sixteen figures

Every figure is four rows, and each row holds either one dot or two. Four binary rows give exactly sixteen possibilities, and the tradition uses all sixteen, which is why the system is closed in a way that tarot is not. The rows correspond, from the top, to fire, air, water and earth.

The two ways of laying the figures

The tradition lays the generated figures out in two forms. The shield, worked in full below, is the self-contained form: sixteen lines of marks yield four Mothers, and everything else is derived from them until a single Judge answers the question. The second form borrows the frame of astrology: the first twelve figures (Mothers, Daughters and Nieces) are set into the twelve houses of heaven, and the chart is judged like a horary figure, the question assigned to its house and the figure falling there examined, with the significations the astrology of Chapter 21 gives. Agrippa’s treatise on geomancy sets out the house method, and it is given below in his own words; the shield is older, simpler, and complete in itself, which is why this chapter works that one in full.

Agrippa gives both, and declines to choose between them in the terms a reader might expect. Having set out the ordinary geomancers’ layout, he neither endorses nor dismisses it:

And this which we have declared is the common manner observed by Geomancers, which we do not altogether reject, neither extoll; therefore this is only to be considered in our judgments: now therefore I will give you the true figure of Geomancy, according to the right constitution of Astrological reason, which is thus.

What follows is the astrological assignment, in which the Matres take the four angles rather than the first four houses in sequence. It is worth noticing that he has printed the method he thinks is inferior, in full, before printing the one he prefers, and has said in one clause both that he will not reject it and that he will not praise it. That is a third position, and this literature almost never takes it.

The true figure, and two numbers that cannot stand

What follows that clause is the assignment itself, and it is short enough to give entire. The four Mothers take the angles, the four Daughters take the succedent houses, and the four cadent houses are not cast at all but computed from the eight already placed:

As the former Matres do make the four angles of an house, the first maketh the first angle, the second the second angle, the third maketh the third angle, and the fourth the fourth angle; so the four Filiæ arising from the Matres, do constitute the four succedent houses; the first maketh the second house, the second the eleventh, the third the eighth, and the fourth maketh the first house; the rest of the houses, which are cadents, are to be calculated according to the rule of their triplicity; that is to say, by making the ninth out of the fourth and fifth, and the sixth out of the tenth and second, of the seventh and eleventh the third, and of the fourth and eighth the twelfth.

Two of those numbers cannot stand, and the passage corrects itself if it is read whole. The succedent houses are the second, fifth, eighth and eleventh. Three Daughters are given the second, the eleventh and the eighth, so the fourth cannot be given the first, which is an angle and is already held by the first Mother. It has to be the fifth. The same slip runs into the next clause. The cadents are derived by triplicity, and the triplicity of the ninth house is the first, the fifth and the ninth; so the ninth comes out of the first and fifth, not out of the fourth and fifth. The three remaining derivations are exact as printed, and they are what shows the rule: the sixth out of the tenth and second, the third out of the seventh and eleventh, the twelfth out of the fourth and eighth, each cadent house made from the other two houses of its own triplicity.

Neither correction is a guess, because the whole assignment falls into one pattern as soon as they are made. The text numbers the angles without saying which houses they are, and the Daughters are what settle it: each Daughter takes the succedent house that follows her own Mother. The second follows the first, the eleventh follows the tenth, the eighth follows the seventh, and the fifth follows the fourth. So the Mothers stand on the first, tenth, seventh and fourth houses, in that order, and each Daughter on the house after her Mother’s. Printed as it stands, the scheme puts two figures in the first house and leaves the fifth empty. Read as corrected, it fills all twelve houses exactly once.

The rest of the passage is instruction for reading the chart, and it is worth having because it shows how much of the borrowed frame comes with it:

the figure which shall be in the first house shall give you the sign ascending, which the first figure sheweth; which being done, you shall attribute their signs to the rest of their houses, according to the order of the signs: then in every house you shall note the planets according to the nature of the figure: then from all these you shall build your judgment according to the signification of the planets in the signs and houses wherein they shall be found, and according to their aspects among themselves, and to the place of the querent and thing quesited.

Notice what has happened by the end of that sentence. The geomantic figures have been turned into signs and planets, and the judgment is then made by the rules of the horary astrology of Chapter 21. The sixteen figures are a way of generating a chart without observing the sky, and everything after the generation is astrology. That is the whole of the relation between the two arts, and it is what the claim quoted earlier in this chapter means: that geomancy has the same radix with the art of Astrological questions. The shield worked below needs none of this, which is the argument for learning it first.

Casting a chart

The shield

  1. Frame one question. Geomancy answers the question asked, and an unclear question produces an unclear judge. Write it down before casting.
  2. Make sixteen lines of marks: dots in sand, or on paper, made rapidly and without counting. Then count each line: an odd number gives one dot, an even number gives two.
  3. The four Mothers. Take the sixteen results four at a time; each group of four is one figure. These are the Mothers, set down right to left.
  4. The four Daughters are read out of the Mothers: the first row of each Mother, taken in order, forms the first Daughter; the second rows form the second Daughter; and so on.
  5. The four Nieces. Add each adjacent pair (Mothers one and two, then three and four, then the Daughters likewise) row by row. Two dots plus one dot gives one; two of the same gives two. This is addition modulo two, and the whole engine of the method is that operation.
  6. Two Witnesses from the Nieces the same way, then the Judge from the two Witnesses.
  7. Read the Judge as the answer, the Witnesses as how it comes about: the right Witness for the querent’s side, the left for the matter’s. A Judge that cannot be reached by an even number of dots indicates the chart is void; recast.

Why this one earns its keep

Every other divinatory method in this book asks the practitioner to see something. Geomancy asks them to compute something and then interpret the result, and the computation is checkable by anybody. That makes it the honest place to start: the arithmetic either works or it does not, and a reading that goes wrong cannot be blamed on a failure of vision.

It also makes the system falsifiable in a way the rest of the tradition is not, which a reader may take either as a recommendation or as a warning.

The passages quoted above are not from that facsimile. Plate VI is leaf 26 of that scan, p. 13, the one figure in the geomancy section that the 1655 sheets draw rather than describe. Long s is set as round s; the printing’s spelling and punctuation otherwise stand, including quesited, certifie, commixture and extoll. The same volume carries Of Astronomical Geomancy under the name of Gerard of Cremona, and the Heptameron quoted in Chapter 10. The four-row binary structure, the derivation of Daughters, Nieces, Witnesses and Judge, and the modulo-two addition are the system’s own and are not in copyright to anyone. Arabic origin: ʿilm al-raml; the Latin transmission belongs to the twelfth-century translation movement of Chapter 6.

The Index, and the tie-breaker

One further device belongs to the method and is easy to miss, because the treatise introduces it as a secret and then gives it away in a sentence. Where the Judge and the Witnesses disagree, or agree so evenly that nothing is decided, there is a separate number to fall back on.

But here we shall give you the secret of the art of finding out the Index in the subsequent figure, which is thus: that you number all the points which are contained in the lines of the projections, and this you shall divide by twelve: and that which remaineth project from the ascendent by the several houses, and upon which house there falleth a final unity, that figure giveth you a competent judgment of the thing quesited; and this together with the significations of the judgments aforesaid. But if on either part they shall be equal, or ambiguous, then the index alone shall certifie you of the thing quesited.

Count every dot in the whole projection, divide by twelve, take the remainder, and count that many houses round from the Ascendant; the figure standing in the house you land on is the Index. Normally it is read alongside the judgment. When the judgment will not resolve, it decides alone. Two things follow. The first is that the system has a deliberate answer to deadlock, which is more than most of the divinatory methods in this book can say: the reader is not left to intuit a verdict out of a tie. The second is arithmetical, and the treatise does not point it out. A remainder of zero has no house to fall on, so the count runs one to twelve rather than zero to eleven, which is why the text speaks of the house where a final unity falls rather than of the remainder itself.

Chapter XXVTarot Adept

Twenty-two trumps; twenty-two letters in the Hebrew alphabet; twenty-two paths on the Tree of Life. That arithmetic is the whole reason tarot belongs in a book of ceremonial magic rather than in a history of card games, and somebody had to notice it first. Éliphas Lévi did, in 1856. Forty years later the Golden Dawn changed his answer, and the version in every modern handbook is the second one. Both are set out below, because they disagree about twenty-one cards out of twenty-two and a reader who has only seen the winner would never guess there had been a contest.

Where the cards came from, and where they did not

Playing cards reach Europe in the later fourteenth century. The tarot pack (four suits plus a fifth sequence of picture cards used as permanent trumps) appears in fifteenth-century Italy, and for something like three hundred years it is a card game. That is not a debunking; trick-taking with a trump suit is what the pack was made for, and it is still played.

The earliest date usually given for cards in Europe does not survive being looked at, and it is worth watching one dissolve. Alphonso XI of Castile is said to have banned cards in the statutes of the order of La Banda in 1332. Willshire, cataloguing the British Museum’s cards in 1876, points out that no early Spanish edition of the epistles that report those statutes says a syllable about cards, and that the passage first appears in a French translation of 1588. A second Spanish prohibition, de jugar dados ne naypes en publico ne escondido, is real, but the word naypes is absent from the editions of 1508 and 1545 and turns up only in the Recopilación of 1640, where, as he puts it, it was “simply an addition.” What is left is solid enough without it: a Flemish traveller of about 1540 who could not buy bread or wine in Spain but could buy cards in every village, and Montezuma watching the Spaniards play in 1519.

Divination by tarot is an eighteenth-century development, and the moment it acquires an ancient pedigree can be dated. In 1781 Antoine Court de Gébelin published an essay on the Jeu des Tarots arguing that the pack was a survival of Egyptian priestly wisdom. Waite, who had no reason to be generous about it, gives the citation exactly: Monde Primitif, analysé et comparé avec le Monde Moderne, volume 8, Paris, 1781, the articles “at pp. 365 to 410”; and the citation is good: the essay opens at p. 365 under the title Du Jeu des Tarots, with a subtitle promising its origin, its allegories, and the proof that it is the source of the modern playing pack. Its second section states the whole claim in a sentence: Le fait est cependant très-vrai: ce Livre Egyptien, seul reste de leurs superbes Bibliothèques, existe de nos jours: the fact is nonetheless quite true: this Egyptian Book, sole remnant of their superb Libraries, survives to our day. The pack he describes he also counts: LXXVII feuillets ou tableaux, même de LXXVIII: seventy-seven cards, or even seventy-eight.

The Egyptian claim has no evidence behind it and never had. It was made before the hieroglyphs could be read, on the strength of the pictures looking old, and it survived because it was useful. This is the same shape as the Hermetica in Chapter 2 and the Zohar in Chapter 4: a misdating that made the material matter, and that the material then outlived.

The attribution, and the man who changed it

The step that made tarot part of ceremonial magic rather than a fortune-telling pack was Éliphas Lévi’s, in 1856: twenty-two trumps, twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, therefore twenty-two paths on the Tree of Life of Chapter 4. Lévi’s own assignment is unambiguous and he states it through the figure rather than in a table: of the first trump he writes that “his body and arms form the letter aleph.” The Juggler is Aleph, the numbered trumps take the letters in order, and the Fool falls near the end.

The Golden Dawn moved the Fool to the front. Under its scheme the Fool is Aleph, the Magician is Beth, and every numbered trump from one to twenty shifts one letter along. That single decision is the difference between the two systems in the table below, and its effect is total: the two schemes agree about exactly one card.

The World is the only row where the columns match, and it matches for an uninteresting reason: it is last in both. Every other card in the pack has been given a different Hebrew letter, a different path on the Tree, and therefore a different meaning by anybody reading meaning off the Tree.

One thing about that table has to be said before it is used. The names in it are the modern ones, which is to say Waite’s. In 1856 the eighth trump was Justice and the eleventh was Strength; they exchanged places in 1909, for the reason Waite declined to give, as the next section describes. The letters in both columns follow the numbers and not the names, so the comparison itself is unaffected. A reader setting the table beside a nineteenth-century pack should simply expect those two cards to be the other way about.

And a second change, which Waite refused to explain

Traditionally Justice is the eighth trump and Strength the eleventh. In the Waite–Smith pack of 1909 they are the other way round, and Waite says so in the Pictorial Key two years later, in one of the more remarkable sentences in the literature: “For reasons which satisfy myself, this card has been interchanged with that of Justice, which is usually numbered eight. As the variation carries nothing with it which will signify to the reader, there is no cause for explanation.”

A four-hundred-year-old sequence altered, and the reason withheld on the ground that the reader would not understand it. Every deck descended from Waite–Smith, which is most of them, carries the change, and most of their users have never heard that it is one.

Waite against Waite

The sharpest thing in this chapter is that both attributions above are Waite’s doing, and he knew it. The English translation of Lévi quoted throughout this chapter is his: he translated Dogme et Rituel as Transcendental Magic, and it is in his English that an English reader meets the sentence about the Juggler’s body forming the aleph. Then, having put Lévi’s attribution into the language, he issued a pack built on the one that contradicts it.

He does not hide this either. Of the traditional placement of the Fool he writes that the zero card “is allocated, as it always is, to the place which makes it equivalent to the number twenty-one. The arrangement is ridiculous on the surface, which does not much signify, but it is also wrong on the symbolism.” That is a man rejecting, in print, the scheme he had himself translated: not quietly, and not without argument, but also without ever setting the two side by side for a reader to compare. The table above is that comparison; Waite appears never to have printed one.

The other fifty-six

The trumps monopolise the theory, but the pack Court de Gébelin counted has seventy-eight cards, and the other fifty-six are described here before their meanings are given below. They are the four suits of the ordinary mediaeval pack (wands, cups, swords, and coins or pentacles) each running ace to ten with four court cards. The ceremonial systematisation is the Golden Dawn’s: the four suits to the four elements (wands to fire, cups to water, swords to air, pentacles to earth) and to the four letters of the divine Name in order, so that the whole pack becomes a diagram of the Name working through the elements, ace to ten mapping the ten sephiroth of Chapter 4 in each element in turn. That scheme is a construction of the 1890s, exactly like the path-attributions above. Divinatory meanings for the small cards are older than the Golden Dawn but not ancient, they descend from eighteenth-century cartomancy, and the familiar pictorial minors, with a scene on every numbered card, begin with the Waite–Smith pack of 1909: before it, the small cards of a tarot pack look like playing cards, pips and nothing else. A reader who finds the fifty-six “meanings” less stable than the trumps’ has noticed something real: they are younger, they were never argued over by the theorists, and no two manuals agree.

How the cards were read: the meanings, and the Celtic Cross

Everything above is the history of the cards; none of it deals a spread. Both halves of the practice (what the cards mean, and how they are laid) were fixed for the modern world by one book: Waite’s Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), the companion volume to the Waite–Smith deck. Its divinatory meanings are the ancestors of the little white booklet in every boxed deck since, and its “Ancient Celtic Method of Divination” (which Waite says had “been used privately for many years past in England, Scotland and Ireland” and had not, he thought, been published before) is the Celtic Cross, the most used spread in the world. Both are printed here from a 1916 page-image witness whose own story belongs in this book’s collection of frauds: see the sources note.

First the meanings of the twenty-two trumps, compressed from Waite’s own list. Note his numbering as you read it: Fortitude stands at VIII and Justice at XI; this is the swap he refused to explain, printed as he printed it. And note where the Fool sits: Waite prints Zero between XX and XXI (second from last, which is Lévi’s placement) in the companion volume to a deck built on the order that moves the Fool to the front. The table keeps his sequence, because on the evidence of this chapter it is not a detail. Note also how unglamorous the list is: the Magician’s meanings include sickness and loss, the Hermit’s lead with treason, and the Star, every modern reader’s card of hope, opens with “loss, theft, privation, abandonment,” hope being “another reading.” The gentler senses now current are largely later accretion.

Then the fifty-six, with their meanings, from the same volume, one card to a page under each of Pamela Colman Smith’s plates. They are set out in Waite’s own order, which runs downwards: the four court cards first, then ten to ace. Three features of the list are worth seeing before it is used. The first is that Waite repeatedly declines to reconcile his sources and says so on the card itself: of the Ten of Wands, that some of the readings “cannot be harmonized”; of the Seven of Pentacles, that they are “exceedingly contradictory”; of the Five of Pentacles, that destitution and love are alternatives which “cannot be harmonized” either. He prints the disagreement rather than settling it, which is the same habit the trumps show. The second is that the court cards are largely descriptions of persons by complexion, and that is the system the Significator is chosen by in the method below. The third is that the Two of Cups is given no reversed meaning at all.

What follows is the whole of the Celtic Cross as first printed, restated as a procedure; the position formulas in quotation marks are Waite’s.

An Ancient Celtic Method of Divination

  1. Choose the Significator. A card to stand for the person or matter asked about. For a person: a Knight for a man of forty and upward, a King for a man under forty, a Queen for a woman over forty, a Page for a younger woman. Suit by colouring: Wands for the very fair, Cups for light brown hair and grey or blue eyes, Swords for hazel or grey eyes and dark brown hair, Pentacles for the very dark: with Waite’s own reservation that temperament may override appearance. For a matter rather than a person, take the trump or small card whose meaning corresponds: his example is Justice for the question “will a lawsuit be necessary?” Lay it on the table face upwards.
  2. Shuffle and cut the rest of the pack three times, faces down.
  3. Turn up the first card and cover the Significator with it: “This covers him.” The general influence and atmosphere of the matter.
  4. Lay the second across it: “This crosses him.” The nature of the obstacles; and if it is a favourable card, the opposition is not serious, or a good thing will fail to be good in this particular connection.
  5. Third above: “This crowns him.” The aim or ideal; the best that can be achieved and has not yet been made actual.
  6. Fourth below: “This is beneath him.” The foundation: what has already passed into actuality and been made the Significator’s own.
  7. Fifth on the side the Significator faces away from: “This is behind him”: the influence just passed or now passing. If the Significator is a card that faces neither way, decide before beginning which side it shall be taken as facing.
  8. Sixth on the side it faces: “This is before him”: what is coming into action in the near future. The cross is complete.
  9. Turn the next four up in a rising line at the right: the seventh is himself: the Significator’s own position or attitude; the eighth his house: environment, and the influence of immediate friends; the ninth his hopes or fears; the tenth what will come: the final result, the culmination of everything the other cards have shown. It is on this card, Waite says, that the diviner should concentrate his memory of the official divinatory meanings and whatever he has divined from the rest of the table.
  10. Two closing rules, both the text’s own. If the tenth card is of a dubious nature from which no decision can be drawn, repeat the whole operation with that tenth card as the new Significator, the pack shuffled and cut three times as before, to obtain “a more detailed account of ‘What will come.’” And if the tenth card is a court card, the matter falls ultimately into the hands of the person it represents, and its end depends on that person: take that court card as Significator in a fresh operation and discover what their influence is.

And then the sentence that belongs beside everything else this chapter has found. Waite closes his list of trump meanings, in the same book that fixed those meanings for the century, like this: what the divinatory art extracts from the Trumps Major “is at once artificial and arbitrary, as it seems to me, in the highest degree,” and “the allocation of a fortune-telling aspect to these cards is the story of a prolonged impertinence.” The man who gave the world its card meanings and its favourite spread thought fortune-telling an impertinence, and published the method anyway, and said so on the same pages. That is Waite against Waite once more; and it is why this section is printed with his warning attached rather than with the modern industry’s enthusiasm.

What this means if you use a modern deck

Any correspondence table in a modern handbook (this trump to that path, that path to this colour, planet or angel) is downstream of the Golden Dawn column above and not of anything older. It is coherent and it is usable. It is also about a hundred and thirty years old, it disagrees with the nineteenth-century French system on every card but one, and neither of them is attested in a fifteenth-century Italian card game.

None of that stops the system working as a system. It does mean that a claim of the form the Tower has always meant this is a claim about the 1890s.

The Spanish pack

A reader who wants the cards read in Madrid, Buenos Aires or Mexico City is not usually handed a tarot. They are handed a baraja española: forty cards, four suits of coins, cups, swords and clubs, three court cards, and no queen anywhere in the pack. The natural assumption is that this is a tarot with the pictures taken out. The relation runs the other way, and setting it out settles exactly which of the meanings above a reader holding a Spanish deck can use.

Willshire, cataloguing the British Museum’s cards in 1876, lists what makes a pack Spanish, and his first observation is the one this chapter has to reckon with:

It should be observed, in the first place, that Spanish tarots are unknown, and it is doubtful if such ever existed. All Spanish playing-cards are of the numeral kind. Secondly, in a legitimate Spanish pack there are only forty-eight cards, instead of fifty-two. This arises from the suppression of the ten in each suit. Thirdly, in agreement with certain Oriental and some German cards, not any queen, dame, or woman is admitted among the honours. Her place is supplied by a caballero or caballo. Fourthly, the old Italian marks are retained as copas, oros, espadas, and bastos, but the Spanish designs differ from the former, as they do likewise in the figures on the coate-cards.

Four things follow. The suits are the tarot’s own suits under Spanish names. The queen is not missing from a Spanish pack; she was never in it, and the horseman occupies the place an Italian pack gives her. The ten is gone from every suit. And no Spanish pack has ever carried trumps, so the twenty-two cards this chapter spends most of its length on have no Spanish counterpart whatever.

The forty-card pack sold today drops two further ranks, and the reason has nothing to do with divination. Willshire catalogues one such pack, from Madrid, of the second quarter of the nineteenth century:

SERIES of forty cards from a pack of forty-eight of the usual kind of Spanish numerals. From the eight and nine as well as the ten of each suit being absent, it is clear that these cards were intended for that particular modification of the old Spanish game, El Hombre (or Ombre)

The deck a fortune-teller shuffles in Seville has the shape it has because three people wanted to play ombre. The Compleat Gamester, which Willshire quotes on the same page, gives the arithmetic: at renegado “three only can play, to whom are dealt nine cards apiece; so that by discarding the eights, nines, and tens, there will remain thirteen cards in the stock.” Every Spanish reading anybody has ever done has been done on a pack cut to fit a three-handed trick-taking game.

What that leaves is exact. Every card in a Spanish pack appears in the tables above under an English name, so the meanings can be read straight off them, and the Celtic Cross needs ten cards without caring which pack they came from. What cannot be carried across is anything that needs a card the pack does not hold: no trump is available at all, the queen cannot be used as a significator, and a forty-card baraja is missing the eight, nine and ten of every suit as well, which is sixteen of the fifty-six cards those tables cover.

What the cards mean: a Madrid manual of 1876

The pack can be described from a museum catalogue. What it means needs somebody who read the cards for a living, and there is a printed source: the Arte de echar las cartas por medio de la baraja española, seguido de las profecías gitanas y de una detallada explicación de cada uno de los naipes, published at Madrid by Saturnino Calleja in 1876 as the third number of his Biblioteca Popular. It is a cheap pamphlet of a hundred and fifty pages with a woodcut of every card, and the last clause of its title is exact: it explains all of them.

Two things about it settle questions this chapter has been circling. The first is the heading over the catalogue itself, which reads Explicación de los naipes egipcios arreglados á las 48 cartas de la baraja española: an explanation of the Egyptian cards, arranged to the forty-eight of the Spanish pack. Court de Gébelin’s invention of 1781 is still doing its work in a Madrid street pamphlet ninety-five years later, and the pack it is fitted to is the forty-eight, exactly the pack Willshire was describing in London in the same year.

The second is that the pamphlet makes no claim to a Spanish descent at all. It says whose method it follows: Madame de Normand, meaning Mademoiselle Lenormand, the Paris card-reader of the Napoleonic years, and el célebre Etteilla, titulado el Grande. So the meanings below are not an old Spanish inheritance that happens to use Spanish cards. They are the French cartomancy of this chapter’s own subject, translated and refitted to a pack that has no queen and no ten.

How the pamphlet reads them

The method it prints is the one it calls the gypsies’. Shuffle, then deal twelve heaps of four cards, which uses the pack exactly. Each heap owns a department of life: the first the querent’s constitution and the length of it, the second business and fortune or poverty, the third family, the fourth love and children and every unhappy accident, the fifth affections and offspring, the sixth health and what would cure it, the seventh marriage and the enmities that come with it, the eighth the manner of death, the ninth the querent’s trade, the tenth politics and the state, the eleventh generous feeling and friendship, the twelfth the harms and persecutions of a life. Take the question to its heap, draw four cards, one from each of the heaps concerned, and read them. The pamphlet then gives a second and more theatrical way of laying the twelve out in rows, and recommends it for the frank reason that it makes the procedure impossible for the sitter to follow.

The catalogue runs from p. 55 to p. 150, one card to a spread, each with its keyword upright and reversed, a list of allied senses, and a page of combinations. The keywords are below. The senses are the pamphlet’s, not this book’s, and one of them is a trap for a modern reader: embarazo at the two of oros is glossed there as obstacle, impediment and perplexity, and means hindrance rather than pregnancy.

Why this will not work with the deck in the shops

The pamphlet is arranged to forty-eight cards and it means it. Its combinations refer to an eight twenty-four times and to a nine nineteen times, and to a ten not once, which is the forty-eight-card pack of Fig. 3 described from the inside. A reader who buys a baraja today gets forty cards, and the eights and nines are the two ranks that went out for the sake of ombre. Work the 1876 system with a modern pack and a sixth of its cross-references point at cards that are not in the box.

The remedy is a forty-eight-card pack, which is still made and still sold for the games that need it. Failing that, the upright and reversed keywords above stand on their own, and it is only the combinations that break.

What is still missing

One thing the pamphlet is not is disinterested about its own descent, and another is alone. It is a single popular printing, and a single printing cannot establish what the cards meant to Spanish readers generally, still less what they mean in Latin America now. The tradition since is largely oral, and the modern books that set it down are in copyright and are not used here. What is above is one dated, named and readable witness, which is better than the nothing this section had, and it is not a survey.

Sources: Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), for the trump meanings, the court cards and lesser arcana, the Celtic Cross, the interchange of Strength and Justice and his refusal to explain it, the judgment on the placing of the Fool, and the bibliographical citation of Court de Gébelin. It was read on the page images of The Illustrated Key to the Tarot (Chicago: de Laurence, Scott & Co., 1916), Internet Archive illustratedkeyto01dela, which is de Laurence’s piracy of Waite’s book with “By Dr. L. W. de Laurence” set on the title page of another man’s text; the scanned copy’s title leaf carries a librarian’s pencilled correction, “Waite, Arthur Edward.” It is the same Chicago house whose pirated Goetia this book reads in Chapter 11, and the same behaviour: the title-page fraud is named here so that the text below it can be used with open eyes. Read by eye: the trump meanings at pp. 146–147, leaves 0154–0155; the court cards and lesser arcana at pp. 90–145, leaves 0098–0153; the Celtic Cross at pp. 153–156, leaves 0161–0164; the title page on its own leaf. The “prolonged impertinence” passage is from p. 147.

The lesser arcana are printed one card to a page, each under its Pamela Colman Smith plate, and the tables above keep Waite’s order for them, which descends: the four court cards, then ten to ace. They compress his wording without altering any term and keep his numbering in the trumps (Fortitude VIII, Justice XI); at the Ten of Wands, the one place where he sets a reading aside in the first person, he is reported in the third. They Anglicise the American printing’s spellings where they differ, in the trumps succour and ardour, and in the lesser arcana honour, honourable, favour, favourable, unfavourable, neighbourhood, valour, dishonour, demeanour, labour and defence; the French bien-être and métier stand as printed, and Waite’s parenthetical dashes are set as commas or semicolons. Where a cell reads none given, the source supplies no reversed meaning for that card; this happens once, at the Two of Cups. Word-spacing is closed up in both scans used here and nothing else is altered; no reading required repair.

Three further page-image copies of de Laurence’s printings exist and were not needed (illustrated-key-to-the-tarot-1916, and the 1918 resettings illustratedkeyto00dela and keytotarot0000lwla); no page images of an authorised Rider printing were found. Two transcription copies circulate as scans and were rejected as witnesses (a.-e.-waite-the-pictorial-key-to-the-tarot, A.EWaiteThePictorialKeyToTheTarot, both set from the sacred-texts keying); the one photographic copy of an authorised printing found, pictorialkeytota0000wait, is a 1959 reprint behind a lending restriction.

Lévi, Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie (1854–56), quoted in Waite’s English as Transcendental Magic, read from the de Laurence printing of that translation, transcendentalma00levi_0; the attribution of the first trump to aleph is at his description of the Juggler, and the Fool is placed in his table of lunar days at the twenty-ninth. I. at its head, with a later hand’s ink note keying it to p. 373; the plates are bound at the end and not beside the essay, which is why they are easy to miss in a scan. The four trumps are read by eye on the plate and the names are the standard ones; no claim is made here about what any of them meant to the engraver.

The table of attributions is this book’s own construction and is the point at which it should be checked hardest. The Golden Dawn column is the standard modern attribution, a construction of the 1890s, set out here from that standard scheme and not from an order document, because the order’s own papers reached print through Regardie and are in copyright. The Lévi column is derived: he gives the first trump and the sequence, and the rest follows from taking the letters in order, which is what he describes rather than tabulates. A reader who needs either column for scholarly purposes should go behind this book to the sources. The dating of playing cards and of the tarot pack is given in outline from general reference and no primary source for it was consulted.

The Spanish pack: William Hughes Willshire, A Descriptive Catalogue of Playing and Other Cards in the British Museum (1876), read on the page images of the Internet Archive scan descriptivecatal00brituoft. How far the table was checked, since it is long. The keywords were taken from the library’s own OCR of the pamphlet and are printed here in its spelling and accentuation, ó for o included. That layer is good on the bold keyword lines and poor in the body, so five entries were read on the page images to test it: the ace and two of oros, the ace of bastos, the knave of bastos and the knight of copas. Where the OCR mangled a keyword it was corrected against the entry’s own list of senses, which repeats the word: Einb’razo at the two of oros is Embarazo, glossed there as obstacle and impediment.
