Chapter XXVIFolk Magic Beginner

Everything so far in this book belongs to a learned tradition. It is written by men with libraries, in Latin and Greek and Hebrew, for readers who can afford instruments and virgin parchment and a room set apart. There is another stream entirely, and leaving it out would misrepresent what magic in the West has mostly actually been: charms, said aloud, by people with no equipment, for the ordinary catastrophes of a working life: a burn, a bleeding cut, a house in a storm, a fire in the barn.

The book this chapter follows is the best-documented example in English: The Long Lost Friend, published in German at Reading, Pennsylvania in 1820 by John George Hohman and in English from the 1840s. It is the handbook of Pennsylvania Dutch Braucherei or powwowing, a folk practice still alive, and it is a genuinely different object from the grimoires of Chapter 10: cheap, small, in the vernacular, and organised by complaint rather than by planet.

Three features mark this book, and the third of them marks the whole tradition. The charms are Christian in idiom, not Solomonic: the names invoked are the Trinity and the saints, not Hebrew godnames. They are spoken, not written, and Hohman requires no instrument at all. And most are built on epic precedent: a holy event is narrated, and the narration is expected to make its outcome recur here. That form is very old (the same shape appears in Anglo-Saxon and Old High German charms centuries earlier) and it is entirely absent from the ceremonial chapters of this book.

Hold the first two of those loosely. They are true of Hohman, and it is tempting to read them as the definition of folk magic against ceremonial magic. The Anglo-Saxon material later in this chapter will not support that reading: it has instruments, timed hours, a silence taboo and a consecration, and it is folk practice throughout. The chapter states the neat division here because it is the one most readers arrive with, and then takes it apart.

The rule that governs everything in this chapter

Hohman states one instruction that applies across the whole book, and it should be read before any charm in it:

“Every thing prescribed in this book must be used three times, even if the three crosses should not be affixed. Words are always to have an interval of half an hour, and between the second and third time should pass a whole night, except where it is otherwise directed.”

Three repetitions, half an hour apart, with a night between the second and the third. That timing rule is to this tradition what the planetary hour is to Chapter 20: the thing that makes an utterance an operation.

Four charms

These are printed exactly as the 1850 English edition has them, misspellings and all: “firy oven,” the mangled names of the three men in the furnace, “Thus they shalt abate.” The errors are part of the record: this is a cheap book, set by a jobbing printer, for readers who were not going to check it against a Bible.

How to cure a Burn

Three holy men went out walking,
They did bless the heat and the burning;
They blessed that it might not increase;
They blessed that it might quickly cease!

Four lines, no apparatus, and the epic-precedent form in its purest state: three men walk out of scripture, bless a fire, and the blessing is expected to carry into this burn. Nothing is asked of any spirit; the charm works, on its own account, by re-narration.

A certain remedy to stop Bleeding

Which cures, no matter how far a person be away, if only his first name is rightly pronounced while using it.

Jesus Christ, dearest blood!
That stoppeth the pain, and stoppeth the blood.
In this help you, [first name] God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Ghost. Amen.

A Benediction to prevent Fire

The bitter sorrows and the death of our dear Lord Jesus Christ shall prevail. Fire, and wind, and great heat, and all that is within the power of these elements, I command thee through the Lord Jesus Christ, who has spoken to the winds and the waters, and they obeyed him. By these powerful words spoken by Jesus, I command, threaten, and inform thee, fire, flame, and heat, and your powers as elements, to flee forthwith.

The holy, rosy blood of our dear Lord Jesus Christ, may rule it. Thou, fire and wind, and great heat, I command thee, as the Lord did by his holy angels command the great heat in the firy oven when those three holy men, Sadrach and his companions, Mesach and Obed Rego, to leave them untouched, as was done accordingly.

Thus they shalt abate, thou fire, flame, and great heat, the Almighty God having spoken in creating the four elements, together with heaven and earth: Fiat, Fiat, Fiat! that is: It shall be, in the name of God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. Amen.

Note what the operator does here: commands an element, and does so on a precedent: the furnace of Daniel 3, whose three men Hohman’s printer garbles into “Sadrach and his companions, Mesach and Obed Rego.” The threefold Fiat at the close is the folk register reaching for ceremonial speech, and it is the one place in the chapter where this tradition and Chapter 8 sound alike.

Protection of one’s House and Hearth

Beneath thy guardianship, I am safe against all tempests and all enemies, J. J. J.

These three J’s signify Jesus three times.

A complete operation in one sentence; and the three initials are the whole system in miniature: a name said three times, compressed so far that only its first letter survives, with the book’s own gloss appended in case the reader has forgotten.

Where the form comes from

The three-part shape described above (a holy event narrated, then the outcome expected to recur) is not a Pennsylvania Dutch invention, and it is not a vague family resemblance either. It has a name, a documented mechanism, and a scholarly statement of both that is old enough to be quoted here. Felix Grendon set it out in 1909, working from the Old High German and Vedic material rather than the American:

The exorcist, desiring to cure a disease or to invoke favors from the deity, recounts a mythological incident presenting circumstances analogous to the situation in which the patient is found. The procedure of the supernatural beings in the narrative is to serve as a precedent in the case with which the conjurer is dealing.

In the two Old High German and in many of the Hindu incantations, it will be observed that the recitation of the mythological precedent frequently concludes with a precise formula, supposedly uttered by the deity or hero who appears in the incident. The potency of a phrase having been proved by its use under supernatural auspices, the conjurer believes that a recital of the same formula will insure the attainment of his end.

Read that as a piece of legal machinery, because that is what it is. The narrative is not decoration and it is not scene-setting. It is a cited precedent: a case in which the desired outcome already occurred, chosen because its circumstances are analogous to the present ones, and adduced so that the present case must be decided the same way. The words that closed the precedent then carry the authority of having worked once under conditions no human can reproduce. Almost every popular account of these charms treats the opening story as poetry. It is the argument.

The same charm, twice, four centuries apart

What makes this more than a theory is that one charm survives in both its heathen and its Christian form, and Grendon prints them within two pages of each other. The older is the second of the two Merseburg incantations, from a tenth-century manuscript, for a dislocation. Grendon gives the opening in English:

Phol and Woden rode to forest
Where sprained was the foot of Balder’s foal.

He describes the rest rather than printing it: three goddesses attempt the cure and fail; then Woden, who in Grendon’s paraphrase knew well how, effects it; and the charm closes on the formula Woden himself is supposed to have spoken, which is the part the human operator repeats. That formula is the bone-to-bone, blood-to-blood binding that every reader of folk charms has met somewhere.

And here is the same charm as it was still being used after the conversion:

Our Lord rade

Our Lord rade, his foal’s foot slade;
Down he lighted, his foal’s foot righted.
Bone to bone, sinew to sinew,
Blood to blood, flesh to flesh:
Heal in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.

The rider has changed and nothing else has. The horse still stumbles, the rider still dismounts, the joint is still set, and the operative formula (bone to bone, blood to blood) survives word for word into a charm that ends on the Trinity. Grendon states the substitution flatly: the Christian versions are plainly related to the Old High German charm, the principal modern changes being the invariable substitution of the words “Jesus,” “Lord,” or “God” for the names “Woden,” “Phol,” “Sindgund,” “Frija,” and “Volla.”

What this does to the charms above

Go back to Hohman’s cure for a burn. Three holy men went out walking, they did bless the heat and the burning. Four lines, no apparatus, an unnamed trio walking out of scripture, and a blessing expected to carry into the present injury. It is the identical machine: precedent narrated, formula applied. Hohman is publishing in Reading, Pennsylvania in 1820, in German, for farmers. The manuscript Grendon is reading was written in the tenth century. Nothing connects them but the form, and the form survived the entire Christianisation of northern Europe by the simple expedient of changing who is riding the horse.

This also explains something the ceremonial chapters of this book cannot: why the folk register needs no instruments, no hour, no circle and no consecration. A ceremonial operation builds a situation in which a thing may be commanded. A charm of this kind does not command at all. It argues, and the whole of its apparatus is one remembered story.

The English charms, and what they undo

This chapter has so far set an 1820 book printed in Pennsylvania beside a German manuscript of the tenth century. Between them lies a large English corpus, and reaching it complicates the neat division this chapter opened with. Anglo-Saxon charms are not simple. Several are more elaborately staged than anything in Chapter 8, and they achieve it without a single instrument.

Start with the smallest complete operation in the book:

For much travelling

For much travelling on land, lest a person tire: let him take mugwort in his hand or put it in his shoe, lest he grow weary; and if he would pluck it before sunrise let him first say these words:

Tollam te artemesia, ne lassus sim in via.

Sign it with the sign of the cross when you pull it up.

Two lines of instruction, one line of Latin (I shall take you, mugwort, that I be not weary on the road) and a gesture. There is a herb, a time, a formula and a sign, and nothing else. Put it in your shoe. It is the whole of the tradition compressed into something a person could actually do on a Tuesday, Hold it in mind against the nine-foot circle.

A rite in the folk register

And then this, which is the reason the English material belongs in this book. It is a remedy, and it is also a staged ceremonial operation running over two days:

For elf-disease

On Thursday evening when the sun is set, go where you know that elecampane stands; then sing the Benedicite and a Paternoster and a litany, and stick your knife into the herb; let it stick fast therein and go away.

Go again thither, just as day and night divide. During this same daybreak go first to church and cross yourself and commend yourself to God.

Then go in silence, and, though something of a fearful kind or a man should come upon you, say not a single word to it until you reach the herb you marked the night before.

Then sing the Benedicite and a Paternoster and a litany, delve up the herb, letting the knife stick fast in it. As quickly as you can, go to church and place it with the knife under the altar; let it lie until the sun has risen.

Afterwards wash it and make it and bishop’s-wort and lichen off a crucifix into a drink; boil the drink three times in milk, pour holy water into it three times, sing over it a Paternoster and a Credo and a Gloria in excelsis deo, and sing a litany over it; and also, with a sword, inscribe a cross round it on four sides, and after that let the patient drink the draught.

Count what is in there. A fixed day and a fixed hour, twice over: Thursday at sunset, and again at the exact division of day and night, which is the same interest in the threshold moment that drives the planetary hours of Chapter 20. A knife left standing in the plant overnight, marking it as claimed and returned to. A silence taboo with an explicit clause covering the case where something frightening addresses you, which is one of the strongest injunctions of its kind anywhere in this book. A consecration under an altar until sunrise. Threefold repetition, twice: three boilings, three pourings. And a cross inscribed on four sides with a sword, which is a circle-casting by another name.

Every structural element of a ceremonial working is present: election of time, purification, a marked boundary, a triple repetition, a spoken formula, a consecrated instrument. What is absent is the entire apparatus: no circle drawn on the ground, no wand or pentacle, no Hebrew, no spirit named, no hierarchy. The instruments are a knife and a sword the operator already owns, and the words are the ones any parish knew by heart.

What this does to the division this chapter began with

The opening of this chapter drew a clean line: ceremonial magic has libraries, instruments and Hebrew godnames; folk magic has a spoken charm and nothing else. On the evidence of the English material that line is too clean. The elf-disease rite is not a charm; it is a liturgy, performed by a layman, using the parish church as its temple and the parish’s own prayers as its words.

The honest description is not two traditions but one grammar with two vocabularies. Where the grimoires say in the day and hour of Mercury, this says on Thursday evening when the sun is set. Where they consecrate on an altar of their own construction, this walks to the one down the road. The difference between the registers turns out to be a difference of access (to Latin, to materials, to a private room) far more than a difference of method.

Herbs addressed as persons

One habit in this corpus stands against the ceremonial chapters, because it is the same move made on a different object: the plant is spoken to, in the second person, and reminded of its own history. The Key of Solomon does this to water (I exorcise Thee, O Creature of Water, by Him Who hath created thee and gathered thee together into one place) reciting the material’s own past as the ground of the demand. What differs is not the grammar but the warrant: the ceremonial text addresses the water through the God who made it, and the charm addresses the plant directly, on its own record. The Nine Herbs Charm opens:

Remember, Mugwort, what you revealed,
What you prepared at Regenmeld.
Una, you are called, eldest of herbs.
You avail against three and against thirty,
You avail against poison and against infectious sickness,
You avail against the loathsome fiend that wanders through the land.

And you, Plantain, mother of herbs.
Open from the east, mighty from within.
Over you carts creaked, over you queens rode.
Brides exclaimed over you, over you bulls gnashed their teeth.
Yet all these you withstood and fought against…

That is not a correspondence table. The herb is not being used; it is being reminded (of what it once did, of what has been driven over it, of what it withstood) and the reminding is the operation, in exactly the way the narrated precedent was the operation in the charms above. Plantain grows in cart-ruts and doorways and is walked on by everything, and the charm makes that its qualification. Something trodden by carts and queens and bulls alike, and still there, is precisely what you want against a sickness.

Grendon, describing how the older layer of this material was handled once the Church took an interest, gives the mechanism its best short formulation. Of a line in the field-blessing appealing to Earth to be fruitful in God’s embracing arm, he writes that it shows admirably the method of toning down the Paganism of the spell. Not deletion. Adjustment, which is why so much of it survived.

What this chapter is and is not

These are historical charms, printed as evidence of what people did. That applies to the Anglo-Saxon remedies above exactly as it applies to Hohman: for elf-disease is a treatment for a condition no modern reader has, made of a plant no modern reader should be boiling into a draught on the strength of a tenth-century manuscript. It is given for its structure, not its pharmacy. Several of Hohman’s remedies are dangerous, some are unpleasant, and a great many address serious illness in place of medicine. The four above are given because they are harmless in themselves; the bleeding charm in particular is not a treatment for bleeding, and The Long Lost Friend was written in a world where the alternative to a charm was frequently nothing at all.

The living tradition should also be named rather than mined. Braucherei is practised today in Pennsylvania and elsewhere, ordinarily within a Christian frame and often transmitted only across the sexes and within families. A reader who wants to learn it should go to it, not to a book.

Modern Practice

The folk register never went away, and it is where most people actually meet magic: a charm said over a child’s scraped knee, a horseshoe over a door, salt thrown over a shoulder, a phrase repeated three times. The ceremonial tradition of this book has libraries and vocabulary and a documented history. This one has survived four centuries in the mouths of people who left no records at all, which is a different and not obviously lesser achievement.

Sources: Hohman, The Long Lost Friend (Harrisburg, Pa., 1850), translated from Der lange verborgene Freund (Reading, Pa., 1820): the three-times rule at p. 22 and the four charms as printed, spellings and all; read from the Wellcome copy b33030467 and verified against its page images. The witness matters more than usual here. Another 1850 printing, the National Library of Medicine copy, is a different English rendering whose rule reads “an interval of several hours” where this one has “half an hour,” so the wording quoted above belongs to this copy and not to “the 1850 edition” at large. Modern editions carry their own editorial apparatus and are not the source used here.

Grendon, The Anglo-Saxon Charms (1909): the statement of the doctrine at p. 111, the English charms For much travelling (B 2), For elf-disease (B 3) and the opening of the Nigon Wyrta Galdor (B 4) in his facing English at pp. 191 and 194, the remark on toning down from his discussion of the field-blessing at p. 156, the English of the second Merseburg charm at p. 148 n. 9, and Our Lord rade with the account of the substituted names at p. 149. His Old English is printed opposite and is not reproduced, and no Old High German is quoted. In the Latin tag of B 2 the scan reads ne bssus sim in via; lassus is printed above as an expansion of an obvious corruption, the sense being fixed by his own instruction lest he grow weary, and the expansion is declared here rather than made silently. Unlike the Agrippa material in Chapter 22, these were read in the scan’s text layer and not on page images; the OCR is clean in these paragraphs and was checked against the surrounding argument, but the distinction is stated because this book has made it a standard elsewhere. The goddess-name Sindgund rests on that single witness, and Grendon’s own footnote elsewhere records that the form was already contested in his day.

Chapter XXVIIThe Modern Occult Revival Reference

Nearly everything a modern reader will meet as the tradition was made between 1875 and 1978, and each stage of it believed it was continuing something much older. Theosophy, the Golden Dawn, Thelema, the witch-cult thesis, Wicca and chaos magic follow one another within a single century, and each inherited the previous one’s invention as an antiquity. Setting them in a row is the only way to see the shape of it.

Lévi, 1854, the stage before the curtain

One name belongs before the figure’s first row, and Fig. 1 should be read with him standing ahead of it. Éliphas Lévi (Alphonse Louis Constant, a Parisian ex-seminarian) published Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie in 1854–56, and nearly every structural idea the revival ran on is in it: magic presented as a single coherent tradition rather than a heap of curiosities, the tarot joined to the Hebrew alphabet (Chapter 25 gives his attribution and what the Golden Dawn did to it), and the astral light as the medium of the whole art. He wrote in the wake of the spiritualist wave that began at Hydesville in 1848 (the séance room is the unacknowledged background of the entire period) and he reached English occultism in Waite’s translation, cited in Chapter 25. Every movement in the figure below inherited him, usually without saying so.

Theosophy, and the reason so much of this is Indian

Helena Blavatsky and the Theosophical Society, from 1875, are why a Western esoteric handbook of the twentieth century talks about karma, reincarnation, chakras and root races. Before Theosophy those are not part of this tradition; after it they are inseparable from popular versions of it. One of her importations is now so thoroughly naturalised that its source is rarely named: “as above, so below” is not in the Emerald Tablet, and it circulates because Blavatsky quoted it as a received Hermetic axiom: see Chapter 6.

Theosophy also supplied the form of the modern claim: a hidden brotherhood of masters, a secret doctrine older than the religions, a text received rather than composed. Every movement below borrows that shape, whatever it fills it with.

The Akashic Records, and the year they got their name

One Theosophical importation has travelled further than any of the others and is now the common property of people who have never heard of the Theosophical Society: the Akashic Records, the idea that everything which has ever happened is permanently written somewhere and can be read by the properly trained. It is offered almost everywhere as ancient wisdom, usually Eastern. The word is certainly Sanskrit. The compound is not ancient, and because the people who assembled it published monthly, the assembly can be watched.

The doctrine is complete thirteen years before the phrase. Here is The Theosophist in September 1882, explaining how a dead man’s face came to appear on a medium:

The images we find in the endless galleries of space, nailed on to the indestructible walls of Akasa, are but lifeless and empty masks after all, the pictorial records of our thoughts, words and deeds.

Records, on the walls of Akasa, in 1882. The following June the same magazine gives the reading method and the metaphor that has stuck to the idea ever since: the psychometer, once “landed in the world of Akasic impressions,” finds “the book of Nature opened at every page and the images of all that was, being as though photographed on the etheric waves.” By 1884 the thing has a settled formula, quoted as such in a book review: the reviewer commends Edwin Arnold for showing “an understanding of the fact which occultism teaches, that ‘the Akasa is Nature’s Book of Record’ otherwise called the ‘Book of Life.’” By the end of the decade the whole doctrine is being set out for beginners in Theosophical Siftings, and so is the objection to its name:

Theosophy also teaches the existence of a universally diffused and highly ethereal medium, which has been called the “Astral Light” and “Akasa.” It is the respository of all past, present, and future events, and in it are recorded the effects of spiritual causes, and of all acts and thoughts from the direction of either spirit or matter. It may be called the Book of the Recording Angel.

Akasa, however, is a misnomer when it is confused with Ether or the Astral light of the Kabalists.

That is 1889. The repository of all events, the recording, the Book, and in the very next sentence the warning that the word is wrong. Blavatsky is making the same complaint in The Secret Doctrine the year before, where the adjective names a substance and not an archive, and where her whole concern is that everyone is calling the substance by the wrong name:

The Earth was in her first Rûpa, the essence of which is the Âkâshic Principle named * * *, that which is now known as, and very erroneously termed, Astral Light, which Éliphas Lévi calls the “Imagination of Nature,” probably to avoid giving it its correct name, as others do.

That ties this section to the one on Lévi above: the substance the Theosophists called Âkâsha is the substance Lévi called the astral light, and Blavatsky accepts the identification while rejecting the label. Her Theosophical Glossary, printed the year after her death, has an entry for Akasa and none for anything Akashic. And the notion has already escaped the Theosophical press by then, which is how one can tell it was current rather than merely printed. In August 1889 the Religio-Philosophical Journal of Chicago, a Spiritualist paper hostile to Blavatsky, runs a satirical dialogue about a leak of Theosophical documents in which one speaker says: “Why, I should think the Madame would roam out in her astral and just read in the Akasian record the whole business.” That is an adjective and a record, six years before Besant, and it is a joke. Nobody makes a joke out of a phrase the readership does not already know.

So by 1891 there is a doctrine, a reading method, a photographic metaphor and a standing argument about names, and no fixed phrase. The phrase assembles in two steps. In September 1894 Olcott, writing his reminiscences of Blavatsky, complains of psychic force wasted on parlour phenomena when it might have been spent to convince “some great scientist to believe in the existence of the records of the Âkâs’a.” The genitive, not yet the compound. Eleven months later, in August 1895, four years after Blavatsky’s death, Annie Besant writes in Lucifer, the magazine Blavatsky had founded:

a scene from the past may be reproduced in all its living reality, correct in every detail of its far-off happening; for in the Âkâshic Records it exists, imprinted there once for all, and a fleeting living picture of any page of these Records can be made at pleasure, dramatised on the Astral Plane, and lived in by the trained Seer.

Besant does not introduce the term, define it or defend it. She uses it as though her readers already have it, which is how a phrase looks when it has been in conversation before it reaches print. The article was reissued the same year as the booklet Karma, where the circumflexes are quietly dropped and the spelling becomes the modern one. Four years after that Leadbeater, explaining to a general readership how visions of the past are obtained, answers that they are read from the âkâshic records and at once takes it back: the word “is in truth somewhat of a misnomer,” and the alternative in circulation, “records of the astral light,” is “still worse.” He is not making a new objection. He is repeating one that had been in the Theosophical press for ten years, about a phrase that had by then won anyway.

YearWhereWhat is actually said
1882The Theosophist, September“the pictorial records of our thoughts, words and deeds,” on “the indestructible walls of Akasa”
1883The Theosophist, Junethe reading method: “Akasic impressions,” “photographed on the etheric waves”
1884The Theosophist, Julya settled formula, in quotation marks: “the Akasa is Nature’s Book of Record”
1888The Secret Doctrine“Âkâshic” three times, always a substance: a Principle, an Ocean, a primal nature. Never a record
1889Theosophical Siftings“the Book of the Recording Angel,” and “Akasa, however, is a misnomer”
1889Religio-Philosophical Journal, August“the Akasian record,” in a hostile paper, as a joke
1892Theosophical Glossaryan entry for Akasa; nothing Akashic
1894The Theosophist, September“the records of the Âkâs’a”: the genitive, eleven months early
1895Lucifer, August“Âkâshic Records,” the compound, used without explanation
1899Leadbeater, Clairvoyancethe phrase in general use, and the misnomer charge repeated
1904Steiner, Lucifer-Gnosisa separate German lineage begins, and it says Chronicle rather than Records

What can be claimed from this is a sequence, not a coinage. The earliest printing of the compound that could be found for this edition is Besant’s, and the search behind that sentence is described in the sources below, along with what it could not reach. The whole of the archive it could have appeared in has now been searched, so if it is earlier it is somewhere that archive does not hold, or in a letter. What will not change is the order: the doctrine was in print for thirteen years before it had this name, the objection to the name is older than the name, the name itself was fixed after the founder’s death by her successors, and the man who did most to spread it told his readers in the same breath that it was wrong.

Thelema, 1904

Aleister Crowley is the hinge between the Golden Dawn and everything after it, and the founding document is Liber AL vel Legis, the Book of the Law, which he held to have been dictated to him at Cairo in April 1904. Two of its verses have entered general use far beyond anybody who would call themselves a Thelemite:

Every man and every woman is a star.

Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law.

The second is routinely quoted as a licence and was not meant as one; the Law pairs it immediately with “Love is the law, love under will,” and Crowley’s thou wilt means a true will discovered rather than a preference indulged. Whether that is a meaningful distinction is not this book’s question. That it is the text’s own reading is checkable, and the misquotation is one of the most common in the subject.

Murray, 1921, and the claim that made Wicca possible

Margaret Murray was an Egyptologist who argued, in The Witch-Cult in Western Europe, that the people tried as witches in early modern Europe had been practising a real religion: an organised pre-Christian survival, which she named the Dianic cult. Her statement of it is admirably plain, and the first four words are the trouble:

The evidence proves that underlying the Christian religion was a cult practised by many classes of the community… It can be traced back to pre-Christian times, and appears to be the ancient religion of Western Europe.

The evidence does not prove that, and the thesis is no longer held by historians of the subject. Murray built it by reading confessions extracted under torture as ethnographic reports and by treating what the interrogators supplied as what the accused described. The book was influential for forty years, it was in the Encyclopædia Britannica, and it is the indispensable link in the chain, because the next stage depended on it being true.

Wicca, 1954, and chaos magic, 1978

Gerald Gardner published Witchcraft Today in 1954, presenting the practice he taught as a surviving remnant of exactly the religion Murray had described; and Murray wrote the introduction. Chapter 18 already dates one piece of that practice in detail, and the finding there is representative: the eightfold Wheel of the Year, presented as immemorial, was assembled between the 1940s and 1958, with the equinoxes added after Witchcraft Today had gone to press. This book’s treatment of Gardner is deliberately thin because his work is in copyright and this edition describes rather than quotes it; the dating is Ronald Hutton’s, and it is cited there.

Chaos magic, from the late 1970s and associated in print with Peter Carroll and Ray Sherwin, closes the sequence by breaking the pattern. Its founding move is to drop the lineage entirely: no ancient tradition, no received text, no masters: technique treated as technique, belief treated as a tool to be adopted for a working and dropped afterwards. Whatever one makes of it, it is the only stage in Fig. 1 that never claimed to be old, and it arrived after a century in which every previous stage had. That is also in copyright and is described here and not quoted.

Why the pattern needs a name

Read down the last column of Fig. 1 and the shape is unmistakable: each generation received the previous generation’s invention as an inheritance. The Golden Dawn took a cipher manuscript for a German lineage. Gardner took Murray’s thesis for a surviving religion. Modern handbooks take the Golden Dawn’s correspondence tables for immemorial doctrine. In every case the material outlived the claim, and in every case it is still in use.

That is the argument of this whole book, arriving in the century that made it: the dating being wrong is not the same as the practice being worthless. It is only the same if the practice was being recommended because it was old, which is exactly why the dates belong on the page.

The dating rests on a search of three bodies of text: HathiTrust full-text, which holds Lucifer complete from 1887; Google Books to 1896; and the periodical archive of the International Association for the Preservation of Spiritualist and Occult Periodicals, which neither of the others holds and which supplied the scans above. That archive was searched in full: every issue it has of every one of its journals dated to 1895, seventeen thousand nine hundred and seventy-one numbers of fourteen hundred and fourteen periodicals, fetched and read one at a time. The test could not be a match on the adjective, because one scan renders it Ak&shic in the very number that carries the earliest use; it looked instead for every occurrence of record with a word beginning Ak within eighty characters, which survives whatever a scanner does to the diacritics. Of the twenty passages it flagged, five are false, four of them the name of the Russian spiritualist Aksakov and one the Sanskrit Rakshasas. The compound occurs nowhere in that archive before August 1895. What the sweep cannot cover is print outside it, and no search of print can speak for what was said aloud, so the claim above is the earliest printing that could be found and not the first use of the words. The Internet Archive’s own full-text search is no use for dating: sorted by date, its earliest results carry publication years of 1200, 1337 and 1740 for books written in the last thirty years. Steiner’s Aus der Akasha-Chronik, the separate German line, began as a serial in Lucifer-Gnosis in July 1904 and is later than everything above.

Gardner, Witchcraft Today (1954), and Carroll, Liber Null (1978), are in copyright and are described and not quoted, which is this book’s standing practice for modern order and movement material. The dating of the Wheel of the Year is Hutton’s and is cited in full in Chapter 18. The judgment that Murray’s thesis is no longer held is reported from the general state of the field; no historiographical survey was consulted, and a reader who wants the case against her in detail should go to Hutton. Fig. 1, its last column, and the observation that only the final stage declined to claim antiquity are this book’s own.

Chapter XXVIIIMaterials Reference

This chapter exists because the rest of the book does not answer an obvious question. The sources specify their materials scrupulously and in scattered places, and a reader who wants to actually perform something has to reconstruct the list by hunting back through five chapters. Here it is in one place, built from the rites themselves rather than from a general impression of what magic requires.

It covers all forty-one rites this book gives outside the laboratory. The six laboratory operations of Chapter XXIX are deliberately not in the table: what they require is a working laboratory with a fume hood, and that chapter states the requirement for each operation where it belongs, alongside the hazard it exists to control.

The first thing the table shows should come before the table: eleven of the forty-one rites in this book need no equipment at all. Not improvised equipment: none. That includes all four of Hohman’s charms, the Merseburg charm beside them, the vibration of a divine name, the assumption of a godform, and the reckoning of the planetary hour. If the apparatus is what has been putting you off, better than a quarter of the book is already open to you. (Not every folk charm qualifies: the Anglo-Saxon rites in the same chapter are among the most demanding in the book.)

The minimum, and what it covers

Ten ordinary things cover twenty-four of the forty-one rites between them. None is specialist and none is expensive:

Add a wand (which in the sources is a cut rod, not a purchase) and a dark bowl for scrying, and the rest is the odd particular the rite itself names: a metal blank, a length of cord, a sword, a flask of strong spirit, a compass.

Substitutions the sources themselves allow

This matters more than it might seem, because the impression that these operations require rare materials is largely an artefact of reading the most demanding text and assuming it speaks for the rest. The traditions are more accommodating than their reputation:

  • Paper for parchment. The Key of Solomon prefers virgin parchment and allows paper. Talismans are now made in paper and ink far more often than in engraved metal, and the text permits it.
  • Any knife, once consecrated. The consecration in Chapter VIII is what makes the instrument, and the rite is given in full. Nothing in it depends on what the blade cost.
  • A cut rod for a wand. Where a wand is specified the sources describe cutting one, not buying one.
  • Resins over sticks. If you want the historical thing, the sources name gums and resins (frankincense, myrrh, mastic, aloes) burned on charcoal. Perfumed sticks are a modern convenience and no source knows them.
  • Kitchen technique for herbs. Infusion, decoction and expression (Chapter XVI, Fig. 1) need a pan and a sieve.

What not to buy, and what not to do

Nothing in this chapter requires a toxic material, and nothing in it should send you looking for one. The historical alchemical literature is full of mercury, antimony, lead and corrosive acids, and this chapter treats that material historically and gives no procedure for handling any of it. Chapter 29 does give the procedures, hazard before method every time, for a reader who already has a fume hood and a waste-disposal route. If a source hands you one of those operations without the hazard attached, the source is being reckless with you.

Incense needs ventilation. This is the one genuinely common hazard in the book. Burning resins in a small unventilated room is a real respiratory risk, and the tradition (which worked in larger, draughtier rooms than yours) is no guide at all here. Open a window. Every time.

Open flame, unattended, near cloth. Robes, hangings, paper and a candle on a table is how a working becomes a house fire. The historical texts do not warn you about this because their rooms were built of stone and their attention was undivided.

No animal materials requiring harm. Several sources call for them. None is reproduced here, and where a passage was cut for that reason the cut is stated on the page.

Fasting. Several rites prescribe it. Do not, if you have any condition that makes it unwise, and note that the sources prescribe it for people whose ordinary diet and medical expectations were nothing like yours.

Modern Practice

The honest summary of this chapter is that the barrier to practising almost anything in this book is not equipment. It is the two things the sources ask for that cannot be bought: a time you have decided on in advance, and an hour when you will not be interrupted. Chapter XX is about the first, and no chapter is about the second; though the sources are not quite silent on it: the Key of Solomon asks for a room set apart where you will not be interrupted, and then says no more about how one is to be had.

Practitioners who assemble a full kit before beginning almost always assemble it instead of beginning. The kit above is ten items, most of them already in your kitchen, and a quarter of this book needs none of them.

Sources: This chapter is derived, not sourced: every entry in the table was taken from the text of the rite it names, in the chapter where that rite is printed and under that rite’s own citation. The permissions listed under substitutions are the sources’ own: the Clavicula Salomonis in Mathers’s 1889 translation for parchment and paper, for the vessel of tin or glazed earth, and for the consecration of the instruments. The safety notes are this book’s: they are modern, and they are in no historical text. The sources are uniformly silent about ventilation, and one of them recommends shutting the room up.

Chapter XXIXThe Laboratory Advanced

Chapter 5 stops at the third of John French’s four degrees of fire and says so plainly: everything it gives is done with warm water, a water bath or a sand bath, and everything it refuses is on the far side of the naked fire, where the metals and minerals are. This chapter crosses that line. It is written for a reader with a working laboratory, and it assumes that reader would rather have the real operations, properly hazarded, than a gap.

What follows is history and chemistry together. Each operation is given as its source gives it, then as it would actually be run now, then as what was chemically happening, which is very often the most interesting part, because it explains why intelligent, careful people concluded they had witnessed a transmutation. They had witnessed something. It was not nothing.

Read this section before any other in the chapter

The operations below injured the people who invented them. That is not a figure of speech and it is not a moral: it is the documented occupational history of the trade, and it is set out at the end of this chapter. The controls that make these operations survivable did not exist until the twentieth century. You have them. Use them.

The four things that actually cause harm here:

  • Metal fume and dust. Antimony trioxide and lead oxide are produced as fine fume the moment these charges are hot and open to air. Both are inhalation hazards; antimony trioxide is classed as a suspected human carcinogen. Fume does not smell and does not warn you. The corrosive sublimate belongs under this head too and is the worst of the three: a metal dust that is acutely lethal rather than slowly cumulative, produced by an operation that ends with opening a vessel coated in it.
  • Mercury vapour. Mercury evaporates appreciably at room temperature and copiously when warmed. It is a cumulative neurotoxin, it is absorbed efficiently through the lungs, and a spill in a warm room is a chronic exposure that persists for months in floor cracks.
  • Corrosive and oxidising acids. Nitric acid distillation liberates nitrogen dioxide, which is the classic delayed-onset lung injury: you feel fine, and hours later you do not. Aqua regia is worse and cannot be stored.
  • Deflagration. Several historical charges are nitre-based. A mixture of saltpetre with a sulphide and an organic reducing agent is, chemically, a low-order pyrotechnic composition. Some of these procedures do not melt quietly. They go off.

The controls, none of which are optional: a fume hood with verified face velocity, or genuine outdoor work with the wind at your back and nobody downwind. Nitrile under leather for hot work, splash goggles and a face shield for acids, and a lab coat that stays in the lab. A mercury spill kit within reach before mercury is opened, never a domestic vacuum cleaner. Proper waste routes for heavy-metal residues, which are regulated waste and not drain waste. No food, no drink, no phone in the room. Never alone.

One thing this book does not give you. The fulminates are primary explosives. They detonate on friction and impact rather than burning, they are what an initiator is made of, and they are not alchemy at all: mercury fulminate was first prepared by Edward Howard in 1800, long after every source in this book. It is excluded because it does not belong here and not because the chemistry is secret. Everything that is alchemy is below, including the poisons.

Calcination and roasting

The first operation of the tradition and the simplest to state: heat a substance in air until it changes. Applied to a metal it produces the calx, the powdery oxide, and the observation that a calx weighs more than the metal that made it is one of the loose threads that eventually unravels the whole theory. The alchemists recorded the gain and could not explain it. Oxygen explains it.

Applied to stibnite (antimony trisulphide, the grey striated ore that is the raw material of every antimony operation) roasting in air drives off sulphur as sulphur dioxide and leaves antimony trioxide.

Roasting stibnite to the white oxide

Hazard first. Both products are the hazard. Sulphur dioxide is an acute respiratory irritant. Antimony trioxide is a fine white fume, a suspected carcinogen, and the reason this is a fume-hood or genuinely-outdoors operation and nothing else.

Procedure. Grind the ore coarsely. Spread it thin in a shallow refractory dish: thin matters, because a deep bed sinters and stops reacting. Bring it to a dull red under a fume hood with the sash low, and rake it occasionally to turn fresh surface up. Sulphur dioxide comes off first and is obvious. The charge lightens toward grey, then toward white as the trioxide forms. Do not chase the last of it: overheating volatilises the trioxide, which then condenses everywhere in your hood as the fine dust you least want.

What is happening. Sb2S3 + O2 gives Sb2O3 + SO2. The white powder the texts call the calx or flowers of antimony is the oxide, and the sublimate that forms on cool surfaces above the charge is the same thing recondensed, which is why flowers is a good name for it.

The regulus of antimony, and its star

This is the central operation of early modern chemistry and the one that most persuaded people that metals could be made. Basil Valentine gives it in three lines:

Take equal parts of best Hungarian Antimony and crude tartar, and half the quantity of saltpetre; pound together, melt over wind fire, pour into copper dish, allow to cool, and you will find the Regulus. The Regulus is thrice, or oftener, purified with tartar and saltpetre till it becomes of a brilliant silvery white.

What that recipe actually is

Read the charge as a chemist rather than as a reader of alchemy. Saltpetre is an oxidiser. Tartar is an organic fuel. Antimony sulphide is a sulphide. Potassium nitrate, carbon and sulphur, in one pot, in a hot dish. That is a description of a deflagrating mixture, and the historical accounts of this operation are full of it going off, throwing the charge, and burning operators.

It does work, and it worked for four centuries. But it is the single most energetic thing in this chapter, and if you run it you run it in small charges, behind a shield, in a heavy crucible with room to spare, outdoors or in a hood with the sash between you and it, with nothing flammable in the vicinity and a route away from the bench. Never scale it up because a small one went well. The iron-reduction route below does the same job without the oxidiser and is what a modern reconstruction should use unless the nitre route is specifically the object of study.

And that recommendation turns out to have a precedent of three hundred and forty years. Theodore Kerckring, whose commentary accompanies the text above, appends a footnote to this very charge telling the reader to use salt of tartar in place of crude tartar and adding that “the sal nitri is useless in this operation.” He gives no reason and says nothing about the charge going off; he is correcting a recipe, not warning anybody. But the commentator printed on the same page as the recipe had already reached the conclusion this chapter reaches, that the oxidiser earns nothing, and the recipe went on being copied with the saltpetre in it anyway.

The regulus by iron reduction, the controlled route

Hazard. Antimony fume; a melt near 700 °C; a crucible that will destroy anything it is dropped on. Fume hood, face shield, leather over nitrile, dry tools: any moisture in a tool put into a melt throws the melt.

Charge. Stibnite with iron (clean iron filings or cut nails, roughly a third the mass of the ore) and a flux of sodium carbonate with a little sodium sulphate.

Procedure. Preheat a clay-graphite crucible empty; a cold crucible charged and heated hard will spall. Charge it no more than two-thirds full and bring it to a full melt, dull orange and quiet. Hold it there until the surface is still and mirror-like rather than boiling; this is the part everyone rushes and should not. Pour into a preheated iron mould, greased and truly dry, and let it cool undisturbed.

You will find two layers, cleanly separated: a brittle grey-white button of metal beneath, and a dark glassy slag above that lifts off. That button is the regulus, and it is antimony metal.

What is happening. Iron has the greater affinity for sulphur; it takes it, forming iron sulphide which goes into the slag, and the antimony is left as metal and sinks. The alchemists described this as the iron seizing the sulphur, and about the mechanism they were not wrong: only about what it meant.

The star. Cooled slowly and under the right conditions, the surface of the button crystallises in a radiating pattern that looks unmistakably like a star. This is the famous star regulus or regulus stellatus, and it was taken as a sign that the operation had succeeded and that the antimony had drawn down a celestial influence, the star of the metal made visible. It is dendritic crystallisation, and it depends on purity and cooling rate. Knowing that does not make it less impressive to see, and it explains why a careful person looking at it in 1650 concluded what they concluded.

Cupellation: the assay that actually works

If any operation in this literature deserves to be called a genuine analytical technique, it is this one. It is old, it is exact, it is still done, and Agricola describes it in 1556 in terms a modern assayer would recognise. It is also the origin of a good deal of transmutation belief, for a reason that becomes obvious once you see it.

Cupellation

Hazard. Lead. The whole operation is a hot open lead melt producing lead oxide fume, which is a cumulative neurotoxin and by far the most under-respected hazard in this chapter because it is so undramatic. Hood, always. Litharge-soaked cupels and the spent lead are regulated waste. Wash before you touch anything.

The cupel. A shallow porous dish of bone ash, pressed damp and thoroughly dried. Bone ash is not decorative: it is calcium phosphate, and its porosity and its chemistry are what make the operation work.

Procedure. Bring the cupel to a bright heat in a muffle and let it come to temperature: a cold cupel cracks and takes your assay with it. Add the lead button containing the sample and let it melt and drive, which is the assayer’s word for the moment the surface goes bright and mobile and begins to fume. Hold it there with air reaching the surface. The melt shrinks steadily. Toward the end the button becomes a small bright bead which suddenly flashes brilliantly and goes still: the brightening or fulguration, the moment the last of the lead leaves.

What is happening. The lead oxidises to litharge; the litharge dissolves the oxides of the base metals, copper and iron and the rest; and the whole of it soaks into the porous bone ash, which does not absorb gold or silver. What is left standing on the cupel is the noble metal that was in the sample, and nothing else.

Why it convinced people. Watch that without knowing the chemistry. A large dull button of lead is put in. It smokes, shrinks, and vanishes into the dish. Left behind, sitting alone and unmistakable, is a bead of bright silver or gold that was not visible before. Every appearance is of a base metal being consumed and a noble metal being born. It is in fact a separation, not a creation; but the person who insisted otherwise was not being stupid, and could point at the bead.

The mineral acids

The isolation of the strong acids somewhere around the thirteenth century is the single most consequential thing this tradition did. Nothing else it produced changed the world remotely as much. They dissolve what nothing else dissolves, and the whole later chemistry of separation depends on them.

Agricola gives the charges for aqua valens (the strong water, nitric acid) plainly enough. One of his is three parts vitriol to one of saltpetre with asbestos and baked brick; another is saltpetre with alum and sal ammoniac. He then describes the furnace: brick, about two feet square, plated over with iron, with a hole in the top for the earthen vessel that holds the glass ampulla, and air holes beside it.

Distilling the strong water

Hazard, and this one is different in kind. The gas that comes off is nitrogen dioxide, red-brown, and it is a delayed lung injury: exposure can feel minor and develop into pulmonary oedema many hours later. There is no version of this that is safe outside a working fume hood, and anyone who has taken a real breath of it needs medical attention even if they feel well. Nitric acid also attacks skin instantly and stains it yellow, which is your protein.

Procedure, in modern glass. Charge a retort or a distillation flask with the nitrate and the sulphuric acid; this is the modern equivalent of vitriol and saltpetre, and it is the same reaction. Ground-glass joints, no grease that the acid will attack, and a receiver cooled in ice. Heat gently in a sand bath or mantle. The acid distils over; the red fume in the neck is the nitrogen dioxide and tells you it is running. Take it slowly. Stop before the flask goes dry.

Aqua regia is made by combining the strong water with spirit of salt: nitric with hydrochloric, classically one part to three. It dissolves gold, which nothing else in the historical laboratory would do, and the alchemists named it royal water for exactly that reason. Make it in the quantity you are about to use and no more. It decomposes as it stands, it evolves gas, and a stoppered bottle of aqua regia left on a shelf is a bottle that will eventually burst.

Amalgamation

Mercury dissolves gold and silver at room temperature into a soft amalgam, and the amalgam gives the metal back when heated. That single property made mercury the most important reagent in the tradition, and it is also the property that has poisoned more people than everything else in this chapter combined.

Before you open mercury

This is the operation on which this book is least relaxed, and the reason is not historical. Gold amalgamation is currently the largest source of mercury pollution on earth and the direct cause of chronic mercury poisoning in artisanal mining communities today. The mechanism is precisely the step below: heating the amalgam in the open to drive off the mercury, and breathing what comes off.

Mercury vapour is invisible, odourless, and neurotoxic; a droplet lost in a floor seam evaporates for months. If mercury is opened at all it is opened in a hood, over a tray that will catch a spill, with a spill kit already open, never over a drain, never near a warm surface, and never in a room anyone sleeps in. The mercury is never driven off in the open. It is done in a closed retort that condenses and recovers it, which is both the safe way and, as it happens, exactly what the better historical sources already tell you to do.

Amalgamation and recovery, in a closed retort

Procedure. Bring finely divided gold into contact with clean mercury and work them together until the gold is taken up; the amalgam is a soft grey paste. Press the excess mercury out through fine leather or a close-woven cloth, which is the historical method and still a good one; what remains is a stiff amalgam holding perhaps two parts gold to one of mercury.

Charge that into an iron retort with its neck led into a water-cooled condenser discharging under water. Heat the body of the retort. The mercury distils off, condenses, and is recovered under the water; the gold stays behind as a porous sponge. Let the whole apparatus cool before opening it, and open it in the hood.

What is happening, and what is not. No transmutation and no compound: an amalgam is a solution of a metal in mercury, and the operation is dissolution and recovery. But watch it from outside. Gold vanishes into a silver liquid and is gone. Heat is applied, the liquid departs, and the gold reappears. A substance is destroyed and restored, which is solve et coagula performed in front of you in an afternoon, and it is not hard to see why mercury got the philosophical career it did.

Sublimation, and the corrosive sublimate

Sublimation, a solid vaporised and recondensed without ever being liquid, is one of the tradition’s favourite operations, because it looks like purification made visible: the substance leaves its dross behind and re-forms above, glittering, in needles. Sal ammoniac sublimes beautifully and harmlessly and is the one to learn on.

The important sublimate of the corpus, though, is mercurius sublimatus corrosivus: corrosive sublimate, mercuric chloride. It appears constantly from the Arabic writers onward, it is a reagent in a great many operations, and it is one of the most lethal substances handled routinely in a historical laboratory.

What this substance is

Mercuric chloride is acutely and severely toxic by ingestion, by inhalation of its dust, and through the skin. A gram is around a lethal dose for an adult. It was for centuries the standard agent of both suicide and homicide in Europe, and it remains the reason old chemistry cupboards are treated as hazardous sites. It is also, in many jurisdictions, subject to poisons regulation; check what applies where you are before acquiring or preparing it.

It is described here because it is genuinely and unavoidably part of the subject, the texts are full of it, and because the chemistry has been in every history of chemistry for two hundred years. Handle it, if at all, as an experienced worker handles a serious poison: weighed in a hood, on a tared paper, never as loose dust, with dedicated glassware that does not return to general use.

The chemistry, in outline, is a partner-exchange followed by a separation by volatility: a mercury salt and common salt are heated together, and the mercuric chloride leaves as vapour where the by-product does not, recondensing cool as a hard translucent crust. It is an elegant piece of work and the alchemists arrived at it by experiment.

The clearest account this edition could reach is Nicolas Lémery’s. His Cours de chymie of 1675 was reprinted for decades: the London printing of 1720 calls itself on its title page “The Fourth Edition” and “Translated from the Eleventh Edition in the French, which has been revised, corrected, and much enlarged beyond any of the former.” Walter Harris put it into English as A Course of Chymistry in 1677. Lémery gives the preparation in Chapter VIII, Of Mercury, under the head Sublimate Corrosive, and gives it in four movements: dissolve the mercury in spirit of nitre; evaporate that solution down to a white mass; grind the mass together with calcined vitriol and decrepitated salt; sublime the mixture in a long-necked flask.

Put a pound of Mercury revived from Cinnabar into a Matrass, pour upon it Eighteen or Twenty ounces of Spirit of Niter: Set your Matrass upon Sand a little warm, and leave it there until it be all dissolved; pour your dissolution, which will be clear as water, into a glass-vessel or earthen pot, and evaporate the Liquor gently over a Sand-fire, until there remains a white Mass, which you must powder in a glass mortar, and mix with a pound of Vitriol Calcined white, and so much Salt decrepitated: put this mixture into a Matrass, whose two thirds at least remain empty, place your Matrass on Sand, and begin with giving a small fire, which you must continue so for three hours, then encrease it with coals to a pretty good violence, there will arise a Sublimate to the top of the Matrass; the Operation must be ended in six or seven hours, let the Matrass cool, then break it, avoiding a kind of Farine, or light powder that flies up into the air when the matter is stirred…

Harris’s English of 1677, p. 93, read from the Wellcome copy. The text layer reads every long s as an f, and it is set here as s; the scan’s broken word-spacing is closed up; encrease is his spelling and stands. Five readings are repaired, and are declared here rather than passed off as the scan’s. The italic fount defeats the capital M, so the text layer gives Aercury and AZercury throughout for Mercury: the chapter is headed Of Mercury in roman and comes through clean, which settles it. Then (inna bar for Cinnabar; 4 slafs-veffel for a glass-vessel; mortat for mortar; and Farine-or for Farine, or. Those four are legible in the English edition of 1686, which was consulted to settle characters and supplied no wording. The ellipsis is a refusal and not a trim. Lémery closes the paragraph by stating the yield, and both editions are corrupt at exactly that point, 1677 reads you’l. have a pound aa very good Sublimate Corrofive, so the figure is not printed here. He ends by directing that the red scoriae at the bottom be thrown away as useless. The two short quotations in the paragraph below are from p. 95 of the same edition and are set the same way; the second of them also heals a line break, the scan reading very inconve-nient and unwholfom.

Read the last clause of that quotation again, because it is the nearest thing in this chapter to a historical source protecting its reader. There is one other, named here so that the claim stays honest: Kerckring warns twice, in so many words, about vessels bursting; he sets out an apparatus “in order to avoid bursting your vessels, during the distillation of the spirits of metals,” and cautions that too much mercury poured in at once “may burst and overturn the retort and the furnace as well.” Both are mechanical hazards, and both are about protecting the operation as much as the operator. Nobody in this literature writes about what the operation does to the body of the person running it, which is the distinction that matters. Lémery tells you to avoid the farine (the flour, the light powder) that flies up when the cold flask is broken open, and he is right: that is the single most dangerous moment of the operation. But he does not connect the dust to the poison he says two pages later will kill a man taken inwardly “in a very little time,” and of the dry route he rejects he says only that it raises a dust to the nose that is “very inconvenient and unwholsom.” A nuisance, in his account, rather than the thing itself made airborne.

The corrosive sublimate, how it would be run now

Hazard, before anything else. This is the most acutely poisonous product in the chapter, and the procedure stacks three separate hazards on one bench. Dissolving mercury in nitric acid evolves nitrogen dioxide in quantity, Lémery’s red clouds, which is the delayed lung injury set out under the strong waters above; it is evolved from an open flask of warm mercury, so mercury vapour is coming off the same flask at the same time. The product is mercuric chloride, of which about a gram is a lethal dose and which is taken up through skin, and the operation finishes by breaking a vessel whose entire inner surface is coated in it as a friable crust. All of this is fume-hood work with the sash low. The last part is fume-hood work with the sash low and a respirator you have been fit-tested for.

The controlled route. The nitric stage exists only to get the mercury into a salt that will exchange partners in the heat, and it can be dropped. Mercuric sulphate ground with dry sodium chloride sublimes to mercuric chloride directly: the same reaction with the worst stage of the preparation removed, and the route to use unless Lémery’s own procedure is specifically the object of study. Sublime in an all-glass apparatus, cooled above, that can be opened wet: flood the condensed crust and take it into solution rather than scraping it dry, which is the whole of what Lémery could not do, because his sublimation vessel had to be broken to be emptied. And if the compound rather than the operation is what is wanted, do not sublime at all: mercuric oxide dissolves in hydrochloric acid, and the chloride crystallises out of the cooling solution in the same white needles, with no dust stage anywhere in it.

Waste. Every residue here is a mercury residue: the wash water, the spent glassware, and the red scoriae Lémery tells you to throw away. None of it is drain waste. Dedicated glassware that does not return to general use; the bench wiped down afterwards and the wipes bagged with the rest.

What is happening. Nitric acid takes the mercury up as mercuric nitrate, and that is the white mass left behind when the solution is evaporated. Vitriol calcined white is green vitriol, iron sulphate, dried by heat until it loses its colour; that it is the iron vitriol and not the copper or the zinc one is confirmed by the residue, because iron oxide is what makes the scoriae at the bottom of the flask red. In the fire the sulphate passes to the mercury. The mercuric sulphate so formed exchanges partners with the common salt: sodium takes the sulphate, mercury takes the chloride, and of the two products only mercuric chloride is volatile at that temperature. It leaves the mass, travels up the cold neck, and recondenses there as the crust. The separation is by volatility and by nothing else, and the reason the product comes out pure is that nothing else in the pot will follow it.

The 1686 edition is not a reprint, and two of its changes are worth having. The first is a correction, and Lémery leads his remarks with it: a pound of mercury does not need anything like the spirit of nitre he had allowed it, and less than half will do. The recipe above is the earlier and wasteful one, and he found that out by running it. The second is an argument. Readers had objected that a sublimate made with spirit of nitre was unfit for making mercurius dulcis, the calomel that went into patients, because the nitre would leave its saline and sulphureous parts behind in the product. Lémery answers from the bench rather than from doctrine: red vapours pour out through the neck of the flask for three hours at the least, those vapours can be nothing but the spirits of nitre, and a fire that small cannot raise the spirits of salt and vitriol to follow them. The volatile thing leaves first, and by the end of the operation it has left. He is right, and the form of the argument, an observation of the process answering an objection from theory, is why this book takes him as the clearest account it could reach. Nothing is quoted from the 1686 here. The phrase this paragraph most wanted, the objectors’ saline sulphureous parts, is corrupt in the scan at both of the places it occurs, and the argument is therefore given in this book’s words from a reading of it.

What this book advises, having given the operation. Buy it. Mercuric chloride is a stocked laboratory reagent; it is subject to poisons regulation in many jurisdictions, and that paperwork is itself part of the control; and nothing in this chapter needs it made rather than bought. The preparation is set out because it is a real and central operation of the corpus and a book that gives the regulus and the strong waters and then goes quiet here is not being careful, it is being squeamish about one thing and not another. It is also the one operation in this chapter where the historical route and the modern one part company so far that the honest modern route is not to run it.

What the sublimate is for in the corpus matters regardless. It is a chloride donor and a powerful oxidant, and it is the route by which mercury enters dozens of other preparations: including the various mercurius vitae and mercurius dulcis of the medical writers, the latter being the calomel that European medicine then administered to patients for three centuries with results that do not bear thinking about.

What it did to them

The occupational toll of this work is documented, and it belongs in the chapter rather than in a footnote, because it is the strongest argument for the controls at the top of it.

Paracelsus wrote what is generally reckoned the first monograph on occupational disease, on the illnesses of miners and smelter workers: Von der Bergsucht, the mountain sickness. He was describing the people who prepared the materials this chapter uses, and he was describing metal poisoning, from the inside of the trade, in the sixteenth century. The knowledge was available. What was not available was any means of avoiding it.

Isaac Newton spent decades at this bench, and the analyses performed on surviving samples of his hair have been widely reported as showing greatly elevated mercury. His biographers have connected that to the episode of insomnia, paranoia and derangement he suffered in 1693 and recovered from. Causation is not established and this book does not assert it. What is certain is that a man of extraordinary carefulness worked mercury for years in a small room and that his hair carried the record.

Set that beside the tradition’s own language and something uncomfortable comes into focus. The literature is full of warnings that the work destroys the unworthy, ruins the greedy, drives men mad. This book has generally read that as moral instruction dressed as chemistry. Allow that some of it was straightforwardly a description of what was happening in the room.

Modern Practice

Historical chemistry is a live and respectable field, and reconstruction is how a good deal of it is now done: the operations are run, the products characterised, and the texts read against what actually comes out of the crucible. That work has repeatedly shown the sources to be more competent and more literal than a century of commentary assumed. Recipes that read like nonsense turn out to describe real products, once you know that Hungarian antimony means a particular ore and crude tartar a particular grade of potassium bitartrate.

If you are going to do this, do it that way: run the operation, keep a real notebook, weigh everything, and record what actually happened rather than what the text said would. That is what the better alchemists were already doing, and it is the part of their practice worth inheriting.

Sources: Agricola, De re metallica (1556), in the Hoovers’ English of 1912, for the cupel of bone ash, the conduct of the assay, the charges for aqua valens and the furnace built to hold the glass ampulla, all in Books VII and X. John French, The Art of Distillation (1653), for the degrees of fire, cited in full in Chapter 5. Paracelsus’s Von der Bergsucht is named for what it is and is not quoted; no edition was consulted.

Basil Valentine, The Triumphal Chariot of Antimony, with Kerckringius’s commentary (1893), for the regulus charge quoted above at p. 142, verified against the page; Kerckring’s note on the sal nitri is the footnote to that page, and his two warnings about bursting vessels are the footnotes to pp. 136 and 137. Three things about this volume are worth stating, because the chapter leans on it. Its title page describes it as “being the Latin version published at Amsterdam in the year 1685 translated into English,” so what is printed above is English out of Kerckring’s Latin and not out of whatever German stands behind Valentine: a translation of a translation, and the wording quoted is the 1893 translator’s. That translator is not named on the title page; catalogue records give Waite, and the publisher is the house that issued his Hermetic Museum in the same year, which is suggestive and is not proof. This edition does not treat the attribution as settled. And “Basil Valentine” is a persona rather than a documented person; the authorship question is real, this book did not investigate it, and no position is taken here.

Lémery, Cours de chymie (1675), in Walter Harris’s English of 1677, for the corrosive sublimate in the First Part, Of Minerals, ch. VIII, Of Mercury, pp. 93–96: the long quotation above from p. 93 and the two short ones from p. 95, read from the Wellcome copy b3033696x, with characters checked against the English edition of 1686, Wellcome b30326618, which supplied no wording. The five readings repaired in the long quotation, and the normalisations applied to all three, are declared beneath it. The edition statement quoted above is from the title page of the London printing of 1720, read from the Eighteenth Century Collections scan bim_eighteenth-century_cours-de-chymie-englis_lemery-nicolas_1720; that page sets the long s properly and needs no repair, though a stray point after in the is dropped. The booksellers named in its imprint are not given here because two of their initials are damaged in the scan and expanding them would be a guess.

The hazard assessments, the control measures and all the modern procedural detail are this book’s own and are not in any historical source. No text in this chapter warns its reader about metal fume, mercury vapour, delayed lung injury or cumulative neurotoxicity, because none of that was known. One partial exception goes on record, since it is the only one: Lémery tells his reader to avoid the light powder that flies up when the sublimation flask is broken open, and says of the dry route he rejects that it raises an unwholesome dust. He had noticed the dust. He frames it as a nuisance rather than as the poison he elsewhere states the substance to be, and about the vapour he says nothing at all. Where a historical method and a safer modern one differ, both are given and the difference is stated.

Sources & Bibliography Reference

The principal sources of this grimoire are listed below by period, with dates, authors or translators where known, and copyright status where it affects availability. It is not exhaustive, and it is not the only apparatus. Each chapter carries its own sources line, and the two divide the work between them: the chapter note says what was read, on which page or leaf, in which scan, and what was repaired or left out; this list gives the edition it was read in, with place, printer and copyright status. A note that names a work in short form is pointing here for the rest. For several texts printed verbatim (Goodwin’s papyri, Budge’s rubrics, Grendon’s charms, Culpeper, French) the full citation lives in the note rather than here. Entries are grouped by period so that the shape of the tradition’s actual chronology is visible at a glance, which is, in itself, the argument of this book.

On what “verified” means here

Each entry below was checked for author, date and status before being included. That checking was done at two different depths, and the difference should be stated. A first pass used reference scholarship and encyclopedic sources. A second pass went to primary materials (the 1849 Rheinwald edition of Andreae’s Vita, Waite’s 1887 and 1924 volumes in full text, Yates, Chapel’s 2013 article) for the claims this book’s argument actually rests on: the Kybalion attribution, the dating of the Hermetica, Casaubon’s redating, Andreae’s ludibrium, Edighoffer on the Brotherhood, and the provenance of the Papyri. Entries touched only by the first pass are therefore less securely verified than those touched by the second.

Four further rules follow from that checking, and each guards against a failure this kind of book is prone to. A paraphrase acquires false authority the moment it is given quotation marks and a name, so no sentence is printed as a scholar’s words unless it was read in that scholar’s text. A text printed verbatim is set from the edition its citation names (never from a secondary copy, however close) and where a second scan was used to settle characters, the sources line says so. And correction has failure modes of its own (a lexicon cited for a sense it does not carry, a causal chain no scholar asserts, a hedge hardened into a flat denial) so repairs were held to the same standard of verification as the claims they replaced. And this book does not print quotations it has only read through corrupt OCR: where a scan’s text layer is unusable, the leaf is read by eye on the page images (as it was for Agrippa, for Trithemius and for Court de Gébelin) or the passage stays unprinted.

Where the record is genuinely unsettled (who assembled the Lesser Banishing Ritual and when, the precise origin of individual Golden Dawn exercises, the relative priority of the Greek and Latin Solomonic texts, the ownership of the Theban Magical Library, the meaning of ludibrium) the relevant chapter reports the dispute rather than choosing a convenient answer. Claims in the body text that carry no citation are ones where a specific attribution could not be verified; they are written as general statements for that reason. A bibliography’s usefulness depends entirely on the reader being able to trust that nothing was added to make it look longer.

Ancient: the primary material (c. 100 BCE – c. 400 CE)

  • Corpus Hermeticum: seventeen Greek treatises, composed c. 100–300 CE. The collection’s date and compiler are unknown; first attested in Byzantium in Michael Psellos (c. 1017–1078), with surviving manuscripts late medieval and later.
  • Nag Hammadi Hermetica (three tractates in Codex VI: The Discourse on the Eighth and Ninth (VI,6), the Prayer of Thanksgiving (VI,7) with its Scribal Note (VI,7a), and Asclepius 21–29 (VI,8)) a single continuous excerpt, not scattered fragments. The Coptic is ancient, but there is no public-domain edition or translation of it: the codices were found in 1945 and first published in the 1970s. The Prayer of Thanksgiving is nonetheless printed in Chapter 2, because its parallel Latin text, Asclepius 41, exists in Mead’s 1906 translation, which is out of copyright.
  • Asclepius: surviving mainly in Latin translation, with Greek and Coptic fragments.
  • Papyri Graecae Magicae (PGM): extant texts from the late 4th c. BCE (PGM XL, the curse of Artemisia, an isolated outlier) and 1st c. BCE down to the 5th c. CE, Christian magical texts into the 6th; the bulk 3rd–5th c. CE. In Greek, Demotic and Old Coptic. Provenance largely the Theban material assembled by Jean d’Anastasi (vice-consul and from 1828 Consul-General of Sweden and Norway at Alexandria) acquired through agents before 1828 and dispersed to Leiden (Dutch government purchase, 1828), the British Museum, the Louvre, the Bibliothèque Nationale and Berlin. Ownership of the “Theban Magical Library” is disputed; Betz’s single-collector suggestion is hedged, and Dosoo argues for multiple collectors.
  • Leyden papyrus X (P. Leid. I 397) and the Stockholm papyrus (P. Holm., Kungliga Biblioteket): alchemical texts of the 4th c. CE from the same reconstructed Theban group, in the same hand or very nearly as PGM XIII. Not to be confused with Leiden W (P. Leid. I 395), which is PGM XIII itself.
