Both are edited in Berthelot and Ruelle, Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs (Paris: Steinheil, 1887–88). edition public domain
  • Defixiones (curse and binding tablets): the earliest from the late 6th and early 5th centuries BCE, the oldest of them Sicilian; recovered from Sicily, Athens, Asia Minor, Rome and Egypt, over a thousand texts in all. Jessica L. Lamont, Greece & Rome 69, no. 1 (2022), 27–51, for the dating. Audollent, Defixionum tabellae (1904), remains the standard corpus. edition public domain
  • Apuleius of Madaura (b. c. 125 CE), Metamorphoses (the Golden Ass), Book XI: the only first-person account of a mystery initiation surviving from antiquity, and a novel, which is why Chapter 19 uses it for the shape of the thing and not for the facts of the rite. Quoted from the translation of H. E. Butler, 2 vols. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1910), read on the page images of the Internet Archive scan metamorphosesorg02apuluoft. Apuleius’s own defence against a charge of magic, the Apologia, survives beside it. translation public domain
  • Testament of Solomon: Greek pseudepigraphon; the core placed around the first century CE by F. C. Conybeare, “The Testament of Solomon,” The Jewish Quarterly Review 11 (October 1898), 1–45, whose English is quoted in Chapter 11. The dating literature since ranges from the first to the third century; the frame is Jewish, the transmission Christian. public domain
  • Zosimos of Panopolis (fl. c. 300 CE): the earliest alchemical writer whose substantial corpus survives under his own name; the source for the colour stages and for Mary the Jewess.
  • Pseudo-Democritus, Physika kai mystika: often described as among the oldest surviving alchemical writings. Ancient testimony names four books under the name, on gold, silver, stones and purple. Whether the Greek stage-names melanosis, leukosis, xanthosis and iosis all occur in it was not checked for this edition against Matteo Martelli, The Four Books of Pseudo-Democritus (2013), which could not be obtained. Liddell–Scott’s citations for iosis are the Leiden magical papyrus, Olympiodorus and Zosimos, not Democritus.
  • Mary the Jewess (Maria Hebraea), Greco-Roman Egypt, most likely between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE (the specialist literature declines to name a city (some scholars: no later than the 1st)) credited via Zosimos with the tribikos, the kerotakis and the bain-marie; the Axiom of Maria. Named among the alchemists listed in Ibn al-Nadīm, Kitāb al-Fihrist (10th c.): the figure of fifty-two that popular accounts give was not checked against Dodge’s translation for this edition. The claim in George Syncellus (active c. 800; the Chronography c. 808–810) that she was among the initiators of Democritus is chronologically impossible.

Medieval and Arabic (8th – 15th centuries)

  • Kitāb Sirr al-Khalīqa wa-Ṣanʿat al-Ṭabīʿa (Book of the Secret of Creation and the Art of Nature): compiled in Arabic in the late 8th or early 9th century; contains the oldest known recension of the Emerald Tablet. Dating contested: Ruska (1926) 6th–8th c.; Kraus (1942–43) c. 813–833; Weisser (1980) c. 750–800. Presents itself as a translation of a treatise by Apollonius of Tyana (Balīnūs).
  • Pseudo-Jābir ibn Ḥayyān, Kitāb Usṭuqus al-Uss al-Thānī (Second Book of the Element of the Foundation): a shorter version of the Tablet: nine lines against the Sirr al-khalīqa’s fifteen, with lines 6, 8 and 11–15 absent and other parts corrupt. Published and analysed in Holmyard, “The Emerald Table,” Nature 112 (1923), 525–26, and Ruska (1926), p. 121, who takes this version to be dependent on the Sirr al-khalīqa rather than earlier than it.
  • Ibn Umayl (Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Umayl al-Tamīmī, c. 900–960; Latin “Senior Zadith filius Hamuel”), Book of the Silvery Water and the Starry Earth: c. 10th century; later translated into Latin as the Tabula Chemica. Quotes the Tablet and glosses it clause by clause (Stapleton, Lewis and Sherwood Taylor, Ambix 3 (1949), 69–90, sect. XXI at p. 81). Its own frame story (a seated figure in a birbā, rendered “the Pyramid” in Stapleton’s translation, holding a stone slab) concerns a different object; the Tablet text appears separately later in the treatise. He is not the source of the discovery narrative, which belongs to the Sirr al-khalīqa.
  • Pseudo-Aristotle, Sirr al-Asrār (Secretum Secretorum, Secret of Secrets): 10th century; the long version carries the Tablet toward its end. Latin text in Steele (ed.), Secretum secretorum cum glossis et notulis (Oxford, 1920), pp. 115–17, where it is described as appearing “in its earliest known form.”
  • Jābir ibn Ḥayyān; Abū Bakr al-Rāzī: the Arabic-Islamic alchemical tradition through which much of this material reached Latin Europe. Note that al-Rāzī wrote his own Kitāb Sirr al-asrār, which is a different work from the pseudo-Aristotelian Sirr al-Asrār above.
  • Latin transmission of the Emerald Tablet: Robert of Chester (1144), Book on the Composition of Alchemy: generally considered the first Latin translation of an Arabic alchemical treatise, though the attribution to Robert rests only on a prologue that Marion Dapsens, Studia graeco-arabica 6 (2016), 121–40, concludes is genuinely his yet probably not written for this text; the vulgate version, probably 12th century, tentatively attributed to Plato of Tivoli (active c. 1134–45), surviving embedded in an anonymous Latin compilation of commentaries on the Tablet and itself the most circulated version and the basis of all later editions; Hugo of Santalla (c. 1145–51), from the Secret of Creation itself, surviving in a single contemporary manuscript (Paris, BnF lat. 13951) and one copy; Philip of Tripoli (13th c.), via the Secret of Secrets, whose more than six hundred manuscript witnesses (Williams, 2003, p. 349) are what give “by some measures” its content.
  • Commentaries on the Emerald Tablet: Hortulanus (Ortolanus), probably active in the first half of the 14th century: the commentary that circulated most widely in print (1541, 1545, 1560 as the Compendium alchimiae under Johannes de Garlandia’s name, and 1571), reading the text as laboratory recipe; Albertus Magnus, On Minerals, c. 1250; Roger Bacon, c. 1275–80, who believed the Secret of Secrets genuinely Aristotle’s; Johannes Trithemius, early 16th century, who shifted the reading toward the Pythagorean monad and the anima mundi; his letter to Germain de Ganay, printed 1613, is quoted in Chapter 6 from the page images.
  • Ars Notoria: 13th century (Véronèse’s version A); the glossed version at the end of the 13th, surviving in three 14th-century MSS; the core Flores aurei possibly later 12th. Later absorbed as book five of the Lemegeton.
  • Clavicula Salomonis (Key of Solomon): the Latin/Italian Clavicula is now generally placed in the 16th century, possibly the 15th: Mathiesen (2007) argues it was translated in Italy from a Greek original that had reached Italy by the 15th century, and that no Western manuscript is securely earlier than the 16th. The older attribution to the 14th or 15th century derives from A. E. Waite rather than from modern scholarship. Surviving Western MSS are chiefly late 16th–18th century: of 122 recorded by Mathiesen only eight are 16th-century. Notable witnesses: Bodleian MS Michael 276 (Italian; undated by Mathiesen, 17th c. per Peterson) and BL Sloane MS 3847 (English, 1572). Pseudepigraphic.
  • Magical Treatise of Solomon (Apotelesmatikē pragmateia Solomōntos), also circulating as The Little Key of the Whole Art of Hygromancy: known from sixteen or seventeen Greek manuscripts, six of them 15th-century, including BL Harley MS 5596. Priority against the Clavicula is not finally settled, but the specialist literature leans to the Greek as the ancestral form, from which the earliest Western version was almost certainly translated. Armand Delatte transcribed one Athens manuscript in Anecdota Atheniensia (Liège/Paris, 1927), pp. 397–445: not the Harley manuscript. Fuller editions: Pablo A. Torijano, Solomon the Esoteric King (Brill, 2002); Ioannis Marathakis, The Magical Treatise of Solomon or Hygromanteia (Golden Hoard, 2011).
  • Sworn Book of Honorius (Liber Juratus): 14th century, in manuscript; untitled, but understood from its own text to be the sworn book of a Honorius. Not to be confused with the printed Grimoire of Honorius of 1629, which trades on the name; see Chapter 10. Dating and description from Waite (1911), below.

Renaissance and early modern (15th – 17th centuries)

  • Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499): Latin translation of the Corpus Hermeticum (treatises I–XIV), Liber de potestate et sapientia Dei / Pimander, completed 1463 on Cosimo de’ Medici’s order and dedicated to him (d. 1464), from Laurentianus LXXI, 33; first printed at Treviso by Gerardus de Lisa, 18 December 1471, in an edition Ficino neither prepared nor authorised. Lodovico Lazzarelli (1447–1500).
  • Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim (1486–1535), De occulta philosophia libri tres: Book I 1531 (Paris: Christian Wechel; Antwerp: Johannes Grapheus: the Cologne 1531 imprint often listed alongside these is unattested in the catalogues); complete three books [Cologne]: Johannes Soter, July 1533 (VD16 A 1180). English translation by “J.F.” (probably John French), 1651. public domain
  • Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy: earliest imprint Marburg, 1559 (VD16 A 1185), twenty-four years after Agrippa’s death; spurious, denounced as a forgery by Johann Weyer, who had been Agrippa’s own live-in student. The Latin words usually quoted from that denunciation are not quoted here: Weyer’s Latin was not read on page images for this edition, and the phrase could not be found in the 1563 first edition or in the 1660 Opera omnia. public domain
  • George Ripley, Compound of Alchymy (1471): the Twelve Gates. The fourteen stages usually given under the name of Samuel Norton (16th century) are in fact numbered in Mercurius redivivus, ed. Edmund Deane (Frankfurt, 1630), and not in Norton’s Key of Alchemy of 1578; see Chapter 5.
  • De Alchemia, ed. “Chrysogonus Polydorus” (probably a pseudonym for Andreas Osiander), Johann Petreius, Nuremberg, 1541: the editio princeps of the Tablet as a free-standing alchemical text, and the first to print it with Hortulanus’s commentary; a different Latin version was already in print inside the Secretum secretorum by 1501 at the latest (Achillini’s Bologna edition), and possibly in the incunables of the 1480s. public domain
  • John Dee, Monas Hieroglyphica (1564). Dee and Kelley’s Enochian diaries (1580s).
  • Johann Weyer (1515–1588), De praestigiis daemonum (1563, libri V): argued against the witch persecutions and criticised the Malleus Maleficarum. The Pseudomonarchia Daemonum was not in the first edition: it was appended to the fifth (Basel, March 1577) and retained in the sixth (1583), and Weyer edited rather than authored the list. Weyer became a live-in famulus of Agrippa’s at fifteen. The Pseudomonarchia is quoted in Chapter 11 through Scot’s English; its Latin was not read on page images for this edition.
  • Reginald Scot, The discoverie of witchcraft (London, 1584): the most radical English attack on witch-belief of its century, and, in its fifteenth book, the carrier of Weyer’s catalogue into English. Quoted in Chapter 11 from the 1886 reprint of the first edition, read on the page images of the Internet Archive scan discoverieofwitc00scot. public domain
  • King James VI of Scotland, Daemonologie, in forme of a dialogue (Edinburgh, 1597): written expressly against Scot and Weyer, both named in its preface; quoted in Chapter 11 from the page images of the Early English Books scan of the 1597 printing. public domain
  • Malleus Maleficarum (first printed c. 1486): the inquisitors’ handbook; named and described in Chapter 11 and not quoted: the standard English translation of 1928 is in copyright, and no public-domain rendering was consulted for this edition.
  • Paracelsus (1493 or 1494–1541; the birth year is inferred rather than documented): iatrochemistry and the medical application of alchemy. public domain
  • Heinrich Khunrath, Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae: first printing Hamburg, 1595; the familiar Hanau 1609 edition is the second and last, published posthumously (Khunrath d. 1605), edited by Erasmus Wolfart, with nine engraved plates. public domain
  • Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), De rebus sacris et ecclesiasticis exercitationes XVI (London, 1614), written against Baronius’s Annales: argued the Greek Hermetica were composed partly out of Plato and the Platonists and partly out of Christian scripture, in Greek later than that current around the birth of Christ. His own formula is primis illis seculis nascentis Christianismi; he gives no numeric range. public domain
  • Fama Fraternitatis Rosae Crucis: MS circulating c. 1610; published Cassel, 1614. public domain
  • Confessio Fraternitatis: Cassel: Wilhelm Wessel, 1615, appended to Philippus a Gabella, Secretioris Philosophiae Consideratio brevis (reissued 1616). public domain
  • Chymische Hochzeit Christiani Rosencreutz (Chymical Wedding): 1616; acknowledged by Johann Valentin Andreae (1586–1654) in his posthumous autobiography, and described by him as a ludibrium. public domain
  • Johann Valentin Andreae, Vita ab ipso conscripta: unpublished in his lifetime; first printed in German translation by D. C. Seybold, Selbstbiographie Joh. Valentin Andreä’s (Winterthur, 1799), the Latin original ed. F. H. Rheinwald (Berlin, 1849). Lib. I, p. 10 for the ludibrium passage; Lib. II, p. 46 for “that Rosicrucian ludibrium.” public domain
  • Michael Maier (1568?–1622; VD17 and GND give 1569), Atalanta fugiens (Oppenheim: Hieronymus Galler for Johann Theodor de Bry, 1617, plates engraved by Matthäus Merian the Elder; a further Oppenheim printing followed in 1618, neither title page carrying an edition statement); Silentium Post Clamores (Frankfurt am Main: Lucas Jennis, 1617, with a German translation the same year). Robert Fludd (1574–1637); Elias Ashmole (1617–1692). public domain
  • Lemegeton (Lesser Key of Solomon): compiled mid-17th century from older materials; five books: Ars Goetia, Ars Theurgia Goetia, Ars Paulina, Ars Almadel, Ars Notoria.
  • William Lilly, Christian Astrology, modestly treated of in three Books (London, 1647): the first substantial treatment of the art in English: chart erection, horary and nativities. Used in Chapter 21, from the Wellcome copy. public domain
  • Meric Casaubon (ed.), A True & Faithful Relation of What passed for many Yeers Between Dr. John Dee… and Some Spirits (London: D. Maxwell for T. Garthwait, 1659): the first printing of Dee’s angelic diaries, issued with a preface holding the spirits real and evil; the editor is the son of the Isaac Casaubon of 1614, above. Used in Chapter 14. public domain
  • Christian Knorr von Rosenroth, Kabbala Denudata (Sulzbach and Frankfurt, 1677–84): the Latin anthology through which the Zohar reached Christian Europe, including the Idra Rabba and Idra Suta in its second volume. Named in Chapter 4 on the authority of Ginsburg and Mathers; not consulted for this book.
  • Georgius Agricola (Georg Bauer, 1494–1555), De re metallica (Basel, 1556), published the year after his death: the standard description of sixteenth-century mining and assaying, and the source in Chapter 29 for cupellation, for the charges for aqua valens and for the furnace built to hold the glass ampulla. Quoted here in the translation of Herbert Clark Hoover and Lou Henry Hoover (London: The Mining Magazine, 1912): the work of a mining engineer who later became President of the United States, and of his wife, who was a geologist. public domain
  • “Basil Valentine” (Basilius Valentinus), The Triumphal Chariot of Antimony, with the commentary of Theodore Kerckringius: a persona presented as a fifteenth-century Benedictine rather than a documented person; the authorship question is genuinely open and is not settled here. Used in Chapter 29 in the English of 1893 (London: James Elliott), which its own title page describes as a rendering of Kerckring’s Latin published at Amsterdam in 1685; so the English is at two removes from anything Valentine may have written. The 1893 translator is not named on the title page; catalogue records give A. E. Waite. public domain
  • Nicolas Lémery (1645–1715), Cours de chymie (Paris, 1675): reprinted and revised for decades; the London English of 1720 announces itself as “The Fourth Edition” translated from “the Eleventh Edition in the French.” Walter Harris’s English, A Course of Chymistry (London: printed for Walter Kettilby, 1677), is the text used in Chapter 29 for the corrosive sublimate. The English edition of 1686 is not a reprint: it corrects Lémery’s own quantities and adds his defence of the method against its critics. public domain

The eighteenth century

  • Antoine Court de Gébelin, Monde Primitif, analysé et comparé avec le Monde Moderne, vol. 8 (Paris, 1781), the essay that gave the tarot its Egyptian pedigree, Du Jeu des Tarots, opening at p. 365, with the Recherches on divination by the cards, signed “M. le C. de M.”, following. Read on the page images of the Internet Archive scan mondeprimitifana08cour and quoted in Chapter 25; Waite’s page range, cited there, proves exact. public domain
  • The printed French grimoires: Grimorium Verum (“1517,” actually mid-18th century), Grand Grimoire, Grimoire of Honorius (1629), True Black Magic (“Rome, 1750”), The Black Pullet and its relatives (late 18th century): surveyed in Chapter 10, with every date from Waite (1911), below; none of them was seen for this edition, and their title pages are quoted from his catalogue of the imprints.

Modern: orders, editions and interpretation (19th – 21st centuries)

  • Éliphas Lévi, Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie (Paris, 1854–56): the book that joined the tarot’s twenty-two trumps to the Hebrew alphabet. Quoted in Chapter 25 in the English of A. E. Waite, Transcendental Magic: Its Doctrine and Ritual. public domain
  • Anonymous, Arte de echar las cartas por medio de la baraja española, seguido de las profecías gitanas y de una detallada explicación de cada uno de los naipes (Madrid: Saturnino Calleja, 1876), Biblioteca Popular III: the source for the Spanish card meanings in Chapter 25, and the only dated printing of them this edition could reach. It credits its method to Mademoiselle Lenormand and to Etteilla, and heads its catalogue naipes egipcios, so it is a witness to the French system in Spain rather than to anything native. Biblioteca Nacional de España, bdh0000082803. public domain; the library’s scan of it is issued under a Creative Commons licence, which is a claim over the photography and not over the sheets of 1876.
  • The history of playing cards, three nineteenth-century authorities used in Chapter 25 for the Spanish pack, all public domain: Samuel Weller Singer, Researches into the History of Playing Cards (London: Bensley for Bulmer, 1816); William Andrew Chatto, Facts and Speculations on the Origin and History of Playing Cards (London: John Russell Smith, 1848), p. 46 for the forty-card game; and William Hughes Willshire, A Descriptive Catalogue of Playing and Other Cards in the British Museum (London: printed by order of the Trustees, 1876), p. 41 for what makes a pack Spanish and p. 98 for the pack cut down to forty for ombre. Willshire is a museum catalogue and is descriptive throughout; where he reports a date he is usually quoting Singer, and he is at his most useful where he takes a received date apart, as he does with the Castilian prohibition of 1332.
  • Christian D. Ginsburg, The Kabbalah: Its Doctrines, Development, and Literature (London, 1865): the spine of Chapter 4: the En Soph and the emanation of the sephiroth, the four worlds, and the case for Moses de León’s authorship of the Zohar, citing Jellinek (1851) and Graetz (1863). Read in the verbatim Routledge reprint of 1920. public domain
  • S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Kabbalah Unveiled (London: George Redway, 1887): three books of the Zohar in English, from Rosenroth’s Latin collated with the original; its introduction reprints Ginsburg’s dating essay, so the case against the text’s antiquity travelled inside the translation itself. See Chapter 4. public domain
  • Aleister Crowley, Liber AL vel Legis (received 1904; first published in The Equinox, 1909): the founding document of Thelema; quoted in Chapter 27 from the 1904 text, with Crowley’s later introduction left aside. public domain in the US
  • A. E. Waite, The Book of Ceremonial Magic (London: William Rider & Son, 1911; 1913 printing also cited here): his hostile but exactly dated catalogue of the printed grimoires, the authority for the survey in Chapter 10. public domain in the US; Waite d. 1942
  • A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (London: William Rider & Son, 1911): the companion to the Waite–Smith pack of 1909; source for the Strength–Justice interchange and its refused explanation, and for the citation of Court de Gébelin. See Chapter 25. public domain
  • Margaret A. Murray, The Witch-Cult in Western Europe: A Study in Anthropology (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921): the witch-cult thesis, no longer held by historians and indispensable to the history of what came after it; see Chapter 27. public domain
  • A. E. Waite, The Real History of the Rosicrucians (London: George Redway, 1887): source of the “reprehensible hoax” verdict on Andreae (p. 240) and of “before he was sixteen” (p. 232) public domain; The Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross (London: William Rider & Son, 1924); where Waite argues at length that the hoax hypothesis should be dropped (pp. 122 n., 207), a position already implicit in 1887 (pp. 225, 234). Citations of either book for the hoax reading misread him.
  • S. L. MacGregor Mathers (trans.), The Key of Solomon the King (1889): “first Translated and Edited from Ancient MSS. in the British Museum” (the British Library did not exist until 1973); seven codices, incl. Add. MS 10,862, Sloane 1307 and 3091, Harleian 3981, King’s 288, Lansdowne 1202–1203. Limited to 500 copies. public domain
  • Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn: founded 1887–88 by William Robert Woodman, William Wynn Westcott and S. L. MacGregor Mathers; Isis-Urania Temple, London, 1888; the original order fractured in 1903, successor bodies continuing for decades. Cipher Manuscripts in Trithemius cipher, decoded by Westcott in 1887.
  • [S. L. MacGregor Mathers (trans., uncredited)] and Aleister Crowley (ed.), The Book of the Goetia of Solomon the King, Translated into the English Tongue by a Dead Hand … The Whole Edited, Verified, Introduced and Commented by Aleister Crowley (Boleskine, Foyers, Inverness: Society for the Propagation of Religious Truth, 1904): Book One of the Lemegeton only, not the complete Lesser Key. Mathers, the uncredited translator, was alive until 1918; “a dead hand” is Crowley’s insult. public domain
  • Joseph H. Peterson (ed.), The Lesser Key of Solomon: Lemegeton Clavicula Salomonis Regis (2001), based on BL Sloane MS 3825: the authority for the dating and manuscript basis of the whole five-book work. in copyright
  • G. R. S. Mead, Thrice-Greatest Hermes, 3 vols (London and Benares: Theosophical Publishing Society, 1906): Theosophically inflected; scholarly superseded, but the most accessible free route to the Hermetica. public domain
  • Three Initiates [William Walker Atkinson, 1862–1932], The Kybalion (Chicago, 1908): New Thought; source of the Seven Hermetic Principles. public domain
  • Karl Preisendanz, Papyri Graecae Magicae. Die Griechischen Zauberpapyri, 2 vols (1928, 1931): the critical edition; vol. 1 available at the Internet Archive. A third volume was set and reached galley proof, its preface dated Pentecost 1941, when Teubner’s Leipzig house was bombed on 4 December 1943; the proofs survived and circulate in photocopy, and the 1941 preface is reprinted in the second edition. 2nd edition with Albert Henrichs, 1973–74. in copyright: Preisendanz d. 1968, Henrichs d. 2017; in the United States only volume 1 has entered the public domain (1 January 2024), volume 2 following in 2027, so the Internet Archive recommendation above is sound for US readers only. Superseded for the formularies by Faraone and Torallas Tovar (2022).
  • Walter Scott, Hermetica, 4 vols (1924–36): foundational; editorial choices now contested. Scott died in 1925 after only vol. 1 had appeared; A. S. Ferguson (1883–1958) saw vols 2–3 through the press and wholly authored vol. 4, the Testimonia. Catalogue hazard: some records misattribute the work to Walter Scott the novelist (1771–1832). mixed: Scott’s own matter is public domain, but Ferguson d. 1958, so volume 4 entire and his additions to volumes 2–3 remain in copyright in the UK and EU until 1 January 2029.
  • Israel Regardie, The Golden Dawn: The Original Account of the Teachings, Rites and Ceremonies of the Hermetic Order, 4 vols (1937–40): the publication of the order’s reserved material. in copyright: Regardie d. 1985, so protected in the UK and EU until 2056; scans on the Internet Archive are not evidence to the contrary. The underlying Golden Dawn documents are themselves out of copyright (Mathers d. 1918, Westcott d. 1925, Woodman d. 1891); Regardie’s compilation and commentary are a separate protected layer.
  • Bernard Gorceix, La Bible des Rose-Croix (1970): translations and commentary on all three manifestos.
  • Paul Arnold, Histoire des Rose-Croix (Paris, 1935), p. 50: renders ludibrium “une farce.” Charles Webster, “Macaria: Samuel Hartlib and the Great Reformation,” Acta Comeniana 26 (1970), p. 149: “derisive terms.” Against these, Yates (pp. 68, 184–85) reads it as theatrical fiction: “not a hoax, but a dramatic presentation.” Lexicography: Lewis & Short, s.v. ludibrium.
  • Renko Geffarth: archive-based study of the Gold- und Rosenkreuzer; its reviewer (Michael Driedger, H-German, Feb. 2010) describes it as covering circles existing “from around 1760 until sometime after 1790”: a statement of duration, not a founding date.
  • Frances A. Yates, The Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972): the standard modern treatment; see Brian Vickers’s critique, Journal of Modern History 51:2 (1979). in copyright
  • Alan F. Segal, “Hellenistic Magic: Some Questions of Definition” (1981).
  • Garth Fowden, The Egyptian Hermes: A Historical Approach to the Late Pagan Mind (1986).
  • Hans Dieter Betz (ed.), The Greek Magical Papyri in Translation, Including the Demotic Spells (University of Chicago Press, 1986; 2nd ed. 1992): the standard English translation. in copyright
  • Brian P. Copenhaver, Hermetica: The Greek Corpus Hermeticum and the Latin Asclepius (Cambridge, 1992): the standard modern scholarly translation. in copyright
  • David Frankfurter, “Ritual Expertise in Roman Egypt and the Problem of the Category ‘Magician’” (1997).
  • Roland Edighoffer, “Rosicrucianism I: First half of the 17th Century,” in Wouter J. Hanegraaff (ed.), in collaboration with Antoine Faivre, Roelof van den Broek and Jean-Pierre Brach, Dictionary of Gnosis & Western Esotericism (Leiden/Boston: Brill, 2005), 1009–1014, at 1009 and 1014; and Edighoffer, “Rosicrucianism II: 18th Century,” ibid., 1014–1017, at 1015, for the 1763 date. in copyright
  • M. David Litwa, Hermetica II: The Excerpts of Stobaeus, Papyrus Fragments, and Ancient Testimonies (2018). in copyright
  • Nicholas E. Chapel, “The Kybalion’s New Clothes,” Journal of the Western Mystery Tradition No. 24, Vol. 3 (2013): the detailed study of the work’s relation to the historical Hermetic current; source of the David Hartley (1705–1757) origin for the principle of vibration: a derivation that is Chapel’s own reconstruction, his only supporting citation being Barbara Oberg, “David Hartley and the Association of Ideas,” Journal of the History of Ideas 37, no. 3 (1976), 442–43, a study of associationism that does not mention Hermeticism.
  • C. G. Jung: the reading of the alchemical corpus as a symbolic account of individuation; 20th-century interpretation. in copyright
  • Isaac Newton: English rendering of the Emerald Tablet, Keynes MS. 28, King’s College Library, Cambridge, ff. 2r–2v; text from The Chymistry of Isaac Newton, ed. William R. Newman (Indiana University, 2010), ALCH00017, transcribed by John A. Johnson. His Latin copy on a later leaf of the same manuscript reads pater omnis perfectionis where the vulgate has telesmi; B. J. T. Dobbs argued the English was made from a French version, probably the Bibliothèque des philosophes (1672–8). The variant is older than his copy: the Trithemius letter printed in 1613 already reads Pater omnis perfectionis totius mundi hic est. No line of transmission is asserted here. Newton’s wording public domain
  • Helena Blavatsky, Isis Unveiled (New York: J. W. Bouton, 1877), vol. 1, pp. 294, 306, 507; The Secret Doctrine (1888): popularised the paraphrase “as above, so below,” which she quotes as an existing “Hermetic axiom” rather than presenting as her own. The earliest attestation of the maxim in this Hermetic sense is not established; the words occur in English before 1877 in unrelated devotional use, which makes “the wording is hers” harder to assert rather than easier. public domain
  • Robert Steele (ed.), Secretum secretorum cum glossis et notulis (Opera hactenus inedita Rogeri Baconi, fasc. V; Oxford: Clarendon, 1920): the critical edition of the Latin Secret of Secrets; the Emerald Table at pp. 115–17, described there as appearing in its earliest known form. public domain
  • Robert Steele and Dorothea Waley Singer, “The Emerald Table,” Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine 21 (1928), 485–501: the source of the English of the vulgate’s second verse quoted in Chapter 6. A separate Steele and Singer article on the Tablet appeared in the Journal of Chemical Education 3, no. 8 (1926); the two should not be merged. public domain
  • Françoise Hudry (ed.), “Le De secretis nature du ps.-Apollonius de Tyane, traduction latine par Hugues de Santalla du Kitāb sirr al-ḫalīqa,” Chrysopoeia 6 (1997–99), 1–154: the critical edition of Hugo of Santalla’s translation. in copyright
  • Marion Dapsens, “De la Risālat Maryānus au De Compositione alchemiae,” Studia graeco-arabica 6 (2016), 121–40: the current specialist treatment of the Robert of Chester attribution. Open access, not public domain.
  • Steven J. Williams, The Secret of Secrets: The Scholarly Career of a Pseudo-Aristotelian Text in the Latin Middle Ages (University of Michigan Press, 2003): p. 349 for the manuscript count; and “Roger Bacon and His Edition of the Pseudo-Aristotelian Secretum secretorum,” Speculum 69, no. 1 (1994), 57–73. in copyright
  • Lawrence M. Principe and William R. Newman, “Some Problems with the Historiography of Alchemy,” in Secrets of Nature: Astrology and Alchemy in Early Modern Europe, ed. Newman and Anthony Grafton (MIT Press, 2001), 385–431; and Principe, The Secrets of Alchemy (Chicago, 2013), pp. 90–105, 98: the argument that the inner-discipline reading descends from Mary Anne Atwood (1850) and Ethan Allen Hitchcock. Neither was reached directly for this edition; both are reported from Zuber. in copyright
  • Mike A. Zuber, Spiritual Alchemy from the Age of Jacob Boehme to Mary Anne Atwood, 1600–1900 (PhD diss., Universiteit van Amsterdam, 2017), Introduction: the route by which the Principe–Newman positions, the list of their critics (p. 24) and the Khunrath material (pp. 50–51) were verified for this book. Open access, which is not the same as public domain.
  • Hereward Tilton, “Michael Maier: An Itinerant Alchemist in Late Renaissance Germany,” in Furnace and Fugue: A Digital Edition of Michael Maier’s “Atalanta fugiens” (1618) with Scholarly Commentary, ed. Tara Nummedal and Donna Bilak (University of Virginia Press, 2020): the source for Maier’s laboratory work, the Carpathian mines, the aurum potabile, and his judgement of Khunrath. Open access, in copyright. Tilton’s The Quest for the Phoenix (de Gruyter, 2003) is cited at p. 97 through Forshaw’s note and was not reached directly.
  • Peter J. Forshaw, “Michael Maier and Mythoalchemy,” in the same volume: for gold-making as part of Maier’s repertoire and against relegating Atalanta fugiens to a “spiritual quest.” Open access, in copyright.
  • Lawrence M. Principe, The Aspiring Adept: Robert Boyle and His Alchemical Quest (Princeton, 1998): not reached directly; quoted through Linden, p. 234. William R. Newman, Newton the Alchemist (Princeton, 2019): not reached; the 1936 Sotheby’s sale and the “experimental chymistry” characterisation come from the publisher’s description page, which is marketing copy rather than scholarship. The word count and the composition of the corpus are better anchored: The Chymistry of Isaac Newton project (W. R. Newman, gen. ed., Indiana University) gives about a million words across some hundred and thirty manuscripts, and describes the 1936 Sotheby’s sale as three hundred twenty-nine lots, over a third of them alchemical. The project’s own pages decline to settle what the papers were for. in copyright
  • Stanton J. Linden (ed.), The Alchemy Reader: From Hermes Trismegistus to Isaac Newton (Cambridge, 2003): Introduction, p. 17, for the caution on the alchemical operations in Chapter 5; p. 16 for the coexistence of the metallic, medical and spiritual goals; p. 234, reporting Principe on Boyle. Verified for this edition from a full-text scan rather than the Cambridge printing, with the page fixed from the running heads of the adjacent leaves. in copyright
  • The Mirror of Alchimy (London: printed by Thomas Creede for Richard Olive, 1597): the Elizabethan English of Hortulanus’s commentary. public domain
  • Stapleton, Lewis and Sherwood Taylor, “The Sayings of Hermes Quoted in the Māʾ al-Waraqī of Ibn Umail,” Ambix 3, nos 3–4 (1949), 69–90. in copyright
  • Allen G. Debus, Alchemy and Early Modern Chemistry: Papers from Ambix (Jeremy Mills, 2004), p. 415: for Trithemius’s metaphysical reading and its adoption by Dee, Agrippa and Gerhard Dorn. in copyright
  • The Chymistry of Isaac Newton, ed. William R. Newman (Indiana University, 2010): diplomatic and normalised transcriptions of Newton’s alchemical manuscripts, including Keynes MS. 28 (ALCH00017). Newton’s wording is public domain; the project asserts rights over its editorial matter.
  • Julius Ruska, Tabula smaragdina: ein Beitrag zur Geschichte der hermetischen Literatur (Heidelberg: Winter, 1926), pp. 121, 166–67 (dates the Sirr al-Khalīqa 6th–8th c. Paul Kraus, Jābir ibn Ḥayyān, vol. II (Cairo: IFAO, 1942), pp. 274–75) c. 813–833. Ursula Weisser, Das “Buch über das Geheimnis der Schöpfung” von Pseudo-Apollonios von Tyana (Berlin/New York: de Gruyter, 1980), p. 54: c. 750–800. Three datings, not two; “Kraus 1926” conflates Kraus with Ruska. Weisser’s text was not reached for this edition; the dating is reported from the literature.
  • Ronald Hutton, “Modern Pagan Festivals: A Study in the Nature of Tradition,” Folklore 119, no. 3 (2008), 251–74: the standard account of the eightfold Wheel of the Year as a staged mid-20th-century assembly: quarter days alone in the 1940s liturgy, solstices c. 1953, equinoxes after 1954, equal status early 1958; Nichols instituting the Wiccan eight in his Druid order in 1964; Aidan Kelly applying Ostara, Litha and Mabon (his own account dates the calendar to 1974), spreading via Green Egg and reaching British usage in the 1980s. Of the eight names, Yule and the four Gaelic quarter days are old and were put to a new use; Ostara, Litha and Mabon are the modern coinages. in copyright
  • Ethan Doyle White, Wicca: History, Belief, and Community in Modern Pagan Witchcraft (Sussex Academic, 2015), ch. 13. in copyright
  • Christian H. Bull, The Tradition of Hermes Trismegistus: The Egyptian Priestly Figure as a Teacher of Hellenized Wisdom (Brill, 2018): for the dating of the Hermetica, the older underlying material, and Psellos as reader rather than compiler. in copyright
  • Ellic Howe, The Magicians of the Golden Dawn (1972): for the Cipher Manuscripts, the grade numbering and the order’s documentary problems. in copyright
  • Graham John Wheeler, “A Microcosm of the Esoteric Revival: The Histories of the Lesser Banishing Ritual of the Pentagram,” Correspondences: Journal for the Study of Esotericism 8, no. 1 (2020), 5–44: the first detailed source-analysis of the ritual, and the authority for the derivations given in Chapter 15. Open access under CC BY-NC 4.0, which is not the same as public domain.
  • Christopher A. Faraone and Sofia Torallas Tovar (eds), Greek and Egyptian Magical Formularies, vol. I (California Classical Studies, 2022): renumbers the formularies, joins PGM VI to II, re-dates PGM I to the 3rd century, and describes Preisendanz’s second edition as obsolete. Open access, not public domain, and it qualifies the “numbering runs to LXXXI” framing of Chapter 9.
  • Jessica L. Lamont, “Orality, Written Literacy, and Early Sicilian Curse Tablets,” Greece & Rome 69, no. 1 (2022), 27–51: open access (CC BY-NC-ND), not public domain.
  • Marcellin Berthelot and Charles-Émile Ruelle, Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs (Paris: Steinheil, 1887–88): Zosimos, pseudo-Democritus, Leyden X and the Stockholm papyrus. public domain
  • Auguste Audollent, Defixionum tabellae (Paris, 1904): the curse tablets. public domain
  • Paul Oskar Kristeller, Studies in Renaissance Thought and Letters, p. 223: the pioneering study of Ficino’s Hermetic translation. in copyright

What this edition could not reach

A bibliography that lists only what was found is half a bibliography. Below are the things this edition went after and did not get, with enough detail that the next person need not repeat the work. In every case the material exists and is out of copyright; what failed was access, or legibility, or both.

The Picatrix, in any language

This is the hardest gap in the book, and it is not an accident of scanning. No public-domain edition of the Picatrix exists. The work was not printed at all before the twentieth century, and the modern editions (Ritter and Plessner’s German of 1962, and the English translations) are all in copyright. What is freely available amounts to perhaps two hundred and fifty words of authentic Latin, transcribed inside Lynn Thorndike’s History of Magic and Experimental Science (1923), plus a good deal of Thorndike describing the text in his own English.

That second category is the trap. Thorndike paraphrasing the Picatrix reads exactly like the Picatrix if it is set in the same type, and a chapter built from it would have manufactured a Picatrix that does not exist. The images of the decans, which are what most readers want from this book, are not obtainable from any public-domain source, and substituting Agrippa’s images for them, which is what circulates, would be the same error in a different direction. Nothing is printed here rather than something misattributed.

The Hebrew Sefer Raziel ha-Malakh

Chapter 20 uses Sloane MS 3846, which is an English witness to the Latin Liber Razielis. The Hebrew book of nearly the same name, first printed at Amsterdam in 1701, is a different work and is not used here. No public-domain English translation of it was found, and the public-domain authorities do not even agree on its date: one line of scholarship puts the first part no earlier than the eleventh century, another reports its ascription to a thirteenth-century writer and holds that there is no criterion for dating its parts at all. That disagreement is itself worth knowing, and it is a large part of why no accessible English version was ever made.

Three habits of method are worth recording alongside these, because each cost time to learn. The 1651 Agrippa is invisible to a title search: the Early English Books collection generates its identifiers mechanically, and the volume surfaces only by wildcarding the collection prefix. And a keyword search on the Internet Archive queries metadata, not the contents of books: a zero result there is not a negative finding, and the only sound test is to fetch each candidate’s text layer and search it locally.

A third is about which scan to fetch once you have found the book. Legibility does not track age or prestige; it tracks how the scanner’s software was set up. Of Lémery’s Course of Chymistry, the 1677 first English is the edition this book needs and its text layer reads every long s as an f, so a passage has to be repaired word by word and every repair declared. The 1720 fourth edition, scanned by a different programme, sets the long s correctly and can be quoted almost as it stands. That is a reason to open more than one scan even when only one edition will do: the others will settle characters the one you need has lost, which is how the five repairs in Chapter 29 were made.

The fourth is the one that cost most, and it is a rule rather than a trick. A search that returns nothing should be assumed broken until it has been shown able to find something. The dating in Chapter 27 was first attempted by matching the word itself, which reported the compound nowhere in the archive. That was false, and it was false for a reason no amount of care about the argument would have caught: one scan of the very number carrying the earliest use renders the word Ak&shic. A negative result is a claim about the test before it is a claim about the world. The way to make one honest is to invert it, searching for a common word the scanner cannot damage and asking what stands near it, and then to check that the inverted test finds the cases already known.

Where to begin

A reader who wants to go to the primary sources rather than to summaries should start with Copenhaver for the Hermetica, Betz for the Papyri, Gorceix or a modern edition for the manifestos, and Yates for the historical context of the Rosicrucian episode. Of the public-domain texts, Mathers’s Key of Solomon (1889) and Waite’s Real History (1887) are freely available and remain worth reading, with the caveat that both are over a century old and neither reflects current scholarship. Preisendanz’s first volume is on the Internet Archive for anyone who reads Greek, though only US readers can rely on that being lawful. Three further public-domain routes are worth naming: Mead’s Thrice-Greatest Hermes (1906) for the Hermetica, Berthelot and Ruelle (1887–88) for the Greek alchemists, and Audollent (1904) for the curse tablets.

One caution about free texts, since this book has just spent a bibliography insisting on precision: open access is not public domain. Several of the works recommended here (Lamont, Wheeler, Bull, the Faraone and Torallas Tovar volume) are free to read and still fully in copyright, and one carries no licence at all. Free to read is a permission to read, not a permission to reproduce.

The single most useful habit, in this field more than most: when a source tells you a text is ancient, check the date yourself. It is often findable in a few minutes, and it is frequently not what you were told.

Final Warning

This grimoire contains material that should be used responsibly and ethically. Approach these practices with respect, humility and proper preparation. The path of Hermetic study is a long one, and it rewards patience far more than enthusiasm.

May this grimoire serve as a guide to Hermetic wisdom and Rosicrucian practice; and to the histories from which both were made. Use it wisely and with pure intention.
